c19feb2b8f24.text: By — Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press By — Rebecca Boone, Associated Press Rebecca Boone, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/abc-and-trumps-fcc-battle-in-federal-court-over-free-speech-and-jurisdiction-issues Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter ABC and Trump's FCC battle in federal court over free speech and jurisdiction issues Politics Oct 6, 2026 7:51 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A lawyer for ABC on Tuesday asked a federal judge to prevent the Trump administration from conducting an unusual, early review of its broadcast licenses, likening it to a looming execution by guillotine that was already chilling the network's editorial decisions just weeks before the U.S. midterm elections. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan did not immediately rule on ABC's request for a preliminary injunction prohibiting the Federal Communications Commission from conducting its early review, which it said was unconstitutional, a violation of free speech and a retaliation for content President Donald Trump dislikes. WATCH: ABC says FCC waging a retaliatory campaign violating free speech rights A government attorney argued that, as a procedural matter, the court doesn't have jurisdiction over ABC's case because it belongs in a different venue. The government also challenged the network's First Amendment arguments, and said ABC had failed to show it suffered irreparable harm. A ruling was not expected until at least mid-October. After extensively questioning both sides, she asked them to submit brief additional arguments by Oct. 9, for the government, and Oct. 14, for ABC. ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC and FCC Commissioner Brendan Carr in August, several months after the commission ordered eight ABC-owned stations to submit renewal applications for their broadcast licenses years ahead of schedule. The case is one of several ongoing legal battles between Trump's Republican administration and news outlets — including The Associated Press — over their coverage and access to the executive branch since Trump returned to the White House for a second term. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. At Tuesday's two-hour hearing, ABC attorney Beth Wilkinson harkened back to the French Revolution to illustrate what she called the chilling effect that the renewal process was having on the network. It was, she said, like having one's "head on the guillotine," forced to wonder "if anything we say is going to make it come down." "Our editorial decisions are being affected right now," Wilkinson said, noting that the U.S. midterm elections are fast approaching. "We are watching everything that we do." She reiterated the First Amendment argument ABC has been making since the beginning — that it was being targeted for its content. "President Donald Trump has made his stance clear over and over again," Wilkinson said. "What he says is because of that content, because of that speech, ABC should lose its license. "These are blatant violations of the U.S. Constitution," she said, calling it a threat not just to ABC but to all broadcast media. Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel, the Department of Justice attorney, explicitly rejected the guillotine analogy. Georgiev-Remmel argued that the court lacked jurisdiction, but that even if it decided it had jurisdiction, a preliminary injunction should still be denied. He said ABC had not established a likelihood of success on the merits of the case, and also had not established irreparable harm, because the network's eight licenses remain valid. Issuing a preliminary injunction at ABC's request would mean "allowing them to sidestep" the path that Congress has set up for regulatory action appeals, Georgiev-Remmel said. Asked by the judge what irreparable harm ABC had suffered, Wilkinson answered: "The irreparable injury is the chill, and the threat of retaliation for First Amendment speech and editorial decisions ABC makes every day." In its lawsuit, ABC had asked the judge to temporarily prohibit the FCC from taking any further action related to its license renewal proceedings. ABC also sought to prohibit the commission from trying to coerce or threaten the network to alter its "exercise of editorial discretion." "The First Amendment demands an immediate end to the Commission's retaliatory campaign," ABC attorneys wrote. Carr, a Trump ally, ordered the early review of the stations' licenses in April — just after a joke by ABC's late-night host Jimmy Kimmel infuriated Trump, who called for the comedian's firing. ABC also had been fighting Carr's efforts to make the morning talk show "The View" subject to equal-time rules. Carr defended his agency's actions against ABC by saying broadcasters have a duty to "operate in the public interest." Government attorneys urged the court to dismiss ABC's lawsuit, accusing the network of trying to prematurely ward off scrutiny by federal regulators. "To foreclose the Commission from using all the tools at its disposal to investigate whether Plaintiffs are meeting their statutory and regulatory duties would seriously harm both the government and the public," Justice Department lawyers wrote. AliKhan was nominated to the bench by President Joe Biden, a Democrat. Noveck reported from New York, and Boone from Boise, Idaho. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. a018d348e092.text: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says it is monitoring reports of a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia and says it is prepared for any threat that emerges. Why it matters: Pneumonic plague is the most dangerous form of plague and is almost always fatal unless if left untreated. The latest: President Trump told reporters Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to discuss the suspected plague case and would speak with him "very soon." Asked what U.S. intelligence was saying about the situation, Trump said officials were in "very deep discussions" and that "we'll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow." Catch up quick: Darya Shipilova , a worker at a Russian anti-plague institute, died after reports that she may have been exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. Russian authorities say testing has not linked her death to plague or to pathogens she handled at work. However, at least five hospitals in the area remain in quarantine and almost 200 people who had contact with Shipilova have been placed under medical observation as a precaution. What they're saying: "We are working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available," the CDC said in an X post Tuesday. "At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely." Context: The CDC said the plague is a dangerous bacterial disease that can be treated with antibiotics, especially when caught early. Pneumonic plague can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact. The CDC says "rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals, and monitoring of potentially exposed individuals" are important for keeping people safe. State of play: The concerns have drawn attention on social media and from government officials and the White House. President Trump acknowledged Monday that he is aware of the situation. "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday, but said he hadn't spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about it yet. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." The Department of Health and Human Services and the State Department are also monitoring the situation. What we're watching: Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia Tuesday to share more information about Shipilova's death, per Reuters . ​Rubio told reporters: "I ​think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously ⁠share more information with the world." Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from President Trump.

da4714b0da0f.text:
The Pentagon’s autonomy command should draw on lessons old and new
AUTOWARCOM will have a big task. Luckily, it’s not starting from scratch.
As Pentagon leaders launch their latest effort to accelerate the development and deployment of autonomous and robotic systems, they can draw on key lessons from past attempts and recent breakthroughs.
The planned Autonomous Warfare Command, slated to launch by next October, will promote “not a particular drone, but the ability to adapt in combat” against “realistic opposition,” according to a Sept. 30 memo from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who added: “We do not have a decade to transition our procurement and doctrine.”
That’s because on today’s battlefields, effective adaptation to “realistic opposition” is something that happens in weeks, not the months and years it typically takes defense contractors to update designs or even issue software patches. Fortunately, the Pentagon isn’t starting from scratch.
Start with the mission, not the robot
Start with asking commanders and operators what they want from autonomy and robots, rather than trying to dazzle them with an experiment or demonstration that isn't relevant to what they need.
One example is Maven Smart System, an AI intelligence platform widely adopted by the U.S. military and NATO forces—and a model for getting emerging technology to the force faster. A noted 2024 report for CNAS wrote, “A clear, urgent, but broad problem definition permitted Maven to more directly meet user needs.”
So what do combatant commanders want now? Here’s Gen. Frank Donovan, commander of U.S. Southern Command, speaking in May at a Defense One event:
“Most of the systems we're looking at are primarily our domain awareness systems, and…We can match the robots to the environment whether it swims, it flies, it has feet, whatever it does.”
Donovan had just finished leading the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group, the special-operations effort to apply autonomy and robotics to missions. He discovered that robots were needed not just to replace humans in combat but to better understand what was happening in the places where boots weren’t on the ground.
“Our partners, who have the access and placement where they live, have to work in, in the rough terrain, the jungle, over the horizon, thousands of miles at sea.”
Build communicative autonomy
Donovan said most of his work at the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group was about getting people partners to talk about what information they needed from robotic systems and what information they wanted those systems robots to have.
“We don't talk about robots. We talk about the data environment, right? With the different data layers that we need at the very forward edge so our [special operations forces] and our conventional force teammates with a...cell phone they can actually plug into that data network, and whatever robot shows up with the capability, they can leverage it instantaneously.”
Autonomous systems will become even more important when network access is blocked by adversary electronic-warfare capabilities, said one former senior defense official who worked to field AI software to U.S. and allied forces.
“The next step is getting these systems to true autonomy that can handle the operating environment. In any conflict, GPS and comms will be denied and degraded. We see it today in Ukraine and the Middle East, and it's a certainty in any future fight,” they said.
Buy the brains and body separately
Another lesson comes from the auto industry, which has turned to external partners for its autonomy needs.
By contrast, the former senior official said, “The Department has mostly asked industry to self-organize to deliver autonomy alongside the vehicle.” For example, Pentagon buyers seeking autonomous drones have simply asked manufacturers to build autonomous versions of their remote-controlled aircraft.
That’s the wrong approach, the former official said. Drone makers “build excellent platforms, but autonomy is its own discipline. Commercial self-driving figured this out years ago: the automakers build great vehicles and partner with autonomy companies for the driver,” they said. “Defense needs the same model.”
Make it modular
The former official added that Pentagon buyers should specify that the autonomy package should be modular—that is, able to be upgraded as threats change and technology improves.
That’s true not just for individual weapons, but across the force and indeed across alliances, they said. “Open standards are what make that partnership work at scale.”
This was underscored by a recent NATO experiment in Portugal. In September, the alliance’s Centre for Maritime Research and Experimentation, or CMRE, wrapped up its biggest annual exercise: Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping with Maritime Unmanned Systems. This year’s edition featured a demonstration that showed what an Autonomous Warfare Command will look to replicate: robots receiving orders not from humans but from software.
“For the first time, we had materialized our vision for future operations. We had algorithms looking at what the mission was looking like and automatically giving tasks to drones,” said João Alves, a principal scientist at CMRE.
That wasn’t the result of a new sensor or piece of AI software but rather a policy change: partner militaries agreeing to adopt a standard for the systems that they were buying.
Instill trust
The biggest challenge any military office, command, or unit will face when using autonomous weapons is knowing when to rely on them.
That’s the big conclusion of a 2017 study of autonomy safety failures involving Patriot missile batteries.The most dramatic case was the 2003 downing of an F-18 by a Patriot in Iraq.
“The tactical director at the battalion command and control node gave the order, ‘Bring your launchers to ready.’ That directive was tantamount to an order to engage. But that was not what the tactical director intended,” Army engineering psychologist John Hawley wrote i

Former Australian bishop Christopher Saunders has been jailed for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men during his time as a Catholic cleric.
Saunders - who resigned as Bishop of Broome when first accused of wrongdoing in 2020 - was found guilty of one charge of rape and 12 counts of indecent assault.
The 76-year-old was sentenced to six and a half years' imprisonment, but will be eligible for release on parole in February 2031.
He is one of the most senior Catholic leaders in the world to face charges of this nature.
His trial in the state of Western Australia heard Saunders systematically groomed the two young men, inviting them to "shirts-off" gatherings and plying them with alcohol, often using church funds and church-owned properties to do so.
He was convicted of kissing and molesting the men, and in one instance forcing oral sex on one of them.
In a victim impact statement provided to the court, that young man said he struggled to talk about what happened.
"I was a toy that he was using," the victim said.
"My head is pounding now, I'm in so much pain."

Pornhub has returned to Australia, eight months after it went dark due to age verification laws, but only adults with Apple devices will be able to access the site.
On Wednesday, parent company Aylo said it was restoring access for "eligible adult users in Australia" who have "confirmed their age through Apple's Australian age-verification process".
The world's biggest porn site left the Australian market in March, saying new laws requiring users to prove they were over 18 would not protect children and "instead creates harms relating to data privacy" and exposure to content on non-compliant platforms.
Apple recently introduced new age checks in Australia, following a rollout in the UK.
In March, Australia introduced stricter laws requiring users to prove they were over 18 in order to access adult content such as porn, R-rated video games and sexually explicit AI chatbots.
The country's online safety regulator said the changes would protect children from harmful content and platforms would be fined for breaches.
Critics said there would be issues with data privacy and users finding ways to trick age-verification technologies such as facial recognition, digital IDs and credit card details.
Aylo said it was returning to Australia as Apple has "set a benchmark" by setting default child safety features on all devices unless owners confirmed they are adults.
This, in effect, makes "every phone or tablet kid-safe as a starting point," it said.
"For years, Aylo has advocated for device-based age verification as the most effective and privacy-protecting approach to help prevent minors from accessing age-inappropriate content online," said Aylo's vice-president of brand and community Alex Kekesi.
Australians with Apple devices that have been "age-verified" will be "served a standard adult users experience", she said.
Kekesi added that having devices with child safety features as a default meant adults don't have to "surrender unnecessary personal information to multiple apps and websites".
It also limits the usefulness of virtual private networks (VPNs) to circumvent age-verification technologies, she said.
VPNs are commonly used to trick a site into thinking a user is logging on from another country, giving the user access to the site.

Famed for its puffins, the picture-perfect island of Lundy attracts birdwatchers from all over. But the island is on the cusp of being evacuated as water levels drop to the lowest levels ever, forcing residents to take drastic measures to ensure supplies do not run out.
Located in the Bristol Channel off the north Devon coast, the 5km (3.1 mile) long island is not the first place you expect to be running out of water.
It is rich with wildlife including puffins and seals and its rugged landscape makes for breathtaking views.
But speak to the handful of residents here and they will tell you of the battle waged since summer to ensure the taps do not run dry.
Entirely self-sufficient, the National Trust-owned island relies on a combination of rainwater and boreholes drilled into the granite for supplies.
Severe water shortages in Lundy are not new, with islanders and visitors previously resorting to bottled water.
But the hottest and driest summer on record has been a "steep learning curve" for islanders, said Lundy managing director Derek Green.
He said there had been no significant rainfall since April and it had barely seen 20% of the typical 1.5m (4.92ft) rain it expected by this time of year.
Reservoir levels dropped to 13% at their lowest, forcing emergency shipments of water from the mainland to the 28 people who live on the island.
Water restrictions are also in place for residents and visitors. Among the more extreme measures is the removal of plugs so tourists are not tempted to take a bath.
The island, which is managed by the Landmark Trust, is now pumping water from ponds used by wildlife to a treatment works as a "last resort".
"Bringing in pond water is something we've never had to do before," Green explained. "It's really our last chance saloon here.
"If we didn't do this, we would be facing the reality of closing Lundy... it would be devastating for us."
Green stressed pond levels had started to drop and a seasonal passenger ferry that has been shipping water to the island is due to end later this month.
"Hopefully the reserve in the pond will last until it rains but because it hasn't rained in so long, this is desperate measures," he said.
"We've got a working farm here and the animals need water every day... so to evacuate those animals, those people and to cancel all those holiday is something that has never happened in the history of Lundy before.
"It would be hugely significant... we're on the cusp of having to make that decision."
The use of pond water led to some recovery in reservoir levels, now at 23.7% full, but Green said islanders were simply "praying for rain".
BBC meteorologist David Braine said there was some rain in the forecast for Lundy but it would take weeks to top up the groundwater and reservoirs the island relied on.
The very dry spring and summer followed record rainfall in the later part of the winter and it was only in March when most of our reservoirs were full.
Shipments of water on passenger ferry the MS Oldenberg from north Devon began in August.
The first delivery of about 67,000 litres was the biggest and cost about Â£7,000, said Green.
Since then they have shipped 4,000 litres of water three times a week, with islanders using between 9,000 litres to 11,000 litres of water a day.
Getting the water from the port to residents has not been an easy process as the island only has a granite track and a handful of vehicles including three 4x4s, tractors, quadbikes and a fire engine.
Adding to the logistical pressure, a landslip in June closed off part of the track to the tiny village at the top of the island about 400ft above sea level.
Green said: "We have to offload the tanks off the ship and we have to bring them up to a staging post halfway up the hill.
"We then have to pump water with a fire hose past the vulnerable part of the road to another tank where it's then staged pumped to the reservoir at the top."
Island manager Matt Scantlebury said the shortages had been a "logistical nightmare".
He said the island's pub, The Tavern, closed toilets and removed bath plugs to help conserve supplies.
"We can't have baths... all the plugs have been removed to resist temptation," said Scantlebury.
"People are showering with buckets to catch the water and then using that to flush the toilets and that's saving water.
"We've had to close the pub toilets so the visitors have all been funnelled to the back shed toilets because they aren't on our mains water supply... we now have to fill them from our pond water."
Green, who started working on Lundy in 2004, said water shortages had become more frequent and in September last year they also considered shutting the island when reservoir levels hit 33%.
He said the changing climate was more "pronounced on Lundy" and islanders needed to adapt.
"Forecasters are predicting it will be even warmer next year," he said.
"We've got to learn from this and be better prepared next year in terms of increasing the reservoir here.
"People need to learn to use a little less water over the winter... it's a sharp learning curve for us and the wider region."
Scantlebury said he was concerned for the future, and without meaningful rain over autumn and winter, it would hard to keep levels at a "reasonable level".
"It's a trend we have to watch out for," he said.
Assistant warden Tara McEvoy-Wilding said 2026 had been eye-opening and the "brown, sad and crispy" vegetation was a visual reminder of how dry it had been.
"This year feels like the real first year people have been noticing climate change," she said.
"For Lundy, it's going to be a challenge going forward. We're going to have to be extra mindful and plan further in advance to maintain our water security."
As Green looks out over the "beautiful, remote and tranquil" landscape, he is fearing for the future.

Research is being carried out to find out how a microplastic spillage has affected coastal sea bird populations.
On 19 July tonnes of microplastics known as nurdles were spilled into the River Tyne following a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne.
A series of necropsies are now taking place at the Dove Marine Laboratory in Cullercoats on dead birds gathered after the spill.
Dan Turner, coordinator at North East England Beached Bird Surveys said: "We've already seen samples from contents of stomachs of suspected regurgitation which contain nurdles."
Necropsies will be carried out on a variation of seabirds gathered from across the North East including eight guillemots, five herring gulls, a gannet and a pink-footed goose.
The research was prompted over concerns birds could "starve" if they confuse the nurdles for food and fill their stomachs.
"We've seen evidence previously of fulmars eating plastic and they've been found in their stomachs, so it is highly likely we could come across the same in some cases," Turner added.
Charities like the RSPB have also warned the pellets could enter the wider food chain, affecting fish, seals and dolphins.
External and internal studies into the seabirds has started with stomach rinsing also taking place to see if the birds have been consuming the nurdles.
"It is quite possible that the seabirds have mistaken the plastic for fish eggs.
"The nurdles when they float attract pollutants and contaminants, which stick to them, if the birds swallow them it can be the case that they get into the bird's system.
"We may need more testing to see if the plastic can make its way into the bird's bloodstream which could cause a drop in the bird's fitness," Turner said.
Researchers have confirmed 28% of 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles which spilled into the river have been recovered since the spill.
Scientists predict that the plastic pellets will continue to wash up on North East beaches as the clean up continues.
Colin Porter who has been assisting the clean up in South Tyneside said: "We are very concerned about the wildlife populations, we've seen birds eating them and we know the fish have too."
The research on the birds is expected to continue into December.

Roosting birds now coo among the ceiling tiles in the deserted dining room of Kibbutz Nir Oz, once the bustling heart of a close-knit, 400-strong Israeli community which was devastated by the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023.
"We used to come and see each other, eat together. There were lots of activities here, also holidays to celebrate," remembers Dalit Ram Aharon, who is showing me around with her husband, Achi.
By the glass entrance doors, dotted with bullet holes, there is a shocking reminder of what happened to the missing residents.
The postboxes for each household bear stickers put there after the attacks three years ago: red indicates those killed, and black those taken hostage. "That's one out of four of us: murdered or kidnapped," Dalit says. "Including children and babies."
As Israel marks the third anniversary of its deadliest-ever day, this is another painful time of reflection for residents of the kibbutz, which sits just a mile (1.6km) from the Gaza border and was one of the worst-hit places.
Time stands still at the nearby burnt-out house of the Siman Tov family, where a wind chime dangles by the door. A picture shows Tamar and Yonatan with their three children, twin girls Shahar and Arbel, five, and their two-year-old son, Omer.
The parents were shot through the door of their bomb shelter - designed to protect from rockets launched from Gaza, not gunfire.
Dalit, who survived with Achi and their three children by hiding in their own shelter for nearly 12 hours that day, recalls the last social media messages sent by Tamar to her neighbours.
"On that day in the morning, she wrote in the woman's group, at the beginning, 'Is everyone fine?' Then, at another point, she wrote, 'They are shooting us.' And after that she wrote with a lot of mistakes, 'We are very injured,'" Dalit tells me.
"From what we understand, they torched the house and the children died from suffocation, so all the family was killed."
An estimated 500 Palestinians, led by Hamas's elite Nukhba force fighters, but including civilian looters, some of them children, joined the assault on the unsuspecting Nir Oz.
Forty-one Nir Oz residents and foreign workers were killed, along with six people who had fled to the kibbutz from a party nearby.
Seventy-six people from the kibbutz were kidnapped to Gaza, including nine bodies, with 14 hostages taken alive and killed in captivity. The last living hostages from Nir Oz were returned to Israel on 13 October 2025 and the remains of the last deceased hostage, Amiram Cooper, were brought back two weeks later.
As we walk through the greenery, it is eerily quiet bar bird song and the mewing of hungry, stray cats. Dozens of fire-damaged homes, which were simple, one-storey buildings in Nir Oz, have now been torn down, leaving just rows of the reinforced concrete safe rooms, which failed to keep people safe.
The Aharons want some damaged houses to be left as evidence of what took place. "We really support that," Achi says. "People should see what happened, should see the destruction, the pure hatred that happened here."
The couple point out where a teacher, Maya Goren, was killed while in the kindergarten and the makeshift memorials where three of the seven members of the kibbutz security team were killed after battling Hamas gunmen.
The findings of the Israeli Defense Forces investigation into what happened at Nir Oz underscored how the army - left in a state of disarray by the unprecedented simultaneous assault on more than 20 communities and multiple military posts - completely failed to come to the rescue here.
On 7 October, the first soldiers arrived in the kibbutz some 40 minutes after the last Palestinian attackers left. Nearly every household experienced killing, violence, including sexual assaults and rape, looting and kidnapping.
Dalit pauses to show me a tree planted long ago by her parents, who were co-founders of the kibbutz, known for its farming and peace activists. They survived the 7 October attacks physically unharmed but died just months afterwards.
Next door is the small home of Shiri Bibas, the mother of ginger-haired boys Ariel, four, and nine-month-old, Kfir. The three, snatched from their home, became symbols of the Gaza hostage crisis.
"This is the hardest house for me because Shiri was a very, very good friend of mine," Dalit confides. "She was like a sister. We even got pregnant together - me with my daughter and her with Ariel. They became best friends also. We used to laugh that they were going to marry."
"Shiri was very, very funny. She was a happy person - a mother," Dalit says. "She lived a simple life. She never did anything to anyone."
While Shiri's husband, Yarden, was released alive by Hamas in a Gaza ceasefire deal in February 2025, she and her sons - held by a different armed group - were killed.
Hamas blamed an air strike early in the Gaza war for their deaths, but Israeli forensic experts, who examined the bodies after they were returned later that February, said they were murdered by their captives and their bodies mutilated.
Many of the bereaved from Nir Oz, including Yarden Bibas, have moved away for good. However, with 20 houses renovated or rebuilt, a few former hostages have come back to live here.
They include Gadi Moses, another kibbutz co-founder, and the oldest living male hostage released during the Gaza war, and Yair Horn, who stops to chat with the Aharons as he passes in a golf buggy. Dalit and Achi are determined to return too.
"We'll come back for the memory of Shiri and for the people that didn't have the chance to live here, and for the memory of my parents, and to continue our roots, and for my children, because this is our home," Dalit says.
However, she, Achi and their children - currently displaced and living in an apartment in a town further north - face a two-year wait for Nir Oz to reopen fully.

As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.
"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.
While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.
Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aï¬ordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".
The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (Â£3.30) a gallon and beef prices are at a record high.
According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.
Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.
"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."
That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump?
Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free.
The economy looming large
There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida.
But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns.
Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement.
When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight.
"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive."
He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents â retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet".
In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.
When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces.
But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages.
Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds â who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" â isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices.
It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction.
"Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long."
Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable".
"We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America."
And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda".
"Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said.
Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war â a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran.
For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital â from the White House to both chambers of Congress. Inevitably, that makes for a challenging rhetorical pirouette among Republican candidates this time round when it comes to touching on Trump's less popular policies.

The World Health Organization has asked Russia for more information on the death of a worker at a Siberian plague research laboratory.
It is still not clear exactly what led to the worker falling ill, but media reports have led to a flurry of speculation.
Russian officials are still investigating the cause of the death, but they say those who came into contact with the researcher all tested negative for pneumonic plague.
So what is pneumonic plague, and how dangerous is it?
What is pneumonic plague?
Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
There are two other types of plague: bubonic, which affects the lymph nodes; and septicaemic, which affects the blood.
Pneumonic plague can occur after an initial infection of one of these other types.
Symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and often coughing up blood.
It's regarded as being more serious but less common than bubonic plague.
The global number of infections of all three types of plague varies each year, but it is probably somewhere between 1,000 to 3,000 cases.
Most of these are bubonic plague, and many of them occur in central Africa, but cases also develop in other places, including Russia, India, China, and the United States.
Prof Piero Olliaro is Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford.
He said: "Plague itself has not disappeared: the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, persists in animal reservoirs across many parts of the world.
"Around 200 rodent species can harbour the bacterium, with reservoirs found across the Americas, Eurasia and Africa.
"Sporadic human cases therefore continue to occur, but established surveillance, infection-control measures and effective antibiotic treatment are important tools for limiting their impact."
How does it spread?
Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria usually found in small mammals and their fleas.
You can catch it by getting bitten by an infected flea or handling an infected animal.
But human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague is also possible through coughing infected droplets into the air, which are then breathed in by another person, although this normally requires quite close contact.
You can also develop it if you have had septicaemic plague and the infection then spreads into the lungs.
It's thought that pneumonic plague was the main type of plague behind what is known as the Black Death, the massive outbreak that killed millions of people across Europe in the 14th Century.
Dr Zania Stamataki, Associate Professor of Viral Immunology at the University of Birmingham, says it is important that researchers are able to study diseases like plague.
"I understand why people find the idea of plague in a laboratory alarming, so it is worth saying why that work exists," she said.
"Plague is not a historical disease. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form.
"Diagnostics, vaccine development and surveillance for antibiotic resistance all require laboratories that hold and study the live organism.
"This work is vital to prepare against outbreaks."
Can it be treated?
According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours.
If it isn't diagnosed and then treated quickly, experts warn it is nearly always fatal.
But the good news is that plague responds well to antibiotics if the treatment starts early.
Dr Malick Gibani, Clinical Associate Professor in Bacterial Vaccinology at Imperial College London, says the infection is widely recognised as a serious threat to public health.
"Pneumonic plague is a very severe manifestation of plague disease.
"Some textbooks will say it has 100% mortality if left untreated, and it's difficult to have accurate figures in the modern age.
"It is treatable with antibiotics, particularly if started early.
"That's why anyone with high-risk potential exposure might be offered post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics and/or quarantine."
In the Russian case, it is still not yet clear whether the person who died was infected by pneumonic plague.
The authorities in Russia have issued a statement saying that tests had shown "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" â and so at this stage it is still not quite clear what has happened.
US President Donald Trump said Washington was looking "very strongly" at the case, while the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said there was "no indication of a broader threat to the United States".
The UK's Health and Safety Authority said it was seeking more information, but that the risk to Britain's population was "very low".

On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall.
Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology.
The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours.
This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below.
Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska.
Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat.
"It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says.
Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation."
Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General AntÃ³nio Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished, external", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers, external in more than three decades.
Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles.
Nevertheless, more than 50 countries, external are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain.
As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it.
Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times.
He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable."
Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation.
Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain.
Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region."
Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas.
While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground.
"With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center.
What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges.
In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive."
What is sprayed into clouds may also be undergoing a major shift. Recast Systems in San Francisco is experimenting with a type of protein made from amino acids found in the soil, says CEO Olivia Li.
While still undergoing tests at Texas A&M University, this new seeding agent moves Recast away from silver iodide as the go-to compound.
"It's safe, biodegradable and nucleates ice at a higher efficiency than silver iodide," says Li, whose company currently uses silver iodide to seed clouds in several US states.
Meyer is optimistic this technology's trajectory will only continue to rise. "We're going to see more demand for these services as so many regions are experiencing water demand," he says, "and they're going to be looking for ways to help bridge that gap."

Trump on Iran: 'Let them take out LA, let them take out San Diego'
US President Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.
California Governor Gavin Newsom responded to the comments - made by Trump during a midterms rally in Nebraska - as "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".
According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.
The cities are the largest in southern California and house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.
Read more about President Trump's comments here.

6f2dd5ea2339.text: Hurricanes have long dominated efforts to make the power system more resilient to extreme weather . But America's energy buildout is running into growing risks from severe thunderstorms. Why it matters: New energy infrastructure and data centers are being built in harm's way as severe weather risks shift , leaving more for developers and insurers to lose when storms hit. Driving the news: Severe thunderstorms account for 40% of modeled global insured catastrophe risk, compared with 27% for hurricanes , according to analysis from risk analytics firm Verisk. The U.S. accounts for $117 billion, or 68%, of Verisk's modeled global insured catastrophe losses . Threat level: A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, potentially creating more favorable conditions for powerful thunderstorms. But the effects of climate change on severe storms are complicated. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration research scientist Harold Brooks told Axios that other atmospheric conditions needed for severe storms may become less favorable as the planet warms. Reality check: Verisk's Jay Guin said growing exposure, more than climate change, is the dominant driver of rising insured losses, as more and increasingly valuable property is built in harm's way. Guin says climate change contributes, but expanding development and higher reconstruction costs are much larger drivers. Zoom in: America's changing energy system is creating new kinds of exposure. Verisk is assessing risks to renewable projects in tornado- and hail-prone areas, where Guin said large hail can cause major damage to solar farms. "While they are renewable, you have a new asset class that is quite vulnerable," he said. Data-center developers must balance natural-hazard exposure against access to land, power and water. Some sites have billions in property and hardware, raising the stakes for siting and engineering. State of play: Tornado activity has increased about 10% in the Mid-South while declining by roughly the same amount from the Texas Panhandle through western Kansas, Brooks said. Population densities in rural areas of the Southeast are roughly 100 times those in the High Plains. "It's 10 people per square kilometer in rural areas of northern Mississippi and Alabama, and so a tornado in that area can't miss buildings and can't miss people," Brooks says. Zoom out: For infrastructure, Brooks said the biggest thunderstorm-related concern is flooding. Heavy rain and flooding are "a huge threat to virtually all of our infrastructure," he said. The bottom line: "There is no ... safe climate zone," Guin said.

1960c1d025b4.text: Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately lamented the impact of the Iran war and gas prices on his campaign in a meeting last month, telling a group of donors and lobbyists, "I don't make the decisions," according to audio obtained by Axios. Why it matters: It's a candid admission from a close Trump ally about the challenging environment Republicans face this cycle. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, was speaking to donors and lobbyists at a closed-door fundraiser in Washington, D.C. The audio was provided to Axios by a person, granted anonymity because it was a private event, who was in the meeting and is opposed to Paxton. President Trump is set to rally with Paxton in San Antonio on Wednesday. Driving the news: Asked by one attendee what issues are "dragging" on his campaign, Paxton responded, "It's not tariffs. ... It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," according to an audio file obtained by Axios. "When it's over $6 per gallon for diesel ... people are feeling the pinch," he continued, adding that the rising cost of fuel "drives up food prices and everything else." The Republican candidate said affordability is "by far our biggest problem" and "why we're having a hard time with numbers." Paxton pointed to his tax cut plan — which includes new housing and health care write-offs and an expansion of the child tax credit — as his proposed remedy on affordability. "I'm just trying to figure out ways I can help people. That's the only way: I can propose legislation," he said. When an attendee posited that Paxton "can't stop the war," the candidate responded "right" and said he has "no control over gas prices." "So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable. I don't make the decisions, and I don't ... know what's behind some of the decisions," he added. What they're saying: "This is a non-story. The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store," a Paxton campaign person told Axios. "President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families' pockets." Between the lines: Paxton said in the same meeting that Trump's midterm convention in Dallas "dropped our numbers," and that control of the campaign is "all coming ... from D.C.," according to separate audio obtained by The New York Times and Politico . State of play: Paxton is facing off with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico after unseating Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in a May primary runoff . Polls of the race have largely shown Talarico narrowly leading. He would be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since the 1980s. Paxton has for years been one of Trump's most loyal allies. Trump returned the favor in the primary by endorsing Paxton despite Senate Republicans' pleas for him to back Cornyn. e5f94e130f1b.text: Israel is marking the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 terror attacks three weeks before an election where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's personal culpability for the country's worst-ever security failure will be a central issue. Why it matters: Netanyahu has never looked more politically vulnerable than in the weeks after Oct. 7, but he has defied expectations by keeping his government afloat — presiding over simultaneous wars and an atmosphere of perpetual emergency. Though the polls are tight, they leave a clear path for the ultimate political survivor to hang on yet again. But Oct. 7 still looms over the country and his candidacy. The opposition lambasts him for refusing to take responsibility or allow an independent inquiry into the Hamas attacks that killed around 1,200 people. Every other senior national security official who was in office at the time of the attacks has resigned, except Netanyahu. Netanyahu's chief opponent, former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, lost his son and two nephews during the war in Gaza. Sources close to Eisenkot say he sees his main mission as replacing the man he holds responsible for allowing the Oct. 7 attacks. Netanyahu blames the deep state. His political and media allies — as well as his wife, Sara — have even spread conspiracy theories implying Israel was betrayed by its own security chiefs. Netanyahu himself has claimed those security chiefs deliberately kept him in the dark and suggested he could have prevented the massacre if only they'd woken him up when early warning signs came in. Driving the news: Recent reporting suggests Netanyahu had at least some warning. Haaretz reported that United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu days before the attacks that Hamas was planning a major operation. Three sources with knowledge confirmed to Axios that UAE intelligence gave a general warning to its Israeli counterparts and that MBZ spoke to Netanyahu to make sure he received it. A former U.S. official said then-CIA Director Bill Burns was told several months later by MBZ that he had warned Netanyahu. Other outlets including the New York Times also confirmed the story. The Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal reported that Netanyahu received a similar warning ahead of Oct. 7 from Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel. Netanyahu denied ever receiving warnings from the UAE or Egypt and sued several media outlets and journalists that reported he had. Between the lines: While those stories have been widely discussed in Israel, the three violent years that have passed since Oct. 7 — the leveling of Gaza, the release of the hostages, the attacks on Hezbollah and two wars with Iran — have given Netanyahu ample opportunity to restore his reputation among many Israelis as a strong and decisive leader. By the numbers: Most polls show Netanyahu's Likud party with 20-22 seats in the Knesset, down from 32, and his right-wing coalition with 50-54 — short of the 61 needed for a majority. But the opposition is also unlikely to secure a majority without the support of Arab-Israeli parties, which are projected to win a combined 12-14 seats. Polls reported by Netanyahu mouthpiece Channel 14 show the opposite, projecting the prime minister and his coalition winning a decisive 63-seat majority. Seizing on the right-wing turn in Israeli society, Netanyahu has pressured his main opposition to rule out forming a coalition with the Arab-Israeli parties. That taboo could keep Eisenkot from taking power, though he could try to cobble together a minority government. One possible scenario, if the polls prove accurate, is a hung parliament with Netanyahu staying on as a caretaker prime minister until another election is held. The vote could determine not just Netanyahu's political survival, but his legal future as well. Losing power would also mean losing any levers to delay or influence his ongoing corruption trial. But if he wins, Netanyahu could argue he was acquitted by the people of Israel — and take stronger action to thwart the proceedings. The intrigue: President Trump could give Netanyahu a boost by endorsing him, but so far he's declined. Asked several times recently by Time magazine whether he supported Netanyahu, Trump dodged the question. He added, however, that he didn't believe the press reports that MBZ had warned Netanyahu. Trump has privately blamed Netanyahu for the Oct. 7 failures, according to two people who have discussed the matter directly with the president. He's also mused about Netanyahu damaging Israel's international reputation. However, Trump has stuck close to Netanyahu during the war in Iran and may still endorse him. What to watch: Israel's election takes place a week before the U.S. midterms. If Democrats take back one or both houses of Congress, that will set up a battle over arms sales to Israel and even over the fate of $3.8 billion in annual military assistance. The tenor of that debate may hinge in part on whether Netanyahu remains in power.

20d71cd0261c.text: Common Sense Media is urging OpenAI to keep teens off ChatGPT, saying its new teen experience poses an "Unacceptable Risk" after extensive testing found shortcomings in safeguards meant to protect younger users. Why it matters: OpenAI has made protecting younger users a central part of its effort to make ChatGPT safer, but the findings suggest some of those protections may give parents more confidence than they warrant. "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Driving the news: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute said it tested more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds. The group found ChatGPT generally did not provide instructions facilitating suicide or self-harm, eating disorders or sexual or romantic roleplay, but said it was less reliable at recognizing when a teen needed outside help. Common Sense Media said ChatGPT missed more than one in four instances in which its testers determined a crisis referral was warranted. The group also said that on more than a dozen newly created, parent-linked accounts, testers could spend up to an hour discussing suicide, self-harm or disordered eating without triggering a parental alert. Common Sense also found that Study Mode could be circumvented: Teens could choose "Show me the answer" and, during parent-set Study Hours, could easily bypass the rules. OpenAI confirmed to Axios that the ability to exit Study Mode during Study Hours is intentional, not a loophole. The company said it designed Study Hours as a more flexible experience after consulting education experts and teens, rather than as a hard parental lock. What they're saying: "ChatGPT is not safe for kids to use," Common Sense Media Youth Safety Institute head Tom Siegel told Axios. Siegel said that what the company announced in August still has the potential to be industry-leading, but gaps remain between what was promised and the current reality. "It feels much more of a marketing announcement that really was not backed up with the engineering work." The other side: OpenAI says it has issues with Common Sense Media's methodology and findings. OpenAI says much of Common Sense's testing of parental alerts occurred before the parent and teen accounts had finished linking, a process the company says can take several hours. As for its age prediction system, OpenAI says it deliberately relies on multiple signals rather than simply accepting a user's stated age and can take up to two weeks to make a prediction. During that time, the company says users are given added content protection, though not as strong as the ones used in ChatGPT for Teens. On crisis referrals, OpenAI says its larger-scale data shows an increase in hotline resources being displayed to under-18 users during the period studied. Between the lines: Some of the disagreement reflects different ideas of what the safeguards are supposed to accomplish. Common Sense treats the ability to exit Study Hours as evidence that the parental control is ineffective; OpenAI says that flexibility is deliberate. Similarly, Common Sense's age test treats a user repeatedly identifying themselves as 13 without being moved into ChatGPT for Teens as a failure, while OpenAI says it intentionally requires multiple signals before making an age determination, while offering some strengthened protections during the time it is making its assessment. Bottom line: Siegel says parents need to have strong conversations about AI and its risks with their teenage children and find other ways to make sure they are getting support, whether it be for homework or the challenges of life. "We just can't outsource taking care of our kids to a tech product that is very early on and still quite buggy," he said.

The News
The largest privately held janitor service in the US is either a thriving business or a bankruptcy waiting to happen. It depends on which numbers youâre looking at.
Shares of Kellermeyer Bergensons Services, whose janitors clean 2 billion square feet of commercial property every day, have been written down to nothing. And valuations on several loans held by its biggest financial backer, a private-credit affiliate of KKR, range from nearly 100 cents on the dollar â a full recovery that is nearly unheard of when equity is wiped out â to around 10 cents. The chief investment officer of the fund, FS KKR Capital Corp., said on an earnings call a year ago that Kellermeyer had stabilized and was receiving interest from buyers. None has materialized.
Kellermeyer is one of a number of companies referenced in lawsuits filed in recent months that accuse funds managed by some of Wall Streetâs biggest names of inflating their marks, often to increase their own payouts. The cases against FS KKR, Ares, and Blue Owl strike at the biggest question hanging over private credit: Can anyone trust its marks?
The firms dispute the allegations and say the fees they charge are fair and industry-standard. Kellermeyer didnât respond to requests for comment.
Step Back
Unlike stocks and bonds, whose prices are quoted on screens across Wall Street, managers of private lenders have broad leeway to value their loans, with varying degrees of input from third-party services. These firms charge fees based on the value of their holdings, adding a financial incentive to keep the marks higher to avoid public scrutiny.
Last week, the Securities and Exchange Commission sent a rare warning shot to accountants, urging additional ârigorâ in how private-credit firms are valuing the loans they hold and how risks are disclosed to investors. While it was couched in a technical note to in-house accountants, it signaled a watchful eye from regulators that have so far left the market alone.
The second-order effects are also crystallizing. Semafor reported this week that the Federal Reserve has been probing how banks that lend to private-credit firms vet the loans that serve as their collateral, an admission that has spooked investors on Wall Street and around the world.
FS KKR said it plans to âdefend the matter vigorously through the appropriate legal process.â A Blue Owl spokesman said the lawsuitsâ claims were âwithout merit and we intend to zealously defend ourselves.â
Know More
The series of lawsuits, filed on behalf of investors in the funds, come not from a Wall Street ankle-biter but one of its consummate insiders. Jim Woolery was a dealmaker at the white-shoe law firm Cravath before leaving to run M&A at JPMorgan. He later became a hedge fund investor and now runs a boutique law firm, Woolery & Co., which is accusing Wall Street firms of clinging to high valuations to boost their own fees. Â
The lawsuits also attack the practice of charging fees on paper IOUs that are racked up by borrowers unable to make cash interest payments. The additional debt, known as âpayment-in-kind,â gives temporary breathing room to companies but can encourage can-kicking by lenders reluctant to acknowledge a dud in the portfolio.
In other words, the lawsuits claim, fund managers are charging fees based on interest they may never collect. More than one-third of the net investment income Blue Owlâs technology-focused lending fund reported last year was PIK interest, according to securities filings. The fund charged $468 million in fees, including an estimated $62 million of incentive fees related to PIK income that the lawsuits say investors should be able to claw back.

‘Medicare for All’ Message Attracts Voters Buckling Under Medical Bills
LANSING, Mich. — Christina Starks-Clay doesn’t know how “Medicare for All” would work exactly, but she’s willing to bet it’d be better than what she has now.
Standing in line for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s town hall in the state’s capital in September, she whipped out her phone to pull up a screenshot. It was of the $1,000 cashier’s check she’d picked up at the bank that day to pay down a chunk of her son’s dental bills. An early childhood special education paraprofessional, she still owed $389, even with good dental insurance. Her own cleaning a few weeks before cost $600.
She tried to talk herself down at the bank, to focus on being grateful for what she could afford.
“I’m like, ‘Tina, OK, you were in a position for this moment to do this,’” she said. “A lot of people couldn’t do what I had to do today. I couldn’t do it. But I did it. So I need to hear, how are you going to make this better for everyone?”
Many who waited in the hot sun that afternoon in a line stretching blocks through downtown Lansing shared similar anxieties. A man ahead of Starks-Clay talked about watching his brother rack up thousands of dollars in medical debt. A professor emeritus at nearby Michigan State University worried aloud about his grandkids’ medical care, because his adult kids were struggling to meet a $9,000 insurance deductible. Healthcare workers who’d turned up for the event described patients choosing between affording medication or food, or how they themselves had been financially devastated by a medical crisis.
They all knew Michigan Democrat El-Sayed’s rallying cry by heart, chanting it when the candidate took the stage: “Money out of politics! Money in your pocket! Medicare for All!”
Support for Medicare for All is at its highest in at least a decade, according to a new KFF poll. The survey found two-thirds of Americans now favor expanding the government health program that largely covers seniors (about half of whom are enrolled in private plans through Medicare Advantage).
But many people don’t actually know how to define Medicare for All. Traditionally, the idea has been to establish a single health insurance program, run by the federal government, that would guarantee coverage for Americans and minimize or even eliminate private insurance. How much people like the idea depends on what they’re told about it, pollsters have found.
Still, at a time when fewer than half of Americans say they can afford their healthcare, Medicare for All has become a progressive shorthand for radical, systemic change.
“Too many people don’t have health insurance, too many people who do have insurance can’t afford medical care, and many people are terrified about the costs of being sick,” said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill who specializes in the politics of healthcare reform.
“And in an electorate that wants change, that is disenchanted with the status quo, Medicare for All is an important symbol,” he said.
That’s why Democrats running for Senate seats in the midterm elections in such states as Maine, Minnesota, and Florida tout their support for scrapping the current health insurance system in favor of broad Medicare coverage. But nowhere is the issue as central to a race as in Michigan, where Medicare for All has become synonymous with El-Sayed.
El-Sayed, who trained as a doctor and served as Detroit’s top public health official, has campaigned on Medicare for All since his unsuccessful bid for governor in 2018. To Starks-Clay, that means he has a plan and will “stick to it,” she said.
That’s appealing to voters right now, said Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. “When we ask people what do they want to hear from candidates in regards to healthcare, it’s a plan to bring down healthcare costs.”
American Dream or Pipe Dream?
Medicare for All has been the shiny object of progressive politics in previous campaigns, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential bid and the 2020 Democratic presidential primary. Its popularity rises and falls in cycles, Oberlander said. And today people are painfully aware their care is getting more expensive and harder to access.
In the first decade or so after the passage of the Affordable Care Act in 2010, the nation’s uninsured rate was cut nearly in half. Insurance companies could no longer deny people coverage based on preexisting conditions. Since then, to cover more people, 40 states plus Washington, D.C., have expanded Medicaid, the government health program for those with low incomes or disabilities.
Now it feels as if we’re moving backward, Oberlander said. “We are now, in the past two years, in an era where the Trump administration and congressional Republicans have reversed that progress.”
Michigan, a battleground state that President Donald Trump won in 2024, saw some of the steepest ACA plan enrollment drops after the GOP-controlled Congress allowed enhanced tax subsidies, which helped people afford their premiums, to expire at the end of last year. Insurance companies in Michigan hiked individual marketplace rates by an average of 20%. And up to 355,000 Michiganders are expected to lose their Medicaid coverage in 2028 because of cuts included in Trump’s signature law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to estimates from the Urban Institute, a left-leaning think tank.
At El-Sayed’s town hall in Lansing, Darleana Ash said patients at the medical diagnostics lab where she works are increasingly skipping tests because they can’t afford them. Others drive hours from rural areas because their local labs have closed or are no longer in their insurance networks. She worries about the patients who must choose between their medications and groceries some months.

Food Aid Enrollment Tanks After SNAP Rule Changes
After President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act more than a year ago, enrollment in the federal food assistance program dropped rapidly across the nation as states enforced new restrictions and prepared to take on more of the costs.
Nationally, an estimated 5 million, or 13%, fewer people were enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP or food stamps, this June than in July 2025, when the law was enacted. Louisiana saw one of the most precipitous declines, dropping about 170,000 people, or 21% of state enrollees, according to federal data.
“We haven’t seen a decline of this magnitude in about three decades,” said Joseph Llobrera, senior director of research on food assistance at the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, which did the analysis.
Meanwhile, food prices rose nearly 3% from August 2025 to this August, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Elected officials, policy analysts, and anti-hunger advocates are pressing Congress to delay provisions in the law that will cut federal funding for food benefits and steeply increase the cost for states. They want to insert the delay in the Farm Bill, which is pending in the Senate.
The provisions required states to start paying for 75% of the cost to operate SNAP on Oct. 1. Previously, the USDA and states split SNAP’s administration cost 50-50.
Beginning in October 2027, some states may also have to cover part of the cost of SNAP benefits that had been paid fully by the federal government. The amount that a state pays toward benefits will depend on its payment error rate, or how often it underpays or overpays enrollees. The higher the error rate, the higher the state’s share of SNAP benefit costs.
In Louisiana, the state may have to cover up to $199 million of the cost for benefits, according to an analysis by the Food Research & Action Center. Its error rate increased from 6.62% in fiscal year 2024 to 8.14% in FY 2025, the most recent data available.
Many states, including Louisiana, have placed pressure on applicants to submit more information more often to verify their eligibility to reduce the state’s payment error rate and limit how much the cost of benefits shifts to the state.
“It’s been a race to drive down those error rates,” Llobrera said.
He said the challenge of implementing new program restrictions and requiring more documentation has increased the burden on applicants and state agencies. The agencies have to process more paperwork on a tight timeline without enough staff. This can increase the likelihood of errors when processing applications, potentially leading to rejection of benefits for more people. It’s also harder for applicants to meet additional verification requirements.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act expanded work requirements for SNAP, made it harder for states to waive the work requirements, and revoked access for many noncitizens with legal status.
The Louisiana Department of Health did not respond to requests for comment.
Tia Fields, the safety net policy analyst for the nonpartisan Invest in Louisiana think tank, said the cost increase to the state has contributed to two crises: a projected shortfall in the state budget and eligible families’ losing access to help.
In Louisiana, state data shows that 75% of people who lost SNAP from July 2025 to June 2026 did so for procedural reasons. When the program’s strict deadlines for documentation and verification aren’t met, applications and renewals are closed.
Fields said applicants may miss forms and interviews or fail to recertify or report changes in their status. Other times, the problem is on the state’s side. Agency notices may reach applicants past the deadline due to mail delays, they may be sent to the wrong address, or caseworkers may have backlogs in processing paperwork.
“Families are still hungry, and they’re actually eligible for the program,” Fields said. “This is a tax bill that we really cannot afford.”
The additional administrative burden and the financial penalties tied to having a high payment error rate give states an incentive to deny more applications, Llobrera said.
“The pressure that states feel now to really get their error rates down is pushing states to just ask for a lot more verification and more frequently,” Llobrera said.
Anti-hunger advocates say the need for food assistance has increased as barriers to SNAP have grown.
A Steadily Increasing Need
Aaranika Macon and her son received SNAP benefits for more than three years, continuing when she began nursing school last year. But she no longer qualified when she took a job in healthcare. After three months of trying to juggle work and school, her grades started to slip and she quit the job to focus on school.
So she reapplied to SNAP in February but did not receive benefits until April.
“I’m waiting, like, two months with nothing, because I stopped working,” Macon said. “Usually when you fill out, they’ll get back with you in, like, two weeks.”
According to the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, SNAP-eligible households are required to receive benefits within 30 days of application.
When Macon’s SNAP application was finally processed, she received less assistance than she previously did. She was deemed ineligible as a student, though she’s taking the same number of classes as she did last year when she was considered eligible. In Louisiana, higher education students are eligible for SNAP if they attend school at least half-time and meet other requirements.
Only her 11-year-old son was approved for benefits. Instead of the roughly $500 a month for two people that she received previously, she said, the $298 for her son feeds them both.
She said she had to stretch a $5 balance in her SNAP account over six days at one point this summer.
“I’m in the same position as before the job. So, why is it cut?” Macon said. “You’ve got to fight to communicate with them.”
