If there was a year the world began waking up to climate change, it might have been 1988. That June, the NASA climatologist James Hansen testified to Congress that the climate was warming and would continue to do so as long as humans pumped fossil fuel pollution into the atmosphere. Months later, the United Nations established the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
And, just weeks before the U.N. vote, Frank Sprow of Exxon’s corporate research department warned his colleagues in an internal memo, “If a worldwide consensus emerges that action is needed to mitigate against Greenhouse gas effects, substantial negative impacts on Exxon could occur.”
Sprow’s memo is part of a batch of previously undisclosed documents released earlier this year without fanfare as part of an ongoing lawsuit Massachusetts filed against ExxonMobil in 2019. While the memo was quoted in a 2023 article by The Wall Street Journal, it has not been published in full. Several other documents included in the filings are being reported on here for the first time, including more recent statements from Exxon scientists challenging the company’s climate-solution claims about its work on biofuels and carbon capture and storage.
While the documents align with hundreds of confidential files that have previously come to light through reporting by Inside Climate News and other news organizations, as well as lawsuits and other sources, experts say they provide new details on internal deliberations at Exxon from the 1980s to the 2010s.
The release of the documents comes at a pivotal time for the oil industry and for efforts to hold it accountable for its role fueling climate change. This week, the U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments from Exxon and oil producer Suncor Energy that a lawsuit filed by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, should be halted. The outcome of that decision could decide whether more than two dozen other claims against oil companies proceed.
Aaron Regunberg, director of climate accountability at the advocacy group Public Citizen, said the documents from the Massachusetts case underscore why Exxon and other companies are fighting to block the lawsuits from even proceeding to the discovery phase.
“They are really scared of the public finding out about this reality,” Regunberg said of oil companies. The Massachusetts filings, he said, suggest “that we have seen just a sliver of the evidence that they actually have that they’ve spent decades knowingly deceiving the public about this crisis. How many more reports are they sitting on?”
Most of the lawsuits assert that oil companies should help pay the escalating costs being imposed on the public by climate-fueled extreme weather because they knew the risks their products posed but worked to publicly question climate science and stymie efforts to curb emissions. Those costs have surged, topping $100 billion in the U.S. in four of the last five years. Exxon, meanwhile, reported nearly $19 billion in earnings over the first six months of this year alone.
Exxon did not respond to requests for comment, but it has denied misleading the public or investors about climate change. In its annual securities filing, the company said of the lawsuits, “We believe the legal and factual theories set forth in these proceedings are meritless and represent an inappropriate attempt to use the court system to usurp the proper role of policymakers in addressing the societal challenges of climate change.”
The case brought by the Massachusetts attorney general’s office in state court is slightly different from others, arguing that the company deceived the state’s consumers and investors into thinking it was taking action to limit warming when those efforts were more about public relations than real action. The state is seeking fines and an injunction blocking Exxon’s allegedly deceptive practices.
The new documents, filed as part of a dispute over whether Exxon should be forced to hand over more files and testimony, help lay out the state’s case.
Take biofuels. For years, Exxon ran a sustained public relations campaign touting its research into using algae to make fuel, which it said could be a sustainable alternative to petroleum.
In March, The Wall Street Journal reported on internal documents that showed Exxon’s scientists told executives the company’s targets were not feasible. The new disclosures in the Massachusetts case add to the evidence with excerpts from a deposition by an Exxon scientist who worked on the program.
Asked whether a 2018 press release, which said Exxon anticipated “10,000 barrels of algae biofuel per day could be produced by 2025,” was misleading, the scientist said “yes,” adding, “All the clauses in there are patently false.”
The scientist testified that the 10,000-barrel-per-day target was “completely impossible to achieve,” and that he told this to others at the company before the press release was issued.
In another instance, the scientist said a research development on algae that Exxon publicly claimed as a breakthrough was, in fact, “a dead end.”
Exxon later dropped its research into algae biofuels but has continued to promote carbon capture and storage as a climate solution. The documents include some statements which, according to the attorney general’s office, show Exxon knew that technology was also unlikely to present a scalable solution to cutting emissions.
A 2014 presentation on Exxon’s carbon capture portfolio included a slide listing challenges to reaching commercial scale. It noted widespread deployment would require a “massive investment” and an eventual storage rate “comparable to current oil and gas production.” It said costs were high and there were no market-based incentives.

Democrats are much more likely than Republicans to have confidence in the honesty of US elections, despite President Donald Trump and his party controlling Washington.
Sixty-three percent of Democrats say they have confidence in election integrity, according to Gallup polling, compared with 37% of Republicans and just 35% of independents.
For the first time this year, the Americans who disapprove of current US leadership are much more likely to have confidence in US elections than those who approve of it.
The polling punctuates widespread Democratic warnings about Trump laying the groundwork for interfering in the midterm elections by asserting more control over mail-in voting and dispatching Justice Department monitors to polling places.
It also makes the US an outlier: In the more than 100 countries Gallup polled, people who approve of the countryâs leaders almost always have higher confidence in election integrity than those who disapprove.

MONTGOMERY, Ala.—The Alabama Public Service Commission approved a new set of rules for future data center projects Tuesday that require more transparency and disclosure from data center companies and public votes by the PSC for data center approval. But they leave in place what critics call a “disappointing” provision allowing for approval by default of large data center projects if the commission does not schedule a vote on them.
Under the new rules, Alabama Power will have to release public summaries of data center contracts that include the name of the company the utility is contracting with, along with parent entities, where the project is located and the maximum amount of electricity the project could use.
Unredacted versions of those contracts would be reviewed by the commission and the Alabama Attorney General’s Office to ensure the projects are “consistent with the public interest.”
PSC President Cynthia Lee Almond said the new procedures will help keep the public better informed about data centers that may be developed.
“Currently, the redacted [public] filings of Alabama Power pretty much blacks out most everything that you might find important,” Almond said. “And so we required certain information in the filing that is not currently required.”
Currently, data centers undergo the same approval process as any other large industrial site, which does not require a separate vote by the commission. The new rules would change that for the massive server farms,, many of which sprawl across dozens, even hundreds, of acres and use as much electricity as cities.
“To me, it was important, because of the size of the data centers and the amount of energy they’re using and all the public concern about data centers, that we take a public vote on data center contracts,” Almond said.
Despite Almond’s support for public votes on data centers, the final version of the new rules includes a provision that could allow projects to be approved by default without a vote by the commission.
The rules say that the commission “shall” vote on each new data center project larger than 150 megawatts, but a late amendment stated that if the commission failed to vote on the contracts within 90 days, those projects would be approved by default.
Data center contracts will also have to include more financial details showing that the facilities are paying all the costs they incur, including whatever new infrastructure may be required.
The new rules were drafted in response to an Alabama law passed this year requiring stronger data-center disclosures.
The commission order instructs Alabama Power to create a new rate schedule for data centers complying with the terms of the order within 10 days, with the changes to take effect not less than 30 days after that.
Alabama Power, through a spokesman, said it was committed to following all regulatory requirements, including the new data center rules.
“Alabama Power will continue to require large load data center customers to pay the full cost to serve their energy needs, so costs are not shifted to existing customers,” the company said in a statement after the PSC adopted its new rules. “Alabama state law affirms that same standard and the Alabama Public Service Commission approves contracts that meet that standard while promoting positive benefits for other customers.”
Critics Point to Potential Loophole
The default approval provision was first introduced by Commissioner Chris Beeker III, who said it would spur the commission to take timely action on submitted contracts.
“We don’t have anything specific in this verbiage that says when we will take it to a vote,” Beeker said. “That’s what I’m trying to kind of right. So it’s deemed approved unless you want to disapprove it.”
Almond responded that she understood Beeker’s position but said it was important for the PSC to vote publicly on each proposal.
“I feel strongly that we should take a public vote as a commission on data centers, and we should not follow the deemed approved process that we’ve been following for a number of years,” Almond said during the meeting.
Commissioner Jeremy Oden said he understood both points of view.
After about 20 minutes of discussion among the commissioners and Luke Bentley, the PSC’s administrative law judge, the commissioners agreed to an amendment that included the 90-day deemed approval provision.
Currently, data center contracts submitted to the PSC for approval are deemed approved unless the commission takes action within 10 days of receiving them. The new rules essentially extend the deemed-approved period to 90 days.
The Southern Environmental Law Center said in a statement that the default approval provision was “a blow for data center accountability.”

The SELC also notes that the new rules do not call for public hearings or other opportunities for the public to comment on data center proposals.
“I am hopeful this is only the beginning of a deeper conversation about how to protect Alabama Power customers from the costs and risks of the data center boom,” Jaclyn Brass, an attorney in SELC’s Birmingham office, said in a news release.
“It’s disappointing the commission would not commit to taking public votes on all contracts,” Brass said. “However, requiring Alabama Power to disclose basic information about these contracts, including the name of the data center and the maximum contracted electric capacity, are all important steps toward greater transparency.”
Daniel Tait, executive director of clean energy advocacy group Energy Alabama, said data center contracts are unique in their requirements and the commission should vote publicly on them.

The Trump administrationâs recent changes to Trump Accounts could come under fire from the next Congress if Democrats win a majority.
The Treasury Department moved last week to automatically enroll tens of millions of children and greenlight donations of individual stocks as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent touts the accounts ahead of midterms.
President Donald Trump âbelieves that the American dream belongs to every child and every family â and today, through Trump Accounts, we are equipping the next generation to claim it,â Bessent said in Pennsylvania this week.
But Democrats believe that the individual stocks lack statutory authority and that the automatic enrollment could prevent savers with religious or other concerns with the stocks from opting out, House aides told Semafor.

In the Southern Ocean, whales, penguins, seals and seabirds feast on massive swarms of krill that underpin much of the region’s marine food web. Meanwhile, a growing fishing industry in Antarctica is also targeting the tiny crustaceans, used to make Omega-3 supplements, pet food and feed for farm-raised salmon. Now, a coalition of more than 30 scientists and ocean advocates, who call themselves the Antarctic Avengers, are asking shoppers to boycott these products to protect marine life.
“We are now witnessing the expansion of industrial fishing into one of Earth’s last great wildernesses. This is happening at a time when these waters are already under immense pressure from climate change, making it all the more urgent that we act to protect them rather than open them up to further exploitation,” said Sylvia Earle, a renowned marine biologist who is part of the Antarctic Avengers group and founder of a global marine conservation nonprofit, Mission Blue. “Krill are not a commodity to be extracted at scale for aquaculture feed, consumer supplements and cosmetics,” she said in a statement.
Krill populations are already suffering as sea ice continues to disappear due to rising temperatures. This loss of critical habitat, which krill depend on for food and shelter, has a direct impact on predators that feed on the crustaceans, like whales. Some research shows whales may not be getting enough food in years where there is less sea ice, and are consequently less likely to reproduce.
“We have shown that in years with poor winter sea ice extent there is a reduction in subsequent pregnancy rates that we believe is the direct result of prey limitation,” said Ari Friedlaender, an ecologist and professor at UC Santa Cruz who has studied whale foraging behavior in Antarctica for more than two decades. Industrial fishing, he said, could further add to the pressure whales face by reducing krill availability in key feeding grounds.
For this reason, Friedlaender said he is in favor of boycotting krill-based products even though he is not part of the Antarctic Avengers group. “It represents an opportunity that we have to reduce a known threat to krill predators,” he said.
The Antarctic Avengers are asking consumers to avoid buying Omega-3 supplements that advertise Antarctic krill as a key ingredient, as well as pet food and treats made from krill meal and oil.
“This is one of the few environmental problems where the fix is genuinely in our hands: read the label, put it back on the shelf, buy the algae version instead,” said Antarctic Avenger and National Geographic explorer and filmmaker Andy Mann, in a statement.
As alternatives, campaigners urge shoppers to seek out krill-free alternatives that include algae, flaxseed, hemp and chia oils. Consumers are also encouraged to reconsider purchasing farmed-raised salmon or other fish that are raised on krill meal.
Other marine conservation groups like Sea Shepherd, which has an ongoing campaign to stop industrial krill supertrawlers from overfishing the Southern Ocean called Operation Antarctica Defense, are also calling on major retailers to stop selling krill products in their stores to help change consumer behavior. Several have agreed.
Last year, as a result of Sea Shepherd’s advocacy, Holland & Barrett, a leading health and wellness retailer in the United Kingdom, committed to phasing out krill supplements.
“Our decision to exit krill products is part of our ongoing journey to become a more sustainable, nature-positive business that protects the ecosystems we all depend on,” said Jessica Long, sustainability and impact director at Holland & Barrett, in a statement.
This year, one of Germany’s largest drugstore chains, commonly known as dm, confirmed that it will stop selling krill products. Two of Australia’s large supermarket chains, Woolworths and Coles, have also stated they will no longer be stocking their shelves with krill supplements.
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.
Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.

Anduril wades into traditional shipbuilding arena with major submarine play
The defense tech company plans to build submarine components at a shipyard outside of Baltimore in which the government will have an approximate 40 percent stake, President Donald Trump said Tuesday.
SPARROWS POINT, Md.—Defense tech company Anduril aims to speed up Virginia-class submarine production by building components, such as torpedo tubes, at a future site outside the nation’s capital by 2030.
The new facility, to be called Arsenal-2, will be the company’s second manufacturing plant and is part of a $6.6 billion effort funded by Anduril, at $3.7 billion, and the U.S. Navy through a $2.9 billion contract award. That contract tasks Anduril with building “critical components and large scale assemblies of the Virginia-class” to be delivered to General Dynamics Electric Boat in Connecticut, and HII Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia, which are the prime contractors on the Navy’s submarine programs, according to the company’s announcement.
Flanked by two of Anduril’s Dive-XL vessels, President Donald Trump spoke to a mostly Navy audience Tuesday on a range of topics, from Venezuela to tariffs, and even gave a quick endorsement of subsea autonomous vessels before he announced the U.S. government’s stake in the new shipyard.
“The ultimate proof of our commitment to ensuring the shipyard's enduring success: American taxpayers will receive a 40 percent stake in the new shipyard. We get 40 percent,” Trump said, without providing more details.
That stake is in a new Anduril subsidiary created to operate the future shipyard. The government is not taking an equity stake in Anduril, the company said.
Additional specifics on the deal were not immediately available.
Submarines are “our oceans' apex predators” that are needed “now more than ever” for deterrence, Vice Adm. Robert Gaucher, who oversees the Navy’s submarine construction, said during the event at Tradepoint Atlantic near Baltimore. But he also acknowledged the nation’s lack of shipbuilding capacity.
“As other nations challenge the rules-based order that keeps our oceans free and open, we need the deterrence and denial of our submarines now more than ever,” he said. “At the same time, we must reckon with the fact that we have lost industrial capacity. Today, we start to rebuild it.”
The shipyard is being designed with reconfigurable production lines and will be underpinned by Anduril’s ArsenalOS industrial software platform.
“What we're really focused on here is being able to build an entire shipyard with a software and digital foundation. So that covers everything from how the factory is laid out, how work moves through the factory in a logical way, how all of that work is managed,” Chris Brose, Anduril’s president and chief strategy officer, told reporters.
That means “automating things that you can automate, keeping digital records of things like precision welding, so that you have traceability back to all the work that was done and an ability to understand, in very precise detail, for the purposes of certification and other types of kind of safety critical measures, what was done at what point all along the way, and having that traceability throughout the entire yard.”
The idea, he said, is for software to make it easier for new or inexperienced shipbuilders to perform tasks because they “can come in with a modicum of training enabled by technology—with digital designs, technical augmentation—and really understand how they can [be] contributing much, much faster.”
The company plans to break ground by early 2027 on Arsenal-2, which will span approximately 40 football fields on nearly 200 acres just outside of Baltimore. Initial operations are slated to begin by 2030.
The Navy contract also ties payments to “demonstrated production outcomes,” Anduril said in its news release.
Having a non-traditional defense company like Anduril building submarine components is an example of the Navy’s strategy to increase shipbuilding throughput by distributing the workload across multiple suppliers in the industrial base.
“Today, roughly 10 percent of shipbuilding work is performed at distributed sites. Our goal is 50 percent. New hulls will prioritize modular, digital designs that enable distributed shipbuilding across multiple yards and suppliers,” the Navy wrote in its 2026 shipbuilding plan earlier this year.
The move also deepens the Pentagon’s relationship with the company, which has several contracts across the military, and its leaders. Last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth named Anduril’s founder, Palmer Luckey, as part of an advising committee for Project Meridian, which will analyze future warfare needs.
Once operational, Anduril’s Baltimore plant is expected to increase overall Navy submarine production by 15 percent or about 9 million production hours per year. That should then translate into more ships produced through the Newport News and Electric Boat shipyards, Gaucher said: “Situated geographically between these two prime shipyards and connected to them by a network of sea, rail, and road, Arsenal-2 will take on the heavy component manufacturing.”
The facility will also build “components our prime shipyards need today, like precision torpedo tubes and impulse tanks,” he said, eventually “moving on to complex rafted module assemblies.”
The company also plans to eventually build sections of the ship’s hull.
Tuesday’s audience included about 100 sailors, and 200 midshipmen bused an hour from the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and Hegseth also spoke at the event.
The USS Billings, which was recently deployed in the Caribbean, served as a prominent backdrop to the stage. Sailors aboard the Freedom-class littoral combat ship could be seen standing at attention during the president’s address.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.
The Nobel Committee explained: "Molecules used by all life, such as the amino acids that are building of proteins, are what is known as chiral.
"This means that they have two versions that are mirror images of one another."
The building blocks to make living organisms on Earth only works with one version. The two scientists answered the question of why life favours one of these mirror image molecules over the other.
In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality" - where there are two symmetrical versions of a molecule, each with different properties.
You can think of them as looking like our hands - each a mirror image of the other.
When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant. One version of a molecule might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing.
Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions so they produce much more of the correct, desired version.

France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials.
Several groups have complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
The disruption continued on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut, and Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu is due to speak about the school protests in an evening address.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt.
NuÃ±ez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions.
"There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said, and confirmed the use of stun grenades was being suspended "until the facts surrounding this case have been clarified".
The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near the Auguste BÃ©hal high school in the northern city near Lille.
Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired.
According to the local prefect, the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks.
The stun grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon, but sends out small rubber pellets when it detonates.
"When there is suspicion of disproportionate force, there are always judicial investigations," NuÃ±ez said, affirming that the government was "here to protect high school students".
Concerns have also been stoked by the case of a 14-year-old hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week. The boy's lawyer said he had lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw in the incident at Saint-Ouen-l'AumÃ´ne, north-west of Paris, and a police officer has been charged.
Meanwhile, prosecutors said on Wednesday that an investigation for attempted murder had been opened after a 17-year-old student protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river in the north-eastern city of Belfort.
The prime minister has condemned violence seen at some of the protests which began in mid-September - noting on Tuesday that 215 students, 85 staff, and 715 police officers had since been hurt.
More than 6,500 people have been stopped or arrested in that time, according to the interior ministry.
President Emmanuel Macron held an emergency meeting late on Tuesday with Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis after almost a quarter of all lycÃ©es were disrupted by the day's protests - with government figures putting the number of protesters at more than 250,000.
Students' unions put the number at 450,000 and say a fourth round of protests is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities.
The head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, told French radio on Wednesday: "We are telling M. NuÃ±ez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint."

US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
"So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with Putin "probably" on Thursday.
Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death. They say that those who came into contact with the victim all tested negative and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague - a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for transparency from Russia.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
- infected flea bites
- contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
- the inhalation of respiratory particles
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked - or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
But Russian officials have played down those reports. The country's health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology".
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

Sri Lanka's former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations raised for a children's hospital.
Anti-corruption authorities arrested the 73-year-old wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa at their Colombo home on Wednesday.
They are questioning her over the 10 million rupees ($30,300; Â£22,800) of donations collected by the Siriliya Saviya charity, meant to be spent on a specialised scanner for Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital.
But officials say such a scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government.
Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing and says the money has not been appropriated.
She returned to Sri Lanka on Monday from Singapore, where she was receiving medical treatment. She had filed a court petition to try to prevent her arrest, but the hearing was set for 12 October.
Ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa's spokesperson, Manoj Gamage, has said the money is safe in Siriliya's accounts and that no fraud has occurred.
Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president of Sri Lanka from 2005 to 2015 and for years, his family held a tight grip over the country's politics. He was hailed by many as a hero for bringing an end to nearly three decades of civil war when Tamil Tiger rebels were crushed in 2009, during his first term as president.
But in 2022, protests broke out across the country as inflation surged and Sri Lanka ran out of fuel, food and medicine.
Mahinda's brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was serving as leader at that time, was eventually toppled.
Sri Lanka's current government, under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has since revived long-stalled corruption investigations involving various members of the Rajapaksa family.
Mahinda and Shiranthi's eldest son, Namal Rajapaksa, was arrested earlier this year over allegations linked to an aircraft procurement deal made during his father's presidency. He is currently held in remand.
His brother Yoshitha was also arrested earlier this year on corruption charges.

A California pair has been charged with multiple counts of abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children - some as young as two months old - and dissuading a witness.
"The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented," Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J Hochman said in a statement.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who US media describe as a couple, were arrested at their Arcadia mansion on Tuesday.
The pair pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
Xuan, 66, and Zhang, 39, are accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in their home to repeated physical abuse, after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.
The pair ran their own surrogacy company and are accused of making false statements to at least two women who became surrogates, indicating that Zhang was struggling to conceive, according to the criminal complaint.
As of May 2025, Zhang maintained a spreadsheet that tracked 21 children, including those born to surrogates.
Officials said the investigation began that month when Zhang brought a two-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury, telling medical staff that the baby had fallen from a bed.
The couple's lawyer Mitchell Krems said the allegation was a "mischaracterisation" based on the evidence he has reviewed, CBS News in Los Angeles reported.
Hospital staff informed law enforcement, and when police arrived at their home they discovered three different rooms called "learning centres" under the supervision of multiple nannies, which Hochman described as a "house of horrors".
The mansion allegedly had 32 motion-activated cameras which Hochman said were used by the couple to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.
Footage allegedly shows the nannies spanking, slapping or hitting the children.
One nanny, Chunmei Li, is accused of hitting the two-month-old baby who suffered the head injury two days before he was brought to the hospital.
Krems said Li was quickly fired, CBS News LA reported.
Li, 58, was previously charged with one felony count of child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death. Hochman said she was on the run with a $105,000 (Â£88,800) warrant for her arrest.
In July 2025, the couple's home was first raided by authorities, who took 21 children into state custody.
Arcadia Police Department said at the time the couple's house was first raided that the children ranged in age from two months to 13 years old, but most were between one and three years old.
Fifteen of the children were taken from the couple's home while six others were living elsewhere and also later taken into custody.
Krems said his client Xuan was innocent.
"He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family," CBS News quoted the lawyer as saying.
Investigators believe the surrogate mothers were from around the country and they were unaware they were carrying embryos for the couple at the same time.
Melissa Brisman, the attorney for two of the surrogates, told CBS News: "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system".
If convicted as charged, Xuan faces a possible maximum sentence of 17 years and four months in state prison, while Zhang faces up to 11 years and eight months. Li faces up to 12 years.

The News
Africaâs long-planned credit rating agency launches in Mauritius on Wednesday, the continentâs most concrete answer yet to years of complaints that the worldâs biggest agencies overstate African risk and drive up borrowing costs.
The creation of the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) comes as global agencies face growing criticism for relying on offshore models that some African leaders and policymakers say misread local realities â a debate sharpened this year by Afreximbankâs public break with Fitch.
AfCRA will rate governments, cities and companies, and it is meant to complement the three US firms, which control 95% of global ratings markets.
The new ratings agency âwill add another opinion in the market place of opinions,â said Marie-Antoinette Rose-Quatre, head of the AU body that incubated it. She called it âa very tangible outcome of our aspiration to build our own financial institutionsâ.
Only three African sovereigns hold investment grade ratings, according to a background note from the AUâs African Peer Review Mechanism (ARPM). Thirteen are rated at very high risk or in default, and 23 have no rating from the big agencies, which cuts them from international bond markets. The AU has also said the continentâs external debt service costs climbed from roughly $60 billion in 2010 to more than $160 billion in 2024.
Know More
The launch is part of a wider push by developing countries, at the G20 and the UN, to change how global finance prices their risk. South Africa used its 2025 G20 presidency to put borrowing costs on the agenda.
In an op-ed published in Africa Renewal, the UN magazine, Rose-Quatre and Ahunna Eziakonwa, the UN secretary-generalâs special adviser on Africa, said unfair ratings cost Africa $74.5 billion a year â an estimate which was first published by the UN Development Programme in 2023.
Key details of the new agency remain unclear. The APRM describes it as privately owned and self-funded but has not named its shareholders, chief executive, or board. Mauritius Commercial Bank and the pan-African lender Afreximbank took part in a 2025 meeting to raise support for the project. According to the APRM note, AfCRA âwill require a licenceâ from Mauritiusâ financial regulator.
People close to the project say trust will take time. âCredibility in credit rating is accumulated rather than declared,â said Daniel Cash, a UK-based law professor who has advised the APRM on credit ratings. The real test, he told Semafor, will come when AfCRA issues a rating that a member state, âparticularly an influential oneâ strongly dislikes. âIndependence is demonstrated at the point of disagreement.â
The launch also comes as global agencies expand on the continent. Moodyâs owns GCR, the largest issuer of ratings in Africa, and in July S&P agreed to buy a majority stake in Nigeriaâs Agusto & Co. S&P Global declined to comment, while Moodyâs and Fitch did not respond to requests for comment.
Tiisetsoâs view
For half a century, the cost of African borrowing has been set largely in New York by three firms that rate the 55 countries from a distance. AfCRA is the continent finally taking a seat at the table where its risk is priced.
Every 10 basis points shaved off a $1 billion Eurobond saves an issuer $1 million a year. Twenty-three states have no rating from the big agencies at all, which locks them out of mandates that require one. Thatâs the prize.
True, AfCRA has no track record and no named shareholders, but the quickest route to credibility runs through pain: an early, well-argued downgrade of one of the governments that cheered the launch.
Room for Disagreement
Critics question whether investors will trust any agency created by the governments it rates. David Lubin of UK think tank Chatham House asked whether AfCRA amounts to Africa âmarking its own homework,â adding that fund managers compare African borrowers with the rest of the world and an African agency âdoes nothingâ for them.
Misheck Mutize, AfCRAâs chief architect, acknowledged that the agencyâs main role would be to steer Africaâs $4 trillion savings into African assets rather than changing how foreign investors see the continent.
âThe challenge here is that this is the bare minimum disclosure required before international investors can even begin to take AfCRA seriously,â said Bright Simons, head of research at IMANI, a think tank based in Accra, writing on public policy platform Katanomics Society.
Notable
- Nigerian President Bola Tinubu made the case for an African rating agency, arguing that the Big Three misjudge African risk and that a homegrown agency could spot progress early, which the global firms would later confirm.

Eva Marie Saint, the Oscar-winning actress who starred in Hollywood classics such as On the Waterfront and North by Northwest, has died aged 102.
Saint won the Academy Award for best supporting actress for her movie debut in director Elia Kazan's 1954 crime drama On the Waterfront, playing Edie Doyle, the love interest of Marlon Brando's conflicted boxer-turned-docker.
Five years later, she portrayed femme fatale Eve Kendall, dangerously seducing Cary Grant's entangled advertising executive in Alfred Hitchcock's spy thriller, North by Northwest.
She died on Tuesday of natural causes, surrounded by family and loved ones at her home in Los Angeles, family representative Jeff Sanderson confirmed.
Until her death, Saint was the oldest surviving Oscar winner and one of the last remaining stars of Hollywood's golden age.
Started in live television in the late 1940s, she also won an Emmy in 1990 for her role as a rich widow in the acclaimed TV miniseries People Like Us.
Born in Newark, New Jersey in 1924, Saint had originally intended to become a teacher before developing a passion for theatre.
She trained in New York at the Herbert Berghof Studio and then the Actors Studio - the home of method acting - co-founded by Kazan.
Saint burst on to the Hollywood scene with her performance in Kazan's classic, On the Waterfront.
Brando was known as an intense method actor and Saint admitted to having found him "adorable" but "a little frightening".
"I felt that he could see right through me," she told Turner Classic Movies (TCM) in a 2013 interview.
She was considered a surprise choice, though, to play one of "Hitchcock's blondes", as they were known at the time, in his masterpiece North by Northwest.
Her co-star Grant was known for being very demanding of his leading ladies.
"He worked with me from the outside in," said Saint.
"My hair, my makeup, my shoes, my jewellery, my purse, my gloves, everything. And just from creating that exterior for me, he gave me the sense of a spy lady."
Saint also starred opposite Paul Newman in Otto Preminger's Exodus in 1960, and she was Warren Beatty's love interest in John Frankenheimer's All Fall Down.
But she then stepped away from the limelight to raise a family with director Jeffrey Hayden.
Half a century later, Saint - by then in her early 80s - made a big screen comeback as Superman's adoptive mother in the 2006 blockbuster Superman Returns.
And she later had parts in the supernatural fantasy Winter's Tale, alongside Colin Farrell and Russell Crowe, and the 2019 nun drama Mariette in Ecstasy.
Saint, who has two stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame for her movie and TV work, said her longevity in acting had given her work extra depth.
"The longer you live, the smarter you get, because you've been around, you've seen things," she told TCM.
"You've gone through different emotional experiences in your own life, and hopefully, you understand things better.
"And that makes you a better actress."
Saint's marriage to Hayden lasted for 65 years, until his death in 2016, and she is survived by their two children.

9d455c24146c.text:
The News
The Nigerian state oil companyâs disclosure that it spent $8 billion to protect energy infrastructure has sparked calls for an inquiry into how the funds were used and cast fresh light on the countryâs inability to protect key economic assets.
Nigeria is Africaâs top crude oil producer and exporter, with sales accounting for around 90% of foreign exchange earnings. But oil revenue has been particularly constrained by theft and pipeline vandalism that has cost the country about $300 billion in recent years, compounding in a worsening security crisis that has hampered the overall economy. At the same time, there have long been concerns about the alleged misuse and diversion of Nigeriaâs oil money, with the state company NNPC often at the center of the storm.
Analysts and government critics are now raising fresh questions about the companyâs $8 billion security costs in 2025, which marks a 26% increase over the previous year.
âNigerians cannot tell from these totals what was spent on pipeline surveillance,â Atiku Abubakar, a leading challenger to President Bola Tinubu in upcoming elections in January, said in a statement. âWhat was paid? Who was paid? For what work? Where are the results?â
Tinubu ended a fuel subsidy scheme three years ago that cost $10 billion in 2022. NNPC did not respond to a request for comment.
Know More
NNPC reported a 33% rise in post-tax profit to $5.4 billion for full year 2025 on the back of Nigeriaâs highest crude oil production output in five years. But its revenues fell year-on-year by 24% due to lower crude oil prices in the dozen or so months that preceded the onset of the Iran war this year.
It owns a 5,000 km crude oil and petroleum products pipeline network across Nigeria and recorded more than a dozen breaks along its pipelines last year and five in the first six months of 2026.
Alexanderâs view
Election season in Nigeria comes with heightened sensitivity around money flows, especially when it involves the governmentâs largest moneymakers. And so the discourse around NNPCâs announcement that it will charge the government $8 billion for securing oil and gas facilities has assumed political undertones with polls set to open in about 100 days.
It may not account for much, however. NNPC has scaled through several inquisitions over the years, mostly unscathed, and is a much larger, consequential company for the Nigerian government than ever before.
Earlier this year, a Nigerian senate committee headed by an opposition party lawmaker ordered NNPC to account for nearly $160 billion in unreconciled figures in the companyâs audited financial statements between 2017 and 2023. That matter remains unresolved. Calls for a probe into the latest controversial figures â which are far much smaller by comparison â already seem to be falling on deaf ears.
Room for Disagreement
Attempts to damage Nigerian oil pipelines fell by 87% between 2022 and last year, a private company contracted to guard the Trans Niger Pipeline in the southern Niger Delta region said in November. It credited the improvement with increased participation of communities in providing intelligence for security.

At least 15 people have died in overnight strikes across central and eastern Ukraine, in what Volodymyr Zelensky has described as one of Russia's "most vile" attacks.
Ukraine's president said a residential building in Pryluky in the Chernihiv region was destroyed as a "birthday 'gift' to Putin", who turns 74 on Wednesday. Strikes also hit Kyiv, Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Zaporizhzhia and Oleksandriya.
Zelensky said Ukraine had struck targets in attacks on Russia's Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions in the past 24 hours, adding there was "also a response in the Black Sea", without providing further details.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest strikes.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," Zelensky said, adding that 70 missiles were fired in total.
In the social media post on Wednesday morning, Zelensky said five people had been killed and 26, including five children, injured in a strike on a five-storey apartment building in Pryluky.
He added that people could still be trapped in the rubble.
Chernihiv Oblast police later reported that the death toll had risen to nine after the bodies of three children were recovered, with emergency workers continuing a search operation.
Two people were also killed and eight injured after Russian missile strikes damaged five apartment buildings in Dnipro and four high-rise buildings in Kremenchuk, said Zelensky.
Two people were also killed in the capital, Kyiv, and two others in Oleksandriya, he added.
Ukraine's national police posted pictures online showing what it says is an unexploded Russian Iskander missile in the middle of a Kyiv district. BBC Verify has confirmed the images are genuine and the apparent missile fragments came down in an area of open land surrounded by high-rise apartment buildings.
A video posted by the police shows people digging through collapsed remains of a residential building in Pryluky. Another verified video shows damage to cars and what appears to be rubble and a fallen tree in an area surrounded by apartment blocks in Kremenchuk.
Zelensky renewed a call for allies to provide air defence support packages to Ukraine, saying its military only managed to shoot down "some" of the missiles launched by Russia overnight.
According to Zelensky, one of the "key targets" of the attack was the country's energy infrastructure, which Moscow earlier said it would intensify strikes on following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities.
In a separate post on Wednesday, Zelensky said Ukraine had struck four targets in retaliatory attacks in the past 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions.
"There is also a response in the Black Sea," the Ukrainian president wrote.
On Tuesday evening, footage emerged showing a huge plume of smoke engulfing an oil tanker off the coast of Sochi, along the Black Sea in southern Russia.
The Russian transport ministry later said unmanned boats had attacked the Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio oil tanker. Authorities claim the crew was rescued.
Separately, Bulgaria has halted a search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov from the Maritime Administration Executive Agency said, as reported by Bulgarian television network Nora TV.
Tracking data shows the ship was anchored at the southern end of the Bosphorus strait until Monday when it entered the Black Sea heading north. Its last reported position on ship-tracking site MarineTraffic was at 23:43 GMT on Monday in what is known as the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone of the Black Sea.
Bulgarian specialist news outlet Maritime.bg reported the Alfa Watan was attacked by a drone and sank 70nm (130km) east of Byala.
As well as the civilian cargo ship, a second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, its Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday. The 18 crew members on the second vessel were rescued.
Bulgaria has not said who it believes was behind the attacks.
It comes as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
In an evening address on Tuesday, Zelensky claimed Russia was responsible for the attacks.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident.
Additional reporting by BBC Verify

The News
Ruben Gallego isnât sure if heâs running for president yet, but he still has big plans for his Democratic Party once itâs back in power.
The Arizona senator is launching a huge, wide-reaching policy agenda on Wednesday thatâs aimed at confronting a labor market â and workforce â getting reshaped in real time by the AI boom. He wants to raise the minimum wage and boost overtime pay while imposing taxes on data centers and automated jobs, in addition to creating a federal public works program to ensure US workers can cope with AI.
Itâs a big move by the first-term senator as his party wages a pitched fight for control of Congress in next monthâs midterm elections. He said he recognizes that the public needs to start hearing about what Democrats intend to do with control in Washington, if they wrest some of it from GOP hands this fall.
âPeople that are working right now donât feel like their hard work is actually bringing them anything in return â¦ and going into election season, people want to know where Democrats stand,â Gallego told Semafor in an interview this week.
âWith AI becoming more and more prevalent in peopleâs lives and fears, I think itâs also important that we have a real forward-leaning policy that deals with AI and the workforce,â he added.
Gallegoâs sweeping proposals certainly look like the policy engine undergirding a 2028 presidential campaign. He said heâs ânot naiveâ about his work furthering that speculation, though he demurred on his future aspirations.
âNo matter what,â Gallego said, âIâm going to be involved inâ policy debates after the 2028 race.
âIâm not in the space right now to make a decision,â he added. âA lot of conversations have to happen between me and my wife, especially when it comes to raising kids and potentially running for office.â
Know More
Gallegoâs plan, which he pitches with a personal touch by invoking his upbringing in Arizona and the stateâs recent run of rapid growth and economic change, touches almost every aspect of the American economy.
But heâs chiefly concerned with evident public views that wages are not keeping pace with rising prices â that the American âdream is slipping away from millions of Arizonans,â as he writes in his proposal.
On top of raising the minimum wage to $20 per hour and pegging it to inflation, his agenda would promote sectoral bargaining agreements to establish labor standards for entire industries, require companies to provide paid leave, and raise overtime pay for eligible workers from time-and-a-half to double pay.
Heâs got equally ambitious plans for the AI industry, calling for a 10 percent excise tax on data center revenues and an end to tax incentives for those projects, a ârobot taxâ to discourage job losses due to automation, and consideration of a tax on AI tokens.
He wants to use that money to help fund a âNew Deal-styleâ public works program to ensure the US wonât experience âmassive unemploymentâ from the adaptation of AI.
âData centers and AI companies cannot just be operating untouched and also unbothered in terms of what they do to our labor markets, to our communities. They need to be part of the solution and not just be a problem,â Gallego said in the telephone interview.
He also wants to prioritize reclassifying certain so-called gig workers as employees rather than independent contractors and require companies to give workers more notice ahead of mass layoffs.
Gallego said heâs ready to maximize Democratic authority to get it done. He proposed putting as much of his proposal as he can in a party-line budget reconciliation bill that Democrats can pass with a simple majority if they control the House, Senate, and White House come 2029.
He added that Democrats should not listen to the Senate parliamentarian if, for example, a minimum wage hike gets ruled ineligible for reconciliation (as it was in 2021).
âWe shouldnât be afraid to push the limits on reconciliation, on overruling the parliamentarian,â he said, arguing that Republicans have âalready kind of blown up the parliamentarian primacyâ anyway.
Burgessâs view
The rising class of Democrats has big ideas, and you can already start to see the party nearing a big debate about its agenda ahead of 2028. Gallegoâs plan is one of the most expansive yet, but he isnât the first to jump in.
Sens. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Cory Booker of New Jersey have tax cut ideas. Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey wants his party to give kids universal health insurance coverage.
This bold flurry is a stark contrast with Democratic leaders, who would like to start really shaping their agenda â¦ after the midterm elections.

Yorkshire Water has admitted a Â£1.5m scheme to reduce storm overflow discharges into a North Yorkshire river has not performed as expected.
When the investment was announced in 2024 for the River Ure in Ripon, the water company said the scheme would reduce the issue by about 75%.
But it said the number of recorded discharges from its Clock Tower combined sewer overflow (CSO), near the Ripon by-pass bridge, fell from 75 in 2021 to 43 in 2025, a reduction of about 43%.
The company has described the result as "disappointing", but stressed that comparing individual years was complicated by rainfall levels.
"[2025] was a particularly dry year, which will have further contributed to a decrease in discharges," a Yorkshire Water spokesperson said.
"As such, whilst there has been a reduction, the scheme did not perform as expected, which is disappointing."
Combined sewer overflows are designed as pressure-relief points on sewer networks which carry both wastewater and rainwater.
During heavy rainfall, they can discharge into watercourses to prevent overloaded sewers backing up into homes, businesses and streets.
Such discharges can be permitted by the Environment Agency under specified circumstances.
'Deeply disgusting'
Recent testing by campaign group Stop Ure Pollution and the Yorkshire Dales Rivers Trust further upstream has raised concerns about bacteria and other pollution in the river, the Local Democracy Service reports.
The Skipton and Ripon branch of the North Yorkshire Green Party has now submitted an Environmental Information Regulations request, seeking information held by Yorkshire Water about the performance of the Clock Tower scheme and changes in discharges following work carried out in 2025.
Green Party councillor Andy Brown said the levels of sewage going in the rivers "is deeply disgusting" and called the latest testing further upstream "far from reassuring".
He said campaigners and organisations, including Ripon City Council, would continue pressing for improvements.
"Yorkshire Water must play its part," he said.
"It must act, and it must deliver the facts â straight-up and undiluted."
Yorkshire Water said it was investigating further projects in Ripon as part of a Â£1.5bn investment programme aimed at reducing storm overflow use.
"We know there is much more to do to protect local watercourses," the spokesperson said.

006e169aba8c.text:
The News
Fourteen major mining companies in DR Congo paid at least $20 billion to ineligible subcontractors between 2020 and 2025, the countryâs subcontracting regulator told Semafor, citing recently completed checks.
These findings at mining businesses, among them subsidiaries of Swiss commodities giant Glencore, Ivanhoe Mines and Chinese-Congolese joint-venture Sicomines, have prompted the regulator to plan tougher inspections this month to tackle breaches of subcontracting rules. These include the longstanding use of Congolese figureheads to disguise foreign control.
Glencore declined to comment. Ivanhoe Mines and Sicomines did not respond to Semaforâs requests for comment by publication time.
The regulatorâs move comes as the country courts new mining investment, including from the US, and seeks to ensure that Congolese partners genuinely own and help run the businesses supplying its mines, in line with its laws.
âWe are open to partnership. But we donât want people to come just for an extractive economy and leave us with holes,â Juan Ted Beleshayi, head of the Authority for the Regulation of Subcontracting in the Private Sector, told Semafor.
In recent weeks, he has ordered miners to terminate about 1,800 subcontracts with suppliers lacking valid registration certificates. These include contracts with 1,540 suppliers at two subsidiaries of Glencore, alongside those involving Ivanhoe Mines, Eurasian Resources Group and Sicomines. âWe really only carried out a simple check,â said Beleshayi, who took charge of the agency just over three months ago. He said he had completed checks begun under his predecessor.
This monthâs inspections would be âvery detailed and rigorous,â said Beleshayi. Inspectors will check who owns the suppliers on paper, who calls the shots and who controls the bank accounts. Companies who fail to comply with the regulatorâs decisions could face closure, he said.
Know More
Subcontracting represents billions of dollars to the Congolese economy â in 2025, 167 major companies declared $3.7 billion in contracts. The regulatory agency registers mining suppliers, which typically handle transport, machinery maintenance and construction among other work, and enforces rules based on a 2017 law that requires Congolese investors to own at least 51% of those businesses, with foreign ownership capped at 49%.
Chinese companies dominate DR Congoâs copper and cobalt mines and have often faced criticism from the regulator for shutting Congolese businesses out of subcontracting work. Beleshayiâs predecessor, Miguel Kashal, accused Sicomines, in 2023 of keeping all its subcontracts in Chinese hands. Three years ago, Sicomines pledged to give Congolese suppliers its secondary work. A company representative said that a misunderstanding over subcontracting rules had been resolved.
Beleshayi told Semafor his own inspections had found the same pattern. Sicomines did not respond to this claim. âWeâre not saying foreigners have to leave. We just want a 49-51 split,â Beleshayi said. Limited financing and technical skills prevent Congolese suppliers from handling major mining contracts, researcher Fridolin Kimonge told Semafor.
Ownership checks and contract cancellations alone cannot address those weaknesses. âIt is not enough to cancel; there has to be a plan behind it,â Beleshayi said. Temporary exemptions would allow foreign suppliers to help Congolese businesses become partners or competitors, he said. âWe will look for Congolese who understand American culture or can adapt to it, to build companies together,â he said of incoming US companies.
Rubenâs view
Like many African countries, DR Congo struggles to enforce laws that exist on paper. Part of the problem with its subcontracting law is finding replacements for the suppliers who break it. Congolese businesses often lack the financing and technical skills to take over major mining contracts, limiting how far the regulator can act without disrupting operations.
Washingtonâs push to loosen Chinaâs grip on Congolese minerals could give the regulator more options. Beleshayi expects American suppliers to accompany new US mining investments and form businesses with Congolese partners. If those companies can deliver the work and meet the ownership rules, existing suppliers would face competitors capable of replacing them. âYes, absolutely,â he said when I asked whether that prospect could pressure companies already operating in DR Congo to comply.
Conflict in mining regions, disputed licenses, slow permitting, and unpredictable enforcement have long deterred Western investors, while Chinese operators have been better able to absorb those risks. DR Congoâs recent reforms and Beleshayiâs crackdown could help signal to the US and European companies it is courting that the country is becoming a more reliable place to do business.
Room for Disagreement
Transparency has long been a central demand in efforts to improve DR Congoâs mining governance and local ownership alone offers no guarantee that contracts benefit ordinary Congolese, say critics.
In a 2020 study of six mining companies, researcher Kimonge found that DR Congoâs subcontracting law required majority Congolese ownership but provided no mechanism to trace where the money invested in those businesses came from. He warned that gaps in the rules also allowed political and administrative officials to own suppliers and steer contracts toward their own businesses. âThe situation has not improved much,â he told Semafor.
Mining governance analyst Jean Pierre Okenda called repeated denunciations of figureheads as âpopulist rhetoricâ that does not go far enough and urged the regulator to publish suppliersâ real owners and their ties to officials. Otherwise, he warned, replacement contracts could go to another set of politically connected businesses.

e0ef7bdc55a5.text:
- Published
Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Gulf of Mexico and looks likely to strengthen into the first Atlantic hurricane of this year.
It is expected to reach hurricane strength late on Wednesday or early Thursday with forecasts suggesting it could then intensify to a category two storm.
It has the potential to bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge to parts of the US Gulf Coast with landfall expected on Friday or Saturday. Parts of Mexico could also see gusty winds and heavy rain as the storm moves northwards and eastwards.
Isaias will bring an end to the lack of hurricanes that has led so far to a record-breakingly quiet Atlantic season with development suppressed by the historic El NiÃ±o that continues to grow in the Pacific.
How strong will Isaias get?
In its latest update, the US National Hurricane Center estimates that Tropical Storm Isaias will strengthen rapidly and is likely to reach hurricane strength during Wednesday night. It will intensify further to a category 2 storm by Friday morning.
Parts of Mexico will feel the first impacts as the storm swirls out at sea, with 4in (100mm) of rain possible around the Bay of Campeche and the Yucatan Peninsula, accompanied by strong winds.
Isaias will then make landfall on the Gulf Coast - probably in Mississippi, Alabama or Florida - late on Friday or early on Saturday.
Forecasters predict that 3-6in (75-150mm) of rain could fall across the Gulf Coast, from south-east Louisiana to the north-west of Florida.
A few places could see up to 10in (250mm) with possible flash flooding, especially in urban areas, and the risk of isolated river flooding.
Dangerous winds are anticipated with the chance of a storm surge which could inundate low-lying coastal areas.
The US National Weather Service says it expects to issue Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches later on Wednesday with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis declaring a state of emergency across 25 north Florida counties over concerns about potential impacts.
As the storm moves further inland and loses contact with its warm water fuel source it will weaken but it is still expected to bring some potentially disruptive wet weather.
Between 1-3in (25-75mm) of rain is forecast for large swathes of the south-east USA - as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas - with isolated totals of 5in (125mm).
El NiÃ±o has lead to an eerily quiet hurricane season so far
Forecasters in the US predicted the 2026 hurricane season would be quieter than average due to the developing strong El NiÃ±o in the Pacific Ocean.
Eight to 14 named storms are forecast, three to six of which would become hurricanes, including one to three major hurricanes.
So far it seems this quiet forecast has come to pass.
Isaias is the ninth tropical storm of the Atlantic season, but will be the first to become a hurricane.
On 12 September the season set a new record for the latest date reached without a hurricane forming since the start of the satellite era in the 1960s. Almost another month has passed without one since then.
A major reason for this is the very strong El NiÃ±o that is continuing to intensify over the Pacific.
The heat released into the atmosphere by the very warm seas in the eastern tropical Pacific has weather impacts that ripple across the globe.
It can disrupt wind patterns above the Caribbean and the Atlantic leading to increased wind shear, meaning winds that blow at different speeds and directions at different levels in the atmosphere.
This can rip storms apart before they have time to strengthen.
However this is not the only factor that determines whether hurricanes will form. While it reduces the odds, it does not make it impossible - as Isaias proves.
Isaias has formed over the Gulf of Mexico where sea temperatures are currently 30-31C - around 2C higher than normal.
It is the warm ocean that gives hurricanes their fuel, providing energy and moisture allowing them to grow.
There is currently limited wind shear meaning the storm has chance to strengthen. However, wind shear is expected to increase dramatically in the 24 hours before Isaias makes landfall which may limit how intense it can become.
However the range of factors influencing hurricane development is complex and exact forecasts are likely to shift slightly over the coming days.

88c28cad09da.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/live-map-track-the-path-of-tropical-storm-isaias Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter LIVE MAP: Track the path of Tropical Storm Isaias Nation Oct 7, 2026 9:20 AM EDT MIAMI (AP) — Tropical Storm Isaias formed early Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters said it was expected to strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before hitting the U.S. Gulf Coast later in the week. Track the path of Tropical Storm Isaias below. Isaias was centered about 285 miles (460 kilometers) west of Progreso, Mexico, and about 580 miles (935 kilometers) southwest of the Mississippi River's mouth, according to the Miami-based National Hurricane Center. It had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (65 kph) and was moving east-northeast at 8 mph (13 kph). It was not immediately known where the storm may make landfall on the Gulf Coast. The hurricane center's initial projections said the center of Isaias could come onshore late Friday or early Saturday somewhere between eastern Louisiana and the western Florida Panhandle. People in those areas were urged to prepare for the storm. READ MORE: Where have all the Atlantic hurricanes gone? El Niño might bring record slow storm season "There is an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast," the hurricane center said. "Residents from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place." Florida Gov. 0ed177868d2c.text: Mark Zuckerberg's Biohub is partnering with Google and the federal government in its ambitious effort to use AI for generating vast quantities of biological data that can predict how cells behave. Why it matters: The ultimate goal is an AI model that lets scientists test potential experiments virtually, helping them identify the most promising ones before spending the time and money to perform them in the lab. AI is capable of understanding proteins and other pieces of biology, but modeling an entire living cell is orders of magnitude more complex — and researchers don't yet have enough of the right data to do it. Driving the news: Biohub, the Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, Meta and a collection of scientific organizations are collaborating to create and standardize data for what Biohub calls a "universal virtual cell." The big picture: The goal is to use AI to explore many more scientific questions in biology virtually, allowing scientists to reserve expensive lab work for experiments most likely to teach them something important. "If we can put more and more reasoning and intelligence into every single question that we actually ask in the lab, the value of those empirical results will be far greater," Biohub head of science Alex Rives told Axios. Much of AI's recent progress has come from combining better algorithms, more computing power and enormous amounts of data. Biology presents an additional challenge: Much of the information AI needs doesn't exist yet and has to be painstakingly measured from the physical world. "We're at the beginning of a new scientific paradigm with AI," Rives said. Yes, but: Biology is harder than many other AI domains because researchers need what Rives calls "empirical AI" — models that learn from biological evidence and can accurately predict what happens in the physical world. "The big challenge in biology is to bridge that gap between compute and the digital world and the real physical world of biology and life," Rives said. "The way to do that is through data." Such models could eventually help scientists investigate fundamental questions such as how aging and regeneration work — or medical questions such as which molecular mechanisms are responsible for Alzheimer's disease. How it works: The first phase will create a broad map of cellular biology, gathering different kinds of information about cells and how they respond to changes. Further out, Rives envisions models that could examine an individual's disease and predict its molecular causes and the best way to intervene. The intrigue: The commercial partners will have one year of exclusive access to the data they develop before it is shared publicly. Rives said the temporary advantage is intended to give companies a reason to contribute money while still ensuring the resulting data becomes an open scientific resource. "We have to have some incentive for commercial players to be a part of this, and the embargo period creates that," Rives said. "But it's a one-year embargo. So what that means is that very rapidly, data becomes available broadly to scientific efforts." Zoom in: The effort involves $1.8 billion in funding, data, computing and measurement technology. DOE plans to invest more than $500 million over five years in biological measurement, modeling and computing, while NIH is bringing datasets and other resources resulting from more than $500 million in previous federal investment. Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta are collectively investing another $300 million, while Biohub previously committed $500 million to the effort. Flashback: When Biohub announced its initial $500 million effort in April, Rives told Axios one of the biggest unanswered questions was whether cellular biology would exhibit the same kind of "scaling laws" seen elsewhere in AI — with models becoming predictably better as they are trained on increasing amounts of data. What we're watching: Rives thinks researchers won't have to wait particularly long to find out whether the bet is working. Within a year of having the first large-scale dataset, he said, researchers should be able to train models, measure their capabilities and determine which kinds of additional biological data make them better. "It's worked in every field, and it works in biology too," Rives said, pointing to AI's progress in protein biology.
