When social and affective neuroscientist Naomi Eisenberger’s dad developed dementia, she knew the popular wisdom. Caring for him could shave years off her life. But Eisenberger, of UCLA, was skeptical. Caring for her dad, who died in January, was stressful but also meaningful, she says. “It gave me a lot of joy to bring him some happiness.”
Caregiving kills as an idea first emerged in the scientific literature almost three decades ago. Distressed caregivers were 63 percent more likely to die within four years than non-caregivers, psychiatrists Richard Schulz and Scott Beach reported in 1999 in the Journal of the American Medical Association. The finding has since been cited almost 5,300 times, including almost 300 times in the past two years.
But researchers have largely failed to replicate that finding, with considerable research showing instead that caregiving links with living longer, Eisenberger and colleagues report in September in Biopsychosocial Science and Medicine. Caregiving stress may be softened by humans’ hardwired propensity to help others in need, the researchers suspect.
Silence surrounding caregiving’s positives is probably well-intentioned. In 2025, almost one-quarter of all adults in the United States, some 63 million people, provided care to adults or children with a medical condition or disability, according to a 2025 report by AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Almost 65 percent of caregivers surveyed reported experiencing moderate or high emotional stress and almost half reported financial difficulties. Yet financial and emotional support for caregivers remains limited, the report notes.
Highlighting caregiving’s pros could jeopardize what little help is available, says sociologist and gerontologist Rebecca Utz of the University of Utah in Salt Lake City. “I don’t like to take our foot off the pedal and say that caregiving is so positive because it’s hard, and people need support.”
But painting caregiving as wholly negative, rather than nuanced, erases insight into how caregiving might also protect health, Eisenberger and colleagues argue. Most stressors, such as work-related burnout, link with chronic inflammation. Caregiving is less likely to show that link. Understanding that caregiving paradox could reveal how the body can withstand stress, Eisenberger says.
Moreover, helping a loved one may bring unexpected benefits, Eisenberger says. She cites a 2003 study in The Gerontologist showing that adult children who did not care for a parent with severe disabilities experienced more depression than those who did, though the researchers could not show causation. “I’m not suggesting everyone go out and engage in informal caregiving,” Eisenberger says. “I’m trying to make informal caregiving [feel] a little less scary.”
Caregiving was labeled as life-threatening
In highlighting the need for researchers to take caregiver well-being seriously, the 1999 study was groundbreaking, Eisenberger and colleagues write. But it had design flaws.
Schulz and Beach, both of the University of Pittsburgh, compared mortality rates across a four-year period from over 800 individuals. Roughly half the participants had disabled spouses, with some serving as caregivers and others not; the other half had nondisabled spouses and served as the control. Caregiving spouses filled out self-reports indicating their degree of mental strain.
Over the next four years, 103 participants died. Schulz and Beach zoomed in on mortality rates among one subgroup — spousal caregivers reporting considerable strain. Of those distressed caregivers, 17 percent died during the study period compared with 9 percent of control group members.
But buried in the data was another finding, Eisenberger and colleagues note: Individuals not providing care to their disabled spouses still died at the same rate as caregivers experiencing distress. Individuals with sick and healthy spouses occupy different realities, largely invalidating comparisons between those groups, Eisenberger says. In this case, the findings suggest that having a sick or disabled spouse, and not caregiving status, increases one’s likelihood of dying.
A nuanced picture
More than 6,000 caregivers were asked to evaluate both the sense of purpose and emotional stress associated with caregiving. Their answers illustrate the role’s emotional duality.
The team is not the first to dispute the idea that caregiving kills. That list includes Schulz himself, who coauthored a 2009 Psychological Science study titled, “Caregiving behavior is associated with decreased mortality risk.” (Neither Schulz nor Beach could be reached for comment.) That study, though, has been cited less than 400 times, with just a couple dozen citations in the past two years.
“I … assumed that the field would have taken notice,” says evolutionary and social psychologist Stephanie Brown, an author on the 2009 paper and a similar 2014 review of caregiving in Social Issues and Policy Review. But “slam pieces on caregiving” remain on prominent display in doctor’s offices and other medical settings, says Brown, of the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University in New York.
Caregivers are stressed. Biology may help compensate
More recent research hints at why caregiving, a tremendously stressful undertaking, may not kill.
It’s increasingly accepted that stress can trigger systemic inflammation that then compromises the immune system. In theory, stressed caregivers should be inflamed. They’re not, researchers reported in 2020 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. That study relied on data from more than 30,000 U.S. adults. In surveys taken in the early 2000s and the 2010s, participants indicated their caregiver status, type and intensity of care being given, and experiences of strain. They also provided blood samples.

Ethiopiaâs prime minister reignited the issue of sea access for his landlocked country, potentially further inflaming regional tensions amid renewed fighting in its northern Tigray region. After being sworn in for a second full term, Abiy Ahmed told parliament his government would work diligently to ensure Ethiopia had âan outlet to the sea.â
Abiy, who has described this as an existential issue for his country, was not specific but neighboring Eritreaâs Red Sea port of Assab has long been seen by some in the government as a possible prize. It was part of Ethiopia until Eritrea seceded in the 1990s, leaving Ethiopia without a coastline.
In a statement prior to Abiyâs remarks, Eritrea, along with Egypt, Somalia, and Sudan, said control of the Red Sea was the âexclusive responsibilityâ of countries that border it. The tensions over maritime access come with Ethiopia locked in a domestic conflict, as well: An alliance of rebel groups have pledged to overthrow the government four years after the end of a civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people died.

Ten people who came into contact with a man who died of Ebola in Kenya have been quarantined, health officials in the East African nation say.
They are also trying to trace 57 other contacts of the Kenyan patient after he travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, dying in hospital in Nairobi on Monday.
This is the East African nation's first-ever Ebola case and there is now growing concern about the country's screening measures.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention chief has told the BBC that despite being sick for a month, the patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, driving to Uganda and eventually flying to Kenya without his sickness being detected.
"We know that he left Buta, a city in [northern] DR Congo, to drive to Kisangani. And from Kisangani, he took a flight to Beni. From Beni, he drove to Uganda. And from Uganda, he took a flight to Nairobi," Jean Kaseya told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.
"What are symptoms he was presenting? Why was he not detected?" he asked.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kaseya said the Africa CDC was investigating the case, alongside the Congolese authorities. A team from the organisation was also due to meet the Kenyan health authorities.
Kenya's health ministry official Patrick Amoth said the patient might have passed screening after taking medications that masked his symptoms.
After arriving at the airport in Kenya's capital, he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city where he died, and was buried on Tuesday in line with health safety guidelines.
Kenyan authorities have urged people not to panic, with the health ministry assuring of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
But Dr Dennis Miskellah, a representative from Kenya's main doctors' union, said the Ebola case did not come as a surprise to him and most health workers.
He told the BBC's Newsday programme that he had witnessed "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenyan's main airport.
"How could you have been sick for almost a month plus in DR Congo, come all the way to the country through not just any small border point, but the main entry point, the main gateway into the country and pass unnoticed?
"That's the question that most Kenyans are asking."
The health ministry says it has intensified measures to contain the spread, with a joint response involving county administrations, humanitarian partners and others.
President William Ruto has said that surveillance and rapid response teams are on the ground, building on the systems that the country adopted following the outbreak in DR Congo in May.
His spokesman said Kenya had the capacity to detect, isolate and manage suspected cases, adding that so far more than 650,000 travellers had been screened and 267 samples tested.
Facilities in four main hospitals have been designated for the management of Ebola patients, including at the Nairobi Hospital, where the first Ebola patient died.
In June, a US plan to establish an Ebola treatment facility at a military base in the central Kenyan town of Nanyuki sparked concern, with Kenyans reacting furiously about the risks of cross-border infection. The plan was halted by the courts.
On Wednesday, Health Minister Aden Duale told local television station NTV that pending the outcome of the court case, the government was considering turning the facility into the "first" infectious disease hospital in the region, to deal with outbreaks like Ebola.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.
However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
On Tuesday, Uganda's health ministry emphasised that the country remained free of Ebola and was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
It said the Kenyan Ebola patient had transited through the country for less than 24 hours and screening teams had "observed he had a normal temperature at the time of departure".
According to Africa CDC chief, his organisation was working with all the countries in the region to reinforce response mechanisms.
Kasiye said Kenya was "well prepared" and was therefore able to immediately receive the case, "but it is not the case for all other countries".
"It means the regional approach is more important today to stop this outbreak."
However, Kasiye said there was no quick testing available at border points and the taking of temperatures was unreliable as medication is able to stop a fever.
"I have to make it clear - we don't have diagnostics to test for Ebola. It's just about temperature," he said.
Dr Miskellah, from the Kenyan doctors' union, said he was concerned that governments were counting on the "honesty and full co-operation of the travellers to self-declare, to say the truth" about their health.
This was however undermined by a lack of proper health education to destigmatise the virus, meaning people often wanted to hide their symptoms, he said.

South Africa is facing growing pressure from labor unions and business groups to provide around $600 million in fuel relief, after the Iran war drove petrol prices to record highs in the continentâs biggest economy.
The calls heap pressure on the coalition government to loosen its purse strings, threatening to undermine its reputation for fiscal discipline just as Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana prepares to present his three-year fiscal plan later this month.
South Africaâs biggest labor federation, Cosatu, described the price shock, which sent a liter of fuel above 30 rand (almost $2) for the first time, as âa cost of living crisisâ because workers spend nearly a third of their wages on transport.
In response, the central bank has raised its main interest rate twice this year and warned in its monetary policy review this week that it has adopted a âfirefightingâ stance before energy prices spill over into broader inflation. The raised borrowing costs apply a secondary squeeze on households and businesses demanding fiscal relief.

Chinaâs competitor to the dollar-denominated system that zips money between global banks saw record daily volume in August. A spike last spring, as the Iran war sent sanctioned companies looking for a way around Washington, now looks less like a blip and more like a permanent, if small, leg-up for Beijingâs efforts to build a parallel system of financial plumbing.
This isnât the death of the dollar. New data from Atlantic Council researchers Jessie Yin and Lize de Kruijf shared first with Semafor, shows the greenback still underpins most global trade and foreign-exchange transactions. (Try converting Turkish lira to Indian rupees without going through the greenback.)
âThe top line numbers all remain stable,â said Josh Lipsky, the Atlantic Councilâs chair of international economics. âBut look underneath the hood and thereâs some worrying signs.â
Chinaâs efforts to dethrone the dollar have so far mostly been a curiosity. Renminbiâs place in global central-bank reserve coffers has actually fallen since 2022, despite Beijing shoveling its currency into developing economies through central-bank swap lines. But crises can reset the board: The number of direct participants in Beijingâs cross-border interbank payment system has more than doubled since Russiaâs invasion of Ukraine, and the resulting weaponization of Western financial networks to freeze Russian assets.

Lizâs view
The bull market of the early 2010s was called the most hated rally in history. This one may be a close second.
Back then, investors underestimated the power and determination of the Federal Reserve to prop up a flagging economy. Flatlining corporate earnings, European debt bombs, and runaway government spending disappeared into a sea of free money.
Todayâs problem is hyperscalers spending themselves into oblivion, spreading inflation well beyond Silicon Valley and obscuring problems nearly everywhere else. The S&P 500 hit another record yesterday, even as oil stays trapped in the Gulf and Europe tilts toward another debt crisis. The rally is driven by just a handful of AI companies. Some of them have the earnings to back it up â Goldman Sachs expects Nvidia and Micron alone to account for a third of the S&P 500âs earnings growth in the current quarter â but the return on their investments is far from certain, and far from now.
Alan Greenspanâs declaration that the Fed canât deflate a bubble without wrecking the economy is far from economic canon, but itâs holding up in the AI era. Mark Zuckerberg and Satya Nadella arenât slaphappy consumers who can be sobered up by higher rates. They are self-styled great men of history in an existential race and wonât stop spending until their shareholders make them. Their shareholders are very happy. You see the problem.

One thing was clear on Skydanceâs first day of life: Beneath David Ellisonâs velvet glove is Ynon Kreizâs iron fist. To earn his $40-odd million payout to help run the combined Paramount-Warner Bros., Kreiz will have to serve as a Tom Wambsgans-ian pain sponge â the executor and cost-cutter behind Ellisonâs lofty vision boards.
After Ellison told Skydanceâs assembled employees at a town-hall meeting Tuesday that âthere is something magical aboutâ movie-making, Kreiz stated plainly âultimately, our success will be determined by performance,â according to prepared remarks viewed by Semafor. Thereâs only so far Hollywood and Washington connections can take Ellison before the reality of managing a debt-laden media giant forces him to prove he can actually run one.

Scott Bessent isnât worried. The market is. The US Treasury secretary has been trying to reassure investors that economic growth and budget restraint can put the US governmentâs financial house in order. But heâs 0-for-3 on his 3-3-3 plan of increasing oil production, growing the economy, and cutting the deficit. His bond buyback program landed as a curious half-step â big enough to suggest concern but too small to make a difference. Tempers are flaring, WSJ reports.
Cracks are showing in the riskiest corners of the credit markets, always the first to surface confidence gaps. Take the loan market, where the amount of deeply distressed loans (those made to low-rated companies trading at 60 cents on the dollar or less) has ballooned to a level not seen since March 2020, as JPMorgan strategists pointed out this week. The biggest concentration of these highly distressed loans, of course, is in the technology sector, where SaaSpocalypse fears have eased among stock investors but not sandbag-packing credit investors. Rising global bond yields and Fed tightening havenât helped. If Bessent âis the house now,â investors are calling his bluff.

Elon Muskâs SpaceX is the in-betweener in the AI capex wars. SpaceXâs reported $40 billion debt raise to buy Nvidia chips shows it is stuck between mature tech giants like Google and Meta and startups like OpenAI and Anthropic, whose private status tends to forgive their inability to pay their own bills.
SpaceX carries five times more debt than Alphabet, and three times more debt than Meta, relative to their respective profits, and while money from Starlink helps prop up SpaceXâs cash-guzzling rocket business, it isnât nearly the cash cow that rivalsâ ad businesses are. It needs to borrow because itâs spending more on AI than itâs taking in from the rest of its businesses.
By going public in June, SpaceX locked itself out of the raise-and-pray venture capital world. But its stock priceâs sideways lurch since then makes it unattractive to issue new shares to pay for its growing AI tab. Its BBB credit rating is two notches below Meta and Alphabet, and a tougher sell with blue-chip bond funds; enter Apollo, which has a pot of money to match seemingly every risk out there (including cash-strapped governments!). Oracle finds itself in a similar position.

ed08d38e674d.text: By — Kimberlee Kruesi, Associated Press Kimberlee Kruesi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/what-happened-in-the-first-maine-senate-debate-between-collins-and-jackson Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What happened in the first Maine Senate debate between Collins and Jackson Politics Oct 7, 2026 10:13 AM EDT Republican Sen. Susan Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump during her first Maine Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, arguing she has maintained her political independence by repeatedly voting against Trump's agenda and saying that she's "not exactly his favorite senator." Democrats are trying to flip the Maine Senate seat as they work to win control of the Senate. Trump lost the state in 2024, giving Democrats hope of defeating the five-term moderate Republican, who has been targeted by Democrats in previous elections and survived. READ MORE: Troy Jackson is racing against time in his bid to unseat Susan Collins During the hourlong debate, Jackson focused largely on attempting to connect Collins to Trump. He kicked off the night by pointing out she cast a critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump nominee who eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion. Collins supports abortion rights and said Kavanaugh assured her it was settled law, but she has said recently that she does not regret her vote to confirm him. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?" asked Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger. He also repeatedly brought up her procedural vote to advance the president's 2025 tax and spending bill — though Collins ultimately broke with her party to vote against it. READ MORE: Maine Dems hammer Collins over report of pay-to-play probe. GOP senator calls it 'completely false' Collins countered that she has voted against Trump more than she did Joe Biden when the Democrat was president, and has pushed back against Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement and the war in Iran. "I voted against my party more than another other senator on either side of the aisle," Collins said. The attention on Trump comes as only 31% of U.S. adults approved of how the Republican is handling the presidency, according to a September AP-NORC poll. That's well below where his approval stood when he took office last year. The president has started holding rallies around the country in an effort to help GOP candidates win in November, telling voters to pretend he is on the ballot. At Tuesday's debate, a moderator noted Trump has floated the idea of campaigning in Maine, and asked Collins if she would stand beside him if he does. "I'm not exactly his favorite senator," she said, adding "I would say that he's not coming to Maine." Collins, who has said she didn't vote for Trump in 2016, voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president's ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they "should never be elected to office again." Collins argued that her seniority and experience in the Senate have resulted in money and resources for Maine, saying: "Leadership matters in Washington." WATCH: Gov. Wes Moore, GOP challenger Dan Cox face off in Maryland governor's debate She also spent Tuesday evening attempting to turn the focus of Maine's high cost of energy and housing on Jackson, arguing that he had a larger role in making a difference when he was the state Senate president and criticizing "Augusta's failed policies" as a way to connect Jackson's to the state's struggle to address affordability. Other moments showed how the two candidates were approaching their appeal to working class Maine voters. For example, as Collins touted her ability to remove certain items from Trump's trade war with Canada, including pulp, concrete and road salt. Jackson pushed back by quipping "we can't eat road salt." Jackson and Collins are scheduled to participate in three more debates later this month. Almost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest.
Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade.
According to the study, there were 63% fewer occuplied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011.
The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered.
Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet.
Zavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory.
In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain.
BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork".
A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds.
This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%.
Where did all the penguins go?
The researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change.
Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable.
"With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards.
"Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said.
Hungry whales and active volcanoes
The team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia.
Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater.
Dr Ratcliffe told BBC News: "When you add all the penguin guano on top of that, and you really do have one of the smelliest places in the world.
"It's like a penguin Mordor."
Mount Curry's last major eruption was back in 2016, but the penguin declines that this study analysed have been steady and ongoing since 2011, suggesting that something else was happening.
Another concern was competition for the krill that chinstrap penguins rely on - possibly from migrating humpback whales. But, while the humpbacks eat huge quantities of krill, they also help boost krill production by fertilising marine plants that the krill feed on (with their huge quantities of whale poo).
Researchers say a more fundamental, climate-driven shift in ocean food supplies is to blame.
There is an unexpected element of this story that also adds to the picture of how - and why - this region is changing: While the chinstrap population has been declining, the number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically.
Macaroni penguins, scientists say, are more adaptable, because they have a broader, more flexible diet.
Tracking data from the study showed that the macaronis foraged in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where scientists say they were were likely to be supplementing their diets with fish and other crustaceans.
Dr Ratcliffe said this shift was "biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica".
"Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," he added.
"It is further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems."
As for the title of world's largest penguin colony, scientists say that is now held by a site more than 5,000km away - on the other side of the Antarctic continent - Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
The research is published in the journal Current Biology, external.

The Scoop
Every Thursday afternoon, a cadre of state AFL-CIO leaders meets on Zoom to advance a shared project: the âContract with Working Americans,â a populist economic platform they devised independently of the national AFL-CIO.
These calls are a new organizing tactic for labor, which historically leads top down from Washington, and the goal is new, too: to mobilize not only workers who belong to unions, but the many more American workers who do not.
âWeâre trying to connect two segments of a group that, quite frankly, should be naturally aligned, but just havenât,â said Derrick Osobase, vice president of Communications Workers of America District 6, which covers Texas. âWe are actively talking to working-class people who are not affiliated with the union, and wrapping them into an agenda that they have said will make their lives different.â
The idea for the âcontractâ was born of a paradox: Union membership has declined from 20% of all workers in 1983 to 10% last year, even as union popularity hovers at 90-year highs. Seventy-one percent of US adults approve of unions, according to Gallup, including 52% of Republicans.
The widening gap between those figures is where organizers see an opportunity.
âFor years the labor movement, for understandable reasons, has fought for a narrower set of issues,â said Francis Eanes, executive director of the Maine Labor Climate Council. âBut I think itâs made it easy for some folks to say weâre just another special interest out there fighting for our own.â
Skeptics of labor, he said, say a union is âa private welfare state that provides benefits to its members and no one else. I think itâs an unfair characterization, but itâs not entirely unfair.â
The Gallup numbers suggest Americans of different political shades seem to be concluding that private welfare states arenât such a bad idea.
In a moment of declining trust in Congress, political parties, the media and many other institutions, labor activists believe a union-led movement whose stated aim is to agitate for the benefit of all workers could have real juice in setting a new national agenda as audacious as Newt Gingrichâs 1994 âContract with America,â which helped produce a sweeping congressional majority for Republicans that year.
âBoth political parties are wildly unpopular. Unions are more popular than ever,â said Matt Schlobohm, executive director of the Maine AFL-CIO. âIt is really important that we â working people, the labor movement â define and put out an agenda and demand it. Or somebody else will define it for us, and itâll be culture wars, or itâll be some mealy-mouth opportunity agenda.â

Earthquakes frequently trigger rock falls. Now there’s solid evidence marsquakes can send boulders tumbling, too.
Scientists mined high-resolution imagery of the Red Planet taken shortly after a recent temblor and found hundreds of new imprints left by tumbling boulders, researchers report September 2 in npj Space Exploration. Such rockfalls can be used as a proxy for seismic data, which is difficult to collect across the solar system.
The data were collected with NASA’s InSight lander, which touched down on Mars in 2018. Over the next four years, its seismometer detected more than a thousand marsquakes. Many of those temblors originated in a region known as Cerberus Fossae, just north of the Martian equator. That’s a dynamic landscape riddled with slopes, cracks and rocks on the move, says Vijayan, a planetary scientist at the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad, India, who goes by a single name. “Thousands and thousands of boulders have fallen.”
Vijayan and his collaborators focused on one well-detected marsquake captured by InSight that occurred in July 2019 just a few tens of kilometers from Cerberus Fossae. By comparing images taken in June 2019 and December 2020, the researchers discovered 27 new linelike features. Each was composed of tens to hundreds of distinct marks. These structures were most likely tracks created by boulders bouncing downhill, the team concluded.
Using historical imagery, the researchers calculated that only about two such features form each year on average in Cerberus Fossae. “We have statistics of previous boulder falls,” says Bivas Das, a seismologist at the Physical Research Laboratory and a member of the research team. Recording 27 new structures over a span of just 18 months is wholly unexpected, Das says. “That’s a big increase.” The nearby marsquake recorded by InSight was probably the instigator, the team concluded.
Mysteries remain, however. All of the rockfalls occurred on the north side of a prominent valley in Cerberus Fossae, despite more boulders being located on the south side of the valley. “That puzzles us,” Vijayan says. The complex landscape of Cerberus Fossae might well alter how seismic waves travel, making it difficult to predict how shaking will impact different areas, he says. “The wave propagation is going to be complicated.”
Looking for such boulder falls elsewhere could help space exploration efforts, the team suggests. Human settlements would do best avoiding areas that are seismically active, and tumbling boulders can be the proverbial canaries in the coal mine, Vijayan says. “They’re like a proxy in the absence of seismic data.”

While the case has raised global concerns, Russian state TV and other national state-controlled media have steered clear of the subject. Some state-sponsored news outlets withdrew earlier reports about the case, which has topped independent online news outlets. READ MORE: What to know about a Russian lab worker's death and speculation about pneumonic plague Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Sunday the lab worker was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology," meaning its origin was not known. In its official, tersely worded statements, it does not link the case to pneumonic plague, saying only that "extensive" testing found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported she died Oct. 2 in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk. Officials have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring the contacts of the worker, who died of what unconfirmed media reports said could have been pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person. READ MORE: How Russia and the world are responding to a possible case of pneumonic plague after lab worker death Moscow informed the World Health Organization that no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region in southeastern Siberia. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would speak about the issue "very soon" with Russian President Vladimir Putin and report about it "probably tomorrow." Wednesday is the Kremlin leader's 74th birthday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that a Putin-Trump call hasn't been set yet but could be organized quickly. Trump said the U.S. stands ready to help Russia. Asked what the U.S. intelligence community was saying about the case, Trump said the U.S. is in "very deep discussions" on the topic. The WHO prods Russia for more information In response to the WHO's request to clarify the situation in view of media reports alleging pneumonic plague as the cause of the lab worker's death, Russia has declared that no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk oblast, the U.N. organization said. Russian health authorities reported a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing of the dead woman's contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests, WHO said Wednesday. The Russian note relayed to The Associated Press by the WHO said the test showed "no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts." WATCH: Understanding pneumonic plague after Russian lab worker's death The Geneva-based organization said it has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. The organization said it has remained in contact with Russian health authorities and offered technical support. The Kremlin and other officials stay tight-lipped Peskov has referred all questions to Rospotrebnadzor, which does not mention suspected plague in its reports. In its latest statement Tuesday, the agency said "the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is calm." It said authorities were completing a "complex of prophylactic measures and medical observation over contacts," adding that so far they have found two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus. "No other infectious pathogens have been found among contacts," it said. The lab worker who died was described as highly diligent The news outlet Lyudi Baikala — or "People of Baikal" — identified the dead lab worker as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova and said she first was hospitalized with cold symptoms Sept. 29 and died three days later. It quoted her colleagues as saying she was a highly qualified and diligent researcher. They also emphasized that security rules at the facility, established in the 1920s to monitor and study the plague that is endemic to southeastern Siberia, are extremely strict. The report quoted Shipilova's neighbors as saying a team of disinfection experts did several cleanups of her apartment, leaving a strong antiseptic smell. The hospital where she died was under quarantine, no longer admitting or discharging patients, although its outpatient clinic has continued operating, according to Mayor Maxim Modin. Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said she died of a "particularly dangerous infection" and everyone who came into contact with her has remained under medical supervision. The incubation period for pneumonic plague — the disease's most virulent form — can be as short as 24 hours, according to the WHO. The lung-based illness is a less common but severe form of plague that can spread between people via respiratory particles. Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible.
It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded.
On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach".
Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to healthcare.
A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness.
Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned.
Fraser said the government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely.
That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so. Advanced requests are not currently legal.
"These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said.
Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases.
Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent. In Canada, that mechanism is known as "track two" Maid.
The expansion has been the subject of controversy, with disability advocacy groups reporting cases where assisted dying was offered to people with disabilities without a patient requesting it themselves.
Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery.

Nearly every poster, stump speech or televised debate seems to reference the attack, which has scarred the country and remains fresh in the minds of voters. Three years on, the worst security failure in Israel's history now threatens to end the career of its longest-serving prime minister. WATCH: Brett McGurk chronicles negotiations to free Oct. 7 hostages in 'Brink' "October 7 is kind of a framework for the entire political discussion that is going on," said Tamar Hermann, an expert on Israeli public opinion at the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem think tank. Netanyahu's opponents want him to pay for the failures that led to the deadliest day in Israel's 78-year history and plunged the country into a series of inconclusive wars. His defenders say Netanyahu was betrayed by the military establishment and that he has led Israel through a dramatic rebound from its darkest hour. WATCH: Netanyahu faces pressure after report alleges he brushed off warnings ahead of Oct. 7 A loss in the Oct. 27 election would likely end the career of the soon-to-be 77-year-old Netanyahu. A victory would mark the greatest turnaround yet for a man who has defied naysayers for three decades. A deadly day that has shaken an entire region On the morning of Oct. 7, Hamas militants fired several thousand rockets into Israel and thousands of militants attacked through holes blown in the border fence or with boats or motorized paragliders. Some 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage. WATCH: Netanyahu government defies court, raising constitutional crisis fears as election nears Israel responded with a military offensive that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, according to local health authorities, left the territory in ruins and sparked an ongoing humanitarian catastrophe. Israel later went to war against Hezbollah militants in Lebanon, seized a chunk of Syria, attacked targets in Yemen and joined the U.S. in two wars against Iran. Hundreds of Israelis, mostly young soldiers, have died, and nearly every household has been touched by the violence. Netanyahu promised "total victory," but Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran's theocratic government all remain intact. A visual installation depicting bodies, on the third anniversary of the deadly Oct. 7 attack at a beach in Tel Aviv. Photo by Aviv Atlas/via Reuters Israel's international standing has plummeted, a number of foreign governments have accused it of genocide — a charge it vehemently rejects — and Netanyahu is now wanted by the International Criminal Court. After a string of resignations by top security officials, Netanyahu is the only senior figure from Oct. 7 still in office, making this month's election in many ways a referendum on his leadership. It's the focus of the campaign for both sides Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attends a state memorial ceremony for the three-year anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attack, in remembrance of Israel Defense Forces and security members in Jerusalem, on Oct. 5, 2026. Photo by Debbie Hill/ Pool via Reuters Netanyahu and his opponents have put Oct. 7 at the forefront of their campaigns — for different reasons. His opponents — from across the political spectrum — call his outgoing coalition "the massacre government." Netanyahu says he has led a "war of redemption." READ MORE: Pilot stabbing further unsettles region shaken by U.S.-Iran war His chief rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief whose son and nephew were killed in battle in Gaza. The opponents have pledged to form a government of "repair and reconstruction" — beginning with the formation of an official commission of inquiry into Oct. 7. They also have vowed to end draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox religious men, a long-standing policy that has outraged the secular majority at a time of war, and accuse Netanyahu of threatening Israel's democratic institutions. "The most fateful elections in the history of the State of Israel are between evasion and enlistment," Eisenkot wrote on X. "Between taking responsibility and fleeing from responsibility." Netanyahu has repeatedly rejected calls for a commission of inquiry while trying to shift the blame to security officials. He recently accused the then-head of the Shin Bet security service, Ronen Bar, of withholding information ahead of the attack. Bar has vowed to file a defamation lawsuit. Netanyahu has meanwhile denied reports in American media outlets that the United Arab Emirates and Egypt warned him ahead of Oct. 7. He insists the country is stronger than ever. "Our enemies expected us to collapse," Netanyahu said in a recent address to the United Nations. "Well, we didn't collapse. Instead, we rose and fought like lions." Sir David Attenborough has promised to "venture even further" and uncover marine life that is "more precious than we ever realised" in Blue Planet III.
The broadcaster, who turned 100 earlier this year, narrates the new six-part series exploring the darkest depths of the world's oceans, produced by the BBC Natural History Unit in Bristol.
After almost four years of filming, the latest instalment in the franchise will air on the BBC later this autumn, marking 25 years since the first series premiered.
At a launch event on Tuesday, Sir David said: "When I narrated the first Blue Planet series, it didn't occur to me that I would be narrating a third series in my centennial year."
More from Bristol
The production uses advanced equipment including remote underwater cameras, drones, and manned submersibles to capture newly discovered animal behaviours.
Viewers are taken into some of the world's least understood marine environments, ranging from coral reefs and tropical islands to the darkest depths of the ocean.
In the newly released extended trailer, Attenborough promised to "venture even further" than ever before, describing the ocean as "an endlessly fascinating place".
"We will uncover life that is more surprising, more intelligent, and even more precious than we ever realised," he said.
"We will discover the extraordinary relationship we have with the ocean. One that has never been more important to understand."
Sir David said he was "proud and delighted" to be associated with the project.
The new series is accompanied by an original score from Hans Zimmer and Bleeding Fingers Music.
Zimmer, who also scored Blue Planet II, said the series was the "most important work" he has ever done.
"I think everybody who comes to Blue Planet comes to it with the knowledge that it is something that changes the world by making you fall in love," he said.
"It's not something where you're being lectured or cajoled about things, but it's something that just shows you how spectacular and beautiful our world truly is.
"How we need to preserve it and how we need to love it, and how whatever we love, we need to treat with great kindness and great respect."
It also features an original song, Into The Deep (Seas Cry) co-written by Jade Thirlwall - best known for being a member of the pop group Little Mix.
Thirlwall described herself as a "huge fan" of the franchise, praising Attenborough as "a true hero".
"Being part of Blue Planet III in this way feels incredibly special and a real privilege," she added.
The premiere launch event took place at Piccadilly Circus in London on Tuesday, with footage from the new series taking over the digital displays.

As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.
It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.
The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure.
"I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.
The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.
Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.
And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies.
"Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.
Aside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew.
For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack.
Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza.
"There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored? We need to find out what happened â not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that."
"The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again."
Over the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours â which he denies.
Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation.
Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper.
Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people.
Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop".
Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation.
"God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network.
"What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks.
Yaacov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault.
In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border.
He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters.
"So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference."
But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening.
"You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state."
For years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of aid for Gaza.
A month after the 7 October attacks, he told a German newspaper that claims he wanted to strengthen Hamas were "an absolute lie".
"On the contrary we wanted to continue to weaken Hamas as much as we could," he told Die Welt. "But the money was meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe - that is the only reason."
Months after the attack, the IDF's then-chief of staff, Lt Gen Herzi Halevi, publicly apologised for the failure to defend civilians, saying he carried that weight on his shoulders and in his heart.
He resigned. A raft of military commanders were later fired, and Israel's domestic intelligence chief left his position.

ab80b50c6ce5.text: The good news about the epic shifts in global bond markets is that they mostly reflect economic fundamentals, not the kinds of panicky swings seen in a crisis. The bad news is that there's a risk the disruptions metastasize into a broader crisis in an era of fractured politics across major democracies. The big picture: Turmoil in the streets this week in France is the latest sign of hazards that await elected leaders who try to address yawning fiscal deficits head-on. They are squeezed between voters who want to maintain public benefit levels and tax levels and a bond market that is resetting long-term interest rates higher — meaning that carrying on with wide deficits will come at a greater and greater cost to service debt. That's why even what has been a relatively orderly repricing so far carries risks that are bigger than just high mortgage or corporate borrowing rates. Driving the news: The relentless upward march of bond yields continued Wednesday morning. The French 10-year yield soared 0.18 percentage point, to 4.93%. French yields are also surging relative to other countries that use the euro, especially Germany — the kind of fragmentation seen in the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s that originated in Greece . But France is not alone. U.K. 10-year yields are up 0.12 point, to 5.49%, while the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is up 0.08 point Wednesday morning, reaching 5.36%, the highest since 2002. Reality check: These are massive moves in markets that form the bedrock of global financial markets. And yet they don't appear to be driven by the kind of crisis dynamics and forced selling that fueled bond market volatility in the 2008 crisis, the 2014 Treasury flash crash and the March 2020 pandemic. Rather, they've been driven by bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and deficit-running sovereign governments, exacerbated by surging energy prices that increase inflation risk. What they're saying: "When you look at outright yield levels and/or spreads, a lot of this is still quite rational, and within the realm of what fair valuation should be, just given where nominal growth is and where we are in the cycle," Kunal Shah, the co-CEO of Goldman Sachs International, tells Axios. "At this point, I still wouldn't say that we're anywhere close to the point of this being a broad financial stability risk or issue," says Shah, who is also co-head of fixed income, currency and commodities. "What policymakers in Europe have shown us, though, is that when there's broader issues on contagion and/or disorderly functioning markets, that's when they can be quick to respond." "Whilst the move in spreads has been very quick and sharp, in the broader context, we're still nowhere close to where we had got to in that previous European crisis," he says. "Financial conditions are tightening, but it's still not, I'd say, flashing red to the point that you need a backstop from the policymakers." Yes, but: The European Central Bank has more powerful tools than it did in 2010 to address imbalances between European countries, and has shown willingness to use them. But it can't do much about the fundamentals of governments spending consistently far more than they raise in taxes. And the global nature of the yield surge shows the common fiscal challenge across major economies. State of play: In France, there have been violent clashes with police as teachers and students protest proposed wage freezes and school funding cuts. In the U.K., a central political dispute is over the future of the "triple lock" pension adjustment mechanism, which all but guarantees pension costs will grow faster than the overall economy. The U.S. Social Security trust fund is on track to be exhausted in 2032 . The rate adjustment of the last several weeks will increase already-onerous debt service costs for all advanced countries. Of note: Those forces can create destabilizing effects for business even apart from the impact on rates. Shah, for example, says that U.K. governments lurching from budget to budget has made it hard for businesses making long-term decisions. "I hope that at some point we'll be able to break out of this cycle, because it does stifle confidence and it just makes planning for the long term very hard," Shah says.

Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (Â£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.
Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy 177-year old company on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.
Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a familiar and trusted High Street presence, selling a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.
Galen Weston, chairman of Wittington, said Boots played "a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland".
Boots has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.
Its stores have also seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every week day.
It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK, leaving it with about 1,800 currently and 51,000 employees.
Its ownership status has also been uncertain, with several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed over the last two decades.
But Weston, who will become chairman of Boots, signalled the new owners had fresh plans for the chain, including shop upgrades and an expansion of healthcare services.
"We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come," he said.
Boots was established by John Boot, who opened the first herbalist store in Nottingham offering an affordable alternative to traditional medicines in 1849.
The Weston family will be buying Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. It is set be completed in early 2027.
The Weston family owns the Canadian grocery chain Loblaws, pharmacy business Shoppers Drug Mart, and previously owned the London department store Selfridges from 2003 to 2021, before selling it for $4bn.
The separate UK branch of the Weston family is the majority owner of Associated British Foods, the parent firm of Primark.
The Westons were ranked fifth on this year's Sunday Times Rich List with a combined fortune of almost Â£19bn.
Wittington will have operational control over Boots, it has secured ownership in partnership with Fairfax Financial Holdings, a Toronto-based holding company.
Sycamore Partners, in partnership with Stefano Pessina and his family, will retain ownership of The Boots Group's Farmacias Benavides in Mexico and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland in Germany.

As Mainers prepare to choose a new governor in November, climate and energy issues may not be top of mind for every voter—but they are having big effects on residents’ lives.
The average cost of heating oil recently soared to a record high of more than $6 per gallon, promising an expensive winter ahead for the half of Maine households heated by oil-powered boilers and furnaces. The cost of electricity has also risen steeply, at the third-highest rate in the nation over the past 10 years.
At the same time, the effects of climate change are harming the state. Boom-and-bust rain and drought cycles are making farming more difficult. Rising temperatures are putting pressure on many plants and animals, including economically important species such as lobster. Sea level rise and worsening storms are eating away the coastline and damaging infrastructure.
All three candidates running for governor agree that energy affordability is a priority. And all acknowledge the reality of climate change. But they disagree on whether these problems can be tackled together.
Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett think energy affordability and climate action can go hand in hand. In a September interview with The Maine Monitor, Pingree said she would continue the work of the Maine Climate Council, which created a plan to meet clean energy and greenhouse gas emissions goals set by the state Legislature. Bennett said he also supports transitioning the state to clean energy.
Republican Bobby Charles said that the state government should focus squarely on affordability, and embrace both renewable energy and fossil fuels, including supporting new natural gas pipelines.
Maine is the only state, alongside Washington, D.C., that is currently ahead of pace to meet its 2030 goal of cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 45 percent, though some other states have more ambitious goals.
Much of Maine’s success so far has been thanks to the rapid uptake of heat pumps, an energy efficiency and electrification solution encouraged by rebates and embraced across party lines.
As the federal government stepped back from climate action during the first Trump administration, state governments stepped up to fill some of that gap, said Anthony Moffa, a law professor at the University of Maine who studies climate policy. Maine in particular has been a leader in that regard, he said.
The state Legislature established the Maine Climate Council in 2019, and the group created a climate action plan called “Maine Won’t Wait.” This comprehensive plan has been “a model document” for other states, according to Moffa.
Maine’s goals have ramped up over time, with the latest update in 2025 requiring the state to source 100 percent of its electricity from renewables or other low-emissions sources such as nuclear power by 2040.
The governor plays a crucial role in pushing forward this change, Moffa said. While the Legislature can set goals, the governor is the one who empowers state agencies to create policies and programs that actually implement the law.
Hannah Pingree
Much of the climate-focused work that happened during the administration of Gov. Janet Mills was led by Pingree, who was director of the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from 2019 to 2025. As part of that job, Pingree served as co-chair of the Maine Climate Council, overseeing two iterations of the state’s climate action plan.
“I would continue that work,” Pingree said. “To not do that is going to put lives at risk. It’s going to put public safety at risk and really risk the future of our economy.”
Pingree wants Maine to procure more clean energy through projects such as the Northern Maine Renewable Energy Program, which aims to develop utility-scale renewable energy projects and transmission infrastructure in Aroostook County.
Locals have raised concerns about these projects, and Pingree added that the governor should work with the Maine Department of Energy Resources, the Public Utilities Commission and the Office of the Public Advocate “to ensure that actual community voices are heard, there is public benefit and there is public savings.”
As the supply of clean energy grows, Pingree wants Maine to use less oil and gas, which largely come to the state from other countries.
“We have no energy independence,” she said, and “no control over these international prices of energy.”
That’s become apparent as first the war between Russia and Ukraine and now between the United States and Iran have disrupted the supply of natural gas and oil.
Roughly half of Maine residents’ electricity bills are for this supply side of the equation. The other half pays for transmission and distribution. To help control those costs, Pingree wants the Public Utilities Commission to oppose what she calls “excessive rate hikes” from electric utilities. She also wants to incentivize more people to weatherize their homes, reducing the amount of electricity they need to use in the first place.
Although Pingree played a pivotal role in the Mills administration’s climate policy, she disagrees with Mills on some key issues. Pingree supports Wabanaki sovereignty, which is a priority not just for the Wabanaki themselves but also for many of Maine’s environmental advocacy groups. She also supports a moratorium on large-scale data center development.
Pingree has been endorsed by the Maine Conservation Voters Action Fund.
“It is more important than ever that Maine people elect leaders who will put the protection of our environment and clean energy future at the center of their agenda, while also looking to make our energy more affordable,” said Maureen Drouin, the group’s executive director. Electing Pingree is “one of the most important things that we can do for the future we want to leave our kids,” she said.

Coco Gauff said she had a "draining" few days after receiving racist abuse online before her fourth-round China Open exit.
The American received an "insane" amount of racist comments and direct messages following an incident in her third-round win over 16-year-old Sun Xinran on Monday.
China's Sun thought she had hit a winner late in the first set, but Gauff raised her hand to halt play because of a flickering light in the side panels surrounding the court.
After a video review - which players are allowed to request - the point was replayed, with Gauff winning it and subsequently going on to clinch the match.
The 22-year-old posted a lengthy statement explaining what had happened and later condemned the racist abuse she received in response.
Gauff was beaten 6-3 6-3 in her next match against Elise Mertens on Wednesday.
Asked how she had felt over the past 36 hours, Gauff said: "It has been kind of draining, I'm not going to lie.
"I just turn off my phone and move on. I mean, there's nothing you can do."
A spokesperson for the Women's Tennis Association said it was appalled by the abuse. It said it was in contact with Gauff "to offer our full support".
A statement given to the news agency AFP said the governing body was "seeking action" against the abusive content.
Gauff, who won the title in Beijing in 2024, committed 34 unforced errors and eight double faults against Mertens.
"I was just a bit flat. That's the main thing," Gauff said.
"The level was there at some points, I just didn't sustain it the whole match."
Belgium's Mertens will play former world number one Iga Swiatek in the quarter-finals after the six-time major champion beat American teenager Iva Jovic 6-1 6-3.
Elsewhere, Britain's Arthur Fery beat Marin Cilic 7-6 (7-2) 6-1 in the Shanghai Masters first round.
Fery came back from a break down in the first set before dominating the former US Open champion in the second to claim his first ATP Tour win since August.
The 24-year-old will face Russia's 26th seed Karen Khachanov next.

Gears of War, one of the video games that helped Microsoft's Xbox to win over millions of fans, is back.
Prequel E-Day takes players back to where it all started, telling the origin story of humanity's conflict with The Locust - the series' horrifying enemy species.
The game's been well-received by critics and players, but it's also seen as a big test of Xbox's new direction.
Unlike recent flagship titles from the company's studios, which have been released on PlayStation 5 and, in some cases, Nintendo Switch, E-Day is being pushed as an Xbox exclusive.
The apparent goal is to draw players back to the brand, but critics have questioned whether that's realistic at a time when console prices are higher than ever.
BBC Newsbeat spoke to developer The Coalition - the makers of E-Day - about what staying exclusive means to them.
'Heart, blood and guts'
Gears of War has been one of Xbox's flagship series since it launched back in 2006.
Creative director Matt Searcy tells Newsbeat the sci-fi shooter is a "mix of war story with comic book-y monsters that come out of the ground".
"It's a video game with a lot of heart, a lot of blood and guts," he says.
First released on the Xbox 360, Gears helped to popularise "cover-shooter" gameplay, which encouraged players to shelter from enemy attacks.
It brought a strategic dimension to third-person action games, and also won fans with its co-operative multiplayer modes - a feature that's returned for E-Day.
But, 20 years later, Xbox finds itself in a very different position in the console space.
It's seen as a third-place competitor, behind both Sony's PlayStation and Nintendo's Switch consoles.
Previous CEO Phil Spencer had begun to take the division in a new direction, releasing some of its most popular games on rival consoles for the first time.
E-Day was widely expected to follow other high budget series such as Halo on to other companies' machines.
But new Xbox boss Asha Sharma, who took over the job in June, announced Gears of War would remain a "console exclusive", although a PC version has also been released.
Her strategy has been called into question by critics.
After taking six years to make and an estimated budget in the hundreds of millions, they argue that keeping E-Day away from other platforms could mean it's less likely to make back its development cost.
Coalition studio head Mike Crump says E-Day is a "natural choice to be an exclusive".
"Gears has been an exclusive franchise to Xbox for 20 years now. It's sort of entwined deeply with the brand," he says.
"And we're proud of that."
He says the series "carries the banner" for the console and gives people a "reason to be in the Xbox ecosystem" - something he says has been the company's mission since day one.
However, there will inevitably be discourse around E-Day's sales figures and engagement numbers.
When asked what would constitute success for the game, Crump admits the studio has financial targets and goals for the number of players it wants to reach, but insists it takes a "broader view" than that.
"We measure things like, are we showcasing the platform? Are we pushing the hardware to its limits? Are we showcasing what the Xbox is capable of?
"Our goal basically is to be the best-looking game on the Xbox and really show the industry what's possible with our hardware."
Crump also says it's important to drive players towards Game Pass, Xbox's Netflix-style subscription service.
For onlookers, it's harder to ignore the wider picture at Xbox.
The division has been carrying out mass layoffs and undergoing a wide-scale restructuring since Sharma's appointment.
In July, she told employees there would be 3,200 job losses across Xbox-owned studios over the current financial year.
Last month, the company said it was about three-quarters of the way through this plan, external.
The Coalition has mostly avoided cuts so far, although one of E-Day's narrative directors announced last month he had been let go.
Reports have suggested developers at the studio are worried they could be at risk now the game has been released, external.
When asked about this, Crump says: "What I say to myself, what I say to the team, is we just we need to focus on the things that we can control.
"For us that's about shipping a great game that people are going to love and I feel like, as a team, we've done that."
He says E-Day will provide a "great foundation" for future games in the series, and insists "the next game will not take nearly as long" to make.
Developers at other studios hit by layoffs previously told the BBC they were concerned about a loss of institutional knowledge - experienced staff who've been working on certain series for years and sometimes decades.
Crump says: "We've got a great team here.
"And the leadership team in particular has worked together for upwards of 20 years.
"So there's definitely a continuity of knowledge and experience."

âA flawless face is the fastest way for a character to read as generic AI,â a Higgsfield spokesperson told Semafor.

J.D.âs view
The race in the West to become the top open-source AI model shifted into higher gear this week, as both Nvidia-backed Reflection AI and French lab Mistral unveiled new models they hope will break Chinaâs open-source monopoly.
The challenge looming over Beam and Le Chonkâs debuts (immediately my new favorite model name) is that they lag the top Chinese models and the leading closed systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on prominent benchmarks.
But Reflection and Mistral boasted in their announcements that they do beat other open Western models, such as those from Thinking Machines and Nvidia, suggesting the companies care just as much about the race against each other as the one with Beijing â despite US and European companiesâ shifts to using more Chinese models over the past year.
Reflection CEO Misha Laskin told me his goal isnât necessarily to dismantle the foothold Chinese models have achieved among developers and large companies. Instead, he sees a market in entities that canât or wonât use Chinese models â think heavily regulated industries and governments â and might otherwise have no choice but to pay for closed American AI.
The timing of that pitch is opportune: Many businesses are heading into year-end budget reviews with eye-popping AI spend figures to account for. Governments are also bracing for sticker shock as $1-a-year pilot deals expire. New data from Ramp suggests companies are switching which AI providers they use more than ever.
The question that will determine the fate of these and other Western open-source players is whether businesses and agencies will tolerate less advanced models for some tasks in exchange for affordability and control.

Prick up your ears, and you can hear it â the sound of many different kinds of Democrats grabbing credit for midterm victories that arenât official yet.
Thereâs Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, assessing that when (not if) Abdul El-Sayed wins his Senate race in Michigan, the left will âbreak open the entire political calculus in Americaâ â i.e., that progressives like them can win the Midwest. Thereâs Pete Buttigieg, making sure we know how many states heâs campaigned in (37) and how many candidates heâd endorsed (more than 100).
At this time in any campaign cycle, groups, candidates, and strategists pepper reporters with early claims that they were right. The election, they say, will be a referendum on their issue, a validation of their spending strategy, proof that their ideas moved votes.
These takes arenât immaculate. Iâve never deleted the October 2017 email from a strategist who was ready to explain why Ralph Northam lost the election for governor of Virginia. In fact, Northam won easily, and that strategist got strategically quiet.
As preposterous as it is, though, the pre-spin cycle matters, because anyone not ready to contextualize what happened to their benefit will lose face.
It mattered in 2020, when centrist Democrats burst out to blame âdefund the policeâ activists for their party underperforming the final polls. It mattered after President Donald Trumpâs win in 2024, when Sen. Bernie Sanders instantly blamed defeat on the party having âabandoned the working class.â That quick analysis shaped the conversation.
Populism won. This is the Sanders project â progressivesâ entire project, really. The goal of recruiting swing-seat populists and getting them through primaries was to prove, as Ocasio-Cortez said, that their kind can win anywhere, which should matter for 2028.
This theory may be tough to sell. One of its proof points was supposed to be Maine, where Graham Platner humiliated the party establishment, then himself. Progressives won the insta-caucus that replaced him, nominating Troy Jackson to face GOP Sen. Susan Collins, and Sanders will campaign for Jackson this weekend after some internal grumbling about whether consultants not approved by the left were ruining his campaign.
Michiganâs the ballgame now. An El-Sayed win would, for progressives, be the story of the midterms. Most of the movementâs primary victories came in safe seats, but to take control of the 2028 story, they want to be talking about El-Sayed winning, Will Lawrence flipping back a mid-Michigan district, and Randy Villegas unseating Rep. David Valadao in California. They want to say that hand-wringing moderates were wrong, and pure populism can flip or hold swing seats.
But if El-Sayed becomes the first Democrat to lose a Michigan Senate seat this century, progressives will enter 2028 with empty hands. What to watch: MI-SEN, MI-07, CA-22

Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, is running the most critical ads about âtransgender ideologyâ of any Democratic incumbent.

Governments around the world are hardening their AI stances as more agentic hacks breach critical systems. South Koreaâs president noted âconsiderable public concern and anxietyâ following revelations that hackers used an AI system to execute recent cyberattacks against banks in the country.
And officials from OpenAI and Anthropic faced questions from lawmakers in Australia on Tuesday, after the ChatGPT maker drew criticism for not alerting Canberra fast enough after one of its models gained unauthorized access to a government health data portal during internal training and evaluation.
Tech companies are playing whack-a-mole around the world as their models get up to more hijinks and are used for malicious purposes. Insurers are also taking note, and preparing for multimillion-dollar lawsuits over rogue AI agents â and weighing whether executives could be held liable, the Financial Times reported.
