US and Chinese tech companies are taking differing approaches to bring AI agents to the masses, the industryâs latest fixation. OpenAIâs recently released dots and Metaâs Muse are built around the assistant first and then sent out to use other companiesâ websites and services.
Chinese counterparts, including Tencentâs Xiaowei âÂ which is built into super-app WeChat â can, for example, place orders from businesses that are already on the app. Itâs an obvious use for closed systems like WeChat and Alipay, which Chinese consumers already use for much of daily life.
Xiaoweiâs strategy may not translate into revenue, the Hello China Tech newsletter wrote: Tencent earns no new fees from purchases, and early tests show it making mistakes. It begs the question whether the super-app strategy limits how useful Chinese agents can become since Xiaowei can only assist with whatâs available inside WeChat, and other Chinese platforms have blocked agents from outside.
Muse and dots may not be a seamless experience either, given Muse has already been blocked by Amazon and both require users to turn over access to private systems, but their popularity already suggests markets are watching closely.

f0c7e7265c39.text: Microsoft on Wednesday unveiled a new class of Nvidia-powered Windows laptops, its latest effort to tie the operating system more closely to the AI boom. Why it matters: Microsoft is trying to carve out a high-end laptop category for people who want to run demanding AI workloads locally, rather than rely entirely on the cloud. Driving the news: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former White House AI official Sriram Krishnan were on hand in San Francisco as the company officially launched Microsoft Surface Ultra, a high-end laptop powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark chip that starts at $2,599. "We have reinvented the computer as we know it," Huang said. Microsoft previewed the laptop back in June but left out key details around price and exact availability. It said at the time that Nvidia-powered devices would also be coming from the likes of Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, among others. Those devices, and the Surface Ultra, will be available starting Oct. 16. On the software side, Microsoft unveiled a version of Copilot that can work using local models alongside those in the cloud, and the company also announced that Meta is bringing its Muse personal agent to Windows. The big picture: Microsoft's first push into AI-powered Windows machines, known as Copilot+ PCs, got off to a rocky start after the delay of Recall, its signature feature. Between the lines: Microsoft's pitch for on-device AI is that developers' appetite exceeds what their companies' AI budgets can afford, with the ideal being an approach that uses both frontier models in the cloud and local models when they can be effective. "Hybrid intelligence exists because people's appetite for intelligence is effectively unlimited," Microsoft executive VP Pavan Davuluri said. And before it even got to the hardware, Microsoft spent a fair bit of time outlining how it is making Windows more secure, ensuring that agents' actions are separated from those taken by humans and remain within preset limits.

e5ed4e0e6628.text: Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Nearly nine in 10 voters say using taxpayer money to pay for election-related ads featuring the president or Cabinet members is inappropriate, including 80% of Republicans, according to a recent Reuters-Ipsos poll . Why it matters: The administration's decision to spend millions of taxpayer dollars on Trump-fronted ads weeks before the midterms is facing an uproar and overwhelming public opposition. While the administration insisted the ads were actually PSAs, Trump later announced that a super PAC affiliated with him would foot the bill for future ads (but not reimburse the taxpayer dollars already spent). Friction point: New polling suggests the TV spots, which the White House said "are a reminder for Americans to love their country," might not get much love from voters. The poll of 4,506 adults found that just 9% of Americans find it appropriate to tap taxpayer funds for election-related television ads featuring the president or cabinet members. Zoom out: A majority of Americans also panned other actions Trump has taken: 68% say it's inappropriate to block media outlets from entering the White House, and 72% say the same about naming federal institutions and buildings after a sitting president. Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Zoom in: A White House official contended in a statement to Axios that the "PSAs are clearly not political," saying Trump "is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action." But one is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad, using the same footage and narration, with the campaign sponsorship tagline replaced with a disclaimer: "Paid for by the U.S. Government." Earlier this month, Democrats called on the Government Accountability Office and the U.S. Office of Special Counsel to investigate the use of taxpayer money to produce and air the ads. Between the lines: Axios' Alex Isenstadt scooped late last month that the ads released so far were "just the beginning" and that Trump himself — pleased with the war-room-style social media posts his digital team regularly pumps out — was hand-picking the ads himself. And it's not just the White House that's gotten in on promotional hype that blurs the lines with campaign content: The FBI's rapid response account released a video Tuesday applauding director Kash Patel — and criticizing Democrats, including Senate candidate Abdul-El Sayed. The bottom line: As an election approaches where cost-of-living concerns are paramount, Americans have strong feelings about how their taxpayer dollars are spent. Standing before the Acropolis in Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio swept through the history of ancient Greece to the rise of American industry in a speech on Wednesday that portrayed western civilisation at risk of decline.
Rubio said the world was at an "inflection point". Nations, particularly in Europe, should return to ancient Greek values and "rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together".
"We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago," he said.
While he spoke of cooperation, Rubio also said "nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognise their common interests".
Rubio, often mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2028, touched on what he considered dangers in the world, such as "radical mullahs" in Iran and suicide bombers.
But most of his speech focused on a broader threat, describing the current period as a crossroads.
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century."
Rubio called for a return to the "classical understanding of politics and statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim - reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilisation".
That appeared to include renewed national pride, which he said the ancient Greeks had embraced, but the west had abandoned as "we felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world".
"The word 'nationalism' became a dirty word," he said. "So we tore down our monuments. We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.
"In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay."
Rubio's boss, President Donald Trump, has sought to carry out an "America first" agenda during both his terms in office, and taken a more confrontational stance toward traditional allies and in longstanding trade relationships.
Just six months ago, Trump again threatened to pull the US from the Nato alliance, which he has frequently criticised while pushing members to make larger contributions to defence.
Rubio's visit to the ruins of the Acropolis in Greece was part of his three-country tour of Nato allies that includes stops in Iceland and Portugal.

7f49183c88a0.text: By — Ryan Foley, Associated Press Ryan Foley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/shock-gloves-purchased-by-ice-cause-pain-compliance-and-fear-army-study-found Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Shock gloves purchased by ICE cause pain, compliance and fear, Army study found Nation Oct 7, 2026 4:24 PM EDT The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased Army study. Immigration and Customs Enforcement leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves in August, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with The Associated Press. READ MORE: 'A perfect tool for abuse.' Why experts are concerned about ICE's $17 million electric shock gloves contract The shocks had a profound impact on Army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching gloves to their skin, and were left with "fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again," the study found. "After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE, ... participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply," the authors wrote. Watchdog says gloves cause pain and raise safety concerns ICE has called the gloves "distraction and de-escalation devices" that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance they cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force. But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. The gloves, they note, are easy to discharge, do not leave a mark and have not been extensively used in settings outside of jails. The manufacturer warns they should not be used on high-risk populations such as kids, pregnant women or disabled people. "The military assessment in ICE's own files shows that these gloves can cause 'intense pain' and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe," said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. "Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it." ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group's Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force. Army study found shock gloves triggered 'immediate' compliance The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could. The study found the devices "increased the efficiency" of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not "significantly change" the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members," the study found. "Inmate compliance was immediate" compared to other methods, it added. The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead "works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings" of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward. Senator says ICE hasn't responded to demand for details on glove use ICE's contract requires the manufacturer, Compliant Technologies LLC, to deliver the gloves within six months. Its owner, Jeff Niklaus, said he was unavailable for an interview, citing a busy workload. White House border czar Tom Homan has said it could "be awhile" before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout, but said "officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics." READ MORE: AP report: ICE plans to give its officers gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE has not responded to an Aug. 27 letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wants answers. "Without ICE's responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States Senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received," she said. Ozone pollution from fires, along with extreme heat and drought, is further weakening the Amazon rainforest’s ability to absorb carbon dioxide, new research shows.
The Amazon and other forests absorb more than a quarter of human-caused CO2 emissions each year, more than 11 billion metric tons. But in recent decades, increasingly larger areas of forests have begun releasing more CO2 than they absorb, especially during droughts and heat waves.
One study, published Monday in the journal Communications Earth & Environment, documents how smoke from wildfires, agriculture and forest-clearing burning contributes to leaf-damaging ozone formation far from the flames.
This means fires in the Amazon have a double impact on the climate. They directly release climate-warming CO2 as vegetation burns and reduce the ability of remaining trees to absorb and store CO2. The reduction is equal to about 24 percent of the carbon released by the fires.
That “hidden effect is a significant loss to the Amazon’s carbon budget that hasn’t previously been considered,” said lead author Flossie Brown, an atmospheric chemist at ETH Zürich, a university in Switzerland.
The second study, published Monday in the American Geophysical Union journal Earth’s Future, found that the extreme heat and drought that gripped the Amazon and other tropical forests in 2023 and 2024 during El Niño conditions could occur nearly every year within 20 to 30 years, cutting CO2 uptake severely and even disrupting the self-regulating forest-to-atmosphere moisture cycle.
Repeated extreme heat events can “trigger self-perpetuating rainfall losses,” warned
lead author Johanna Van Passel, an ecologist at Ghent University in Belgium. “You have this feedback loop,” she said. “If the forest is suffering, it will cause less rain to fall in other parts, and those forests will also start suffering.”
All tropical forests stayed unusually hot for an 18-month period overlapping with El Niño conditions, on average, and 80 percent of the forests were drier than average. The Amazon rainforest was particularly hard-hit. After a full two years of drought, water levels at the port of Manaus sank to the lowest level in more than a century of record-keeping. Globally, three-quarters of tropical forests endured extreme heat and drought simultaneously for an average of six months, the study found.
Even if human carbon emissions are eliminated or neutralized by 2075, extreme heat and drought will still be six times more likely across tropical regions by the end of the century than they have been over the past 25 years.
Under any higher-emissions climate scenario, the extreme, forest-damaging conditions seen in 2023 and 2024 are projected to become the annual norm across most tropical regions by the 2040s, with or without El Niño. It’s a “very striking” projection for the near future, Van Passel said.
Brown, the lead author of the ozone study, said the research offered a way to connect the often-invisible atmospheric chemistry of the atmosphere with real-world effects “that felt really relevant and important to me.”

Some of the data came from enclosed growth zones at TropOz laboratory “where we can control conditions like ozone concentration and really measure the trees,” she said. Other measurements used to understand ozone’s effects come from satellites that track vegetation reflectivity and from flux towers installed in the rainforest canopy that detect changes in the air’s chemistry.
One surprising result was that, during the 1997 to 2024 study period, there was “on the whole, a decline in ozone damage, coming from increasing CO2 concentrations,” Brown said. One reason is that, as the concentration of CO2 rises, trees can photosynthesize more efficiently, so they take up less air, and less ozone, through their stomata.
But the overall decline was outweighed by the effects of extreme events. Fires, smoke-driven ozone, drought and heat are becoming more frequent and more damaging, with impacts far greater than similar events would have had in a cooler climate.
The next cycle of extremes is already beginning, with a powerful El Niño driving drought in the region and the season for agricultural burning starting in the coming weeks.
The fires are not intended to become huge or burn the forest, but during droughts, they often escape control and release significant amounts of nitrogen oxides that can be carried distances and combine with other reactive organic molecules to form ozone.
Brown said ozone damage is just one of many pressures on the Amazon, as drought and high temperatures are “already moving the Amazon into conditions that it didn’t grow to withstand.” Limiting the damage requires changes in the way agricultural fires are managed, including using practices other than burning, and slowing deforestation and other degradation, she added.
Her biggest single concern is extreme drought. The Amazon evolved as an environment that is always wet, “and now, this isn’t the case,” she said. “A natural rainforest shouldn’t burn. It’s too wet. So even the fact that we create and see these fires that spread into the Amazon is already some kind of tipping point.”

The botched execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has thrust Tennessee's criminal justice system into uncharted territory.
After state officials administered two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, Pike survived and was transported to a nearby hospital, where she was intubated. Six days later, her lawyers announced she was "conscious and speaking".
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation into what went wrong at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville and suspended all executions for the rest of the year.
The fate of Pike, who has been on death row for 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer, now lies in a mysterious grey area.
Doctor Joel Zivot, an anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defence team, says he suspects the deadly chemical spread under her skin instead of her bloodstream, and, because of the the large dose, it could take days or even weeks for a clear picture of her health to emerge.
At a hearing on Thursday, an attorney for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.
Pike's lawyers are seeking to have Pike's death sentence commuted to a lesser punishment of life in prison without parole. Lee, who has the power to pardon Pike or commute her sentence, has not indicated what the state will do in her case.
The BBC spoke to multiple experts to explore what could happen next.
Attempt to execute Pike by lethal injection again
The Tennessee Department of Corrections could attempt to execute Pike again by lethal injection, but the state would very likely run into legal challenges based on constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
"For the state to attempt to execute her again using the same methodology, they would have severe legal hurdles," Tennessee-based defence attorney Stephen Ross Johnson said.
Ross said Tennessee had botched two executions in one year - it also failed to kill Tony Carruthers in May - which could give lawyers the grounds to argue broadly against the constitutionality of its lethal injection protocol.
Pike's lawyers could also argue a lethal injection is what Ross called "unconstitutional as applied", meaning it is cruel and unusual specifically for Pike, due to her medical condition.
Pike's lawyers had warned before the execution attempt that she has small veins and thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition that would complicate the procedure.
Her medical condition combined with the state's botched execution would make it difficult for Tennessee to present a convincing legal argument for attempting lethal injection again, Ross said.
Attempt to execute her with a different method
But Ross, president-elect of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, could see the state attempting an execution by a different method.
This would require "additional legal hoops", including approval from the governor's office and potentially the state legislature.
Since Pike's survival, political leaders in Tennessee have called for moving her death sentence forward through other means.
Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."
Congressman Tim Burchett, posted on social media that he's already filed a bill to "bring back hanging".
Tennessee could be allowed to use the electric chair because Pike committed the murder in 1995 before the state changed its execution laws.
She would need to waive her right to lethal injection in writing, which means it would have to be her decision, Vanderbilt University law professor Chris Slobogin said.
Given Pike's exact medical state is unknown, Slobogin said there is a scenario where the state could be blocked from attempting to execute her again, regardless of method.
It is also considered cruel and unusual punishment to execute someone who is mentally incapable of understanding why it is happening, he explained.
Historically this has applied to prisoners with dementia or psychosis, but experts have said there is a chance that Pike has suffered brain damage.
Commute her sentence
Tennessee is taking a long pause on carrying out capital punishment.
Only one person was due to be executed this year after Pike, which the governor has now postponed. Earlier, in May, the Carruthers execution was suspended by a year after state officials could not find a vein to administer the lethal injection.
That means it will likely take a while for any movement in Pike's case.
"At a minimum there's going to be some significant delay while this issue is studied by the state", defence attorney Ross said, adding Pike's health would also need to be studied.
Slobogin suspects the governor will commute her sentence, especially if missteps by state officials are uncovered in the investigation he has ordered.
"If the investigation, in any way, shape, or form, suggests that the protocol was not followed, or is hard to carry out, that might be the easy way for him to go, given the complications with the execution and all the bad press," he said.
There is legal precedent for a death sentence to be commuted due to a botched execution combined with an inmate's poor medical state.
The execution of Alabama death-row prisoner Doyle Hamm was called off after more than two hours of attempts to establish an IV line failed.
The state gave up on executing him following a legal settlement that related, in part, to his health. He later died of natural causes.

In 1991, Random House published a picture book called “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: ABC’s for a Better Planet,” in which the masked cartoon turtles trade in their signature nunchucks for signs bearing environmental slogans.
For “A,” the turtles explain the sources of acid rain. Under “B,” the concept of biodegradability.
“Don’t Pollute Dudes!” the turtles exhort under “D.” They designate the letter G for “Green Power!”
Then the book reaches the letter “M”—for meat.
“A lot of the world’s cereal crop is fed to cattle, when it could be used to feed to starving people instead,” the book says. “And cattle expel methane, a gas that makes the greenhouse effect worse.” Underneath is a drawing of one of the turtles, Donatello, eating a salad.
“What can you do?” Donatello says, instructively. “How about not eating so much meat in the first place?”
This message and its potential to harness the power of early-’90s “Turtlemania” did not sit well with the meat industry. Its top lobbying group, then the National Cattlemen’s Association, now the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association (NCBA), publicly called for Random House to cease publication.
This example of meat industry pushback is one of many that Jennifer Jacquet, a researcher with the University of Miami, and her colleague Loredana Loy unearthed while researching the association’s influence, much of it in archives at the University of Wyoming. On Wednesday, they published a new paper in the journal PLOS Climate, in which they document a string of instances of the NCA attempting to tamp down messages and distort facts about the climate impacts of livestock, the researchers say.
“What we found in the archives really reveals the lack of concern about global warming,” Jacquet said, “and yet an incredible concern about the public’s view of the role of livestock in global warming.”
Jacquet and others have long researched the industry’s attempts to downplay its greenhouse gas emissions. Some of Jacquet’s recent research documents that the industry knew about its climate impacts long before the public became broadly aware of them, but worked to obstruct policies and campaigns meant to reduce emissions and consumption.
If those dietary or policy shifts had happened, they could have significantly lowered emissions: Jacquet and her colleagues calculated that lowering meat consumption in the United States by 50 percent per capita could have been up to 80 times more effective in reducing methane emissions than all the efforts to limit methane from the oil and gas industry over a 30-year period, starting in the early 1990s.
The latest paper adds details to the record, citing more examples of the industry’s efforts and specifically homing in on the National Cattlemen’s Association.
The NCBA did not respond to requests for an interview or for comments.
Jacquet said she wanted to look at the period immediately after 1986, when researchers published a major paper estimating the significant emissions of methane from enteric fermentation—the burps of ruminant animals. In 1988, NASA’s James Hansen famously testified about the “greenhouse effect” before a U.S. Senate subcommittee, saying that “non-CO2” gases, including methane, were also warming the atmosphere.
In the years that followed, as a new wave of environmental action arose and governments across the world started to act on climate, influential books advised people to eat less livestock-based food for both health and planetary reasons. “Diet for a New America” by John Robbins advocated a shift toward vegetarian diets and “Beyond Beef: The Rise and Fall of the Cattle Culture” by Jeremy Rifkin traced the long history of beef production, railing against intensive factory farms.

As these books became popular, NCA began strategizing its rebuttal. After the actors Lisa Bonet and River Phoenix appeared on the Phil Donahue Show in support of Robbins’ book and vegetarian diets, the NCA asked researchers at Texas A&M University to refute its main points. When “Beyond Beef” was published in 1992 and Rifkin launched a related campaign urging 16 countries, including the U.S., to reduce beef consumption by 50 percent, the NCA launched the “Food Facts Coalition” to fight “anti-cow” arguments.
F.M. Byers, a researcher at Texas A&M, became the go-to scientist the NCA called on to challenge the mounting evidence behind livestock emissions from cattle. “Cattle are not a significant source of greenhouse gases,” Byers wrote in an opinion piece for USA Today.
Livestock are estimated to produce about one-third of all human-caused methane, and in the U.S. are the biggest source.
As the NCA worked on the public relations front, its members were sufficiently concerned about the growing awareness of livestock methane, to the point that some attended a workshop on “Methane Emissions from Ruminants,” held by the Environmental Protection Agency in 1989. That same year the NCA published its “Strategic Plan on the Environment,” outlining how the industry should respond to growing concerns about its environmental and climate impacts.
At that time, the NCA said climate change was a real threat and was concerned that incoming Republican President George H.W. Bush would enact policies to address it.

86a6a057d305.text: President Trump threatened Wednesday to fire two of his top political consultants if he finds a conflict, after reports that they advised a Russia-aligned government ahead of local elections there. Why it matters: Chris LaCivita and James Blair are leading Republicans' midterm election strategy, putting their foreign consulting work in tension with their prominent roles in Trump's political operation. What they're saying: Trump called the pair "outside consultants" in a Truth Social post Wednesday. "They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them. They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C." "I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there's a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!" The other side: A source familiar with both consultants and the trip tells Axios that it was "a normal weekend full of calls and texts on the various races and our strategy/tactics in each." Context: The nationalist party warned that new voting machines could threaten its hold on power, echoing Trump's repeated attacks on voting machines in the U.S. A national election commission required the territory to use the new equipment. The source said Blair and LaCivita were there for about 48 hours to give "strategic advice on Election Integrity and what to look for to spot and avoid potential election fraud, because it was the first election where Republic of Srbska was forced to use new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment…which obviously made them nervous." Between the lines: Caroline Wren, a registered lobbyist for Srpska, said the republic's abiding interest is in gaining stronger relations with Trump's administration. "It's not about Russia. It's not about Putin. It's about Christians who want their freedom and autonomy," Wren said. "The Trump Administration has made a huge priority of protecting and promoting Christians around the world and there is no better place to do that than the Pro-Trump Christians in the Republic of Sprska who have been demonized by the Europeans and Brussels for their Western values," she said. Blair and LaCivita were "maybe on the ground for 36 hours," she said, observing that she saw Blair constantly on the phone discussing elections back in the U.S. "Chris and James work around the clock to deliver wins for President Trump and Republicans here at home," she said. Zoom in: Blair , who previously served as White House deputy chief of staff, left the administration earlier this year to work for MAGA Inc., a super PAC affiliated with the president. He was also a senior adviser on Trump's 2024 campaign. LaCivita , the former co-manager of Trump's 2024 presidential campaign , is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc. Catch up quick: LaCivita and Blair visited Republika Srpska, a semi-autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of local elections, according to the New York Times. The two were reportedly recruited to advise the government on voting-related issues. They were hired to work for the government, not the nationalist party that controls it, though the party dominates the territory's government. Yes, but: American political consultants have a long history of taking on foreign clients. Zoom out: Trump's family businesses have expanded their foreign dealings since he returned to office. The Trump Organization and its partners have more than 20 Trump-branded projects planned, under construction or opening abroad — more than triple the number of overseas properties operating before his return. His administration accepted a luxury Boeing 747 from Qatar slated to eventually go to Trump's presidential library, while a UAE royal-linked firm bought a 49% stake in the Trump family's cryptocurrency business. Donald Trump Jr. had his wedding bankrolled by a Putin-linked Russian oligarch and later repaid him after public outrage. Go deeper: Trump's presidential profit machine bursts into the open

08b5264d8236.text: Saudi Arabia and Syria are discussing sending Syrian troops to Yemen to join the counteroffensive against the Houthi rebels, three U.S. officials told Axios. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is seriously considering it, but hasn't decided. Why it matters: While the discussion is mostly between Saudi Arabia and Syria, the Trump administration has been consulted by both countries and is not opposed in principle to such a move, the U.S. officials said. But sending Syrian troops could inject a religious dimension into the Yemen war and exacerbate the conflict. The troops could include Islamist Sunni foreign fighters who participated in the rebellion against the Assad regime. They would be fighting against the Houthis, who follow Zaydi Shiite Islam. Driving the news: The Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a massive ground operation over the weekend against the Houthis. The offensive was designed to retake territories the Houthis control, including the capital Sanaa and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait. A U.S. official said the issue of sending Syrian troops to Yemen came up during the meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and al-Sharaa in Riyadh earlier this week. The Saudis want al-Sharaa to send troops in order to boost the Yemeni forces that are less trained than the Houthis. While al-Sharaa hasn't signed off on the decision yet, the U.S. official said it is highly likely the Syrian president will accept the Saudi request. Behind the scenes: The U.S. doesn't oppose sending Syrian troops to Yemen. It would provide more support for the Saudi-backed operation against the Houthis without the U.S. having to get deeply involved, a U.S. official said. Trump administration officials also believe that deploying Syrian troops to Yemen would strengthen the relationship between two U.S. allies, Saudi Arabia and Syria. Two U.S. officials said U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed. The White House and CENTCOM declined to comment. Spokespeople for the Saudi Embassy and the Syrian Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Zoom in: A source with knowledge of the discussions said the Syrian military could send 10,000 to 20,000 troops to Yemen. The units under consideration are the 90th division near Damascus and the 84th division based in southern Syria near Sweida. The 84th division includes thousands of Islamist foreign fighters who came to Syria during the civil war to fight against the Assad regime under the umbrella of the HTS rebel group.

(AP) — Farmers, truckers and economists say a move to cut taxes on diesel will provide little relief from record-high fuel prices that have soared since the U.S. attacked Iran months ago. Industry groups said they appreciate President Donald Trump's executive order expanding the use of a diesel now reserved for off-road work, but farmers already have access to the fuel and many have already wrapped up harvest. Truckers will struggle to navigate differing state rules. WATCH: Trump campaigns with Ricketts in Nebraska, signs order on red-dyed diesel "In the context of diesel prices that are over two dollars more than they were last year, it just doesn't come close to closing that wound," said Matt Perdue, president of the North Dakota Farmers Union. With less than a month to go before the November election, diesel prices continue to hit record highs as some farmers transport their crops for processing and others rush to complete their fall harvest. Many have been feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared thanks to refinery constraints and supply disruptions amid the Iran war. Please check your inbox to confirm. Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon across the country on Wednesday, more than 70% higher than one year ago, according to motor club AAA. The executive order defers the $0.24 federal tax per gallon of regular diesel, used for road projects, until the end of the year. Most states also levy their own tax on diesel. "Dyed" diesel is the same as regular diesel, except for its red dye to help law enforcement enforce penalties for on-road use. It's already allowed for off-road purposes like farming equipment, such as tractors and combines, as well as construction and heating uses. Who will see benefits Savings can compound if states take similar actions; many have eased restrictions or waived taxes on dyed diesel, including South Dakota and Iowa. Perdue said North Dakota has waived the tax on regular diesel. But where the state decision is focused on farmers, he believes the federal decision would largely benefit those on other levels of the supply chain. Farmers who will see the most benefit are those who haul their own product, like livestock or fresh produce, on public roads. Those who have already wrapped up harvesting won't see savings. "Most of our diesel use is behind us," said Perdue, who grows spring wheat, durum and canola on his family farm. READ MORE: 3 things to know about rising diesel prices and how they affect you Both trucking companies and independent truckers may not see much relief either. The effect is likely to be negligible for big trucking companies because the order is on a federal level and states make their own rules, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in a social media post. "The largest diesel users are the least likely to use dyed diesel," he wrote. "A national carrier crossing five or six states in a day faces enormous risk with a patchwork of rules, legal in one state, and subject to fines in the next." WATCH: How the diesel price spike is rippling through nearly every part of the economy Many states exempt road diesel from sales tax but apply sales tax to dyed diesel instead, he said. Easing limits on red-dyed diesel will likely have a minimal effect for small truckers, who pay for fuel up front, said Todd Spencer, president and CEO of trade group the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association. He estimates every $1 increase per gallon in fuel costs independent truckers about $400 more per week. Increased demand for dyed diesel The savings will be small, but it could still increase competition for dyed diesel, said David Ortega, food economics and policy professor at Michigan State University. "I think there's a real chance this could backfire and make the situation worse for farmers," he said. "Basically anybody that's running a truck on the highway on regular diesel can now be using this off-highway diesel. Even someone that owns a diesel pickup truck potentially has access to this other type of diesel." Perdue in North Dakota said he expects a "rush for dyed diesel, and we'll see how the supply responds." READ MORE: Trump calls on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel fuel, saying attacks are causing a shortage But not all dyed diesel pump stations are set up for larger trucks like semis, said Paul Mitchell, a professor of agricultural and applied economics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "It's going to come down to infrastructure ability to get your vehicles to a place that you can use and fill them up with," he said. Supply shortages persist Henry Hanscom, American Trucking Associations chief advocacy and public affairs officer, pointed out that the executive order directs temporary penalty relief and potential tax deferral for using red-dyed diesel, not outright tax forgiveness. He said the ATA would review the Internal Revenue Service's implementing guidance of the policy when it is available. Last month, Trump had threatened a diesel export ban, though he later said it is off the table. On Friday, G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products. b0eda7d0422f.text: By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press By — Derek Gatopoulos, Associated Press Derek Gatopoulos, Associated Press By — Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-rubio-urges-europe-to-defend-western-values-and-strengthen-u-s-alliance-in-greece Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Rubio urges Europe to defend Western values and strengthen U.S. alliance in Greece World Oct 7, 2026 5:22 PM EDT ATHENS (AP) — Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a sweeping speech against the backdrop of the Acropolis in Athens, called for the nations of the West to return to their civilizational roots and restore the values that drove the rise of Europe and North America to global dominance for centuries. Watch Rubio's remarks in the video player above. In Greece to discuss deepening economic, energy and security cooperation, Rubio made the case for nationalism while emphasizing the importance of global alliances during a dramatic speech about ancient civilization that appeared to reflect his political aspirations beyond being America's top diplomat. READ MORE: Cold War memories stir Rubio in Iceland as he champions diplomacy and downplays differences Rubio aimed to remind listeners of qualities he says were born in Greece and later defined the West, such as curiosity, courage, ambition, a restless spirit of exploration and a drive to discover the unknown. Please check your inbox to confirm. "It has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the 'global community' over one's own people," Rubio said. "And I think here, too, we have much more to learn from the men of ancient Greece. They knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else." Rubio touts alliances with Europe but says U.S. pursues 'national power' In his current role, Rubio is seen by many as the gentle face of the Trump administration and has been frequently dispatched to clarify or otherwise address concerns about the president's frequently undiplomatic statements. He is on the second leg of a three-nation tour of NATO allies that has already taken him to Iceland and will end in Portugal on Thursday, aiming to reassure U.S. partners that the Trump administration is committed to their success and security despite what has been an often brusque approach to traditional friends that has stirred unease. "We must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age. And we can," Rubio said Wednesday, maintaining that the U.S. administration wanted Europe to join its bold vision of the future. He also was clear, however, about the United States acting in its own interests around the world. "We will either choose to act now, or lose the choice to act at all," he said. "Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power." Rubio warned European countries that the decisions made in the next decade "will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline." But he also argued that despite "passions" having strained U.S.-Europe relations, allied countries must work to "rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together." The Trump administration has repeatedly accused countries in Europe of backsliding on their traditional values and democratic principles by stifling the free speech of conservatives and falling short on commitments to international partners like the United States. Many of those countries have rejected the complaints and accused the U.S. under Trump of being guilty of similar behavior and worse with its staunch anti-immigration stance that some believe is racist. Rubio's speech offers presidential overtones The tone and tenor of Rubio's remarks, the symbolic backdrop and the State Department's hiring of a local television crew to provide different angles of the speech, including a camera-mounted swiveling crane, were more reflective of a stump speech during a presidential campaign than a public address while on a diplomatic trip. The former Republican senator, who previously ran for the White House in 2016, touched on the history of Western civilization while making mention of his own family's immigration journey, at one point marveling how a son of Cuban immigrants could become the U.S. secretary of state. "Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American Republic, halfway across the world from where I stand now, I stand here today as the Secretary of State of that Republic, and as the great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the New World from Spain," Rubio said. "I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space, can ever extinguish." Along with Vice President JD Vance, Rubio is seen as one of the leading contenders to assume Trump's mantle at the top of the Republican Party, which faces stiff challenges in next month's congressional midterm elections. The speech, however, contained several historically dubious points, including that the founders of the United States had embraced the direct democracy that Athens was known for. The founders were suspicious of direct democracy and so created the Electoral College as a check on the popular will. Rubio also hailed the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés as an heir to the Athenian concept of exploring and pursuing knowledge for knowledge's sake. 4b169566f692.text: By — Annie Ma, Associated Press Annie Ma, Associated Press By — Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-proposes-a-70000-fee-for-international-students-to-work-in-the-u-s Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration proposes a $70,000 fee for international students to work in the U.S. Politics Oct 7, 2026 5:16 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States, the latest effort from the Trump administration to crack down on foreign enrollment. A proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school. Students are generally eligible for one year of work post-graduation, though certain science, technology, engineering and math majors are eligible for an additional two years. Please check your inbox to confirm. Schools would be required to pay the $70,000 for each new student's initial application to the program, and a $30,000 fee for each renewal. Change would be a blow to higher education and some businesses American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. Tech companies and other industries also hire many international students for technical roles. The OPT program allows international students to gain hands-on experience and fill labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields, said Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education. WATCH: Study finds Trump administration cut legal immigration far more than illegal crossings "Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership," Aw said in a written statement. In a statement, DHS described the fee as a response to fraud and abuse of the visa program, which it called a "pipeline for cheap foreign labor." The public has 60 days to comment on the proposal before DHS can finalize it and put it into effect. The proposal also could face legal challenges from higher education groups or business associations that could delay it. Trump administration puts pressure on international students The proposed rule is part of its wider efforts to crack down on immigration and reshape higher education. Last year, the Republican administration began suddenly terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, detaining and deporting many of them. This summer, the administration finalized a rule that sought to prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government. The move drew swift backlash from higher education leaders who said it would increase the burden on schools and noted that many programs are longer than four years by design. A federal court prevented the rule from taking effect in September. WATCH: How college communities are reacting to funding threats, international student arrests Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services during the Biden administration, predicted that the fee would be struck down in the courts, as was a $100,000 fee for the H-1B work visas that many tech companies and universities rely on to fill openings for skilled jobs. The Trump administration is now trying a different way to raise the fee for the visas to more than $100,000. Rand said fees are not the answer. "When we educate international students at our universities, and they want to work and apply their talents here after graduating, of course we should embrace them -- not use an exorbitant fee as a pretext to send them packing," Rand said in an email. Enrollment concerns mount among education groups Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said international enrollment has suffered. Last fall, the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 17%, the sharpest decrease since the COVID-19 pandemic. Overall numbers for this fall are not yet available, but Spreitzer said some individual colleges are reporting drops of 30% to 40%. She said the new Trump plan will not help. "We know that OPT is one of the reasons that international students choose to study in the United States because they're able to have that post-graduation work experience," she added. READ MORE: Visa cancellations and deportations sow panic for international students A similar program that allowed international students to participate in internships and practicums also has faced scrutiny from the Trump administration. New guidance from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that the program, Curricular Practical Training, should only be authorized when the work experience is a degree requirement led to a lawsuit Monday. Education groups, including the Association of American Universities and NAFSA, said that in the past that program was allowed if it was "directly related to the student's major area of study." The groups also said ICE was threatening college university officials with criminal prosecution if they did not comply. "We know the administration has been trying to hinder legal employment-based immigration through numerous means," said Steven Brown, a Houston-based immigration lawyer. "I think this is the next level of attack, and I think it's a design to kill the program without killing the program. I

The spots, which began airing in September, already have cost more than $12 million to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, and a total of $20 million in Homeland Security Department funding has been tapped to pay for them. Some blind people can now find a doorway or spot an object with the help of an experimental treatment and custom goggles.
Participants in a new study had blindness caused by a genetic disease called retinitis pigmentosa, which progressively kills off light-sensing cells in the retina. The treatment improved seven of 10 people’s light sensitivity, researchers report October 7 in New England Journal of Medicine. The findings build on a 2021 report that the same approach helped one blind man see and count objects.
The treatment is based on optogenetics, a technique that uses genetic instructions to make cells respond to light. Rather than repair the retina’s damaged light detectors, it gives that ability to retinal ganglion cells that normally relay visual signals to the brain.
“This is a proof of concept that optogenetics can bring back some visual activity [and] object sensitivity,” says Botond Roska, neuroscientist at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel in Switzerland.
Pioneering work on optogenetics snagged the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on October 5.
Scientists have been experimenting with optogenetic therapies to rewire the eye and restore vision to people with degenerative eye diseases for more than a decade. Just as in the 2021 study, in the new work Roska and his colleagues injected genetic instructions for ChrimsonR, a light-sensitive protein derived from algae, into participants’ worse-seeing eye. The treatment made retinal ganglion cells in that eye sensitive to amber light. A camera in the custom goggles detected changes in brightness in what was in front of a study participant, and the goggles projected those changes onto the retina as pulses of amber light, activating the treated cells.
Four of the eight study participants who completed behavioral testing after treatment were able to find a doorway or follow a line while wearing the goggles. No patient gained the ability to read visual words or see faces, but Roska and his colleagues hope to tackle that next.
But there’s a limitation to this work. The approach requires a working optic nerve to carry signals to the brain, says study coauthor José-Alain Sahel, an ophthalmologist at the University of Pittsburgh. It relies on cells in the retina communicating to the brain, so it cannot restore vision when that connection is damaged.

d85b981b13f9.text: By — Ellen Schmidt, Associated Press Ellen Schmidt, Associated Press By — Gene Johnson, Associated Press Gene Johnson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/fbi-says-it-stopped-a-mall-of-america-terror-attack-by-a-teen-after-agents-sold-him-an-assault-rifle Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FBI says it stopped a Mall of America terror attack by a teen after agents sold him an assault rifle Nation Oct 7, 2026 4:56 PM EDT MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — FBI agents thwarted a terror attack by a teenager on the Mall of America after monitoring him for nearly two years and ultimately supplying him with the assault rifle he planned to use, authorities said Wednesday. The 18-year-old had been on the FBI's radar since December 2024, when he began trading messages with a confidential informant. A criminal complaint says he initially expressed an interest in traveling overseas to fight for the extremist group al-Shabab. As his plans to instead attack the mall solidified, it says, agents sold him an AK-47 and ammunition on Tuesday and arrested him on the spot. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched," U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said. Agents "were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people." Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield, several miles northwest of the Mall of America, after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of ISIS for the rifle and 200 rounds of ammunition, the agency said. Mohamud appeared in a yellow jail uniform for his initial appearance Wednesday in federal court in St. Paul. He told the judge he did not have a job, own a house or a car, or have any money in the bank. He was represented by Siri Carlson McDowell, a federal public defender. Carlson McDowell and relatives of Mohamud declined to comment after the hearing. READ MORE: FBI gives employees a classified 'Patel Report' about times the agency 'fell short' According to an FBI agent's sworn complaint, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed in chat messages to the informant that he intended to attack and kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled Hmong arts celebration. When the informant asked if he was serious about committing the attack, Mohamud replied, "yes i am 100% sure," the complaint said, and added: "I would have backed out by now if I wasn't sure." Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent. The agent wrote that Mohamud's messages expressed admiration for recent terror attacks as well as an interest in traveling to Somalia to join ISIS. Ultimately he decided he couldn't afford to travel there and would attack the mall instead, the complaint said. The teen first came to the FBI's attention in December 2024, the same month the source began exchanging messages with him, the complaint said. By May 2025, agents were concerned enough that they went to his home. His mother told them he wasn't home from school yet and called the boy's father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said. "What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded," Rosen said. Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join ISIS or other terror groups. Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press reporter Philip Marcelo in New York contributed. An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del RÃo said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, UrbagestiÃ³n, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from â¬500 per month (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650 (Â£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.
That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.
Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours,'" it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Protesters gathered at one of Madrid's main squares, Puerta del Sol, following the announcement of Abascal's death. The site has become a protest encampment for protesters over the last two weeks.
Photos show demonstrators lighting candles and holding posters of Maricarmen at the housing protest camp on Wednesday evening.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.
The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.
On Monday SÃ¡nchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.
The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Speaking on Monday, SÃ¡nchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.
Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.

OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short.
The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use.
On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity.
However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail.
When OpenAI this summer released what it called ChatGPT for Teens, external, it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents".
Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive."
The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating.
OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work.
In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder.
The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases.
But Common Sense Media's new research, external determined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable.
An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete."
"We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said.
While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide.
The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents.
It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert.
In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found.
The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour.
"ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said.
The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common.
This year has seen several lawsuits looking to hold companies like Meta, TikTok and others responsible for harming the mental health of children end in unprecedented losses for the firms.
OpenAI, too, has come under increased scrutiny and legal pressure over the way young people use ChatGPT.
The Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in rural Canada in February was carried out by an 18-year old who had for months prior been discussing gun violence with ChatGPT.
OpenAI has previously apologised for failing to flag the shooter's account with law enforcement, and is facing several lawsuits over the incident.

A Chinese fitness influencer has been dropped by her sponsor after she apologised for riding a bicycle during the Berlin marathon.
Sun Yuanyuan, known as Abeeeer on Chinese social media, had claimed a personal best during the event which was held in September.
But an Instagram page dedicated to monitoring inaccurate or misleading race times posted by influencers published a picture which appeared to show Sun on a bicycle between the 35km and and 40km marks.
Sun apologised and admitted to "breaking the rules". Brooks, the running shoe company, has ended its sponsorship deal with her and her finish time has been disqualified by the marathon organisers.
An Instagram account calling itself the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) posted a photo of Sun apparently on the back of a bike being ridden by another person during the marathon.
The page also posted a grid of Sun's "splits" - which are the times taken to complete different 5km segments of the race.
The grid appears to show that she sped up between the 35 and 40km marks, when she was allegedly on the bike.
Sun posted an apology on the Chinese social media platform Rednote, which was shared by OMTIU, admitting that she had broken the rules.
She wrote: "I won't make any excuses for this behaviour.
"I was feeling physically unwell on the course, [but] that is absolutely not an excuse for breaking the rules.
"My attempt to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the fairness of the competition and the spirit of the marathon."
Sun, who has 520,000 followers on Rednote, also said she "deliberately concealed" her actions, adding: "I feel deeply guilty about this."
Brooks confirmed to BBC News that it had dropped Sun.
A company statement said: "Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition.
"After verifying the facts, Brooks China terminated its relationship with the individual and publicly addressed the matter."
OMTIU was set up to highlight "the growing trend of GPS-based fabrication, selective Strava displays and false PR claims" among marathon runners, particularly fitness influencers. Strava is a fitness tracking app.
The page's mission statement says: "We exist to protect the integrity of the sport by ensuring that the times athletes share publicly reflect the times they actually ran."
Its Instagram bio describes it as "satire".
BBC News has contacted the Berlin Marathon for comment.

Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the devastating Hamas-led attack there that sparked the war in Gaza.
Families paid tribute to their loved ones at some of the sites where about 1,200 people were killed in the assault and 251 were taken hostage.
"The nation unites on this day in the longing for our dear ones," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faced calls from protesters for an independent state inquiry into security failures that day.
In response to the attack, Israel launched a military offensive in Gaza which has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN.
Violence has continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed almost a year ago and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire.
On Wednesday morning, bereaved families and survivors gathered at a memorial for the 378 people who were killed at the Nova dance festival in southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
The festival site was near Kibbutz Re'im and not far from the border with Gaza, from where Hamas-led gunmen launched their dawn attack.
Witnesses have described how festival-goers were shot, sexually abused and tortured by gunmen during the raid.
Forty-four people were kidnapped, of whom 25 were brought back from Gaza alive.
Ahuva Yavin Mayze, whose 21-year-old daughter Adi was shot and killed at Nova, told the BBC what happened at the site was "dystopic, unimaginable".
"Today is a difficult day, not only for me but for a large part of the nation," said Shlomo Sharf, a former Israeli footballer, in comments reported by Channel 12.
He paid tribute to his granddaughter, May Naim, 24, who was also killed at the festival.
Former hostage Yarden Bibas, whose wife and two young sons were kidnapped from their home in Kibbutz Nir Oz and later killed in captivity in Gaza, was quoted by the Times of Israel as saying: "Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here."
Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October.
Zion Regev, a community leader, said most surviving residents had yet to return to their homes because of the trauma of what happened.
"This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," he told Reuters news agency. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after 7 October."
A man who reportedly helped to fend off Hamas attackers at Kibbutz Magen praised IDF troops who "fought so bravely" during the raid.
Speaking to crowds at the national memorial event at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday evening, Ido Yakir said Israel would remember everyone "who knew that they had to give their lives in order to save others".
In a statement released by his office on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu said he had lit a memorial candle commemorating every victim of 7 October.
"We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers," he added.
At a ceremony on Monday marking the Jewish calendar's anniversary of the attack, the prime minister said Israel had killed 4,000 out of the 6,000 Palestinians who infiltrated Israel from Gaza that day.
In Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Square, Israeli anti-government protesters dyed the fountain red to mark the anniversary of the attack.
The fountain has been used as a memorial site for those killed, with pictures, flowers and messages laid around the basin wall.
Protesters also briefly blocked one of the main highways in the city to hold a moment of silence on Wednesday morning.
They held banners that read, "the people will remember their sons and daughters", along with others that said "a complete failure" and "guilty" next to an image of Netanyahu.
Many senior Israeli defence and security officials have resigned or been fired since the attack took place. But there has not been an independent commission of inquiry into Israel's worst security failure.
The prime minister has rejected any personal responsibility and has refused to establish a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.
Einav Zangauker became an outspoken critic of the Netanyahu government while her son, Matan, was in captivity in Gaza. He was released last October as part of the ceasefire agreement.
"They're trying to make us forget what happened on 7 October," she told Army Radio. "We won't forget, we will demand the truth."
Memorial events were organised in other countries around the world, including in Germany, where the Jewish students' union held a vigil at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Hamas-led attack marked a "profound rupture".
"We commemorate the victims, we share their pain," he said, adding that antisemitism must be confronted with "even greater resolve".
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Britain's Jewish community: "We stand with you."
"The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day," he said.
Outside Downing Street, a vigil was also held to commemorate British-Israelis killed in the initial attack, later as hostages, or in fighting with Hamas.
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said: "The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again."
She also said that the European Union "remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu and wished the people of Israel well.
"That was a horrible day, a horrible tragedy," he said.
This is the first anniversary of the 7 October attack with no hostages remaining in G
