b7ac2fab5d23.text: Republican super PACs are flooding the airwaves in once-safe states, and pulling down ads for races that look like lost causes. President Trump, his approval ratings near record lows, is popping up in some of America's reddest states. Why it matters: The polls showing Democrats headed toward a blue wave on Nov. 3 may not be quite right. But money — and how campaigns and PACs spend it — rarely lies. Nor do the contrails of Air Force One. While Republicans are scrambling, Democrats are cutting some spending in contests they think are in the bag, such as North Carolina's Senate race. No one wants to pay too much for a landslide, just as no one wants to throw good money after bad. Republicans have been forced to pour well over $100 million into Ken Paxton's Senate race in Texas against Democrat James Talarico, and to plead for millions more to defend Senate seats in Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. Call it political triage. Republican operatives are making the kind of hard decisions that would be familiar to any battlefield medic: Save the wounded, and say a prayer for the lost. Driving the news: Trump was in San Antonio on Wednesday to try to boost Paxton — his second trip in less than a week to Texas, a state he won by 14 points in 2024. During the past week the president also has campaigned in Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska. He's planning another trip to Alabama this weekend for the Georgia-Alabama football game. Vice President Vance showed up in Alaska this week, and will be in Ohio this weekend. What they're saying: Republicans' efforts now appear more focused on calling for party loyalists to show up at the polls than on persuading new voters. "Every time they up a buy [ads] on their end, it's always in the red states," said J.B. Poersch, president of Senate Majority PAC, the Democrats' main outside group working to win the Senate. "Some of these outside [GOP] groups such as the Senate Leadership Fund and others are going to have to figure out where their money is best spent," said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost the GOP primary to Paxton. "It looks like the money has already started to shift." Zoom in: After pulling out of North Carolina (which Trump won by 3 points) last Friday, the SLF — Republicans' main Senate super PAC — put a fresh $14 million in normally deep-red Kansas. This week, it sent a $5 million "insurance policy" to South Carolina (which Trump won by 18 points) to boost Republican Sen. Darline Graham. The other side: Democrats are pulling down some advertising, but in states where polling has solidified in their favor. Their spending moves reflect confidence, not concern. After the Senate Republicans' PAC cried uncle and pulled out of North Carolina, the Senate Democrats' group decided to go dark there as well. One of Democratic group's ad reservations for North Carolina — which was actually in the Greenville market in South Carolina — was gobbled up by an allied group, Fresh Start SC PAC, which will use the time to attack Graham. Between the lines: There's triage campaigning in House races as well, but it's not as pronounced — yet. The GOP's Congressional Leadership Fund pulled down $1.1 million in advertising in Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, one of three GOP-held seats where former Vice President Harris won in 2024. Democrats followed suit, with House Majority PAC canceling the $1.1 million it had reserved for the race. Both sides appear to agree that there's no obvious path for Republican Brinker Harding to win the seat left open by retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon. In a San Diego-area House district, the Democratic group pulled down $200,000 in ads in a redistricted seat Harris would have won. Zoom out: Republicans insist that their reallocation of funds doesn't mean they're admitting that the House or the Senate are lost. One thing neither side disputes: The Senate Leadership Fund, which is closely associated with Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), is well capitalized. That allows it to shore up candidates in red states, which wouldn't be necessary in a better political environment. In Texas, one of its subsidiaries spent $131 million in 17 days — more than $7.7 million a day. The group has announced another $4 million for the Alaska race, bringing its total there to $21 million for Sen. Dan Sullivan, who's being challenged by former Rep. Mary Peltola. In Maine, it has reserved another $8 million, for a total of $50 million for Sen. Susan Collins, who's in a battle with Democrat Troy Jackson. In Michigan, it's putting in another $2 million, for a total of $53 million for former Rep. Mike Rogers in his race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. And in Ohio, it's spending another $14 million, bringing the total to $93 million for Sen. John Husted, who faces former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D). What we're watching: All eyes are on Georgia. SLF announced an initial investment of $44 million there to back Republican Mike Collins, but Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has a healthy lead . The bottom line: Republicans can dismiss bad polls as noise, or the result of liberal bias. But their concern is evident in their thundering attack ads in red states such as Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

a34a872631ed.text: House Speaker Mike Johnson raised $30 million in the third quarter, bringing his total haul this cycle to $156 million as Republicans fight to hold on to their increasingly endangered majority, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Johnson's team says that's the most raised by a Republican speaker or leader at this point in an election cycle. Johnson has distributed more than $91 million to Republican members, candidates, committees and state parties this cycle, according to figures first shared with Axios. That includes $46 million transferred to the National Republican Congressional Committee, putting him on pace to make the largest cycle transfer to the group by a Republican speaker or leader. He's also sent $21.5 million directly to GOP incumbents and $7 million to challengers. Zoom out: Johnson's fundraising operation has brought in more than $220 million for House Republicans since he became speaker in October 2023. That's a notable turnaround from when Johnson first took the gavel, when Republicans worried whether the relatively unknown Louisiana Republican could replace former Speaker Kevin McCarthy's formidable fundraising operation . Johnson is also crisscrossing the country to help House Republicans, traveling to more than 40 districts across 22 states in the final stretch before Election Day, Axios previously reported. What they're saying: "We are focused on getting unprecedented resources to the Districts that will decide the majority," Johnson said in a statement to Axios. "With this continued momentum, we are in place to defy history and defend the House to save America from the far-left!" State of play: House Republicans have a cash advantage over Democrats. The NRCC ended August with $13 million more in cash on hand than the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, its largest-ever advantage at this point in an election cycle. But the House battlefield has continued to move toward Democrats. Cook Political Report shifted 15 House races toward Democrats last month, while Sabato's Crystal Ball moved 11 races toward Democrats days later. Many of the most competitive races are now in districts President Trump carried in 2024.

‘Medicare for All’ Is Back. Now Comes the Hard Part.
Turning an inspirational slogan into law gets gnarly.
As Americans grow increasingly frustrated with their healthcare system, a proposal that has long been kicked around on the Democratic periphery is showing up in debates and on political platforms: “Medicare for All.”
According to a 2025 Economist-YouGov poll, nearly 60% of Americans favor a system of Medicare for All, while 85% of Democrats support it. For years, Democrats in Congress have proposed symbolic Medicare for All bills that have had no chance of passage but have been supported by dozens of members.
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland added his support in December. “I was listening to my constituents,” he said. “It’s just reached the complete breaking point. Our system is unaffordable and unsustainable with premiums going up, copays going up and up.”
At a time when more than 100 million Americans carry medical debt, it’s easy to get behind a promise of free, or free-ish, no-hassle health care. But turning an inspirational slogan into law gets gnarly. Those three words, Medicare for All — a pledge to bring universal healthcare to every American — mean not one thing to supporters but many. And all versions of such a system face considerable obstacles to enactment.
“Medicare for All is a slogan, not a concrete proposal, so it’s hard to have an opinion on,” said Amy Finkelstein, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist who, with Stanford’s Liran Einav, wrote We’ve Got You Covered, which laid out what the pair considered a realistic and fiscally responsible plan for providing basic insurance to every American.
“What we can afford is a basic plan — what we call a shack, not a chateau,” Finkelstein said. Its bedrock would be a government-funded skinny plan less generous than Medicare, with potential constraints such as a limited number of physical therapy visits or stricter criteria for getting a knee replacement, but guaranteed robust basic coverage for catastrophic medical conditions. She estimated that most Americans would opt for supplemental coverage.
The most high-profile political proponent of Medicare for All this election season is Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senatorial candidate in Michigan, who has made a more sweeping proposal central to his platform — far more chateau than shack. It would create one plan that covers a suite of medical needs with no cost to patients, including dental and vision care, which traditional Medicare doesn’t cover.
(Traditional Medicare has increasingly come to resemble private insurance with premiums and coinsurance, and, unlike standard commercial plans, it has no annual out-of-pocket maximum. To fill such gaps, patients buy separate Medigap and drug plans.)
“The most important thing is just to make Medicare whole — meaning no charge for medical care — rolling back the complexity and costs of the last 10 years,” El-Sayed told KFF Health News.
His program would start off covering children and adults five years younger than the current eligibility age for Medicare and close the gap over a period, he has estimated, of eight years. To ease the transition for the healthcare system, he would initially set the Medicare payment rates to mirror the totals doctors and hospitals receive now to avoid a “price shock” to their operations. Future increases would be limited to the rate of inflation.
One big question is how to make the financing work in a highly profitable industry. National health spending was projected to hit $5.7 trillion in 2025, or nearly 20% of the U.S. gross domestic product.
The United States spends twice as much on healthcare per person than many peer countries. And health insurance is often a company’s second-largest expense after payroll.
But how will the government divert financial outlays of employers and households into a new Medicare for All system without new taxes or massive government spending?
When polls ask voters whether they would support Medicare for All if it meant losing their insurance or paying new taxes, support often drops.
“You could decide to raise taxes and cover more,” Finkelstein said. “If you don’t want to cut current Medicare benefits, you could decide to bust the budget, which seems to be a common practice.”
Joe Biden said that, as president, he would veto any Medicare for All bill, given the cost, which was estimated at up to $40 trillion over 10 years. The bills in Congress don’t include very detailed financing plans.
Economists who have mapped out the possibilities are divided on a realistic path.
A group of Yale researchers estimated that converting to a Medicare for All program could save $450 billion annually. That’s in part because a government plan could negotiate — or simply set — far better prices for hospitals, doctors, drugs, and devices than private insurers. It would reduce the overhead created by private insurance with its army of negotiators, coders, and claim deniers — and reduce profits.
Strong forces are pushing back against such “rightsizing” of exorbitant prices, most notably: insurers, hospitals, and drug and device manufacturers. In 2022, they spent over $700 million on lobbying and have been a powerful force for job creation. But a grand Medicare for All proposal may simply be a strategy to open the debate to lesser possibilities. President Barack Obama’s initial Affordable Care Act proposal contained ambitious ideas — such as drug price negotiation — that fell by the wayside to get the votes for passage.
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico supports what he calls “Medicare for Y’all” — allowing people under 65 to buy into Medicare.
“There are versions of Medicare for All that could potentially include our proposal, and versions that could look extremely different,” Finkelstein said.
Support in some parts of the industry is growing.
According to one survey, more than half of all physicians have said they’d prefer some sort of single-payer system.

Medical Debt Is Crushing Hospital Patients in Los Angeles. Health Officials May Have a Fix.
LOS ANGELES — Every Tuesday, Naman Shah sees tuberculosis patients at a small public clinic in Los Angeles’ San Fernando Valley. Shah, a physician and epidemiologist at the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, pores over images of battered lungs, listens to labored breathing, and checks medications.
It’s part of an initiative dating to the early 20th century to control infections so tuberculosis doesn’t spread. “We like doing things upstream,” Shah said, “meaning before they happen, not after the damage is done.”
Today, Shah and his colleagues are applying the same principle to medical debt. A key part of that effort is a new system to allow every hospital in Los Angeles County to easily screen patients for financial aid. The goal: to stop low-income families from getting a bill that buries them in debt.
Shah estimates this system could prevent several hundred million dollars of medical debt every year.
Vicious Cycle
Nationwide, an estimated 100 million adults have some form of healthcare debt. In Los Angeles County, the nation’s most populous, public health officials calculate that about 800,000 residents have medical bills they can’t pay.
“The impacts of medical debt were staggering,” said Shah, who used to staff a rural health clinic in India and, since 2023, has led a county initiative in Los Angeles to tackle the debt problem.
“People end up with credit card debt and then a vicious cycle of high interest rates and poverty,” he said. “People forgo their prescriptions. People forgo appointments. And then you get into worse health.”
Hospitals typically offer financial aid to patients with low incomes. But information about assistance is often hard for patients to get. Applying can be cumbersome. And many eligible patients never seek aid, research shows.
“Most people walk into the hospital and walk out without any knowledge of financial assistance,” said Jared Walker, founder of Dollar For, a nonprofit that helps patients nationwide apply for aid, often called charity care.
That’s fueling debt. It’s also driving costly collection efforts that even hospital officials acknowledge pointlessly target low-income patients who are unlikely to be able to pay.
“They’re turning their wheels trying to collect on debt that isn’t collectable,” said Adena Tessler, regional vice president for the Hospital Association of Southern California.
Presumptive Eligibility
One potential solution is a system that automatically screens and qualifies low-income patients for financial aid without requiring an application. This is called presumptive eligibility.
Some hospitals already use such systems, which rely on software that checks patient eligibility based on publicly available information such as credit history.
The strategy can be very effective. Shah said hospitals that have deployed presumptive eligibility systems have reported as much as a 50% increase in the amount of financial aid they give patients.
Under a state law passed last year, all California hospitals will have to start doing presumptive eligibility screening by next July.
But the systems can be expensive and difficult for smaller hospitals to implement. Only about 1 in 5 hospitals in Los Angeles County currently use them, Shah said.
Public health officials wondered if they could help more hospitals set them up.
The county, which, like many local governments, faces major fiscal challenges, couldn’t pay for this, Shah said. But the public health department could bring together healthcare and hospital officials in the county to figure out another solution.
“The beauty of government is not when it always has to do the work,” Shah said. “We have the ability to make sure that people cooperate.”
The Hospital Association of Southern California, initially wary of the county initiative, came to see improving hospital financial aid programs as beneficial to hospitals, many of which were wasting money on collections. “The billing process is cumbersome and costly,” said Paul Young, a senior vice president with the association.
The association agreed to procure a presumptive eligibility system and make it available to its members. This bulk-purchasing approach, which Young compared to “a Costco model,” would lower the cost for individual hospitals, he said.
At the same time, L.A. Care, a nonprofit health plan that administers Medicaid coverage for more than 2.5 million low-income county residents, committed $2 million to set up the system.
The investment reflected the safety net insurer’s mission to make medical care accessible to more people, said Melanie Fontes Rainer, who leads strategic planning for L.A. Care. “It’s going to make Los Angeles County better,” she said.
Making It Work
Getting the new system up and running by January, as the partners hope, faces challenges.
Hospital officials are figuring out how the system will be funded in the long term. And it’s unclear how many of the county’s 88 acute care hospitals will ultimately use it, even if it’s cheaper and easier to access.
The partners are also working to improve data that the system relies on to screen patients. One goal is to link the system to tax records maintained by the state of California. This would provide hospitals with more accurate information on patients’ income than current systems, which often rely on estimated income.
Walker, the patient advocate at Dollar For, said he’s heartened by the county’s effort. “I’m optimistic that we can make a better charity care system,” he said. “And the fact that hospitals in Los Angeles County are willing to be innovative and creative about ways we can do that is super encouraging.”
For his part, Shah said county public health officials recognize that a better screening system at hospitals won’t by itself eliminate medical debt. But he said the public health department couldn’t ignore a problem that affects more county residents than asthma or

Maryland environmental regulators say jet fuel continues to seep into Piscataway Creek from Joint Base Andrews more than six months after the spill was reported, despite the base’s assurances that it has isolated the damaged fuel system and stopped the leak.
“MDE remains deeply concerned about the ongoing environmental impacts and continues to observe signs of jet fuel coming from the site,” the Maryland Department of the Environment said in a written response. “Jet fuel continues to flush into the creek, particularly after heavy rain.”
In its response to Inside Climate News, the installation acknowledged that they continue to “actively contain and recover” spilled fuel trapped in soil that flushes into the creek during storms.
Piscataway Creek connects Joint Base Andrews, located in Prince George’s County, to the Potomac River near Fort Washington Park. The adjacent Piscataway Park provides public access points to the creek and the river for fishing and boating.
The initial incident drew criticism from lawmakers and environmental advocates over the base’s delay in reporting the spill. The fuel system failed a tightness test on Dec. 11, according to the MDE, which said the base’s leak detection system failed multiple times between January and March, spilling roughly 32,000 gallons of jet fuel into the creek.
The agency said it was not notified until fuel odors and a sheen were seen near the creek’s headwaters on March 23, and the base did not report the full extent of the discharge until April 8. The MDE, which has enforcement authority under state environmental regulations, then ordered the military facility to carry out an emergency soil investigation, install monitoring wells and remediate contaminated soils.
Differing estimates of how much fuel has spilled has complicated the mitigation work. A May letter nine members of Maryland’s Congressional delegation sent to U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink described approximately 32,000 gallons leaking across multiple dates and locations. Approximately 10,000 gallons from January and February incidents were reportedly contained within the fuel infrastructure and approximately 22,000 gallons were discharged into the environment.
The lawmakers asked for an accounting of how much fuel had entered the creek and how much remained underground, along with plans to prevent further contamination during rain events.
In its June 22 reply, the Air Force said the pressure-test failure on Dec. 11 was caused by a faulty valve that did not release fuel into the environment but distorted pressure readings. It said the anomaly delayed leak detection until the fuel was detected in the waters on March 23.
“JBA did not notify MDE of the failed pressure tests,” the Air Force said, adding that the matter is part of an ongoing internal investigation.
The Air Force did not provide the exact volume of the spill, saying it was “not yet possible” to determine how much fuel remained in soil, groundwater and the creek, and said it had recovered more than 35,000 gallons of a fuel-water mixture from the creek, a value the MDE has yet to verify.
“Over six months since the jet fuel leak was reported, JBA has yet to identify the exact location of the leak, diagnose the cause of the failure, or take appropriate action to fix the problem,” MDE representatives told Inside Climate News in the latest response.
In background interviews, agency officials vented their frustration that despite repeated requests over months, the base continues to stonewall requests for site-specific information, such as a basic site model displaying a map of fuel lines, creeks and environmental assets nearby, or the precise location of the crack in the underground fuel line. It has also not carried out standard subsurface probing to map the contamination plume under the tarmac. Under state oil control rules, agency officials noted, handlers of jet fuel are expected to account for every drop and quantify spills and the installation has not met that basic requirement.
The base did not respond to allegations that the MDE’s requests for information have been rebuffed. It offered a different assessment of the situation on the ground.
“The compromised section of the hydrant system was identified, isolated, and completely drained to eliminate any residual risk of fuel contaminating a water source,” a JBA spokesperson said in emailed comments. They did not say when this correction took place.
Asked whether its assertion that “the active leak has been stopped” meant the spilled fuel was no longer entering the creek, the spokesperson clarified that the assessment applied specifically to “fuel escaping from the infrastructure.”
The base further stated that its June testing could not conclusively determine the location and cause of the leak, and a pressure test is planned within the next few weeks. “The exact timeline for repairs will be dependent on the test results and subsequent engineering assessments,” it said, and that the affected sections would remain drained and isolated until repairs and retesting were completed.

Tight polls for Republicans are throwing future GOP leadership of the Senate health panel into question.
With Sens. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, and Susan Collins, R-Maine, fighting difficult reelection battles, itâs unclear who will replace Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy as the top Republican on the Senate HELP Committee.
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., is the next most senior person, but he would have to give up leading the Homeland Security Committee to helm the health panel. And Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, another member, could be in line to be the top GOP appropriator if Collins loses her reelection bid.
Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., would be next up after Paul and Murkowski, but he already leads the Senate Banking Committee.
Itâs not impossible that Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley, a staunch abortion opponent, lands the role opposite Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., on the committee.

The News
Democrats are hoping to persuade Latino voters to get out and vote for their candidates in droves in the midterms. A Latino organization says theyâll have the best chance of doing that by presenting solutions to the economy, housing, and abuses by ICE.
Polling by Voto Latino shared first with Semafor shows 40% of Latinos backing Democrats on the generic ballot, while just 21% support Republicans.
The group argues that bringing more Latinos into the Democratic fold will require running on solutions to pocketbook issues: Latino voters rank the cost of necessities as their top frustration, and view food and housing costs as most unreasonable.
âThis is where Democrats really have an opportunity to really bring back Latinos back to their corner,â said Beatriz Lopez, Voto Latinoâs executive director. âI think this is a pure opportunity, and itâs not to be wasted because if they waste it right now, itâs going to be even harder in â28.â
Know More
Voters are looking for âsome long-term solutions, some short-term solutions,â said Lopez. Among those surveyed, Latinos who didnât vote in 2024 were more likely than those who had voted to have economic frustrations, like struggling to earn enough money or find a good job.
âWhat we see in this poll is the people that are struggling the most are the ones who want the most,â said Voto Latino deputy director Ameer Patel.
Republicans have been hoping that the shift of Latino voters towards Trump and Republicans in 2024 would be part of a more durable trend, and drew new congressional districts in Florida and Texas to favor Republicans that relied in part on the Latino voting trends. Democrats, on the other hand, have hoped Latino voters would return to the left, motivated by economic concerns and the Trump administrationâs immigration enforcement.
Immigration still remains a major issue for Latino voters. Asked about immigration solutions for Congress to tackle, Latino voters polled picked investigating ICE as a top priority, alongside immigration changes like a pathway to citizenship and ending the immigration detention of children and families.

The News
A bipartisan pair of senators wants to do something bold before a new Congress takes over: Fix the Senateâs frequently maligned rules.
No, Sens. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Steve Daines, R-Mont., donât want to end the filibuster. But they have a proposal that would allow more bipartisan bills to get votes, end time-wasting procedures, and actually allow popular bills to come to the Senate floor and pass, according to details reviewed by Semafor.
âMore bills passed, more votes taken, less time wasted. That sums up,â Daines told Semafor in a joint interview with Merkley.
Itâs a big undertaking for the odd couple, but the effort has more momentum behind it than one would expect. Merkley is the Senateâs resident rules expert and has literally written the book on Senate gridlock. Daines, who is retiring, is close to two of the people theyâll need on board to pass the proposal: President Donald Trump and Senate Majority Leader John Thune. When Daines started exploring how to fix the Senate, all roads led to Merkley, who wrote Democratsâ last rules change proposal and spearheaded the push to end the 60-vote threshold for nominees.
The senators told Semafor they hear plenty of complaints from their colleagues about the Senateâs sluggish progress as an institution. One senator can force a week of debate on a popular bill, the government often runs on zombie continuing resolutions, and securing an amendment vote often requires consent from all 100 senators. Whatâs more, plenty of time is wasted for antiquated time rules like the âintervening dayâ on legislation or âpost-cloture timeâ â things Senate hopefuls arenât exactly briefed on when they launch their campaigns.
ââWe had productive professional lives in functional institutions, and what the hell happened to the Senate?ââ Merkley said, summing up complaints heâs heard from colleagues. âThe American people are saying the same thing.â
âOne thing you see here is people thinking about going home and being a governor. Why? Because states are not paralyzed the way the US Senate and House are,â the Oregon Democrat added. Daines agreed: âWe have morale challenges now in the United States Senate.â
Know More
The two senators have four major asks: They want to get rid of procedural (known as cloture) votes to begin debate on nominees, bills, and amendments while retaining the ability for the lawmakers in the minority to oppose efforts to close debate on controversial bills via the filibuster. Under their proposal, the intervening day before a vote to break a filibuster would be eliminated and debate time condensed, removing dead time from the Senate floor.
They also want to establish a fast-track suspension calendar, not unlike the House, that would allow the Senate to more quickly take up bills at a supermajority requirement of two-thirds of the Senate. Debate time for those bills would be limited and require coordination from committee leaders in both parties to get on the fast-track.
Daines and Merkley also want committee leaders to have a one-day fast-track for considering popular bills with strong committee support from both parties that would allow those bills to pass the Senate with a simple majority. Finally, their proposal would give Appropriations Committee leaders a quick route to the Senate floor for popular spending bills with plentiful spending amendment opportunities.
Itâs a tradeoff that would still allow the Senate minority to stop party-line bills or those without broad support and require real work by committee chairs and ranking members to get their products on the Senate floor.
But it would ensure that, like the House, a bill with two-thirds support can come to the floor quickly. It would minimize the ability of a single senator to block bills with huge support, like last week when Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., blocked the popular Kids Online Safety Act.
âThe goal here is to not make this a political fight. I think what we have proposed here is durable, regardless of which party is in power. We realize the benefits, no matter if Ds or Rs have a gavel,â Daines said. âAcross the last four Congresses, there have been 665 bipartisan bills passing through committees that go to the elephant graveyard.â
The pair is already talking to their respective party leaders about modernizing the Senate rules and theyâre optimistic about getting it passed at the required 67-vote threshold for a rules change. Daines is keeping Thune apprised.
Thune spokesman Ryan Wrasse said âThune is always open to discussing ways to make the Senate function in a more effective and efficient way, and he applauds Sen. Daines for thinking outside the box. Since no rules change can be implemented unilaterally, building a bipartisan consensus will be key to any modification of the existing process.â
Merkley said he talked to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic leader âdidnât say, âstop the discussion.ââ
Schumer and Thune ârecognize that there is frustration and dysfunction that merits a conversation,â Merkley said.
Trump, of course, wants to just kill the filibuster entirely. But Daines said the presidentâs team is engaged in their talks too.
âWe also ran the traps with key players in the White House. And got a thumbs up on it,â Daines said.
In an ideal world, they said theyâd also move the Senate more toward a talking filibuster and restrict the use of party-line budget reconciliation bills in order to reduce deficit spending. But they are starting with what they believe are broadly popular proposals that could get the chamber to devote a time to debate the rules â preferably before Daines leaves office.
That hasnât happened for awhile. Recent changes to Senate precedent have been made using the unilateral ânuclear optionâ which can be done in a party-line fashion by the majority. The next time a party uses the nuclear option to change Senate rules, they might nuke the supermajority requirement altogether, Merkley warned.

Peraton wants to bring AI-fueled project management to the Pentagon and beyond—while also changing the perception that it’s just an IT company.
It’s true the company has “a rich history of doing IT services and IT modernization across
government customers,” Gabe Camarillo, the company’s new defense sector president, told Defense One.
But Peraton is also big on defense prototyping and engineering: “We do Tomahawk theater mission planning support for the Navy,” he said, plus “modeling and simulation for Aegis. Also, sonar analysis and acoustic analysis for the Navy at Carderock. And then we also provide engineering support to some Army programs, like, for example, those that do aircraft survivability equipment.”
And those are areas ripe for growth, he said.
“We're looking to expand that footprint across the department, particularly at a time where new capabilities allow you to reduce risk in modernization programs, identify technical risks on system designs…achieve test and evaluation much more quickly. And bring that experience to bear to our customers to help them modernize at the pace they want to,” Camarillo said.
The former Army undersecretary stepped into the role this summer and said his overall vision is for Peraton to become the “go-to provider to manage and modernize enterprise IT across the department” which includes using AI to manage networks effectively.
And part of the vision is to bring what Peraton’s been doing with the $1.5 billion contract to overhaul the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control system to other government customers.
“One of the key aspects of that work that we're doing for the FAA is introducing AI-enabled program management, where it gives the leadership of the agency much better insight into how the program can be executed,” Camarillo said, adding that AI can spot cyber risks and map out an organization’s modernization plan.
“That kind of applied AI usage…[can] enable not just an end user to ask queries of an AI tool, but to really allow an enterprise to use the tool effectively for its own modernization. That’s where I think there's some secret sauce that Peraton has brought to the table, and we're looking to expand that across all of our customer sets, whether it's defense and non-defense.”
Welcome
You’ve reached the Defense Business Brief, where we dig into what the Pentagon buys, who they’re buying from, and why. Send along your tips, feedback, and song recommendations to lwilliams@defenseone.com. Check out the Defense Business Brief archive here, and tell your friends to subscribe!
On a waterfront near Baltimore during a shipbuilding announcement Tuesday, President Donald Trump brought up tariffs, which he now calls his “fourth” or “fifth favorite word.” The comments weren’t new, but they were a reminder of simmering concerns about how U.S. trade relations, particularly with close allies, could affect national security.
- “Our drug industry is coming back. Our car industry is coming back. They're leaving Canada. They're leaving Mexico. They're leaving Japan, Germany, South Korea. We're building car plants,” he said. “It's all because of my favorite word, my fourth favorite…tariff,” the president said. (Context: There are multiple reports that U.S. tariffs on imported goods, such as automobiles from Canada, create uncertainty and the U.S. trade deficit is worsening.)
- The president’s comments reminded me of exchanges last week during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on Golden Dome, in which lawmakers on both sides of the aisle raised concerns that the escalating U.S. trade war with Canada could spill into defense.
- “They're a good ally. They're a good neighbor. They are modernizing NORAD right now…It's my understanding, though, that an agreement hasn't been reached with Canada yet on Golden Dome,” Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., who chairs the Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Strategic Forces, said during the hearing last week. “I think as we progress along there, my hope would be that we can continue to have a good working relationship there to really protect both of our countries.”
- Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., agreed, saying tensions between the neighboring allies have necessitated multiple “peacekeeping visits to Ottawa” and that it’s “unrealistic to expect that you can treat an ally badly in one domain, on the economy, but expect…to work cooperatively in terms of our defense.”
- Some background: The senators’ concerns echo those circulating since last year when the White House issued hefty tariffs on Canada and threatened to make the sovereign nation the 51st state. Those qualms have resurfaced as U.S.-Canada trade talks faltered in August and as a new batch of tariffs—and retaliatory tariffs—took hold this week. On the defense side, Canada has been reviewing its decision to buy 16 F-35As for months. And even if the trade war is resolved, there’s concern about an overall cooling in U.S.-Canada relations.
Making moves + other news
- General Dynamics President Danny Deep will take over as the company’s next CEO in 2027. CEO Phebe Novakovic will become executive chairman of the company’s board of directors.
- Peraton hired two more former Army officials as vice presidents: Jennifer Swanson and Danielle Moyer.
- The Army inked a $9.5 million deal to expand use of Reveal Technology’s intelligence platform Farsight with the service’s Nett Warrior system.
- Ursa Major added ex-Pentagon official David Rader as its chief strategy officer.
- ACMI, which builds defense production hubs, added Limitless Aeronautics to its Indiana campus.
- Kaizen, the company that helped build the Pentagon’s counterdrone marketplace, landed a $49 million deal for unclassified work for the Army.
- Auterion debuted a universal UAS launcher.
- Tiberius Aerospace snagged a $500 million deal to build and distribute its Sceptre precision-guided missile as part of a U.S.-U.K. collaboration.

Environmental groups and citizens are urging Pennsylvania regulators to increase the minimum amount of protective buffer space between gas wells and homes, schools and water sources. The issue has taken on new urgency as the AI data center buildout spurs more demand for natural gas.
On Wednesday, a coalition of environmental and community groups held an event at the state capitol to draw attention to their concerns. They complain they’ve been waiting two years for the Department of Environmental Protection to move forward with a petition they filed in 2024, urging the agency to increase minimum setback requirements.
Katie Weber lives in Hanover Township, Washington County and went to Harrisburg because she’s concerned about plans to build a large cluster of data centers powered by an on-site natural gas plant near her home.
“We are united and our message is clear,” Weber said. “We do not want data centers, and we do not want fracking anywhere near our homes, our schools or our daycares.” The day before, activists argued for a three-year moratorium on data centers in another rally at the capitol.
Gov. Josh Shapiro had been an early proponent of the AI buildout in the state, but shifted his stance earlier this year as public opposition mounted. He has signed executive orders aimed at putting some limits on data centers, including having them “build, bring online, or buy incremental electric capacity” to power their facilities. The goal is for data center builders to foot the bill for the increased power demand instead of Pennsylvania ratepayers.
More Data Centers, More Natural Gas
Environmental advocates, like Lisa Graves-Marcucci of the Environmental Integrity Project, worry Shapiro’s efforts will push data center builders to rely more heavily on natural gas to power the facilities—leading to more pollution on site and negative environmental and health impacts from increased shale gas production.
“We’ve realized now that fracking will fuel the data centers,” said Graves-Marcucci. “Communities that already have a lot of fracking could see an increase, or communities that don’t have fracking may get some. It’s all the more reason we need these protective setback distances.”
Environmental groups argue a growing body of peer-reviewed research shows more space would provide more protection from potential health harms, including chronic stress, excessive noise and light, poor air quality, vehicle accidents, explosions and chemical spills.
Two years ago, the coalition of groups filed what’s called a petition for rulemaking with the state Department of Environmental Protection’s Environmental Quality Board— asking regulators to evaluate whether the existing setback requirements could be expanded. For example, under current law, a gas well could be 500 feet from a home.
“We are looking for a common-sense protective setback of one kilometer, which is a little over 3,000 feet,” said Gillian Graber, executive director of Protect PT, a community group for Westmoreland and Allegheny counties. “The current setback is very old and out of date.”
Their petition also calls for greater distances between gas wells and buildings serving vulnerable populations like schools or hospitals. David Hess, a former secretary of the Department of Environmental Protection, who authors a blog covering state environmental issues, views the push to increase the setbacks as reasonable.
“We’ve been shale gas drilling here in Pennsylvania for more than 20 years, and to not look at those kinds of issues, like setbacks and other things, would be a huge oversight,” Hess said. “We’ve learned a lot from these operations and how they impact people living next to them. If anyone thinks 500 feet is adequate to deal with any of the issues, I think they’re kidding themselves.”
In 2018 Colorado expanded its oil and gas well setback requirements to be 1,000 feet from schools. A 2020 grand jury report about fracking in Pennsylvania led by then Attorney General Josh Shapiro recommended 2,500 foot setbacks for buildings and 5,000 feet for schools and hospitals.
DEP spokesman Neil Shader said the agency is continuing to review the petition.
“DEP thoroughly reviews all petitions submitted, along with the other associated materials submitted with the petition, before delivering a recommendation to the EQB,” Shader wrote in an email. “This particular petition included several scientific studies, which DEP is reviewing using in-house experts (including a toxicologist) to be able to deliver a fully informed recommendation to the EQB.”
The Marcellus Shale Coalition, a natural gas industry trade group, argues the DEP lacks the legal authority to increase the setback requirements via this rulemaking petition, because those limits are already spelled out in state law, and any changes would have to go through the legislature.
Patrick Henderson, vice president of government affairs and communications at the Marcellus Shale Coalition, previously worked in Republican Gov. Tom Corbett’s administration and helped update the state’s oil and gas law in 2012, in response to the drilling boom.
“That process Governor Tom Corbett put forth was the product of an advisory commission that he appointed with environmental, industry, local government officials and academia to develop,” said Henderson. “Those setback requirements derived a lot from that input.”
Lisa Graves-Marcucci of the Environmental Integrity Project, said the environmental groups are hopeful DEP will respond to them before the end of the year.
“There is no draft rule,” she pointed out. “We’re just waiting for the formality for them to say they’ve reviewed the petition. We believe it merits the full process of rulemaking.”

Thirty-three people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting a bus carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Russia is trying to seize as part of Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
However, Thursday's attack follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.
Russia is now launching constant air raids against Ukraine, with sirens ringing throughout the day in the capital Kyiv. According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.
In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack, however rescue officials said the attack caused a fire on two buses that were both carrying passengers.
Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the Donetsk region to move to safer regions of Ukraine.
Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.
Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.
Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".
Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of warned of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the best defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.
For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.
Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk City Council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets."

A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
The incident happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal and there were casualties reported, the UKMTO said.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers, which was reported as laden with cargo on Saturday as it sailed towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).
The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.
This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.
Vanguard also reported a fire on board another tanker on Thursday in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates. It said the vessel was likely to be the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.
The cause of the fire is unclear and the UKMTO has not reported an incident in the area.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

dca65523cfbd.text: Republicans are in a dogfight to defend the Latino gains that had them dreaming of a lasting political realignment just two years ago. Why it matters: Nowhere is that reversal of fortune more visible than in South Texas, where President Trump ran up historic numbers in 2024 — and Republicans redrew the map in 2025, assuming those Latino gains would last. Trump won 55% of Texas Latino voters in 2024 exit polls, carried 14 of the 18 counties within 20 miles of the border and won all four Rio Grande Valley counties. Polling shows Trump's disapproval ratings have skyrocketed among Latinos in Texas since 2024. Democrats and allied groups are now pouring money into races across the Rio Grande Valley. Zoom in: The reversal is starkest in TX-15, where Rep. Monica De La Cruz was one of the GOP's most visible symbols of its South Texas breakthrough. Trump would have carried the newly-drawn district by 18 percentage points in 2024. De La Cruz won her 2024 race under the previous map by 14 points. Cook Political Report moved the race from Lean Republican to Toss Up on Sept. 25, saying public and private polling shows the race tied or even favoring Tejano singer and Democrat Bobby Pulido . By the numbers: Democratic campaigns and allied groups are outspending Republican campaigns and groups on Spanish-language ads in two of the three competitive House districts covering the Rio Grande Valley, according to AdImpact data reported by the Texas Tribune . In TX-34, held by Vicente Gonzalez (D), Democratic campaigns and groups have spent $2.7 million on Spanish-language ads, compared with $1.6 million on the Republican side. In TX-15, Democratic groups have spent more than twice as much as Republican groups on Spanish-language ads. TX-28 bucks the trend: Republicans have narrowly outspent Democrats on Spanish-language ads to unseat Henry Cuellar (D). Zoom out: TX-34 is also a Toss Up, while TX-28 is Lean Democratic. The newly redrawn TX-35 has moved from Likely Republican to Lean Republican. House Majority PAC launched another round of ads Tuesday in TX-15, TX-28 and TX-34, defending two Democratic incumbents while continuing to target De La Cruz. The bottom line: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll shows Latinos nationally favor Democratic control of Congress 59%-35%, a 24-point advantage — roughly double the margin the same poll found for Democrats in 2024. A recent TelevisaUnivision poll found Latino voters in the three competitive Texas House districts shifting from a 44%-44% split in their 2024 presidential vote to 56%-36% Democratic on the 2026 congressional ballot.

South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.
But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.
In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

Police in central Chile have airlifted several residents to safety after rising floodwaters left them trapped in their homes.
Recent torrential rains caused the Mapocho river to burst its banks, flooding large parts of the city of Talagante, 35km (22 miles) south-west of the capital, Santiago.
Santiago has seen 74mm of rainfall in the first seven days of this month, making it the rainiest October for the area in 76 years, meteorologists have said.
They have warned that this year's unusually strong El NiÃ±o climate phenomenon will likely continue to bring unusually wet weather, powerful winds and storms to the region during the southern hemisphere's spring.
Officials said one person had been found dead in a flooded underpass in the city of San Bernardo, south of Santiago, although they have yet to confirm the cause of death.
In Talagante, police used helicopters to rescue people and pets living on the banks of the Mapocho who had been surprised by the fast-rising waters overnight.
Dirt roads turned into rivers in the riverside community which, unlike in July's storms, had not been evacuated ahead of the heavy downpours.
Climate experts have warned that the 2026-2027 El NiÃ±o is likely to cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, intensifying droughts in some areas and floods in others.
In central Chile, it is expected to trigger above-average rainfall.

Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.
Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.
The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature".
The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime's body of work and is regareded as the most prestigious award in global literature with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (Â£900,000, $1.2m).
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement.
"She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind," Carlberg, said.
"She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice."
Anders Olsson, chairman of the Swedish Academy's Nobel committee for Literature, praised the way Carson has "broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature".
"This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms," he said.
Carson's notable works include The Glass Essay, Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse, Nox, Float and The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos.
Carson has also translated ancient Greek literature and has been a professor of classics for more than 30 years.

The EU trade commissioner pressed China to balance trade with the bloc, but major divisions between the sides in negotiations and rising tensions have dampened hopes for a breakthrough. Europeâs trade deficit with China has sparked growing alarm on the continent, which fears Chinese goods will hollow out its industries, driving job losses and economic anxiety that ultimately fuel the rise of nationalist parties.
Brussels had initially proposed Beijing voluntarily cap the number of hybrid vehicles it exported to the EU, but China rejected that proposal. Experts instead warn of a looming trade war, with Germany and France calling for the EU to ready new tools that could combat China.

Franceâs challenges mounted as concerns over its ballooning debt weighed on economic activity and reverberated across Europe. Economists argue planned government spending cuts do not go far enough and political divisions â far-left and far-right parties instead want the European Central Bank to buy up or even cancel French debt â suggest Parisâ proposed budget faces an uphill battle to pass.
Political uncertainty is hampering business investment, Franceâs biggest business group has warned, while anxious consumers are holding off on purchases. Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.
Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.
Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of flouting democracy.
Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.
Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.
The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.
Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.
A party or coalition which emerges with the largest share of the votes - provided this exceeds 42% - will be awarded 105 additional seats in parliament (70 in the lower house and 35 in the senate), which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.
In a debate ahead of the vote, centre-left members accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.
The proposals have also exposed tensions within the ranks of Meloni's coalition, too, with the Brothers of Italy (FdI) party and its allies, the far-right League and centre-right Forza Italia.
Analysts had predicted that Thursday's final vote was unlikely to fail - particularly given the number of lawmakers who would risk losing their eligibility for a parliamentary pension if their term was ended early as a result of the threatened snap election.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided," Meloni wrote on social media after the vote, "today we respond with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens."
She added: "We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary coherence of any government, regardless of its political colour."
Meloni's term officially comes to an end in October 2027, although she could bring elections forward to the spring.

The Scene
As Western governments slash foreign aid, many organizations are seeking Gulf philanthropy to fill the gaps. While wealthy individuals and governments in the region are ready to take on a larger role, a younger generation of donors isnât content with plowing money into existing programs, and is instead seeking new approaches with more effective and measurable outcomes.
Sonia Ben Jaafar, CEO of the Abdulla Al Ghurair Foundation, told Semafor that private donors from the Gulf want to be more involved in designing development programs rather than simply financing them. She said the regionâs charities have developed their own expertise that can help inform changes to improve existing charitable programs. The foundation she runs â established in 2015 by Emirati billionaire Abdulla Al Ghurair and chaired by his son Abdul Aziz â has become one of the Arab worldâs largest privately funded education initiatives, reaching about 500,000 young people over the past decade.
The foundation runs like a business, using performance metrics to evaluate its grants and tying funding decisions to outcomes such as job placement rates, Ben Jaafar said. The approach fits within a broader push by Badr Jafar, the UAEâs special envoy for business and philanthropy, to bring private donors, businesses, and governments together to address humanitarian needs.
In an interview in New York during the UN General Assembly, Ben Jaafar discussed the changing role of private wealth in the region, and why her foundation is quick to drop programs that donât deliver results.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Why is private philanthropy hesitant to step in to cover underfunded programs that have been abandoned by many governments?
The narrative that philanthropic capital will just fill that up is not going to happen. What weâre hearing in the discussions, at least that Iâm in, in the closed rooms, is: What does the new framework look like? Because it cannot be more of the same, and philanthropic capital shouldnât be coming in as a gap filler.
We need a new model of how public, private, and philanthropy â this is the new three Ps â are going to partner together.
How does the Abdulla Al Ghurair Foundation measure the success of its programs?
We have a strategy that would look like any business, except instead of generating revenue, we need to generate impact for the communities we serve.
We have, on average, a [jobs] placement rate of 78%, which is a very high placement rate in my field. We donât count just who we train. We want to know that that training landed them into a revenue-generating life.
You were early to get into Syria after the war ended. What are you focusing on there?
Weâre training young Syrians to learn construction skills, and paying them to attend an apprenticeship program. Those graduates will then work on the schools we started to refurbish there.
During the war, we started a fund in 2018 that was focused on educating refugees in Lebanon and Jordan. Some of those Syrians are now returnees and are being picked up by government administration and companies to support the reconstruction.
Have you funded programs that didnât work?
We have funded programs that we were sure would work, and we were sure we had the right partner to implement it.
Because itâs outcomes-based funding, if you cannot meet the milestone and you donât have a good reason, or we canât find a solution with you, then we will defund that. Weâll stop. Weâll sunset that, and weâll find a new way of doing it.
Notable
- Abdul Aziz Al Ghurair runs his philanthropy like a business. The foundationâs chairman urged donors to set measurable goals and work with governments and businesses to maximize impact.
- The Gulfâs wealth transfer could reshape charitable giving. Badr Jafar, the UAEâs special envoy for business and philanthropy, told Semafor that more than $1 trillion will change hands in the region by 2030, accelerating a shift toward impact-driven philanthropy.

A bear has killed a man and seriously injured a woman after it attacked them in their home near the Mongolian capital, Ulaanbaatar.
Police say the incident happened in the Bayanzurkh district overnight on Wednesday in their traditional Mongolian nomadic tent-like structure known as a ger.
The man, who was in his 40s, died, but the woman, in her 50s, managed to flee and raise the alarm with neighbours. She is in a serious condition in hospital, city official Munkhbayar M told reporters.
Sightings of bears around humans are becoming more common in Mongolia, for reasons that include climate change and food scarcity.
A team of rangers is searching for the bear while officials have warned locals to be vigilant and report any sightings.
There had been 24 bear sightings near the capital this year alone, compared to just two in 2018, Munkhbayar said, in comments reported by the AFP news agency.
Videos showing bears entering or damaging gers, and attacking livestock have reportedly gone viral on Mongolian social media in recent weeks, highlighting the increase in bear and human interaction across the country.
Bear-hunting permits across eight provinces have been issued and officials are seeking to obtain tranquiliser dart guns to support rangers in rural areas, AFP reports.
A significant amount of Mongolians are nomadic, but settled agricultural communities are becoming more common. An increasing number of the population lives in the capital or other major urban areas.

Abu Dhabiâs Technology Innovation Institute, a state-run research body, released AI models trained on the Emirati Arabic dialect, improving translation, transcription, and voice-enabled services. The Falcon-Emirati model and related tools for speech recognition and extracting Arabic text from images and documents are relatively compact. The speech recognition model has 1.6 billion parameters, but is more accurate than a 30-billion-parameter model, according to TII.

An experimental drug may melt away a dangerous type of fat that packs around internal organs.
The drug, called CBL-514, specifically triggers fat cells to enter a death program called apoptosis. People who got injections of the experimental drug in their lower abdomens lost visceral fat, researchers reported October 1 at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy. Visceral fat sits deep in the abdomen where it chokes organs and can spur inflammation and health problems.
Weight loss can shrink fat cells, but the cells are still there, poised to balloon up again.
The team already knew the experimental drug could reduce subcutaneous fat, the pinchable fat that sits under the skin, in the abdomen. That surface fat doesn’t carry the same health risks that visceral fat does.
In the new study, researchers examined MRIs from a subset of participants in two small clinical trials to track visceral fat levels. Study participants, who ranged from healthy weights to overweight, got injections of CBL-514 or placebo every three weeks for up to 12 weeks. The two groups started with about the same amount of visceral fat; 642.5 milliliters on average in the CBL-514 group and 677.4 milliliters in the placebo group. Four weeks after treatment, those who got the experimental drug had dropped almost 71 mL of visceral fat (a 12 percent decrease), while the placebo group gained 31 mL (a nearly 6 percent increase) of the dangerous fat in their abdomens.
Measurements taken at eight to 12 weeks after treatment showed the gap had widened. Those who got the experimental drug lost almost 63 mL — about a quarter cup — of visceral fat on average while the placebo group gained more than 78 mL of visceral fat over the starting point. Those results suggest that the drug might have health benefits by reducing visceral fat, which contributes to diabetes and heart problems. Larger clinical trials to test efficacy and safety of the drug are ongoing.

In Montgomery County, Indiana, utility-scale solar projects appear on an official list of undesirable land uses that also includes “adult-oriented businesses.”
So it wasn’t surprising that the county Board of Commissioners unanimously rejected a 200-megawatt solar project on Sept. 28.
But it still stings for renewable energy advocates. It shows a huge challenge lurking right behind the debate over a U.S. Senate energy permitting bill. Even if the federal government eases the permitting process, much of the country is off-limits for wind and solar development because local residents and their elected officials oppose it.
One person who repeatedly defended the Indiana project at public meetings was John Smillie, a solar power supporter who lives in Crawfordsville, the county seat. He works as a finance manager for an industrial lighting company and does charitable work, written about by Canary Media, to help nonprofits install solar.
I spoke with Smillie this week to explore how Montgomery County and the country are supposed to move into the energy future when a seemingly beneficial project gets smacked down in such a fashion.
“Hearing the disinformation is very difficult,” he said.
For example, people opposing the project said China doesn’t use solar panels, it just sells the panels to the United States.
“That’s radically untrue,” Smillie said. Indeed, China has installed more solar power than any other country.
Video of the meeting shows more than an hour of testimony, including repeated claims that solar is a danger to human and animal health. Such concerns are widely debunked, but they are repeated at government meetings as if they were true.
Commissioners said they were swayed by testimony that the project may reduce nearby property values and change the character of the area.
“This is a large agricultural area,” said Commissioner Jim Fulwider.
Solar will “change the looks and the surroundings of that community for years to come with the size of that project,” he said.
Researchers have looked at how solar and wind projects may affect property values. A 2023 study from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory—which did not include data from Indiana—showed small effects in some states, but nothing close to the drastic changes that opponents have claimed.
Much of the world of environmental and clean energy advocacy is now focusing on the permitting bill in the U.S. Senate, announced on Sept. 30.
Supporters of the bill, including clean energy industry groups, say it would unleash a building boom for interstate power lines, wind, solar and battery projects. Opponents, including many environmental advocacy groups, say the measure would accelerate construction of fossil fuel infrastructure and lock in decades of emissions that contribute to climate change.
I think what happened in Montgomery County and similar communities across the country must be part of the discussion. Even if federal permitting gets easier, developers will struggle to build if local residents and elected officials are not on board.
By the end of 2025, there were 888 state and local laws restricting renewable energy across 48 states, according to Columbia Law School’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. The center’s database shows restrictions in more than 30 of Indiana’s 92 counties.
Notably, Montgomery County is not one of them. Its limits are indirect, stemming from a comprehensive planning process in 2024 that includes wind and solar as undesirable land uses, based on focus groups with residents. The county’s list of undesirable uses also has junkyards, landfills and adult-oriented businesses, among others.
Researchers at Ball State University in Muncie, Indiana, released a policy brief in April showing that county-level restrictions on wind and solar are associated with a decrease in economic activity, while Indiana counties without restrictions saw a net gain. The limits on development also contributed to a net loss of jobs, mainly in manufacturing and transportation, that were partly offset by small gains in agricultural jobs.
I reached out to Engie North America, developer of the solar project, and the Montgomery County Board of Commissioners, and didn’t hear back from either.
The project would have paid more than $40 million in local taxes during its lifespan and generated enough electricity each year to meet the needs of about 32,000 households, according to Engie North America. The company planned to spend more than $300 million to build the solar farm.
It’s not every day that Montgomery County has a company wanting to invest $300 million.
And the project was to be in a location with few houses within view, with greenery planted to partially block the view, Smillie said.
“Most people going through Montgomery County would never have noticed it was there,” he said.
I don’t have a solution to the problem playing out in Indiana and so many other places.
Ideally, developers would get better at connecting with local residents and elected officials, while local officials would find ways to use revenue from renewable energy projects to reduce taxes and fund community priorities.
States could also step in to limit the ability of local governments to block projects, as Illinois, Michigan and others have done. That approach may lead to more projects being built, but it can also deepen resentment from rural communities and probably isn’t a long-term solution.
I asked Smillie how he felt walking out of that meeting.
“Pretty doomy,” he said.
Same.
