The Chrysler Building, one of the most distinctive high-rises in Manhattan's skyline, will undergo a major renovation as part of a multi-million-dollar sale deal.
The skyscraper, opened in New York nearly 100 years ago, will see its Art Deco crown polished and restored during a refurbishment that will also involve the restoration of the building's 77-storey faÃ§ade.
Developer Tishman Speyer has taken over the lease from the Cooper Union for the Advancement of Science and Art, a private college.
Tishman Speyer and its partners will invest $235m (Â£178m) in the project, as part of which it will upgrade the 61st floor, which is home to huge eagle gargoyles and will also feature an "upscale" lounge.
The developer is planning to use most of the building, which is close to Grand Central railway station, for office space. It is following what it calls a "prebuild approach" that will allow firms to move into their new premises quickly.
Tishman Speyer explained that the area "has one of the lowest office availability rates in Manhattan", adding: "Construction of new office supply in the neighbourhood has been virtually nonexistent for decades."
The renovation will include internal work, such as upgrades to the building's mechanical, elevator, electrical and air handling systems.
At 1,046ft (319m), the Chrysler Building was once the world's tallest building - before being usurped less than a year later by the nearby Empire State Building.
Financed by Walter Chrysler, the motor magnate, the skyscraper's construction began in 1928 and was completed two years later.
Architect William Van Alen modelled the eagle gargoyles on hood ornaments found on the 1929 Chrysler car.
The Cooper Union college, whose alumni include inventor Thomas Edison, has owned the land on which the Chrysler Building stands since 1902.
The land was bequeathed to it by the children of Peter Cooper, a manufacturer and industrialist who founded the college in 1859.
As part of the deal, Tishman Speyer will make ground lease payments to the Cooper Union which the college wants to use to finance "a bold plan to restore full-tuition scholarships for all undergraduates".
Cooper Union's president Steven McLaughlin, said: "The significance of this agreement is ultimately about what it makes possible for generations of Cooper Union students."

A former teacher who sexually assaulted a student has been returned to jail in Indonesia after a BBC investigation revealed he was secretly released early.
Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2022 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a female student at his father's prominent Islamic boarding school in East Java, where he worked as a teacher.
A BBC Eye undercover investigation revealed he was secretly released on parole in August 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The woman he had been convicted of assaulting had not been informed - despite her legal right to know.
On hearing he was back in prison, she cried with relief.
"I pray that this doesn't happen to anyone else and that, going forward, the law will be applied justly in Indonesia," the former student, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC.
The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections previously told the BBC that Bechi was released because of sentence reductions granted in accordance with regulations.
But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review.
That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison.
Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions".
"We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said.
For Ira Puspitasari, one of several former students who accused Bechi of sexual abuse and testified at his trial, the decision is a vindication.
"I'm amazed, really. I didn't expect the government would pay such detailed attention to this case and really pay attention to us, the victims," she said.
Ira, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by Bechi for more than four years, from the age of 15.
"I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she said.
She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her.
She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her complaint. She also shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened".
Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube, external.
Watching BBC undercover footage of Bechi smiling and greeting supporters at an event in March, when he should still have been in prison, Ira became tearful.
"It's like nothing ever happened," she said.
Ira was invited to a parliamentary hearing this week into the state's handling of sexual abuse cases in religious and educational institutions, held in response to the BBC's investigation.
Lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has represented several victims of abuse in educational institutions, also addressed the hearing and said authorities were often reluctant to investigate allegations of abuse because they involved "influential religious figures who have large followings".
He told the hearing that he regularly faced threats and intimidation as a result of taking on such cases.
Bechi is the son of prominent Islamic cleric Muhammad Mukhtar Mu'thi, founder of the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in Jombang, East Java.
He was arrested in 2022 after a 15-hour police siege at the school, where supporters had gathered to prevent his arrest.
Prosecutors had sought a longer sentence after Bechi was accused of rape by a number of students, but he was acquitted of the rape charges and convicted of the lesser sexual assault offence of one student.
The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah boarding school as part of its investigation but received no response.

A congressional candidate in Arizona has said she was raped in a car park as she repaired campaign signs late at night in her district.
Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democrat, told the Phoenix New Times, external she was knocked unconscious during the alleged attack in the Phoenix suburb of Sun City on 14 August, waking up to find a man on top of her.
She said she did not initially notify police until filing a report with the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office two weeks later.
Her Republican opponent, Abraham Hamadeh, urged authorities in a statement to "investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place".
"No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community," said Hamadeh, who is running for a second term in office.
Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times she was "embarrassed" and "just wanted to forget", but felt compelled stand up for other victims.
The candidate said she often speaks on the campaign trail about fighting for Arizonans.
She told the Phoenix New Times: "I didn't feel like I could keep saying that if I weren't also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault."
The BBC has contacted the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office for comment. A sheriff's spokesman told the New York Times the investigation was ongoing.
After the attack, Greene-Placentia said she withdrew from the public for two days, staying in an apartment separate from her husband and skipping a campaign event.
When she emerged, her husband, campaign staff and others in her circle noticed she was acting differently, according to Phoenix New Times.
Greene-Placentia said she did not see a doctor following the alleged attack in congressional district eight and did not receive a sexual assault examination.
She said her memory of what happened was spotty and she did not get a good look at either of the two assailants, but described them as white men, according to the New York Times.
She told the Phoenix New Times that one assailant may have made a comment about her political affiliation, together with a misogynistic slur, although she could not be certain.
The candidate said she was concerned voters might think it was a political stunt to win points in a heavily Republican district. She also expressed concern that the allegations might overshadow her messaging around affordability.

In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.
"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.
He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.
"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.
Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.
She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.
But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.
"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.
In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.
The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.
"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."
Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.
The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.
On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.
His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.
Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.
Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west.
Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space.
The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas.
In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters.
In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%.
Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline.
"Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said.
Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own.
Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began.
"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.
"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."
There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.
The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.
Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.
Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.
Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.

Some blind people can now find a doorway or spot an object with the help of an experimental treatment and custom goggles.
Participants in a new study had blindness caused by a genetic disease called retinitis pigmentosa, which progressively kills off light-sensing cells in the retina. The treatment improved seven of 10 people’s light sensitivity, researchers report October 7 in New England Journal of Medicine. The findings build on a 2021 report that the same approach helped one blind man see and count objects.
The treatment is based on optogenetics, a technique that uses genetic instructions to make cells respond to light. Rather than repair the retina’s damaged light detectors, it gives that ability to retinal ganglion cells that normally relay visual signals to the brain.
“This is a proof of concept that optogenetics can bring back some visual activity [and] object sensitivity,” says Botond Roska, neuroscientist at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel in Switzerland.
Pioneering work on optogenetics snagged the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on October 5.
Scientists have been experimenting with optogenetic therapies to rewire the eye and restore vision to people with degenerative eye diseases for more than a decade. Just as in the 2021 study, in the new work Roska and his colleagues injected genetic instructions for ChrimsonR, a light-sensitive protein derived from algae, into participants’ worse-seeing eye. The treatment made retinal ganglion cells in that eye sensitive to amber light. A camera in the custom goggles detected changes in brightness in what was in front of a study participant, and the goggles projected those changes onto the retina as pulses of amber light, activating the treated cells.
Four of the eight study participants who completed behavioral testing after treatment were able to find a doorway or follow a line while wearing the goggles. No patient gained the ability to read visual words or see faces, but Roska and his colleagues hope to tackle that next.
But there’s a limitation to this work. The approach requires a working optic nerve to carry signals to the brain, says study coauthor José-Alain Sahel, an ophthalmologist at the University of Pittsburgh. It relies on cells in the retina communicating to the brain, so it cannot restore vision when that connection is damaged.

1b58aa29b0f6.text: Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that he is suspending Microsoft , Adobe and several other IT firms' ability to hire foreign-born workers for permanent jobs in the U.S. Why it matters: The move will affect hundreds of companies owned by the tech giant, escalating the Trump administration's cracking down on immigrant labor. What they're saying: " We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector," Vance said during a Thursday news conference. "We're the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers." "And so our message to Microsoft is, you're great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants." Zoom in: The program, the permanent labor certification program , administered through the Department of Labor, allows a company to hire a foreign worker to live permanently in America. Driving the news: Vance specifically singled out Microsoft, slamming them for laying off 6,000 workers last year. Vance said Thursday that "[a]t the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. Now that is a scandalous system that we've allowed in this country for far too long." Microsoft owns hundreds of companies, including LinkedIn, Skype and gaming studio Activision Blizzard. He also called out and suspended Adobe and IT outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini from the program. Worth noting: Trump will award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House today. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

408b95737b39.text: Prosecutors accused former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Thursday of orchestrating the torture of people held in his regime's custody, piling onto the narcoterrorism charges they already face. The big picture: The charges add new fuel to the historic prosecution seeking to hold the strongman-turned-prisoner accountable for alleged crimes against Americans and alleged abuse of power. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, pleaded not guilty in January to drug- and weapon-related charges. They have been held in the U.S. since Maduro's stunning capture from Caracas earlier this year. Driving the news: Maduro "authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention, and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition," a superseding indictment filed in the Southern District of New York alleged. The indictment outlines a series of disturbing torture tactics — including electrocution, beatings, isolation and simulated drowning — allegedly employed at Maduro's direction to quell political opposition. "As opposition to the ruling regime intensified," Maduro allegedly "continued to oversee the development of a more systematic approach to unlawfully arresting and torturing dissidents," per the indictment, ordering who would be arrested and tortured. One unnamed victim who the indictment described as "friendly" with "a famous opponent of the regime" was told by his captors that they would kill his young child, whose hair color they referenced. It also details abuse against Americans, including one who was allegedly falsely accused of participating in a conspiracy to kill Maduro. That victim was allegedly tortured with electric shocks, asphyxiation and forced injection of a substance that made him have seizures. Catch up quick: Americans who were formerly imprisoned in Venezuela have accused Maduro of heading a web of corruption that used Americans as negotiating tools. In a lawsuit filed last year, Matthew Heath and Osman Khan, two Americans freed in a 2022 prisoner swap, alleged they were subjected to electrocution, suffocation, severe beatings and food and water deprivation, among other threats and forms of torture. Members of a group of oil executives, known as the CITGO-6, also released in October 2022, alleged they faced physical and emotional torture while in Venezuelan custody. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

Rubio told reporters that he would not discuss the allegations contained in a Wall Street Journal story that said Guilfoyle had asked a donor and supporter of President Donald Trump to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. Sisak, Associated Press By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cornell-gang-rape-accuser-was-misled-about-criminal-investigation-her-lawyer-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cornell gang-rape accuser was 'misled' about criminal investigation, her lawyer says Nation Oct 8, 2026 10:43 AM EDT ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — The woman accusing several men of raping her at a Cornell University fraternity party was "misled" about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said Wednesday. WATCH: What the Cornell case reveals about how sexual assault allegations are handled Even as she took her allegations about a 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house through Cornell's internal disciplinary process, the university's police department gave her the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, lawyer Thomas Giuffra told The Associated Press. In fact, the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, the local prosecutor, made the decision not to go forward with a criminal case within days of the woman giving her first substantial interviews to police. READ MORE: Woman told Cornell investigators she 'felt like bait' during alleged gang rape Van Houten has said that he asked Cornell's police department to convey the decision to the woman, who is referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, but never spoke personally to her or her lawyer. Giuffra said the woman was told that the criminal investigation was ongoing. "I think she was misled. She was told it was still — they weren't going to prosecute, but they were still investigating," Giuffra said. "I was involved with this case early on. I thought they were still investigating. It was news to me that they weren't doing anything." Giuffra added that at the time, he assumed investigators just needed more time to speak with witnesses and build a case. READ MORE: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency "But nothing was being done, and we didn't know that," Giuffra said. A message seeking comment was left for Van Houten. Cornell's media relations office, citing pending litigation, declined to comment on behalf of the university's police department. The district attorney said in a statement last week that he was confident that no further investigation was necessary after prosecutors and criminal investigators from his office reviewed a six-page summary of the woman's account, written by a police officer. Summary left out key details, lawyer says Based on that summary, Van Houten said he believed no crime had been committed, and that the woman's participation in drug use and sex was "voluntary, conscious and consensual." That description differs sharply with what the woman told police and university investigators, and with what she alleged in a lawsuit filed against seven Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others last month. WATCH: New details intensify scrutiny of Cornell's handling of gang rape allegations Among other things, Giuffra said, the six-page report omitted the woman telling investigators, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," that she was subjected to physical violence, and that a fraternity brother had sent a message to a group chat using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman's body was freely available. Last week, citing investigative records it obtained, The New York Times reported that a Cornell police investigator tried to get Van Houten's office to consider additional evidence in the weeks after the alleged rape, but was rebuffed. "At first I thought these police were incompetent," Giuffra said. "It sounds like they were doing the right thing. And they just got shut down." Giuffra said that while he and Jane Doe have received death threats, he has been heartened by an outpouring of support, including rallies and protests on the Cornell campus and more than 1,000 women who have emailed him to share anger, frustration, solidarity and stories of their own assaults. Students rally against sexual violence Some Cornell students staged a sit-in at a dining hall and vowed not to spend money on campus Wednesday to protest sexual violence and how the university has handled complaints, in the latest expression of outrage over an alleged 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house. A handwritten sign reading "Justice for Jane Doe " — the name under which the accuser is suing — was propped on an empty table in the dining hall in the afternoon. Some students sat around the room without eating, while others lunched. Another small group sat outside holding signs with messages such as "we are Jane Doe." READ MORE: Cornell brings in former DOJ official Sally Yates to review handling of sex assault claims The demonstrations were meant to spotlight complaints that the university is slow to respond to reports of sexual assault while quick to protect its reputation. Among other demands, the groups want the university to retool disciplinary procedures for addressing complaints and expel or revoke the degrees of anyone involved in the alleged October 2024 sexual assault. Jane Doe, who was a student then, alleges that Chi Phi members plied her with alcohol and drugs and several sexually assaulted her. One man sent others a message inviting them to participate, according to a lawsuit she filed last month. Lawyers for two of the men have denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the others or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Some of the men who underwent a university disciplinary hearing in 2024 told investigators that the sexual activity was consensual or said they were not involved. Zambia has signed a five-year health financing agreement with the US, ending months of public dispute over whether the country was trading citizens' medical data and mineral rights for aid.
Under the memorandum of understanding, signed in Lusaka on Thursday along with a data-sharing deal, the US will provide about $1.5bn (Â£1.1bn), with Zambia also contributing.
Civil society groups had criticised a leaked draft they said allowed too much data sharing, while activists seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to minerals, which the then-US ambassador denied.
The deal comes after the US Agency for International Development (USAID) was cut.
US President Donald Trump had accused USAID of wasteful spending. After closing the agency last year, Washington has pursued similar deals with a number of African countries, arguing partner governments should take on more of the cost.
Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda are among those that have signed. Ghana and Zimbabwe have rejected agreements over conditions about sharing data and specimens.
Officials say the revised text of Zambia's new deal addresses concerns about privacy, intellectual property and benefit-sharing.
Health Minister Roma Chilengi said earlier this week that clauses requiring Zambia to send biological specimens to the US had been removed, and that the agreement would not allow the sharing of individual patient records.
Data exchange, he said, would be limited to information needed to monitor and evaluate programmes funded under the deal.
A draft leaked earlier this year prompted civil society groups to warn that Zambia was accepting wider data-sharing terms than other African countries, including long-term access to pathogen information and specimens.
The Chapter One Foundation, a human rights group, said the government risked "signing away" citizens' health data. HIV advocates, including the Treatment Advocacy and Literacy Campaign, said the flow of information would be one-way and demanded the text be published.
Opposition figures and activists also seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to Zambia's large reserves of copper and other critical minerals.
In May, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe called the data terms a violation of privacy and "unconscionable", and accused Washington of tying the package to minerals. Then-US ambassador, Michael Gonzales, rejected that account as false.
The row was sharpened by an earlier US suspension of drug funding after the embassy alleged theft of donated medicines, which the government disputed.
Zambia's new deal replaces support that for years flowed largely through US programmes. The money is intended to support HIV/Aids, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, disease surveillance and wider health system work, including the recruitment of community health workers.
The US has described the arrangement as a shift from a donor-recipient model towards shared responsibility, with US funding expected to decline over the five years as Zambia increases domestic spending.
Officials have put the combined package covering 2026 to 2030 at roughly $3.6bn, though figures for the Zambian share have varied.
Shortly after taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump ordered the closure of USAID, in the process decimating health programmes in some African countries that relied on American funding.
Critics say the move has impacted the speed of detecting the current ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the scale of the response, emphasising that the humanitarian agency was crucial to organising logistics, supplies and local outreach.
The US denies its cuts have harmed efforts, arguing that they are more "aligned and effective" under the new arrangement and pointing to the $270m it has donated to tackle the epidemic.
Additional reporting by Mallory Moench

fdf043564df2.text: By — John Raby, Associated Press John Raby, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/how-el-nino-is-playing-a-role-in-hurricane-isaias Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How El Niño is playing a role in Hurricane Isaias Science Oct 8, 2026 12:12 PM EDT The super El Niño has been a nonstop machine cranking out tropical storms that have seemingly rolled through the Pacific region like rush-hour traffic. Now, it's the U.S. Gulf Coast's turn. One of the strongest El Niño years on record meant a quiet first four months of the Atlantic hurricane season, but that's no longer the case. LIVE MAP: Track the path of Hurricane Isaias Isaias is the ninth named storm of the season. None of the previous ones reached hurricane strength. A normal hurricane season has 14 named storms, seven of them becoming hurricanes and three of them reaching major hurricane level, which is more than 110 mph (177 kph). Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The season has been completely dead — and we're still going to have an impactful storm hitting the northern Gulf," Colorado State University hurricane expert Phil Klotzbach said Wednesday. "How impactful it is remains to be seen." READ MORE: Where have all the Atlantic hurricanes gone? El Niño might bring record slow storm season El Niño involves a natural, temporary warming of parts of the equatorial Pacific, setting off a chain of unusual weather around much of the world. While it's one of many factors in play in the formation of Isaias, the current El Niño "still is certainly driving the bus," Klotzbach said. Water temperatures in the Gulf right now are "super hot" and are considered "rocket fuel for hurricanes," he said. Another contributor is the ongoing natural seasonal weather pattern that moves around the globe every 30 or so days called the Madden-Julian Oscillation. Still, overall Atlantic hurricane activity, using a measurement that deals with the number of storms, their strength and how long they last, is on track to be the quietest since modern data started around 1950, thanks to El Niño, which could become the strongest one ever recorded, Klotzbach said. Why is a storm forming so late in the season? During El Niño, low-level surface winds blowing from east to west across the Pacific are weakened or sometimes reversed. It causes a shift in the jet stream and drives record global heat, severe droughts, wildfires and shrinking water supplies. El Niño also typically curtails hurricane activity in the Atlantic basin. When tropical systems form in the Pacific Ocean during El Niños, that increases wind shear in the Caribbean, making it difficult for storms to form there. WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns But now, the wind shear in the Gulf has weakened a bit compared with other tropical regions, so the Gulf is "a little more primed for development," said Lindsey Long, a meteorologist with the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center. "It's actually not that surprising that we're starting to see some development in the Gulf at this time of year," Long said. "It only takes one storm for a lot of possible destruction. So you don't want to put your guard down." Hurricanes have formed in the Atlantic basin during previous El Niños Notable hurricanes that have hit the eastern United States during an El Niño include Lili in 2002, Ivan in 2004 and Idalia in 2023. Hurricane Andrew, the first named storm of the 1992 Atlantic hurricane season, didn't form until August. It caused 65 deaths and more than $26 billion in damage across Florida, Louisiana and the Bahamas. An El Niño that started the previous winter continued through the spring and into the summer of 1992. When Andrew formed, Long said, the world was transitioning into a neutral condition when it comes to the important natural El Niño Southern Oscillation, which warps weather systems worldwide. Neutral is when weather gets closer to long-term averages or normal. Has there ever been a year when there were no Atlantic hurricanes? During the modern satellite era that began in the mid-1960s, there has never been a year in which no hurricanes formed in the Atlantic basin. And "it doesn't look like it's going to happen this year, either," Long said. Before satellites arrived, there were a few years when no Atlantic hurricanes were recorded, but some storms out at sea could have been missed and records were less reliable, she said. Since the start of the satellite era, the latest date for the first Atlantic hurricane to form was Sept. 11, both in 2002 and 2013, the weather service said. Isaias is expected to topple that. This year's Atlantic hurricane season had already set a record for the longest a season has advanced without a storm that reached winds of 74 mph (119 kph) to qualify as a hurricane — at least in the satellite era — said Nick Novella, a meteorologist at the Climate Prediction Center. Where is Isaias heading? The biggest threat for storm surge and initial flash flood risk over the next 48 hours is from the mouth of the Mississippi River in southeast Louisiana to Yankeetown, Florida, north of Tampa. Hurricane-force winds are anticipated over the Florida Panhandle, through the Alabama coast and on to Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Flash flood risks on Saturday and Saturday night go as far north as Memphis, Tennessee, according to the weather service. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 6725229c0c8a.text: By — Rebecca Santana, Associated Press Rebecca Santana, Associated Press By — Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-vance-says-microsoft-is-being-suspended-from-green-card-program-for-h-1b-visa-workers Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Vance says Microsoft is being suspended from green card program for H-1B visa workers Politics Oct 8, 2026 11:54 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration is suspending tech giant Microsoft from a program to apply for green cards for workers who come to the U.S. to live and work using H-1B visas as it accuses the company of fraud. Supporters of the Republican president have long argued that various programs like the one Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing essentially empower American companies to recruit foreign workers for jobs that end up undercutting Americans. In a wide-ranging announcement Thursday, Vance and other top administration officials also called out universities over their use of J-1 visas for international students and IT outsourcing firms. READ MORE: Here's why experts think Trump took 'a sledgehammer' to the H-1B visa worker program The announcement came hours before Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, part of an event at which he is granting some of the nation's most prestigious science and technology awards to his tech billionaire allies. WATCH LIVE: Trump awards Elon Musk the National Medal of Science, among other awards for tech execs "They'll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They'll go out there and say that 'We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.' And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants," Vance said. Vance said H-1B workers are effectively foreign indentured servants because if they lose their job, they have to leave the country, and they earn less than Americans in the same position. H-1B program has been scrutinized The H-1B program has long been a target of Trump supporters who say that the program undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse. H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find American workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India. Trump also has targeted foreign students The Vance announcement came a day after Trump's administration launched another broadside against international students and their ability to work in the U.S. READ MORE: Trump administration proposes a $70,000 fee for international students to work in the U.S. The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States. Campaign group Human Rights Watch (HRW) says the deportation of migrants from the US to third-party African countries is against the law and exploits suffering to deter migration.
"Many, if not most" of the deportees have no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there, HRW says in a report.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, more than 500 people have been sent to African countries where they are not citizens, the group says, citing US data.
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said "third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets".
Tackling immigration was one of Trump's key pledges during the 2024 election.
Eswatini, which welcomed 32 deportees from the US, says three people - from Yemen, Belize and Laos - "voluntarily departed" to their home countries recently.
According to HRW, some of the countries accepting the deportees have "arbitrarily detained" or sent them to their home countries, where they face "the risk of persecution or torture".
The group said that people sent to Eswatini, Ghana and South Sudan, had been arbitrarily detained and faced ill-treatment while in detention.
In Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and Ghana, the deportees had been sent to their countries of origin despite the risk of "violating the principle of nonrefoulement [that people should not be sent to a country where they face torture, cruel treatment, or threats to their life and freedom]", it said.
The group cited an unnamed US official as having told a Senate hearing that the point for the administration was that it could "threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere".
"The point is to scare people," HRW said.
"Deporting people to countries where they have never set foot is part of a US policy designed to cause human suffering as a means to deter migration," said Michael Garcia Bochenek, the group's interim US programme director.
In a statement from to the BBC, DHS said: "ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe. When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them."
None of the African countries named has commented on the report.
However, while announcing the recent departure of three migrants on Wednesday, Eswatini said that it was committed to ensuring that the "rights, dignity and well-being of third-country nationals were respected and protected".
HRW said it interviewed 24 third-country nationals in six countries - Cameroon, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan.
Some described to the group "abusive treatment" during their deportation flights, including being chained for about 18 hours and with no knowledge of their destination. They were also "denied access to essential medication, and often did not receive sufficient food or water".
"The opaque deals that facilitate these transfers, some of which are still secret, are part of a US policy that violates international human rights law," HRW says.
According to the report, at least a dozen people who identified as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender (LGBT) were sent to African states that criminalise same-sex relations.
Among them were refugees granted protection in the US based on the likelihood they would be persecuted back home because of their orientation or gender identity.
In November, a Nigerian man deported from the US initially to Ghana expressed his fears to the BBC after he and five others were secretly transferred to Togo.
He spoke of his fears about returning to Nigeria, where his association with a separatist activist group could lead to his arrest and torture.
In DR Congo, HRW says it was told by a US lawyer that of the 15 people from Colombia, Peru and Ecuador deported to the country in April, none remained there by late September, with 11 having returned to their home countries.
"The uncertainty and other conditions they faced in the Democratic Republic of Congo call into question whether these returns to countries of origin were voluntary," the group said.
Equatorial Guinea, which received 65 people, quickly sent at least two people to their home countries, HRW said.
Burundi announced late last month that it had agreed to take in migrants deported from the US.

The News
The Trump administration on Thursday suspended more than a half-dozen tech companies, including Microsoft, from the program that allows permanent hiring of foreign workers â escalating its long-simmering clash with the tech industry over immigration.
âThe H1-B visa program is meant to allow companies to bring in really the best of the best from outside the United States of America for positions that are completely impossible to fill with American workers,â Vice President JD Vance, who helms the administrationâs fraud task force, told reporters. âUnfortunately, the program has become rife with fraud.â
The administration has tangled with tech companies since President Donald Trump returned to office over its interest in reining in H1-B visas for highly skilled workers.
That tension has resulted in a partial pullback of some attempted policy shifts, such as Mayâs clarification of an announcement that H1-B holders would have to start applying for permanent residency from outside the US.
The administration has also recently moved to charge more than $100,000 for a single H1-B visa.
Thursdayâs announcement formally bans Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and four other companies from the permanent labor certification process. Representatives for Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, and Infosys did not immediately return requests for comment.
Notably, Trump plans to award a medal to the CEO of Microsoft later on Thursday.
In addition, the administration announced it had served subpoenas for a new investigation into multiple universities over their use of J-1 visas for exchange students. Among the educational institutions targeted by the probe are Pitt, Yale, Harvard, Stanford, Brown, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, and MIT, officials said at a press conference.
âWe will investigate whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research,â said the Labor Departmentâs inspector general, former Republican member of Congress Anthony DâEsposito.
Know More
Foreign workers made up almost a quarter of the USâ STEM workforce in 2023, according to the American Immigration Council. Businesses, which challenged the proposed H1-B fee in court, say they need visas to overcome worker shortages that stem in part from lagging workforce development.
Thursdayâs announcement marks a continuation of Vanceâs focus on fraud heading into the midterms and 2028. The vice president has portrayed the issue as bipartisan â though Trump, when he announced the task force earlier this year, suggested it would focus âprimarilyâ in blue states.
Asked Thursday to explain his allegations of visa fraud, Vance pointed to âa couple of certificationsâ companies must make to receive the visas, including âthat the person that youâre bringing in has a specialized, hyper-capable skill set.â
âThatâs clearly not the case if youâre just replacing one American worker with a foreign indentured servant and undercutting their wages in the process,â Vance said. âSo the fraud is that theyâre making representations when applying for this program that are fundamentally illegitimate and therefore ultimately illegal.â
Notable
- Vance declined to directly address a Wall Street Journal report that US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle requested a donor pay off debt in exchange for access to government officials, though he told reporters he doesnât âlove that.â

The News
The Federal Trade Commission is close to sending investigative demands to frontier AI companies, a senior agency official told Semafor â a sign that its AI probe is moving forward after its unusual disclosure to the public.
The FTCâs planned AI inquiry emerged in a New York Post story as the White House raced to project seriousness about the rise of tech that President Donald Trump has made clear he wants to treat with a light touch. Less than 24 hours before news of the FTC probe, the agencyâs chair appeared alongside Trump and AI CEOs to announce a nonbinding accord that pledged industry self-regulation.
Itâs rare for the FTC to reveal an investigation before it sends civil investigative demands, which have subpoena-like force. And itâs even less typical to do so well before any decision has been made about a potential lawsuit or settlement.
The leak of the AI probe raised the question of whether FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson â who was since appointed to Trumpâs AI task force â plans an in-depth inquiry or a probe thatâs more designed to convey the appearance of serious action ahead of the midterms.
Yet the senior FTC official reiterated to Semafor that it plans a significant probe, revealing it to the media due to public health and safety concerns about AI systems. The CIDs being sent to AI companies are dozens of questions long, according to the official, encompassing what the companies have said about the dangers of their products and other questions around consumer harm.
While two people with knowledge of the matter told Semafor that career FTC staff learned from the press â not agency leadership â about the AI investigation, the senior official disputed that. Career staff attorneys in the Bureau of Consumer Protection are drafting the CIDs, the senior FTC official said.
âCareer staff who do not leak to the media are working hard every day on issues of importance to the American people, includingâ the AI inquiry, the official added.
Know More
One well-known exception to the FTCâs practice of not publicizing investigations was its revelation of an inquiry into Metaâs privacy practices after the 2018 Cambridge Analytica data release scandal, a move that responded to overwhelming public interest. A similar step occurred in 2017, when the agency confirmed it was investigating Equifax after a massive data breach.
One former FTC official told Semafor that the agency tries not to âpublicize investigations in advance, because you donât want people to prejudge the investigation. The simple fact that there is an existing investigation will impact a companyâs stock price and operations.â
Yet William Kovacic, a former Republican FTC chair, said confirming an investigation in the press is âunusual,â but not without precedent and ânot in any sense improper.â
âYou donât do this unless you want to make clear to the larger public that youâre looking at a particular issue,â he said.
The announcement, which may also target independent AI evaluator METR, aligned with Trump advisersâ approach to AI safety: Apply the laws on the books without adding new regulatory requirements. That differs wildly from what many bipartisan members of Congress, state regulators, the public and even AI companies have said they want: new rules and restrictions for AI as the technology reaches alarming capabilities.
Ferguson has said that he does not consider the agency to be an AI regulator. The Trump administrationâs 2025 AI Action Plan called for a review of all FTC investigations commenced under former President Joe Biden to âensure they do not advance theories of liability that unduly burden AI innovationâ and even modify existing orders that may âunduly burden AI innovation.â
The AI industry appears unsure about where Ferguson is heading: âWeâre trying to find out more about that,â OpenAIâs chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane said in an interview last week when asked about the investigation.
Anthropic, also named in the initial report, declined to comment. METR didnât respond to a request for comment.
Room for Disagreement
Former FTC chair Lina Khan told ABC on Sunday that she doubts Ferguson is serious: âYou have on the one hand, these CEOs of these AI companies wining and dining at the White House, the idea that the next morning theyâre going to get some type of credible subpoena from the same administration I think just strains credulity.â
Asked about Khanâs remarks, Kovacic said: âWhen youâve tied your destiny so close to the White House, youâre inevitably going to raise questions about the sincerity and the aggressiveness of the inquiry â¦ The only way to dispel those concerns is to carry out a serious inquiry and explain what youâre doing along the way.â
Ashleyâs view
Ferguson is wearing very different hats here, and we are seeing him embody the resulting tension in real time. As Trump embraces a hands-off approach to AI growth, heâs made clear by his task force participation that he aligns with the president.
But heâs also the countryâs top consumer protection official, and he has shown he can go after tech when he wants to. On the antitrust side, heâs taken Meta to court and will face Amazon in court next year; he also previously asked AI companies about kidsâ chatbot practices; itâs not clear what will come of that.
With AI safety is very much on the publicâs mind ahead of Election Day, we might be seeing the Trump administrationâs best recipe to assuage voters for the rest of the year: an investigation alongside a pledge for self-regulation.
That investigation, of course, may not result in much. These probes can take a long time, and AI companies are a long way from any finding of wrongdoing.

de40811e8533.text: President Trump said Thursday the U.S. will not attack Iran ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Why it matters: Trump had been considering for several days the possibility of resuming major combat operations against Iran ahead of the midterms. If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include large-scale strikes on Iranian energy facilities, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say. Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterms, in part because oil prices might rise in response. It could also influence Israel's elections, which are scheduled for Oct. 27. What he's saying: "I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait ... we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Driving the news: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran , Axios reported on Wednesday. Behind the scenes: On Tuesday, Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke with senior U.S. officials who briefed him on the U.S. military's preparations for the possibility of resuming major combat operations against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a U.S. official and another source briefed on the call. Zamir said during the call that resuming the war within that timeframe could lead to the postponement of the Israeli elections, given the assessment that Iran would respond by launching missiles at Israel, the sources said. The IDF declined to comment on conversations between Zamir and his U.S. counterparts. Between the lines: It's unclear whether Trump's statement will reassure Iranian leaders that an attack is not imminent. U.S. and Israeli officials say Iranian leaders are deeply suspicious of Trump's statements. The officials said Iranian leaders want to avoid a third surprise attack. What to watch: Trump said the U.S. and Iran "are having productive discussions". But there are no signs that the major differences between the two sides have narrowed.

40795535ef56.text: Data: U.S. Department of Labor ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios New applications for unemployment benefits have stayed below 200,000 in a stretch rarely seen in modern history. Jobless claims fell by 2,000, to 197,000, last week, the Labor Department said Thursday morning. Why it matters: It points to a remarkable stability on the "firing" side of the labor market, even amid a slower pace of hiring on the other side of the equation. That is helping to keep unemployment low, but it also masks a growing divide between Americans who have jobs and those struggling to find one. What they're saying: "New jobless claims have been under 200,000 for a month now, an incredibly low level of layoffs for a sustained period of time that hasn't been seen since the 1960s," Navy Federal Credit Union chief economist Heather Long said. By the numbers: The four-week average, which smooths out weekly volatility, fell to 198,000, its lowest level since the red-hot job market of 2022–2023. The other side: Jobless claims don't capture every layoff. Some workers receive severance, don't qualify for benefits or find the application process too cumbersome. Still, when layoffs have surged across the economy, claims have surged with them — including during the recessions after the financial crisis and the pandemic. The absence of such an increase now is hard to dismiss. Other data tells a similar story: Announced job cuts fell 20% from a year earlier in September, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The bottom line: Employers may be reluctant to hire, but they appear just as reluctant to fire — an unusual combination that, for now, keeps the labor market on steady footing.

0b12696cc6d1.text: A couple more interest rate hikes are probably on the way. But the Federal Reserve is in no great hurry to deliver them. That's the takeaway from the latest round of communications out of the central bank. Why it matters: It implies that the Fed is not in a full-scale effort to tighten the screws on the economy, but rather a cautious recalibration in light of inflationary pressures and robust growth. With Fed chairman Kevin Warsh declining to offer much in the way of guidance, traders and Fed watchers must look to other communications for clues — and the message has been strikingly consistent across the latest crumbs of information. Driving the news: Speaking Thursday morning in Istanbul , Fed governor Christopher Waller explained, with distinctly non-Warshian detail, what kind of interest rate path he anticipates. "If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal," he said. "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time." That aligns with the language in the minutes of the September policy meeting released Wednesday afternoon, stating that "most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year-end," but that they "approached each meeting with an open mind." Of note: The minutes and Waller comments come after fairly explicit comments last week from vice chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams waving away expectations of a second rate increase at a meeting concluding Oct. 28. Zoom in: That doesn't answer the question of how big this tightening cycle will turn out to be. But the tea leaves point to one more rate hike at this year's final meeting and another early in 2027. That would amount to a total of 0.75 percentage point of rate increases, the same size adjustment as easing cycles in 2019 and 2025. Waller, in an extended musing about Fed communication strategy in Thursday morning's speech, used a 0.75-point adjustment as the hypothetical cumulative adjustment. If nothing else, it's a hint that he sees three rate hikes in this adjustment cycle as the most probable course of action. Between the lines: Warsh is determined to maintain optionality and not pre-commit to a policy path, and he still has that. But talk of leaving rates steady in October and keeping the cumulative adjustment modest tells us something about what kind of rate cycle Fed leadership envisions. This is not — in their view, at least — the beginning of a sustained, open-ended tightening cycle needed to slow the economy and break the back of inflation, as last seen in 2022. Rather, it's a take-your-time, limited operation to better calibrate policy for the mix of solid labor market results, accelerating growth and elevated inflation that they see. What they're saying: "With evidence that economic activity is strengthening in the second half of this year, I am not greatly concerned that tighter monetary policy threatens a damaging slowdown in the economy," Waller said Thursday morning. "But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation." The bottom line: Investors can take solace that the Fed is not preparing aggressive action to take away the punchbowl. The open question is whether this limited tightening will do the trick in getting inflation down faster.

715ce646ee2f.text: President Trump on Thursday called anyone who uses "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Super Intelligence" "THE ENEMY!" — even as the White House continues using the term "AI." Why it matters: Trump's push to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" clashes with established terminology in the technology industry. Trump's branding blurs the distinction between AI and super intelligence , a hypothetical version of AI more advanced than human intelligence. What they're saying: "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday. Zoom out: Trump's executive order from September doubled down on using "SI" over "AI," though it did not offer a penalty for using the term. The order specifically defines "Super Intelligence" using the existing federal legal definition of AI. The order calls on federal agencies to change how they describe AI in official communications. The State Department already ordered diplomats to use the term after Trump's United Nations speech on Sept. 22. Yes, but: The White House still uses "AI" as a term, including on its AI-focused website, AI.gov . The White House's Office of Science and Technology Policy also makes reference to "artificial intelligence." But when an Axios reporter asked the America.gov chatbot about AI, the bot responded: "The executive branch uses Super Intelligence (SI) for this topic, not the older term you used." What we're watching: Whether the White House could update its websites to reflect Trump's preferred terminology. The White House did not respond to Axios' request for comment Thursday.

New figures show sewage was released into rivers, lakes and the sea around Wales for more than 800,000 hours last year.
The charity Surfers Against Sewage, which has analysed data from Wales' water companies, said there were more than 100,000 sewage discharges in 2025 - or one every five minutes.
The figures are down on the year before when sewage was discharged for more than 970,000 hours.
Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it had strengthened its approach as regulators through increased monitoring and tighter guidance, and had overseen "significant programmes of environmental investment" by water companies.
Surfers Against Sewage said part of the reason for the drop was the dry weather seen during the summer last year, but underinvestment and a lack of enforcement remained an issue.
In its annual assessment, it said since 2019 it had received 992 reports of sickness in Wales caused by sewage, with 215 of those coming in 2025.
It said the impact of those sickness reports led to more than 2,200 days off work.
According to the charity, sewage was discharged into Wales' designated bathing waters for a total of 35,669 hours over the year.
At Llyn Padarn, Gwynedd, despite the lake's designated bathing water being classified as "excellent" for water quality, discharges lasted 1,614 hours.
Rules allow a limited discharge of sewage in periods of excess rain, but environmental groups remain concerned the levels pose a threat to wildlife and a health risk to swimmers.
Giles Bristow, chief executive of Surfers Against Sewage, said last year's figures equated to a discharge every five minutes, which he called a "shocking statistic".
He pointed to 90 places that authorities have said are good places to swim, but said they'd "been impacted by over 4,000 hours of sewage pollution".
"It's a really terrible picture that we're seeing of continued underinvestment and a lack of enforcement to ensure that this isn't happening," he added.
"People's lives and their health are being put at risk when they go to enjoy these amazing places."
Welsh Water said it will invest a record Â£2.5bn over the next four years, and understood the concerns about sewage discharge.
"We take our responsibility to protect these waters seriously and recognise that we need to improve," it said.
"In line with Welsh government policy, we are prioritising the overflows causing the greatest environmental harm."
Hafren Dyfrdwy - which operates in mid and north-east Wales - said it was "working tirelessly" to reduce the average number of spills but "we know more needs to be done".
"Which is why we're investing Â£11m at our storm overflows to reduce spills to fewer than 20 a year by 2030," it added.
The Welsh government said it was "taking full control of water in Wales" and would "apply the polluter-pays principle, including prosecuting serious and persistent offenders".
"Water reform demonstrates how Wales and the UK can work together to strengthen and simplify devolution, while keeping effective cross-border cooperation," a spokesperson added.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said water companies must "take responsibility" for record levels of sewage pollution.
It added: "Our strengthened Water Bill will deliver cleaner waters, stronger accountability and will create a powerful new regulator to hold companies to account."

Kilauea has been erupting almost continuously for nearly 200 years, and volcanologists have seen a lot of sides to Hawaii’s most active volcano. But in the last year, Kilauea started doing something new: firing up frequent fountains of lava.
The volcano’s fountain era kicked off at dawn on December 23, 2024, with an eruption inside the summit crater of Halema’uma’u. Since then, Kilauea has put on a recurring pyrotechnic display of lava fountains, researchers report October 8 in Science. It produced 54 different lava fountains by September 2026, some of which shot as high as 457 meters into the sky.
During an eruption, which can last from hours to days, months or even years, occasional lava fountains aren’t unusual. But it’s rare to see repeated fountains — distinct bursts separated by minutes to weeks — during a single eruption. At Kilauea, these clustered spurts have only occurred three times since 1823, and never with such frequency.
Thanks to their rarity, researchers have known relatively little about what initiates, sustains and ends these episodic fountains, say Ashton Flinders, a research geophysicist at the U.S. Geological Survey’s Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, based in Hilo, and colleagues. There have been two prevailing ideas: Water dissolved in magma — the underground, molten mix of rock and gas — rising from deep inside the volcano suddenly escapes as the pressure changes, leading to a burst of pyrotechnics; or a carbon dioxide–rich foam atop the trapped magma, like the pressurized froth over a shaken bottle of soda, suddenly and violently expands.
Kilauea is the perfect laboratory in which to assess these hypotheses, the researchers say. It has been intensely studied by scientists and monitored by instruments for decades. Scientists continuously collect data on its seismic activity, temperature, low-frequency acoustics, how much the ground swells or deflates and the gases that escape. Using these data, researchers have begun to form a picture of what’s causing the relentless spewing.
Before each fountain, the team found, the floor of the bowl-shaped caldera would swell and tilt, suggesting magma was gathering beneath. As the eruption matured and the fountains continued, a pattern emerged, first appearing before the fourteenth fountain. Just before that eruption, the team detected a repetitive sequence of minutes-long bursts of seismic energy and low-frequency acoustics.
Those signals, the researchers say, are linked to the buildup and release of trapped gases in magma, which make it rise and fall through narrow volcanic vents in the rock like a piston in a car. The team also noted that while the volcano burped some sulfur dioxide gas, there was relatively little carbon dioxide, suggesting that the foam hypothesis wasn’t at work.
This is just a preliminary glimpse into this phenomenon, and a lot of questions remain, Flinders and his colleagues say.

Sisak, Associated Press By — Joshua Goodman, Associated Press Joshua Goodman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/new-u-s-indictment-charges-former-venezuelan-president-nicolas-maduro-with-torture Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture World Oct 8, 2026 3:17 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. authorities added new torture charges Thursday to their case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ramping up pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking allegations. Maduro and wife Cilia Flores, already charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., now also face allegations of human rights abuses during his time as president of the oil-rich South American nation. WATCH: Trump says Venezuela is 'not ready yet' for elections after U.S. ouster of Maduro The updated indictment "alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable," New York-based U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the courthouse where the case is being handled. He said thousands of Venezuelans, and some Americans, were tortured to ensure that Maduro and Flores held onto power. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "This is the epitome of corruption," McDonald said. The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on torture methods, sought and got updates on specific victims' treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner's child "as a form of psychological torture." READ MORE: Proud of their oil, Venezuelans view major U.S. stake in their reserves as a surrender Flores, a former legislator and attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends. A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer. Flores' attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations. The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country. They face potential sentences of life in prison if convicted. WATCH: Analyst breaks down challenges U.S. will face to unlock Venezuela's oil Maduro, who served as Venezuela's president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing. Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid. Flores' lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest. Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request. Alleged torture victims included U.S. citizens The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela's feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro's co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York and has offered to testify against his former boss. WATCH: Aid worker describes crisis in Venezuela, one month after devastating earthquakes While the indictment doesn't name the alleged torture victims, three are described as U.S. citizens. One was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said. Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela. Among those who sued is Matthew Heath, a former U.S. Marine corporal from Tennessee. He was arrested at a roadblock in Venezuela in 2020 and held in custody for more than two years. In May, Heath and another former prisoner won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. The lawsuit, brought under a federal anti-terrorism law, included allegations of waterboarding, electrocution, threats of rape with a nightstick, administration of mind-altering medications and the repeated use of a cramped cell nicknamed "El Tigrito." "It's incredible to see a dictator in court," Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. "The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations." Former first lady denied release for medical treatment Meanwhile, Flores' lawyers argued that Flores, 69, has medical problems that cannot be treated effectively in jail. She has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July, has "lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath" and has been told that she might need heart surgery, the attorneys said. They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was "thrown against a wall or dresser" during her capture. Prosecutors opposed the bail
