Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square.
Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis, she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause.
"It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."
She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."
Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees.
"There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own.
"They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."
His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government.
On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".
Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting SÃ¡nchez to call a snap election next month.
Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.
Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday.
Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.
Carmen PÃ©rez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years.
When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent.
"When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."
Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista.
In the centre of the southern city of MÃ¡laga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.
Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern.
A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market.
Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.
However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation.
He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.
Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain.
"When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."
The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes.
The institution's deputy governor, Soledad NÃºÃ±ez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.
There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs.
Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.
Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand.
Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.
However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period.
That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building.
"It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."
He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.
Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries.

02afe174e657.text: Anthropic is launching a new cybersecurity initiative designed to bring its most powerful AI models and engineers to companies protecting power grids, water utilities and other critical infrastructure, the company first shared with Axios. Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are struggling to secure aging, complex systems as AI threatens to make cyberattacks faster and cheaper to execute. Driving the news: Under its new Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, Anthropic will provide its frontier AI models, on-site engineers and threat research to companies already responsible for securing critical infrastructure systems. Participating companies will use these resources to identify and fix vulnerabilities in their customers' systems. The program's founding partners include Accenture, Booz Allen Hamilton, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC and Rockwell Automation. Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same. Zoom in: Anthropic is also launching a free AI-powered vulnerability scanning service for open-source software projects, called OSS Scanner. Participating projects will receive periodic scans from Claude, along with automated reports detailing vulnerabilities, how they could be exploited and suggested fixes. The reports won't undergo human review before being sent to software maintainers, meaning some findings could be inaccurate. The big picture: Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI developers are looking for ways to put their most powerful models in the hands of cyber defenders as hackers gain access to similar capabilities . Anthropic's new initiative builds on lessons from Project Glasswing, which gave vetted organizations access to its most capable AI models to identify security vulnerabilities. The company said the project demonstrated how quickly AI can uncover vulnerabilities, but also how difficult it remains to verify and fix them. Yes, but: It's unclear how participating companies will safely test and deploy fixes without disrupting utilities' operations, one of the biggest challenges in securing critical infrastructure. Anthropic also didn't specify whether partners will receive free model access or who will cover the computing costs associated with using its AI tools. Go deeper : AI is supercharging hacks of everyday utilities

Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.
Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft, along with Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini, of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa program and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.
"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
He went on to claim that the company, one of the most valuable in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."
The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Kieth Sonderling said during the same conference.
Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.
The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.
The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped, external at 85,000 per year.
A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employes more than 200,000 people worldwide.
Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.
The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.
She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.
According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary, external for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.
"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.
Satya Nadella, Microsoft's longtime CEO, is set to be at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.
Nadella was also present at other recent White House events, including a luncheon on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.
Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.
"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.
He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.
Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating, external that grace period altogether.
Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.
None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.
The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.
The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.
During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified, external more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

3237e8952e9e.text: By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press By — Barry Hatton, Associated Press Barry Hatton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/rubio-says-u-s-pressure-on-nato-allies-to-boost-defense-spending-is-not-hostile Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Rubio says U.S. pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is 'not hostile' World Oct 8, 2026 2:45 PM EDT LISBON, Portugal (AP) — U.S. pressure on NATO allies to increase their defense spending "is not a hostile thing," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Thursday, but reiterated that the Trump administration wants the military alliance to be a stronger deterrent against threats. READ MORE: Report alleges Ambassador Guilfoyle improperly asked a donor to pay her credit card bill. Rubio refuses to comment Rubio told reporters during a visit to European NATO ally Portugal that "the stronger the members of NATO are, the stronger NATO is, the stronger the alliances and the stronger the deterrence is." President Donald Trump has long railed against NATO allies for spending too small a fraction of their national budgets on defense, leaving the United States to shoulder what he says is an unfair burden. Some members of the 32-country alliance have been reluctant to divert funds from other government policies, however. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "People sometimes view this call to invest more in defense as a hostile thing," Rubio said. "It is not a hostile thing." Rubio, who was in Portugal on the last leg of a three-nation tour of NATO allies that also included Iceland and Greece, acknowledged that some smaller NATO members, such as Portugal, have difficulty finding the funds for major military projects. WATCH: Rubio urges Europe to defend Western values and strengthen U.S. alliance in Greece "Every country is of a different size and proportion. Some countries can contribute more than others, but every country in NATO needs to be as strong as they can possibly be," Rubio told a news conference in Lisbon. He noted the danger of the war in Ukraine, following Russia's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022, spilling beyond Ukrainian borders. An apparent stalemate in Ukraine could bring a military escalation in Europe, he said. "That escalation could wind up being a sabotage campaign in neighboring countries that are members of NATO," he said. That could "quickly turn what is a war between two countries into a much broader and far more dangerous regional conflict." European officials have accused Moscow of a campaign of sabotage and disruption aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations. READ MORE: Cold War memories stir Rubio in Iceland as he champions diplomacy and downplays differences Rubio also said that the Trump administration will keep trying to facilitate a negotiated settlement to the war, but that it has been difficult. "We have tried, we will continue to try, but we're also not going to invest in pointless processes if we can't make progress," he said, coming after new Russian strikes in eastern Ukraine killed 30 people. Meanwhile, Rubio also praised Portuguese efforts toward meeting the NATO target for defense spending. Portugal, a country of fewer than 11 million people, spends just over 2% of its gross domestic product on defense, according to NATO. The government says it plans to increase defense spending to around 3%, including dual-use investments in civilian infrastructure. That still leaves it below the 5% of GDP set aside for defense spending that Trump has demanded and that requires investment at an unprecedented scale in Europe. Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel said at the news conference that his country views its relationship with the U.S. as "fundamental." Portugal provided support for American operations in the Iran war by allowing the U.S. to use the Lajes Field air base in the mid-Atlantic Azores islands, which is strategically located for military refueling flights. The U.S. Air Force has long had a base there under an agreement with Portugal. Unlike neighboring Spain, where Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, a Socialist, refused to allow the American military to use Spanish bases to stage operations for attacks on Iran, Portugal's center-right government granted Washington "conditional approval" to use Lajes Field. "Portugal is a great ally, very cooperative ally of the United States and a country with which we already have a solid and growing relationship. And we visit these countries in order to reinforce those ties," Rubio said before arriving in Lisbon. "That's the purpose of the trip." Some Portuguese political parties balked at the decision to allow the U.S. to use the Azores islands air base, however. Following a formal complaint by a small left-wing political party called Left Bloc, the country's attorney general's office said last week that it's looking into whether the use of the Lajes Field base was lawful. Rubio visited Portugal a day after delivering a speech in the Greek capital, Athens, urging European countries to save Western civilization by upholding the values and traditions of ancient Greece. Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.
The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.
The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.
The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday.
In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.
The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.
White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.
It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.
This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.
The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".
Adidas, which reported â¬24.8 billion (Â£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.
Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.
In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.
A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.
In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.
White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.
In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (Â£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

ade550d32c12.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday the public will be able to watch the execution of the Fort Hood shooter by firing squad. Why it matters: The U.S. hasn't held a public execution in 90 years , and Hegseth's remarks raise questions about how the military would allow people to watch. It's unclear if Hegseth's remarks mean the execution will be open to public spectators, broadcast on streaming or TV, or made available to select individuals. Driving the news: Hegseth was asked about Nidal Hasan, the man convicted of killing 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood. What they're saying: Hegseth told Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be." "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it's public. Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." State of play: The Department of Defense declined to comment on Hegseth's remarks, leaving many unanswered questions about how the public could watch the execution. The AP reports that the Army has not shared how it intends to conduct the firing squad execution. Zoom out: This would also be the first U.S. military execution since 1961 . The last U.S. military execution by firing squad was in 1945, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, according to NPR . Death by firing squad are rare in the U.S. Only Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah authorize the method, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . Last year, South Carolina executed a prisoner by firing squad for the first time in the state and the first time in the U.S. in 15 years. The last public execution in the U.S. was in 1936, when Rainey Bethea , a Black man convicted of raping a white woman, was hanged in Kentucky.

Coca-Cola is seeking to unwind its $5 billion acquisition of a British coffeehouse, months after a sales process faltered earlier this year.

Coca-Cola acquired Costa for $5.1 billion in 2018, but has struggled to grow the business meaningfully. It explored selling Costa in late 2025, before calling off the sales process earlier this year after a tepid response from private-equity bidders, the Financial Times reported in January.
At least one strategic acquirer mulled what a deal for Costa would look like before passing due to valuation and strategic issues, one of the people said. It couldnât be determined what price Coca-Cola might seek for the asset were it to market it more actively again. Coca-Colaâs on-again, off-again efforts to sell Costa mean it might again choose to wait.
Coca-Cola did not return a request for comment.

Costa Coffee has 2,700 outlets in the UK and Ireland and employs 20,000 people. The coffee chain is targeting younger consumers by adding more iced drinks and matcha to its menus.
Coca-Cola bought Costa from British hospitality company Whitbread. The business lost nearly Â£20 million in 2023 and 2024 combined.

04d9374d41c1.text: By — Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/watch-four-astronauts-return-to-earth-after-8-months-aboard-international-space-station Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Four astronauts return to Earth after 8 months aboard International Space Station Science Oct 8, 2026 3:42 PM EDT CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew. Watch the splashdown in the video player above. SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles. WATCH: NASA launches Crew-13 to International Space Station NASA's Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France's Sophie Adenot and Russia's Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew's homecoming. They couldn't wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports. "We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station," Meir radioed moments after splashing down. While still in orbit, she said the crew had "a lot of mixed, swirling emotions" and would miss the "extraordinary views of our home planet." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. All four were out of their capsule within an hour, waving and pumping their fists in the air aboard SpaceX's recovery ship. After a helicopter ride to shore, they were going to head for Houston. Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA's Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight. The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States' 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert. Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost. In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef's toque. Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity. Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over? "It's kind of become a little bit of my brand up here," Hathaway said in August, "so I don't know if it'll go away right away or I'll end up keeping it for a while." Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA's count. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The Scoop
Continental, a Washington-based law and lobbying firm with close ties to President Donald Trumpâs network, helped arrange a recent trip to Bosnia and Herzegovina by two Trump political advisers, three people familiar with the trip told Semafor.
Republika Srpska, whose Russia-friendly Serbian leaders have sought to align themselves with Trump, agreed earlier this year to pay $35,000 monthly to Continental, which would organize âmeetings and discussions and establish relationships with key stakeholders in the executive and legislative branches,â according to a Justice Department filing.
Since then, former Trump campaign adviser Alex Garcia has helped arrange meetings with White House officials like Walker Bennet, Jarrod Agen and Richard Walters, according to another DOJ filing.
A White House official told Semafor that Garcia, who was in Republika Srpska around the same time as LaCivita and Blair, also set up a recent meeting between Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles and a Serbian official from the region.
The Balkan trip occurred after Garcia initially reached out to LaCivita, multiple people familiar with the situation said. LaCivita and Blair were there for 48 hours, one source said, to consult on voting equipment ahead of elections on Sunday.
Trump on Wednesday signaled his displeasure with LaCivita and Blairâs trip, which was first reported by The New York Times, amid some intraparty criticism that his advisers arenât as focused as possible on the midterms. But Trump wasnât particularly harsh about the trip in private, two people familiar with the situation said.
âIf Iâm the president â¦ traveling the country every day and campaigning â¦ Iâm rightfully annoyed, right?â one of the people said. âWith that being said, do I think James missed a second of work? No.â
Two sources said that Trump and Blair had a call following the news, with one calling it âa good conversation.â And while the duo has faced criticism from some corners of the Republican party, others close to Trump are openly defending them.
LaCivita and Blairâs trip focused on election integrity rather than political strategy, multiple people said; this year marked Republika Srpskaâs first election using new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment.
Asked for comment on whether Continental helped organize LaCivita and Blairâs trip, a spokesperson for the firm said only that Garcia was its only employee in Republika Srpska on Oct. 4 as well as its only employee to lobby the US government on its behalf.
The spokesperson added that Wilesâ daughter Katie, who also works at Continental, traveled to Republika Srpska in August for a separate reason: helping a US-based company complete âa feasibility study.â
Know More
Republika Srpska voters on Sunday decided to keep former President Milorad Dodikâs nationalist party in power.
The US last year lifted sanctions on Dodik, who was banned from holding office after violating his countryâs peace deal.
The Balkans isnât the only place Continental is looking to cash in on the administrationâs agenda abroad: The firm reportedly took on at least a dozen clients in Venezuela after the US captured its former leader earlier this year.
Republika Srpska, for its part, has signed lobbying contracts worth at least $9 million since Trump was inaugurated in an effort to curry favor with the administration (though itâs never signed one with Ballard Partners, Susie Wilesâ former firm).
So far, it seems to be working: Officials have yet to impose recently enacted sanctions on Serbian politicians despite Congressâ urging.
House Democrats already have a plan, reported first by Semafor, to oversee the administrationâs Balkans policy if they win a majority next month.
Notable
- LaCivita has also advised another Continental client looking to ingratiate himself with Trump: Albaniaâs Sali Berisha.
- Trump this term has embraced a number of foreign governments who have moved to politically align themselves with the conservative or MAGA movement, as CBS and Reuters reported.

c68b7f60c1e0.text:
Shield AI expects to fly its unmanned fighter jet within months
The Navy is kicking in $150 million to further develop the X-BAT.
Shield AI expects to start flying its X-BAT prototype unmanned fighter jet by year’s end—and is getting $150 million from the Navy to keep developing it, officials said.
“We've been building two prototype vehicles—they're full scale. The first one will be done in the next couple of weeks here,” said Armor Harris, Shield AI’s senior vice president of aircraft. “And then we'll be getting into flight testing at the end of this year…going straight to the vertical takeoff and landing tests as the final de-risk of the [technology].”
Shield AI also secured $150 million from the Navy to continue developing the X-BAT, a modification to an other transaction agreement. The venture-capital-backed company promised to match the investment with its own funds. That brings total planned development spending on the project, which also received $50 million from the Navy and the Defense Innovation Unit in August and a dollar match from Shield, to $400 million.
“We really developed X-BAT in collaboration with NAVAIR and NAWCAD, which is the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division—the experts for naval aviation,” Harris said. “The Navy has been funding the development through the newly created Rapid Capability Cell. So there was an initial $50 million investment earlier this year. This is basically the next round of investment, which is $150 million to continue the development of the platform.”
The company also recently named two sites for production and flight testing of the autonomous jet.
Under the X-BAT contract, the Navy money will be released to Shield AI as it meets developmental milestones.
“There will be a follow-on phase in the future if Shield AI and X-BAT continue to perform well—all leading up to fielding an early operational capability in about 2029. So basically, the way that the OTA is structured is that there's milestone-based payments for Shield achieving specific objectives along the way,” Harris said.
The company also aims to export the aircraft as well as sell it to the Pentagon.
“There's been a tremendous amount of international interest in X-BAT because of its multi-role capabilities, its ability to be runway independent, and basically what's called the cost-per effect,” he said. Particularly interested countries are “looking to augment F-35 and F-16 capabilities” and those “that don't necessarily have the infrastructure and the size of an air force needed to operate a jet like the F-35.”

9fa086261069.text:
- Published
The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.
An official from the Defense Department told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.
The Pentagon had announced earlier this week that it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said on Thursday. "Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be".
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on whether President Donald Trump supports a livestreamed public execution.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said on Monday that the defence secretary had made the recommendation and Trump approved it.
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The shooting took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The last military execution took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency.
The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of the Second World War.
While Trump has never publicly advocated for a public execution, he has long supported the death penalty. In 1989, for example, he took out large ads in The New York Times calling for the execution of the Central Park Five - who had been convicted of rape and assault charges but were later exonerated.
The US government did not carry out executions for 17 years before the final year of Trump's first term as president, when the government conducted a flurry of 13 executions.
Upon returning to office last January, Trump swiftly overturned predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions and signed an executive order aimed at "restoring" the death penalty and "protecting public safety".

e8a09ce431ec.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/pentagon-says-firing-squad-execution-of-fort-hood-shooter-will-be-livestreamed Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed Nation Oct 8, 2026 6:19 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be "public." Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice News on Wednesday, said the execution of Hasan will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said. Hegseth spoke to the outlet aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier while visiting the long-deployed crew, who supported the Iran war, before their arrival at their home port in San Diego. WATCH: Hegseth welcomes return of USS Lincoln after long, troubled deployment When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Hegseth simply replied: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd." Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution will be livestreamed and that more details would follow. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said Monday that President Donald Trump had approved the execution of Hasan. Trump has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action. Those warnings preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran at the end of February over its ballistic missiles and the risk of it developing nuclear weapons. "We've been told that the killing in Iran is stopping," Trump told reporters on Jan. 14 of this year. "It's stopping and there's no plan for executions." He repeated that claim on Jan. 20 at a White House press briefing, saying: "We let them know that if that happens, that will be a very bad day for them. And they decided not to do it. They didn't hang the people." Slightly more than a month later in his State of the Union address, Trump said, "We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence." The White House on Thursday immediately referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon. However, experts on military law said Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution. "It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions," Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law. Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. During the trial it was revealed that Hasan spent weeks planning the deadly attack, and his preparation included videotaping a sales clerk showing him how to change the magazine on the pistol that he purchased. He would later go to a gun range outside Austin and ask for advice on how to reload with speed and precision from an instructor. Soldiers later testified that Hasan's rapid reloading made it all but impossible to stop the shooting. Investigators recovered 146 shell casings inside the building and dozens more outside, where Hasan shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot. Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his trial. Hasan made almost no effort to defend himself in court, telling jurors when he acted as his own counsel that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides." Hegseth said the military hasn't executed a servicemember by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. What Americans think about the death penalty
Christa Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented.
The failure of Pike's execution has reignited the debate about capital punishment and its use in the United States.
The BBC spoke to Americans as well as international tourists in Washington DC about their views on the death penalty.
Video by Meiying Wu.

9ab73efa88b8.text: Presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet with Ukrainian negotiators and European officials in Miami on Friday to present "new ideas and proposals" to break the stalemate in the Russia-Ukraine war, U.S. and Ukrainian officials say. Why it matters: The Trump administration is hoping to reach a diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the midterm elections and before brutal winter weather grips Ukraine. One of the ideas is a partial ceasefire that halts attacks on energy infrastructure and grain shipments. While Ukraine has said it's willing to take that step, Russia has shown little willingness. "They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop. So the U.S. is trying to mediate with the sides, with the goal of creating a unified proposal," a U.S. source said Driving the news: Witkoff and Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv in early September. Since then, they've been working with the Russians and Ukrainians on an updated peace initiative. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at a press conference in Lisbon Thursday that the war is at a "stalemate." He stressed that the U.S. wants to prevent further escalation of fighting in the coming month and find a way to end the war. Behind the scenes: Witkoff and Kushner met with President Trump Thursday to present the latest U.S. proposal and receive his input ahead of the talks in Miami, which are expected to last two days, a U.S. official said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Deputy National Security Advisor Mike Needham also attended the meeting. Zoom in: President Volodymyr Zelensky's Chief of Staff, Kyrylo Budanov, Foreign Intelligence Director Rustem Umerov, diplomatic adviser Sergey Kyslytsia and Member of Parliament Davyd Arakhamia will participate from the Ukrainian side. The U.S. also invited national security advisers from the UK, France and Germany, as well as officials from NATO and the EU. A U.S. source said the parties will discuss proposals for security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war prosperity plan and other aspects of the conflict. The other side: Zelensky told reporters on Thursday that Ukraine is discussing with the U.S. the possibility of an energy and grain ceasefire. "As for what might be realistic or more realistic, I am not ready to say yet. I do not want to say something and then have Russia, as always, do the opposite out of spite. So let's wait and see," he said. Between the lines: A Ukrainian official said that despite skepticism in Kyiv, the U.S. midterm elections and Russia's need for sanctions relief might lead Vladimir Putin to agree to a ceasefire of some sort. What to watch: Witkoff and Kushner might travel to Moscow later this month for more talks with Putin, a source with knowledge said.

Watch: Why was the sign at the British consulate in East Jerusalem removed?
Israel said in September it would shut the British consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.
The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the building ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.
Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission".
The BBC's Middle East correspondent Yolande Knell says the UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband "sees this as being a good outcome".
The consulate is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.

Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.
"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."
Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.
It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.
For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.
That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.
And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.
His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned".
Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole.
But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant.
It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it?
Meta's 'trust deficit'
It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta.
Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users.
Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed.
And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (Â£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube.
Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution.
Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases.
In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant.
And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes.
The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users.
Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight.
To some, the trust issue feels existential
"Once the public has stopped trusting you, it's kind of a downward spiral," says associate professor Alison Taylor of New York University's Stern School of Business.
"It feels likeâ¦ the trust deficit is so big, I just don't know that they're going to be able to recover."
'Withstanding the blowback'
But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025.
While it has agreed to temper its pursuit of the teen market (which many brands eagerly cultivate to build their future user base), the company has said that teens accounted for less than 1% of its revenue anyway. Competitors TikTok and Google's YouTube are more popular with young users.
And the company's settlement with the 48 states was widely considered a massive win for Meta, because it prevented some Meta bosses (including Zuckerberg) from having to give testimony, and stopped the release of further internal documents, while allowing the company to avoid admitting wrongdoing. The company's stock price surged 4% immediately following the announcement, and is up more than 25% over the last month.

5dbca907d8a5.text: More than half a dozen U.S. House districts in California will send a Democrat to Capitol Hill next year no matter what. Party leadership still has a lot riding on the outcome. Why it matters: Most of these Democrat vs. Democrat runoffs — a quirk of California's election system — are between an establishment candidate and an outsider vowing to make leadership's life hell. Democratic Reps. Mike Thompson, Doris Matsui and Jimmy Gomez are all facing well-funded challenges from younger, less establishment-aligned Democrats. There are also several Northern California races that feature a pro-leadership Democrat facing off against a more left-leaning rival. Sought for comment on this story, Justin Chermol, a spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), told Axios: "Stop wasting our time with your irrelevant stories that have nothing to do with taking back control of the House of Representatives." 4th District: Rep. Mike Thompson vs. Eric Jones Thompson , a 75-year-old first elected in 1998, faces a challenge from 35-year-old former venture capitalist Eric Jones. "I don't think anyone in Democratic leadership today is really doing their job well," Jones said in an interview with Axios. Asked if he would vote for Jeffries as speaker, Jones replied: "As of today, I wouldn't vote for any member." Jones is trying to cobble together a populist, anti-establishment coalition consisting of both progressives and Republicans. He said he does not identify as progressive, telling Axios he prefers "no labels." He said that, if elected, he will "have the benefit of independence ... of not taking party money, and I'm not going to vote a party line." 7th District: Rep. Doris Matsui vs. Mai Vang Matsui, 85, is seen as particularly vulnerable after finishing second to Mai Vang in the jungle primary election in June. Vang, a progressive Sacramento City Councilmember in her 40s, has positioned herself alongside a new bloc of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-aligned candidates including Darializa Avila Chevalier, Chris Rabb and Melat Kiros. She previously signaled to Axios she won't vote for Jeffries as speaker, saying she "cannot support this kind of leadership" and that "we need new leadership and a new direction." 11th District: Scott Wiener vs. Connie Chan The fight between state Sen. Scott Wiener and San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan to succeed former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has been particularly bitter. Chan has positioned herself to the left of Wiener, a longtime progressive who has come under fire from the pro-Palestinian movement for being insufficiently critical of Israel. Wiener told Mission Local he looks "forward to electing Hakeem Jeffries speaker." Chan told the outlet that "any candidate for speaker, including Hakeem Jeffries, will have to earn my vote." 14th District: Rep. Aisha Wahab vs. Melissa Hernandez Wahab , a progressive former state senator, defeated Hernandez, the more moderate former mayor of Dublin, California, in an August special election to replace former Rep. Eric Swalwell . The two are now duking it out for a full term. Wahab has already shown her willingness to buck leadership: She defied Pelosi and Jeffries by running in the special election instead of allowing a "caretaker" to run unopposed, according to The Sunday Times . The Wahab and Hernandez campaigns did not respond to questions about whether their candidates would vote for Jeffries as speaker. 34th District: Rep. Jimmy Gomez vs. Angela Gonzales-Torres Gomez has come under fire after the House Ethics Committee opened an investigation into him in August over allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denies. He has been a longtime target of the left, having survived three consecutive primary challenges from Democrat David Kim since 2020 by 2 to 11 percentage points. This time he faces a challenge from Angela Gonzales-Torres, a progressive local neighborhood councilor backed by many of the same left-wing groups that support Vang and Wahab. Gonzales-Torres , asked in an interview with Axios if she would vote for Jeffries as speaker, said she looks forward to "supporting leaders who are not nearly funded by corporate super PACs." Gonzales-Torres, pointing to her support from DSA, said she considers herself part of the "national slate" of progressive insurgents such as Avila Chevalier, Rabb and Kiros. "Right now [what] we are focusing on is winning this election and hopefully getting to be part of utilizing our bargaining power as this incoming class in Congress," she said. The bottom line: The larger the bloc of Jeffries skeptics that arrives on Capitol Hill in January, the worse a time Democratic leadership will have. That could be tempered to a large degree by the size of Democrats' potential majority, but, as Axios previously reported , many red-seat candidates are also maintaining their independence from leadership. Still, few Democrats think Jeffries will ultimately be denied the speakership. The fights that come after are more uncertain.

A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was ordered by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time.
Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle".
Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent".
A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head.
But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her.
He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut.
Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych.
For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent.
Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev.
He understood it was an official mission.
"As Reut informed me, this operation [â¦] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says.
Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused â he says she was not fully trained â Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead.
Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives.
The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that is it "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies.
The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer".
Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep.
It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force.
Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack.
He called for "the truth, protection, and justice".
Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol.
She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine.
Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting.
The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling.
The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories.
They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine.
Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine.
Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case.
Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us.
He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea.
"In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison.
Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia.
But might this story be even murkier?
At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present.
At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised".
"Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining.
The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court.
Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets.
When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason.
As the investigation continues â into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own.
The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son.
Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" â meaning Russia.
He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation".
Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair.

Some people in the US "still hate the look of solar", Kate Collardson acknowledges.
She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor.
For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles.
This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance.
For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs, external. This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes, external.
Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry.
Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity.
For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US.
Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20â30% since it was established in 2019.
In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat.
Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently".
Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels.
The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'."
Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup.
She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where.
"With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however.
But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road."
Before repair costs are factored in, a solar roof might cost twice as much as a system of solar panels mounted on a roof.
Solar roofs are also less efficient - one reason is that the tiles are just smaller.
Another factor is the energy lost as heat. Since the tiles sit close to the roof, there's less airflow than with standard solar panels mounted on a roof. Heat impairs solar performance.
Coloured tiles are even less efficient, comments Ben Graves, co-founder of UK solar company Sunsave. "The reason why all solar cells are black, and increasingly the whole panel is now black, is because black is the best absorbing colour."
Overall, much more space would need to be devoted to solar roof tiles to produce the same amount of energy.
Sunsave does not offer solar roofs. "Most people in the UK just don't have enough money to pay for it," Graves believes.
While appearance was a bigger factor five years ago, now "the vast majority of consumers are most interested in how much they can save".
But supporters of solar roofs argue that they should not be pitted against standard solar modules on roofs.
"Let's not compare PV roof tiles to a standard PV system, but look at PV roof tiles as generating additional electricity from our roofs instead of just having the roof sit there," urges Martin Heinrich who leads a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Germany.
While standard solar panels have gone from strength to strength, solar roofs have not advanced to the same extent.
One advancement that could especially help solar roofs is matrix shingling technology.
This is a different way of connecting solar cells. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, layered like overlapping shingles, and connected to each other using electrically conductive adhesive, rather than metal wires.
This means that the electrical current can flow around shaded areas, unlike with standard modules. "If you get like a bird pooping on a part of the cell, the current can go around it," Learoyd explains.
In addition to increasing energy output, this improves the appearance as the silver wires aren't visible.
Another advantage, Heinrich says, is that "since we cut the cells into smaller areas, we can fill out special sizes more easily. You don't have to adhere to the regular pattern size."
Freesuns is an early adopter of matrix shingling technology in building-integrated PV. "We see it as a big opportunity for the future in terms of how we would make our tiles," Learoyd says.
What would also help the company is better software for automated design. This would speed up the design process, since each roofing job is unique.
Learoyd believes this would lower costs and give "the whole construction industry much more confidence in using the product".
Ten years after her own solar roof was installed, and despite the sector's setbacks, Learoyd remains optimistic.
She believes that for people with the means, it will eventually become standard to install a new roof with some sort of embedded solar. "It's just a no-brainer."

Widespread snow driven by a polar vortex is rumoured to be heading for the UK this autumn and winter. But is that really the case?
Headlines have been suggesting it is down to the effects of El NiÃ±o but the truth is much more complicated.
For the rest of the autumn, El NiÃ±o actually increases the chance of wet, mild and potentially stormy weather for the UK.
Later in winter it could shift the odds towards cold and snow, something that can be influenced by changes in the polar vortex but none of this is certain.
What is a polar vortex?
The polar vortex is a ring of strong westerly winds encircling the North Pole every winter, around 10-30 miles (16-48km) above the Earth's surface.
It forms because the air high above the Pole becomes extremely cold and dense in winter. The contrast with warmer air further south drives the very strong stratospheric winds that make up the polar vortex.
This is all going on high up in the stratosphere, far above the troposphere - where our weather actually happens.
A strong polar vortex tends to encourage a strong polar jet stream in the troposphere.
This drives areas of low pressure from west to east, bringing mild air from the Atlantic across the UK with spells of wind and rain. The coldest air is essentially locked away to the north of us.
Sometimes, however, the polar vortex can wobble, weaken or even reverse direction.
Over a period of days and weeks this can work its way down through the atmosphere influencing our jet stream, causing it to weaken, become more bendy or reverse.
It can deliver colder northerly or easterly winds which can bring the UK its coldest winter weather
However, it does not always translate into changes in weather patterns at the Earth's surface.
Equally, periods of a meandering jet stream and cold winter weather often occur without significant changes in the polar vortex.
What does El NiÃ±o have to do with it?
El NiÃ±o - the naturally-occurring climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean - is continuing to grow and by some measures is already the strongest on record.
The heat released from the warm Pacific Ocean into the atmosphere impacts weather patterns around the globe.
In autumn it increases the chance of wet and stormy weather in the UK - something that is reflected in the forecasts for this season.
In late winter, the waves of energy released by El NiÃ±o can move upwards through the atmosphere making it more likely that the polar vortex becomes disrupted, increasing the chance of ice and snow.
However, the links are unclear and the evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest winter in three decades - and coincided with an El NiÃ±o.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El NiÃ±o winter and was unseasonably warm.
The so-called Beast from the East in 2018 actually occurred during a La NiÃ±a year, effectively the opposite of El NiÃ±o.
So while El NiÃ±o is already having big impacts on global weather, and may influence the polar vortex later in winter, snow and ice in the UK is far from guaranteed.
Current forecasts suggest no significant cold or snow is likely in the near future.

40596e3286f7.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/how-moscows-secrecy-about-a-suspected-plague-case-follows-a-soviet-era-pattern Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How Moscow's secrecy about a suspected plague case follows a Soviet-era pattern World Oct 8, 2026 6:56 PM EDT The Kremlin has long maintained a culture of secrecy when it comes to controlling public information, especially involving accidents — from industrial disasters to health emergencies. The suspicious death last week of a worker at a research lab in Siberia that has fueled global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague is just the latest example of how leaders in Moscow manage the official narrative that often covers up the truth for years. READ MORE: Russia's public health watchdog denies a second infection in suspected pneumonic plague case Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, has told the World Health Organization that no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region of southeastern Siberia. In tersely worded statements, the Russian agency said the lab worker contracted pneumonia of "unknown" origin and that tests found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The WHO urged Russia to share more information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures and media reports that a second employee had pneumonia of undetermined cause. Scarce official information about the worker's death, which unconfirmed reports in Russia blamed on pneumonic plague, follows the Soviet-era patterns of secrecy in dealing with outbreaks of infectious diseases, accidents and other emergencies. Here are other examples of Moscow censoring public health information: The 1959-60 smallpox outbreak In the final days of December 1959, leading Soviet graphic artist Alexei Kokorekin fell ill and died shortly after returning from a trip to India. Doctors initially struggled to identify the cause of death as smallpox, which was considered eradicated decades earlier. Once it became clear, authorities launched a massive effort to contain the outbreak. The KGB meticulously tracked down Kokorekin's contacts, and thousands of people were put in isolation. An Aeroflot flight carrying one of his contacts was contacted before it landed in Paris and ordered to return to Moscow. Authorities halted all travel to and from Moscow and launched an unprecedented effort in which thousands of vaccination teams distributed shots to millions of residents of the capital and the surrounding region. International news outlets reported the massive campaign, but Soviet state media kept silent about it. The outbreak led to 46 confirmed cases and three deaths in Moscow before it was contained in 44 days. A novel and movie based on the outbreak appeared later, but the true details of what happened were hidden from the public until the waning years of the Soviet Union. The 1971 Aral Sea smallpox outbreak During tests of a smallpox bioweapon on a tightly guarded range on Vozrozhdeniya Island in the Aral Sea in August 1971, a research ship accidentally sailed too close to the aerosolized plume of microbes. A marine biologist on the ship contracted smallpox and spread it to several others in the town of Aralsk in what is now part of Kazakhstan, resulting in 10 infections and three deaths. The town was quarantined and more than 40,000 people were vaccinated against smallpox within days, but the public remained unaware of what happened. The incident only became widely known in 2002 when U.S. researchers publicized old Soviet archives. The 1979 anthrax leak On April 2, 1979, anthrax spores were accidentally released from a secret biological weapons lab in Sverdlovsk, the Ural Mountains city that is now called Yekaterinburg. The accident was caused by a worker failing to replace a faulty ventilation filter, resulting in the release of the deadly spores into the air. At least 68 people died in the resulting anthrax outbreak. Soviet authorities officially blamed the deaths on contaminated meat from a street market and the KGB made sure to keep details of the accident under wraps, confiscating medical records. It wasn't until after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union that the truth about the outbreak became known under Russian President Boris Yeltsin, a former Communist Party boss in Sverdlovsk. The 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster When the reactor No. 4 exploded at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in the then-Soviet republic of Ukraine on April 26, 1986, it spewed a radioactive cloud across Europe. Authorities were slow to report the incident and warn the public about the radioactive threat. When Sweden detected the radiation, Moscow initially denied that any accident had occurred. Soviet officials waited for 36 hours before ordering the evacuation of the town of Pripyat near the plant. Five days later, tens of thousands of people were exposed to radioactive fallout as they marched through the streets of Kyiv during the May Day parade. Despite Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev's policy of "glasnost," or greater openness, authorities heavily censored medical data and casualty figures as part of their efforts to conceal the true scale of the disaster. Immediately after the accident, 30 plant workers and firefighters died from acute radiation sickness, and thousands of people later died from radiation-related illnesses.
