c7ec5583e0fd.text: Millions along the Gulf Coast are on high alert as Hurricane Isaias gains power and moves closer to land. Isaias is now a Category 2 storm, the first hurricane in the Atlantic basin this year. Forecasters are warning of heavy rain, damaging winds, flooding, storm surge and the possibility of tornadoes. Amna Nawaz discussed the latest with National Hurricane Center Director Michael Brennan. Amna Nawaz: Millions of Americans along the Gulf Coast are on high alert due to life-threatening conditions as Hurricane Isaias gains power and moves closer to land. Isaias rapidly intensified overnight from a tropical storm to what is now a Category 2 hurricane, making it the first one in the Atlantic this year. Residents are securing their homes and gathering supplies. Local and state officials are issuing evacuation orders. And forecasters are warning of heavy rain, damaging winds, flooding, storm surges, and the possibility of tornadoes. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said his state will be ready. Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL): And I will just say we have got everyone mobilized, the full monty for the storm. We're taking it very seriously. I hope it weakens. I think there's conditions where it could. But our assumption is that it's going to hit strong as a probably lower-end category 3. Amna Nawaz: Joining us now is Michael Brennan. He's director of the National Hurricane Center. So, Michael, knowing the path could still change here, let's just start with the latest you know on the potential path of this hurricane and when it could make landfall. Michael Brennan, Director, National Hurricane Center: Well, the storm has strengthened over the last several hours, now a Category 2 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale. It's going to continue to move off to the northeast over the next several hours overnight and then turn more towards the north. Right now, we're thinking that the center is going to make landfall somewhere in the Alabama or Florida Panhandle coastline, but where the exact center crosses land is not as important as the impacts. You're going to see impacts all along the Northern Gulf Coast from this system. Amna Nawaz: You mentioned how rapidly it intensified. It's already a Category 2. Is there any way to tell just how powerful this storm could be when it makes landfall? Could it possibly reach Category 3 or more? Michael Brennan: Over water, yes. There's a small window of opportunity for it to continue to intensify tonight, potentially taking it close to Category 3 strength overnight. But we think weakening will commence later tonight or tomorrow as it approaches the coastline. So we're really looking at maybe a Category 1 or 2 as it makes its approach, final approach, to landfall. But, regardless, a lot of people get really hung up on the intensity and the categories. I think the hazards are largely baked at this point, meaning that, no matter what intensity the storm comes ashore as, the hazards are largely going to be unchanged, We're going to see a lot of storm surge, rainfall, flooding, and potential for strong, impactful winds moving inland over some of these Southern Tier states with long-duration power outages. Amna Nawaz: We know those residents are being urged to prepare. What kind of preparations should they be making? How far inland should they be preparing, and when and how do people make that decision to evacuate? Michael Brennan: So, first and foremost, I'm glad you mentioned the evacuations. There are a number of mandatory or recommended evacuations along the Northern Gulf Coast here, especially coastal Alabama, portions of Mississippi and even Florida Panhandle. If you've been ordered to evacuate, you need to go ahead and do that right away. Don't assume that you'll have the entirety of tomorrow to make necessary preparations or evacuate. You can see in the satellite imagery here the conditions are already spreading well out in front of this storm, so we're not going to have all day tomorrow to prepare or evacuate if ordered to do so. Amna Nawaz: That is Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, joining us tonight. Michael, thank you for your time. Michael Brennan: Thank you.

Some campaigns fear it's too late Politics Oct 8, 2026 6:51 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans are entering the final month of the midterm campaign increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping losses as the party reckons with President Donald Trump's unpopularity, persistent cost concerns and the fallout from the war in Iran. The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million in cash on hand at the end of August and began stepping up its spending on critical races in September. WATCH: Who's spending big, and where, in most expensive election cycle ever But that money may have come too late, forcing the president's group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time. Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups. Instead, by waiting until September, Trump-connected organizations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they acted earlier. A representative of MAGA Inc. familiar with the group's strategy said its spending has allowed Republicans to keep races more competitive than they would have been otherwise. In some cases, the group has been the only one on the air criticizing Democratic candidates. Please check your inbox to confirm. The MAGA Inc. representative and the Republican Senate campaign officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy. The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump traveled on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. The state hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. WATCH: Trump speaks at rally for Senate candidate Ken Paxton in San Antonio Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what's normally a safe Republican seat. One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton's estranged wife saying she's supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans. Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price. MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Democratic nominee James Talarico's campaign, also on broadcast and streaming. Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities. For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico's campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact. Elections are a referendum on the power of money The 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics. Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage. Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late. "After the votes are counted, I think we're going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it," he said. "A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket." Thune's group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party's challenge in the Senate race there. The state's outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party's vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, "in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets." "If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state," he said. "Absent endless resources, you've got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win." The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash. Money alone doesn't translate into victory There's plenty of evidence that money alone doesn't translate into victory. Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House. Elon Musk's $25 million didn't lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat last year. ba3a2e6b4197.text: Christa Pike, the Tennessee woman who survived a botched execution, has reportedly taken a few steps in her hospital room six days after she received two lethal injections. Justice correspondent Ali Rogin discussed questions surrounding the state of capital punishment with Austin Sarat, author of "Lethal Injection and the False Promise of Humane Execution." Amna Nawaz: Christa Pike, the Tennessee woman who survived a botched execution, has reportedly taken a few steps in her hospital room six days after she received two lethal injections. Pike was convicted of the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, and it's now unclear how that case will proceed. Justice correspondent Ali Rogin has more on the questions surrounding the state of capital punishment. Ali Rogin: In response to the failed execution attempt, the governor has paused all pending executions through the end of the year, and a judge has ordered Tennessee to preserve evidence of what went wrong. To discuss, we're now joined by Austin Sarat, author of the book "Lethal Injection and the False Promise of Humane Execution." Austin Sarat, thank you so much for joining us. You have been covering executions and failed executions for a long time. How unique, if at all, is what happened to Christa Pike and how often do executions either fail or get botched like this? Austin Sarat, Author, "Lethal Injection and the False Promise of Humane Execution": What happened to Christa Pike was shocking but not surprising. To anyone that's followed the American death penalty, we know that executions are frequently botched, and the method of execution which is least reliable, most frequently botched, lethal injection. But I don't think anyone was prepared for an execution in which the lethal drugs actually reach the condemned person, and that person lives to tell about it. So it's really an unprecedented event in the recent history of capital punishment. Ali Rogin: It certainly also seems unprecedented in terms of what policymakers do now. What options are the leaders in Tennessee who would make these decisions thinking through right now in terms of, do they try again? How does Christa Pike's legal status change? Austin Sarat: Well, the first thing that they are doing, as Governor Lee has announced, is, they're going to do an investigation to try to find out what actually went wrong in the execution chamber. Next, the governor will have to make a decision about whether or not that this governor wants to commute Christa Pike's sentence. If the governor doesn't do that, and the state decides to go forward with a second execution attempt, we will be entering somewhat uncharted territory. A second execution is very rare in the United States. It happened in 1947 in the state of Louisiana. It's happened a couple of times in Alabama more recently. And the arguments will be made, and I think they're persuasive arguments, that to subject Christa Pike to a second execution attempt would be a cruel punishment, in violation of the Eighth Amendment, and would be a form of double jeopardy prohibited by the Constitution of the United States. Ali Rogin: In your research, you have found that lethal injection fails more often than any other method in American history, including hanging and the electric chair. Why is that? Austin Sarat: Well, no method of execution is foolproof. Every method of execution that we have used in the United States, whether it's hanging, the electric chair, the gas chamber, now lethal injection, has run into problems. Lethal injection runs into more problems because, paradoxically, it's a very complicated way to try to put someone to death. You have to find a usable vein. You have to secure an I.V. You have to make sure that the drugs that you are using are up to date and potent. So it's not surprising that a complicated procedure like lethal injection would run into problems of the kind that it has. And, of course, the problems of lethal injection have not been helped by the desire of states, including the state of Tennessee, to keep what happens in the execution chamber as secret as possible, so that the problems of lethal injection, when they occur, often don't make the headlines that Christa Pike's execution attempt made. Ali Rogin: And certainly this execution attempt has made a lot of headlines, but you have opined that it's not likely to change the dial in terms of public perception around the death penalty. Where is public sentiment today and why don't you think something like this might shift it? Austin Sarat: I think the United States is in a period of national reconsideration of capital punishment. Support for the death penalty is down from what it was three decades ago, and even people who support capital punishment tend not to support it as intensely as they once did. The number of death sentences in this country is way down from what it was three decades ago. And if we look at the states that have the death penalty, many of them that have it on the books don't use it in practice. They don't execute anyone. Ali Rogin: Austin Sarat, expert on the death penalty and capital punishment, thank you so much for joining us. Austin Sarat: My pleasure. Thanks for having me.

97745f8091d4.text: Israel is barreling toward elections in less than three weeks, which could extend Benjamin Netanyahu's already-record tenure as its leader. The Trump administration has worked in near lockstep with Netanyahu since the president’s return to office. Amna Nawaz discussed what Israeli voters are considering with Dan Shapiro, the U.S. ambassador to Israel during the Obama administration. Amna Nawaz: Israel yesterday observed the solemn and terrible anniversary of the October 7 attacks. The nation is now barreling toward elections in less than three weeks, which could extend Benjamin Netanyahu's already record tenure as Israel's leader. The Trump administration has worked in near lockstep with Netanyahu since the president's return to office. But an exclusive in today's New York Times reports that a top official in the U.S. Embassy is often rewriting cables that alter the picture on the ground in Israel, Gaza, and the West Bank. To explore that and the wider picture in Israel, I'm joined now by Ambassador Dan Shapiro, who served as an American envoy to Israel during the Obama administration. Ambassador, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Daniel Shapiro, Former U.S. Ambassador to Israel: Thanks for having me on. Amna Nawaz: So I want to start with that New York Times exclusive in which they said they talked to 15 U.S. officials, reviewed dozens of cables and documents and internal communications. And the characterization there is that this top aide was altering information making its way back to Washington in a positive light, in other words, not reflecting accurately some of the things that were making their way up in memos and getting that to D.C. What's your reaction to that reporting? Daniel Shapiro: Well, I don't know the details of this particular case. What I can tell you is that my experience as an ambassador and with an embassy staff is that what Washington policymakers need is clear and unvarnished reporting about what's happening in the country you're serving in. That means that, in a case like Israel, Israel is a security partner and there are aspects of the things that happen in Israel that certainly serve U.S. interests. Certainly, with the case of the current government, which includes very extreme members of the Israeli political system, advocates for mass settlement expansion in the West Bank, people who are looking away from a wave of violence by extremist Jewish settlers against Palestinian civilians, that should also be part of the reporting. So, that's, I think, what an embassy's obligation is, an ambassador's obligation is and those who work for the ambassador. Amna Nawaz: One of the pieces of information The New York Times cites specifically is a memo that staff members in the embassy drafted about Israel expanding some of its West Bank settlements very quietly. They say, according to sources, that memo never made it to Washington. And I should share with you what the ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, said in response to their reporting. He called it a hit piece. He said: "I personally and categorically refute the elements of this proposed story," as he put it. I have to put to you, since you have served in the role. Some will say, isn't it the ambassador's job to gatekeep that information, to edit cables before they go back to D.C.? Do you have any concerns about this reporting? Daniel Shapiro: A good embassy and ambassador gives clear and unvarnished reporting, but there's always judgment calls. And, in the end, the embassy's reporting should reflect what the ambassador believes and the views that he wants to share with the Washington policymakers. Amna Nawaz: As we noted, we're now speaking the day after Israel marked three years since those Hamas terrorist attacks, and we know the shadow of those attacks has loomed large over these upcoming elections. You're there on the ground. We know Netanyahu's faced a lot of questions about what he knew before the attacks. How big a role are those attacks playing in this election? Daniel Shapiro: Yes, I have been here just about 24 hours, and it's very clear that this is the central issue in the closing phase of this election. Who bears responsibility for the October 7 attacks? The opposition candidates led by Gadi Eisenkot as part of a coalition of parties are saying that Netanyahu was asleep at the wheel, had policies that underestimated what Hamas' intentions and capabilities were in Gaza, didn't respond in real time, nor were they prepared before the case for that -- attacks. They did not share information with him. They didn't wake him on the morning of the attack in time to make key decisions. And he is trying to rally his traditional supporters to say he's still the person that can be trusted to deal with the various security threats that Israel still faces. It looks like it's a very close election, and it may be that neither side will really be able to form a coalition government coming out of it, in which case it's entirely possible that Netanyahu will remain in office as a caretaker while another election is run a few months from now. Amna Nawaz: We have seen Netanyahu say that he has no greater partner than U.S. President Trump, but we did see President Trump sort of sidestep a question recently about endorsing Netanyahu. What have you noticed about relations between the two? Have they taken a hit recently? Daniel Shapiro: They certainly have cooled. There was certainly a period earlier this year when it was fully expected, and I know Netanyahu was expecting it, that President Trump would give him a fulsome endorsement. 1f97acb9bf76.text: Fusing faith and politics is almost a no-brainer for many Republicans hoping to hold public office. But this election cycle, 12 pastors, seminarians and former clergy ran as Democrats, with about half securing nominations. Lisa Desjardins discussed more with NPR religion correspondent Jason Derose, who recently spent time on the campaign trail with several of these candidates. Amna Nawaz: Well, with just a few weeks to go until Election Day, Democrats are hoping to flip some seats in deep red states. And some are doing that by talking about religion. Our Lisa Desjardins has more. Lisa Desjardins: Fusing faith in politics is almost a no-brainer for many Republicans hoping to hold public office. But this election cycle, 12 pastors, seminarians, and former clergy ran as Democrats, with about half managing to secure their nominations. Coming from the pulpit to the political stage, these candidates have used their experience as religious leaders to talk about their call to run. James Talarico (D), Texas Senatorial Candidate: I want to speak to you this morning, not as a candidate, but as a fellow Christian. Frederick Haynes III (D), Texas Congressional candidate: But this Republican Party has demolished and torn down. Adam Hamilton (D), Kansas Senatorial Candidate: Jesus himself, there were times he turned over the money changers' tables in the temple, and he still taught us to love our neighbor and even love our enemy. We have seen that this year also, but what's new here is this Democratic cohort. Why do you think this is emerging now? Jason DeRose: Well, for many years, as you said, Republicans really had the market cornered on this. And I think that Democrats finally figured out a way to have clergy, the people best trained and most trained and most used to talking about their faith and how it -- how they use it in public life. And these people emerged through state legislatures. Three of these candidates serve in state legislatures right now. So they realized, this is our moment, I think. I don't think there was a big campaign to get them to run, say, from the Democratic Party. It was much more -- these were people serving their neighbors in state legislatures who said it's now time for a larger stage. Lisa Desjardins: There is news regarding one of these candidates. That's Adam Hamilton in Kansas. The Cook Political Report rated that Senate race in Kansas a toss-up, which is rather incredible for a state that has not voted for a Democrat for Senate in decades. What can you tell us about that race? What does it tell you about what's happening? Jason DeRose: Well, what's interesting to me there is that, when I first started this reporting, it was a pretty solidly Republican race, and this has moved very quickly from solidly red to leans red and now to toss-up, a very big deal. Hamilton is the pastor of a very large, one might call it a megachurch, a Methodist megachurch. He's written many, many books. But he was actually a Republican for many years who, in fact, thought of running as an independent, but decided to run as a Democrat. And it seems to be working out for him, becoming a toss-up. Lisa Desjardins: How do these candidates thread this needle -- we have separation of church and state here -- between talking into a secular crowd and then also speaking of their faith to a religious one? Jason DeRose: Well, it's a really difficult needle to thread for clergy because they're so used to talking about their faith. But, again, these people, some of them have spent time in legislatures talking about their -- how their faith influences their politics, but not how it dictates their politics. And I think that, for James Talarico in particular, he came to prominence talking out against Christian nationalism while being a seminarian, while being a politician. So he's figured out how to do it as well. I think part of what he says and part of what Sarah Trone Garriott in Iowa and Lindsay James in Iowa also do is, they say that their faith influences their politics, it doesn't dictate their politics, and they don't dictate other people's faith. Lisa Desjardins: Republicans are countering some of these candidates by questioning if they are true Christians. I want to play some sound from one of those opposing Republicans. This is Joe Mitchell in Iowa. Joe Mitchell (R), Iowa Congressional Candidate: I call them PINOs, pastor in name only. That's what I call them, pastors in name only, because they're not real pastors, right? They don't profess the truth, Gospel of Jesus Christ. Lisa Desjardins: In our last-minute or so, these are ordained or to-be-ordained members of clergy. That is a fact. But are these attacks working? And what does this say about kind of the battle to define Christianity? Jason DeRose: Well, I don't know that they're working because throughout -- all of these candidates are being attacked that way for not being true Christians, and they have all gained ground. Hall, Associated Press By — Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/christa-pikes-attorneys-say-she-is-walking-with-help-and-eating-after-failed-execution-attempt Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Christa Pike's attorneys say she is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt Nation Oct 8, 2026 8:35 PM EDT NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike has begun walking and eating again at a hospital a week after surviving Tennessee's attempt to execute her with lethal drugs, her attorneys said Thursday. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state sought to giver her a lethal injection eight days ago for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The drug didn't kill her, and her arms were left burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator. WATCH: Botched execution reignites debate surrounding death penalty Her first steps on Wednesday were "limited" and she required some assistance as she walked on Thursday, her lawyers said in a statement. She is also regaining mobility in her arms, and she was able to eat for the first time. But the lawyers warned uncertainty remains about her physical recovery and her legal standing after the attempt to carry out her death sentence. Questions remain about Pike's recovery and legal case The failed execution on Sept. 30 has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty. Texas on Wednesday carried out the first execution in the U.S. since the Tennessee attempt. "While her physical recovery has been remarkable, significant questions remain about the long-term effects of what she endured," her attorneys said in Thursday's statement. "Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die." Pike regained consciousness Tuesday and was able to speak after awakening, they said. They initially described her as "confused" soon after regaining consciousness, and said Thursday that she continued to struggle with concentration and memory. Doctors say it is too early to assess the long-term impacts, the attorneys added. It also remains unclear whether Tennessee will try to execute her again. Her attorneys have said that they will urge Republican Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without parole. "She should never be subjected to another execution attempt," they said in the statement. What went wrong with the execution remains unclear Lee has since postponed the state's only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of why the execution failed. The state's prison chief resigned after the execution attempt. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream. READ MORE: The latest on Christa Pike's case and Tennessee's previously botched executions Pike's attorneys wrote in a court filing that "apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed." State officials have offered no explanation of what occurred. As the process got underway Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital. Chandler reported from Montgomery, Alabama. Associated Press writer Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles contributed. Few details were immediately available about the shooting, which happened around 4 p.m. The person who was shot was conscious and being treated at a hospital, the New York Police Department said in a post on X, noting that its officers didn't witness the shooting and weren't involved. READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows Messages seeking further information were sent to federal authorities. An FBI spokesperson said an evidence response team was responding to the scene "to support our partners at the Department of Homeland Security," but offered no other details. The shooting happened in the Marble Hill neighborhood, a small part of Manhattan attached to the Bronx. Pedro Almaraz, an employee at a nearby restaurant, said he heard about three or four gunshots and saw a man on the ground surrounded by several officers wearing face masks and vests with Department of Homeland Security branding. Witnesses, he said, were screaming. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, said in a post on social media that she had been briefed on the shooting. "We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why," she said. Videos and photos posted by bystanders on social media showed a man sitting on the ground with his hands behind his back, in the immediate aftermath of the shooting. Another video shows New York City police officers picking up an apparently injured man and carrying him into a police vehicle. Nearby, a damaged car sat blocking the roadway with small holes in two of its windows. The videos show agents wearing Immigration and Customs Enforcement badges on the scene, including one carrying a rifle. "This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on X. "I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities." A new report paints a dark picture of the state of global wildlife—but also highlights flickers of light where some populations are on the upswing.
Over the past half-century, populations of thousands of vertebrate species across the globe have decreased in size by 73 percent on average, according to the “Living Planet” report published Wednesday by the nonprofits World Wildlife Fund and the Zoological Society of London. A number of factors contributed to this precipitous decline, including habitat loss, overexploitation and climate change.
However, a closer look at certain regions and biomes offers reasons for hope, the report’s authors say. Roughly half the populations they studied are stable or even increasing. Though these gains are outweighed by the greater magnitude of losses elsewhere, they show that concerted conservation efforts have made a difference for species such as green sea turtles and bluefin tuna, according to lead author Rebecca Shaw, the chief scientist at the World Wildlife Fund.
“The report focuses on hope because even though the headline statistic is really, really stark … what we see underlying the statistic is some real movement in some species,” Shaw said.
Despite these successes, the report stressed the importance of tackling biodiversity loss at a global scale by changing the three major systems driving extinction: food, energy and finance.
Species Losses By the Numbers
The “Living Planet” reports are released roughly every two years. The latest taps into data from tens of thousands of populations of 5,790 vertebrate species across the animal kingdom—from Laysan albatross to ring-tailed lemurs.
Rather than tallying the total number of animals lost or gained, the researchers measured changes in relative abundance of populations. That means a small population of monkeys that has dropped from 200 to 100 would have experienced the same 50 percent loss as a large colony of 20,000 bats that has dipped to 10,000.
This method allows researchers to compare data from different populations and better track overall trends, said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London who works on the Living Planet Index that informs the report.
“The reason we do that is so that we can get a good picture of what is happening across different species by giving them equal weight within this index,” she said. “We’re getting a better signal of the health of the environment.”
So while the new report does not mean there are 73 percent fewer wild vertebrate animals in total today than in 1970, it does show populations the report monitored are plummeting on average. However, diving deeper into the numbers reveals the varied stories playing out for wildlife around the world.
By geography, monitored species populations have faced the most significant decline in Latin America and the Caribbean, with an average 95 percent decrease from 1970 to 2022. In that same timeframe, North America and the combined regions of Europe and Central Asia have seen around 25 percent declines, though the authors pointed out that development in those areas had already had large-scale impacts on nature prior to 1970. Declines in Africa and the Asia and the Pacific region were 80 percent and 49 percent, respectively.
The researchers also broke the numbers down by biome. Freshwater species were the clear losers, seeing an overall decline of 85 percent—significantly more than terrestrial or marine species, though these vertebrates are also seeing major losses.
The report attributed the nosedive in freshwater species to a number of factors, including pollution, overharvesting and habitat loss caused by infrastructure such as hydropower dams. Impacted species included in the report range from migratory fish such as Chinook salmon in the Western United States to the Amazon pink river dolphin in Brazil, which plummeted by 65 percent between 1994 and 2016 alone in the Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve in the state of Amazonas.

For terrestrial species, habitat loss and degradation drove much of the biodiversity decline, while marine life faced major threats from overfishing.
Viorel Popescu, an associate research scientist at Columbia University who wasn’t involved in the report, said it’s valuable to bring these “huge amounts of data” that are largely invisible to most of the public “to the forefront.” But he added that the report may be an underestimate of total biodiversity losses, given that it only focuses on vertebrate species the authors analyzed. Other scientists have echoed this critique.
Popescu pointed to the collapse of many populations of insects, which make up roughly three-quarters of all known animal species on Earth. In fact, beetles alone account for 25 percent of all animal species.
“Those declines could be even more drastic,” Popescu said.
Good News and Bad News
The report also pointed to bright spots around the world. For example, in 2025, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle to be downlisted by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature, which means populations increased enough around the world for the animal to no longer be considered endangered.
But this recovery didn’t happen overnight. According to the report, a roughly five-decade coordinated conservation effort launched across more than 80 countries helped populations rebuild through protecting nesting females and eggs, beach management, lighting regulations, turtle excluder devices and other bycatch reduction measures to help reduce sea turtle entanglements in fishing gear.

(AP) — After more than 10 months at sea, thousands of sailors Thursday poured out of the the USS Lincoln on San Diego Bay to thunderous cheers, streaming tears and emotional hugs, marking a homecoming that included new dads who met babies born while they were away on a historic deployment supporting the Iran war. WATCH: Hegseth welcomes return of USS Lincoln after long, troubled deployment The reunion followed an emotional rollercoaster for families who described crying and losing sleep after hearing reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew during the deployment that spent a record 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea. Many said they only could communicate with family via the occasional email or rare WhatsApp calls. Abel Ramirez, 20, was glad to have that all behind him. He walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over. "It feels amazing," he said while headed out to search for his parents who traveled from Texas. "There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off." Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck after the ship docked at the pier. "It feels really overwhelming," she said about being seeing her mom again. "She missed most of my seventh grade and my birthday." She added that she's happy her mom won't be eating ramen almost every day and can celebrate with her now. Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship's commander, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day. "It's a floating city as you can see and at any moment there might be a clogged toilet," he said. The Navy has downplayed problems on the carrier The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough." WATCH: Trump says USS Lincoln's deployment was 'not nearly long enough' Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive. Hegseth told the crew that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless." Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission." USS Lincoln crew looks forward to family and favorite meals The Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat. The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The Lincoln's deployment of 322 days was just shy of that. Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. With the airwing included, there were 122 new dads, Keeler said. Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress. "She's our deployment baby," said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia. It was tough to hear about the ship's conditions while she was pregnant, she said. "I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn't sure if he was OK or not," she said. When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was "pretty bad," but now she said she feels blessed to have her family home. Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter. "I couldn't grasp the reality of it," he said about coming home. He became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, "seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me," Rivas said, his voice shaking as his eyes teared up. Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few. He had told his wife about "the lack of food and showers" on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said. The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28. In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced for a short time. After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East. Long deployments can tax service members Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment. The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months. f2a962f42b36.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/army-calls-for-safety-fixes-after-finding-systemic-failures-behind-dc-midair-collision Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Army calls for safety fixes after finding systemic failures behind DC midair collision Nation Oct 8, 2026 7:46 PM EDT The U.S. Army found systemic safety breakdowns behind last year's midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., and recommended changes to prevent future tragedies. WATCH: NTSB investigators say DCA midair collision followed years of ignored warnings The Army report — completed in May and released publicly Thursday after months of pressure from the victims' families — identified failures involving air traffic control, helicopter routes, training and safety practices. The Associated Press obtained a copy of the report hours before it was released. The deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil in over two decades happened when the helicopter collided with the descending airliner as it approached the runway, sending both plummeting into the icy Potomac River and killing 67. The Army report highlighted how the air traffic controller at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport could have prevented the crash, but it also acknowledged the military's own failings and other contributing factors. Families demand answers from the Army Tim Lilley, a former Army Black Hawk pilot whose son Sam Lilley was the airliner's first officer, said the report leaves important questions unanswered. Parts were redacted, and responsibility for the Army's failures was assigned broadly rather than to individuals. "The Army owes the families and the American public a full accounting of how these risks were allowed to persist, who was responsible for the decisions that allowed them to persist and what will be done to make sure this never happens again," said Lilley, now a commercial jet captain. The Army acknowledged that in a statement Thursday. "We recognize the families' need for answers and remain committed to transparency regarding the Army's review," it said. Report identifies key factors in the crash While the report largely reinforces the National Transportation Safety Board's conclusions, the civilian investigation was broader and emphasized years of missed warnings by the Federal Aviation Administration along with a weak military safety culture. The Army faulted the air traffic controller for not giving the helicopter crew more precise information about the approaching jet and for not warning the jet's pilot about the helicopter. After the crash, the FAA prohibited controllers from relying on pilots to maintain visual separation in busy airspace. The report recommended looking beyond Washington to examine military helicopter operations in other major cities for similar risks. An Army official said the review of helicopter flights in other cities, including Los Angeles and the Seattle-Tacoma region, is ongoing. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the situation publicly. The lieutenant general who authored the report cited "breakdowns across all layers of conflict management" but singled out two failed radio transmissions that contributed to the helicopter crew not identifying the jet. The military pilots' night-vision goggles also restricted their view and made it hard to spot the plane amid the city lights. The poorly designed helicopter route allowed a scant 75 feet (23 meters) of vertical separation between a helicopter and a plane landing on the airport's secondary runway, assuming helicopters stayed near the riverbank, which the route didn't require. This did not allow enough separation to account for the accepted level of error in a Black Hawk's altimeter, and the NTSB found the helicopter was flying nearly 100 feet (30 meters) higher than its instruments read. NTSB says the Army is making safety changes The NTSB said in a letter to the Army last week that it was pleased with the Army's progress on seven of its eight safety recommendations. That contrasts with the FAA's failure to implement roughly a third of the recommendations aimed at the agency. The Army said it has strengthened helicopter crew training, and has inspected and reconfigured 3,585 helicopters after discovering the crashed Black Hawk's ADS-B Out system, which broadcasts its location, hadn't been working for some time. The military is also improving its monitoring of safety risks and working with the FAA to share information about close calls. Victims' families push Congress for safety reforms Families of the crash victims said the Army's findings strengthen their case for legislation requiring aircraft to have technology that helps pilots detect nearby traffic. "It's a simple concept anyone can understand: aircraft should be able to see each other in the sky. The technology is proven. All that's required is the political will to do the right thing," the Families of Flight 5342 group said in a statement Thursday. "We have waited long enough. We waited for the NTSB. We waited for the Army. Both investigations are complete, and both make clear that collision avoidance technology must be part of the solution. There is nothing left for Congress to wait for," they said. The House and Senate have passed separate aviation safety bills but have yet to agree on a final version. Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. b5b406826ffc.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russian-strike-on-ukrainian-public-buses-leaves-dozens-dead-as-blackouts-worsen-in-kyiv Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russian strike on Ukrainian public buses leaves dozens dead as blackouts worsen in Kyiv World Oct 8, 2026 7:28 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — A Russian-guided bomb exploded next to public buses filled with passengers in eastern Ukraine, authorities said Thursday, killing 30 people as part of a wave of attacks that also worsened power outages in the capital. The morning attack occurred next to a bus stop in the war-torn city of Kramatorsk in Ukraine's Donetsk region, prompting public transport to be suspended in the area. "There is no doubt that Russia is cynically targeting civilians," Oleksandr Honcharenko, head of the city's military administration, said, adding that the rescue effort had been hampered by subsequent Russian attacks using small drones. READ MORE: Ukraine claims its strikes have taken out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Russia has escalated its aerial attack in recent weeks, putting pressure on Ukraine as it prepares for winter and hitting the infrastructure keeping its war-battered economy afloat. Recent targets have included energy systems, key industries, railways, post offices, shopping centers, telecom networks, gas stations and grain exports. Thursday's attack followed a Russian missile strike a day earlier that killed 22, including five children, in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky. Rescuers were searching the rubble of a residential building. At least 54 people were wounded. Several survivors slept in heavily damaged apartments because they couldn't find anywhere else to stay. Ukraine appeals for more defense support from NATO Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy traveled to Pryluky on Thursday with visiting British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who announced new sanctions on Russia. Zelenskyy warned that Russia will likely escalate daily missile and drone attacks as winter approaches. He appealed for additional defense support from NATO countries. "It is important that support in words takes concrete form in new packages for Ukraine's defense," he wrote in an online post. "Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft and investments in interceptors — all of this is directly helping save lives every day." In audio clips responding to journalist's questions Thursday evening, Zelenskyy said a Ukrainian delegation would meet in the U.S. with President Donald Trump's representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff for two days beginning Friday to discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses, among other issues. Ukraine's energy company DTEK said national grid operator Ukrenergo had ordered emergency power outages in Kyiv. Regular, rolling outages that occur on a schedule across the country will be halted during these shutdowns. Officials are urging families to prepare emergency kits, store drinking water and maintain backup power sources, as Moscow keeps up the intensity of its attacks. Kyiv police said bomb disposal specialists defused two unexploded ballistic missile warheads, each weighing about half a ton, after they landed near residential buildings. Late Wednesday, Russian drones struck Kyiv's Obolonskyi and Desnianskyi districts, killing four people and injuring 12, including four children, police said. Ukrainian attacks damage data center and oil refinery Russian technology giant Yandex said one of its data centers in the western Ryazan region was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack, taking the site offline. Also Thursday, Ukraine said its forces struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometers (about 750 miles) east of Moscow. Ukraine's General Staff described the complex as one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities. The claim could not be independently verified. Ukrainian drones also reached Russia's Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said most of the drones were shot down by air defenses, but one "reached a northern industrial hub." He didn't elaborate. Russian independent news outlet Astra reported that the Omsk oil refinery was on fire after the attack. There was no official confirmation of the report. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his government presented proposals to both Russia and Ukraine aimed at protecting civilian shipping in the Black Sea, while warning that commercial trade and grain exports could be disrupted by escalating military offensives. Separately, Lithuania deployed about 100 additional soldiers to help secure the NATO member's border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, the Baltic country's defense minister, Robertas Kaunas, said. Sandwiched between Lithuania and Poland, Kaliningrad is separated from mainland Russia and remains a major security concern for NATO's eastern flank. Associated Press writers Suzan Fraser in Ankara, Turkey; Liudas Dapkus in Vilnius, Lithuania; Derek Gatopoulos in Athens, Greece and Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed. Every voting-age Mainer could get a $167 voucher for home heating oil with what Democrats and Republicans are spending on ads in the Senate race, according to an analysis of AdImpact data.
Why it matters: Every senator gets one vote, but Senate seats aren't created equal — and they don't cost the same.
Zoom in: Like two years ago, the less-populated states have a dramatically higher dollar-per-voter ratio in 2026.
Maine is in first place, followed by Alaska, which is scheduled to be hit with $76 million in ads — enough to suck up most of the state's inventory.
Between the lines: Ohio is only in fifth place on the dollar-per-voter metric, but it's on track to host the most expensive Senate race in the country — for the second cycle in a row.
Sherrod Brown's comeback bid is proving more expensive than his 2024 race, when he was ousted by now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio).
And in New Hampshire, where Democratic Senate nominee Chris Pappas has been warning that his race is actually quite close, both parties are spending heavily to reach the state's voters.
The big picture: Both chambers are likely to come down to a handful of races.
All year, Republicans warned that Texas would get really expensive if Attorney General Ken Paxton won the primary. They were right.
Outside GOP groups spent a mind-blowing $131 million in just 17 days trying to rescue Paxton. And tens of millions more could be on the way.
But in North Carolina, where Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), predicted the race could cost $1 billion, the contest looks like it will come in under $200 million.
Republican super PACs are abandoning the Senate race there as they reallocate money to redder states.
The bottom line: Republicans have a spending advantage, especially when it comes to how many eyeballs they're actually reaching in Texas and Ohio.
But neither side has really figured out how to play moneyball and find a way to reach voters with a dramatically smaller budget.

A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in the Bronx in New York City on Thursday.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the agency, confirmed an ICE officer "discharged his weapon" during "a targeted enforcement operation... to arrest a criminal illegal alien".
In a statement, it added the man was alive and at a local hospital.
New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said it was an "unconscionable and incredibly serious situation".
"Early reports indicate agents surrounded him and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds. We believe the child was physically unharmed," he said.
The BBC has approached DHS for comment about Mamdani's remarks.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said New Yorkers were "outraged tonight" and called on federal authorities to provide answers "immediately".
The DHS said the man, who has not been named by officials, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession".
It also claimed he was associated with the Trinitarios, described by US justice department as a transnational criminal group.

Christa Pike has made a "profound" turnaround after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.
In a statement on Thursday, Pike's lawyers described her recovery as "remarkable" and said she is able to walk with assistance and is eating. She has also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution, they said.
"Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said.
The case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
"Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team said.
Pike's lawyers said they do not know the full emotional and psychological toll of the execution attempt or how long it will take her to recover.
They added that while she struggles to process what happened, she "continues to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim Colleen Slemmer".
Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
A court has ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
On Wednesday, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, such as packaging, inserts and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition before, during and after the failed execution.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions for the rest of the year and said he wants answers about what went wrong.
Pike's lawyers have called on the governor to downgrade Pike's punishment to life in prison without parole.
Proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different method to put her to death.
Killing Death Row
Could the US death penalty ever die out? A surreal story about a man in Acton, London, who supplied the USA with lethal drugs tips Livvy Haydock into the macabre world of Death Row.

A huge data centre planned in a village near a nature reserve would generate "very high noise levels" without extensive measures to block it, experts have said.
Plans have been submitted to South Norfolk Council for a 150 megawatt facility in Keswick on the edge of Norwich, which includes assessments of its potential environmental impact.
The scheme is causing concern, with thousands of people signing a petition against it, due to fears it could harm neighbouring wildlife sites.
But Norwich Apex Data Centre has defended the scheme, claiming assessments showed it would not harm protected areas like Marston Marshes.
The data centre is also causing concern over its potential water usage, noise pollution and the scale of the facility harming the landscape.
Assessments of the noise it could create found it has the "potential to generate very high levels of noise to the surrounding area" and would require extensive mitigation measures.
The majority of noise would come from the 72 chiller units on the roof.
A spokesperson said: "Our environmental assessments conclude the data centre will not harm nearby designated wildlife sites.
"The data centre will use air-cooling technology, meaning no water will be required for cooling. Water will only be needed for everyday uses, such as toilets and staff facilities, with none taken from nearby rivers or marshes.
"The facility has also been designed so that operational noise levels at surrounding sensitive locations are in line with existing background levels."
The firm also said the facility could create up to 150 permanent jobs and that it would create planting and landscaping to screen the development and reduce the visual impact.
It would also be located close to an electrical substation for offshore wind farms in the North Sea, from which it could draw power.
The project has already been met with opposition, with thousands signing a petition against it.
Daniel Elmer, the Conservative leader of South Norfolk Council and county councillor for Keswick, said he will formally object to the proposed facility.
He told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "My personal view, is that it is just too damned big for the site it would be on.
"It is right next to the marshes and the southern edge of Norwich, while it is near a listed church.
"That's the southern gateway into the city of Norwich. I think you have to think, in terms of the Norwich 'brand', what visitors to the city would see when they travel down that road.
"What they see needs to be aesthetically pleasing and I am not sure that is what they will get, given the application which has been submitted at the moment."

The clearance of a notorious illegal waste "supersite" in Kent has been completed after 15 months at a cost of Â£15m to the taxpayer.
The dump at Hoads Wood, near Ashford, which is on a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) known for rare plants and wildlife, was targeted by criminals who dumped nearly 40,000 tonnes of waste over six months in 2023.
It was the first supersite in England to have central government money spent on its clear-up, with work at two other sites bringing the total taxpayer's bill to Â£26m.
The government said the completion of works on Friday showed "just how serious" it was about tackling waste crime and restoring affected countryside.
The Environment Agency-led clean-up operation began in June 2025 and has seen 2,500 lorry loads of waste removed from the woods by specialist contractors to a landfill site in Essex.
The countryside charity CPRE Kent, residents and Kent Wildlife Trust joined forces in 2024 to campaign for the clearance of the waste, which was piled up to 15ft (4.6m) in places.
They welcomed the work's completion but some are concerned the criminal gangs may return to dump waste.
One of the organisers of the 'Rescue Hoads Wood' campaign said the cleared site would now be "catnip" to both organised gangs and opportunist fly-tippers.
He told the BBC: "Our biggest fear now is people are going to be able to access this site and start dumping on it again and unless the authorities are quick it will happen again."
The Environment Agency (EA) said it was extending the current restriction order in place that prohibits access and had dug ditches to make the site inaccessible to waste trucks.
Matthew Higginson, the EA's area environmental manager, said the regulator, police and local authorities had a joint "trigger plan" in place.
"That will bring all law enforcement partners to work together closely and much more quickly to stop anything like this happening in the future," he said.
Meanwhile, there remain conservation concerns over the future of the countryside site.
Ian Rickards, area manager for Kent Wildlife Trust, said it would take decades for ancient woodland species to return.
But he added: "It won't recover as it was but there are benefits to this. You've now got open space within the woodland. You've got wet bodies. You've got ponds. You've got these piles of dead wood as well.
"All of this will start creating, collecting and attracting wildlife back into here so it'll be fascinating to see how the site recovers."
The Hoads Wood illegal waste site is one of hundreds across England that include a number of so-called "supersites" - those that contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish - that were exposed by the BBC earlier this year.
As well as the Â£15m spent on clearing Hoads Wood, another Â£6m has been spent on the clearance of an illegal supersite in Kidlington, Oxfordshire, and a further Â£4.8m of taxpayers' money has been allocated to the clear-up of a third site near Wigan.
Speed of authorities criticised
In August, the government launched a national action plan to tackle waste crime, which it estimates costs the country more than Â£1bn every year.
But Hoads Wood campaigners have criticised the authorities for not acting quickly enough when the illegal tipping was first reported at the Kent site.
At the height of the activity in the summer of 2023, locals said there were as many as 20 to 30 trucks per day dumping waste at the ancient bluebell woodland.
The EA's Matthew Higginson said the agency did respond quickly to reports of the dumping but had to spend time investigating "to make sure we had a robust case to take to court in order to get a restriction order which closed the site".
Investigations into who was behind the dumping are ongoing, with three arrests made in February 2025.
Environment secretary Dame Angela Eagle said: "This government is taking action on the illegal waste sites that have blighted communities.
"Handing this ancient woodland back to local people, alongside our nationwide clean-up of waste sites, shows just how serious we are about restoring the places people love."

As Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities intensify and autumn's cooler temperatures hint at another tough winter to come, Ukrainians are wrestling with how to meet the twin challenges ahead: Russian drone and missile strikes and the biting cold.
"It was a very difficult winter last year in Kyiv," says mother of two Mariia Shostak, who is now packing her bags and leaving her small flat.
With prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts brought about by Russia's attack on the country's power grid, last winter was one of the hardest so far.
"There were some days and weeks that were unbearable. I started thinking I'm not going through another winter like this."
Mariia is not even waiting for winter. Russia's latest assaults on the capital have forced her hand.
"Everything changed in late August and the beginning of September, when Kyiv started being attacked around the clock," she said.
"Earlier, the drones and missiles were intercepted somewhere on the outskirts. Now it was happening in the centre, right above our heads."
After weeks of escalating Russian attacks, which by the end of September had included petrol stations, power plants and key bridges over the Dnipro river, Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko said the city was facing a "very dramatic situation".
Mariia's children, four-year-old Artur and Kira, who's two, were both born after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Unwilling to subject them to another miserable, dangerous winter, she's taking them abroad. They plan to spend the winter in Hurghada, on Egypt's Red Sea coast. It's cheaper than Europe, Mariia explains, and warmer too.
"I don't feel safe in Ukraine in any way," she says.
Polls show that many Ukrainians are feeling the same way, even if not everyone has yet made such a radical decision.
A September survey by the Gradus research company found that 40% of Ukrainians were considering relocating if living conditions continued to deteriorate; 35% said they would not move elsewhere, while 25% were undecided.
"People are thinking about a combination of stress factors," Evgeniya Blyznyuk, Gradus's founder and CEO, told us. "Not just about electricity and blackouts like last winter. Russians are targeting big logistics centres, which means that the population is worrying about products, about food during the winter."
Russia's recent attacks on Kyiv's bridges, petrol stations and schools have increased the sense of danger and foreboding.
For families with young children, the situation feels especially urgent.
Last winter, Iryna, who asked us not to use her surname, says her three-year-old daughter Polina found it hard to cope.
"Sometimes we didn't have heating for weeks and the temperature inside the apartment was zero or five degrees," she tells us. "So being here with a little child that is sick all the time was not OK."
The family's recent experiences have only compounded Polina's difficulties.
"We had two missile attacks this year," Iryna says.
The first explosion, in early June, blew out several windows in the family's home on the north-western edge of Kyiv. A month later, after some of the damage had been repaired, a second blast, close to the foot of their 10-storey apartment block, propelled a wave of earth into the flat, forcing the family to move into temporary accommodation.
Polina's health has deteriorated. She suffers from extreme anxiety, which has brought on bouts of incontinence, vomiting and uncontrollable shaking.
"Now we have this neurological problem with her so that's the reason we're thinking about leaving," Iryna says. "There are new symptoms after each shelling."
Iryna, whose husband is in the army, has not yet decided where to go. Her work with an international NGO may allow her to work remotely from Poland.
"Our president says that it is better to leave Kyiv because this is target number one," she says.
For other Kyiv residents, the solution lies closer to home: in the vast open spaces of Ukraine's countryside.
Olena Konoplia tells us she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital.
"I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explains.
"Everything that can be a Russian target."
On the day we visited, Olena was busy ferrying supplies to the house and supervising the installation of a new door.
In keeping with Ukrainian tradition, a priest has already been around to bless her new home.
The cottage has gas-powered convection heaters, but in an adjacent barn a stack of firewood will help to keep Olena warm in the event of power cuts. She has already installed high-speed internet, necessary for her work at a Kyiv-based charitable foundation.
At a time when air raid sirens sound constantly in Kyiv and explosions can be heard almost every day, the peace and quiet of the village is what Olena says she needs most.
"After several nights here, when I can sleep, just sleep, without any explosions, without any sirens, I feel better," she says. "I can work, write my articles, I feel good."
Olena's elderly mother will soon be joining her.
"She lives in a pretty dangerous district in Kyiv and it's harmful for her health," she explains.
Of course, not everyone can afford a cottage in the countryside or a months-long trip abroad.
Most Kyiv residents will do what they can to survive another tough winter in the capital, just as they have before.
The authorities are taking steps to prepare. Some of Kyiv's most vulnerable citizens â the elderly and women with young children â are being offered places in converted sanatoriums and rehabilitation centres in the city's forested outskirts.
Meanwhile, a network of around 15 small-scale power plants has been constructed around the city over the past 18 months in an effort to shore up Kyiv's battered power grid.

At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two major cities, police say.
Clashes broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country's largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast.
The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling requiring the government to remove barriers that had prevented some migrants from applying for asylum.
South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.
Thursday's demonstration turned violent following allegations that a foreign national had assaulted one of the protesters in Durban.
Three foreign nationals were arrested in connection with the alleged assault, police said.
In Durban, in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, protesters gathered outside a government refugee reception centre demanding that it stop accepting asylum applications.
Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses in the city centre shut their doors.
"There were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," senior local police officer Xolani Fihla told state broadcaster SABC.
"At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported," he added.
Police said 14 vehicles were torched in Durban and 10 in Soweto, where gunshots were also reported during confrontations between residents and foreign shopkeepers.
Acting national police commissioner Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane condemned the destruction of property.
In Orlando West, a neighbourhood of Soweto, residents had initially gathered to demand the closure of small convenience stores, known locally as spaza shops, operated by foreign nationals.
Protesters forced foreign traders out of some areas, while shops were attacked and a building was set on fire, local media reported.
Police said reinforcements had been deployed to prevent further violence.
The authorities have promised to pursue those responsible for the destruction.
The latest unrest follows a July ruling by South Africa's Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, which struck down restrictions preventing some people from seeking asylum because of how they entered the country or missed immigration deadlines.
The judgment means asylum seekers must be allowed to submit applications, even if they entered South Africa without the required documents.
It has prompted hundreds of people to gather at refugee reception centres, fuelling anger among anti-immigration campaigners who fear the decision will encourage undocumented migration.
Government spokesman William Baloyi told Reuters news agency that people had deliberately spread false claims about the judgment, creating the impression that undocumented migrants would automatically be granted legal status.
Baloyi insisted that the ruling does not automatically give migrants refugee status or the right to remain permanently in South Africa.
Officials say applications will still be assessed individually and applicants will remain subject to immigration checks.
Earlier this year, anti-immigration groups staged weeks of demonstrations demanding that undocumented foreign nationals leave the country by 30 June.
The protests forced tens of thousands of migrants to flee, with some returning home through repatriation programmes organised by their governments.
South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.
The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.
Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.
Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.
