Army’s new command plans to streamline autonomous warfare acquisition
Experts weigh in on what it will take to be successful.
The Army is bringing futures back.
The service announced the creation of Futures and Autonomous Systems Command on Friday, a day after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the creation of a new combatant command for autonomous warfare in a speech to troops.
"Secretary Hegseth made it clear: We are done with the bureaucratic inertia holding back modernization,” acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said in a news release.
So how do they cut through bureaucracy with a new bureaucratic organization?
FASCOM will stand up in the wake of last year’s decision to consolidate Army Futures Command and Training and Doctrine Command, part of a multi-year effort by the service to reduce its general officer ranks. Hegseth has since taken the idea military-wide.
The difference is that FASCOM will be led by an acquisition executive, where Futures Command had four-star generals with infantry backgrounds at the helm during its short tenure. Though the command endeavoured to fix the Army’s broken requirements process, ultimately the final decisions and acquisitions were made at the Pentagon, creating a disconnect that FASCOM won’t have to deal with.
“So maybe this is kind of Futures Command 2.0, right?” John G. Ferrari, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and retired two-star general, told Defense One.
Except this time, rather than a standalone four-star command with no joint equivalent, FASCOM could nest under the new Autonomous Warfare Command as a service component.
“I think their theory of the case is that you have too many disparate organizations within the Pentagon working this, and that they're working in some cases counter to each other,” Ferrari said, referring to the Defense Innovation Unit, various service PAEs and the recently created Defense Autonomous Warfare Group.
A combatant command “gives a single military leader the authority, the responsibility, and the resources to drive this,” he said. “So I think it's an admission that the current organizational structure isn't going to deliver in a timely manner.”
It’s also a more permanent solution than another working group or special unit.
“I think what they're trying to do is create an enduring organization that will drive this thing into the future, for the future, and outlast them,” Ferrari said. “Because regardless of who wins the next presidential election, it won't be this president, and so there'll likely be changes…the thing that endures are these combatant commands.”
What we talk about when we talk about autonomy
The Defense Department’s push toward autonomous warfare is not about robot drones finding, fixing, and deploying their weapons at will—at least not yet.
The war in Ukraine is a test bed for autonomous operations, with Ukrainian troops using artificial intelligence to identify targets and help guide a weapon to the target. On the Russian side, according to Center for Strategic and International Studies fellow Kateryna Bondar, there are some indications that fully autonomous drones have attacked civilian targets.
“We can just infer this indirectly, because analysis of those systems show that they don't have any connection or communication system…and also they carry NVIDIA chips, which are able to process AI models on board, and also just observations how they behave,” she said.
And they’re not very accurate, she added, something that the U.S. military isn’t inclined to experiment with.
“So I would say that autonomy that is being deployed right now, it's not some super sophisticated technology, AI-enabled full autonomy, or anything like that,” Bondar said. “It's more a function that assists the human operator in getting the drone to a place where the target is, and then actually engaging it.”
Ukrainians are also using AI-assisted analysis to gather intelligence, but humans still do the decision-making.
“Now they're trying to train agents which can perform as humans, and this is, I think, a turning point where we can actually get to autonomous,” she said. “And I would also call it a weapon system because, if this agent is able to act and activate whatever effectors we have—be it missiles, be it drones, whatever it can employ—then the decision-making system and this agent can actually be called a weapon system.”
FASCOM would bring together the Army’s existing transformation efforts with regard to unmanned systems, with a new push to prioritize autonomy.
Telle’s memo calls on the service’s operations chief to figure out what kind of manning existing units will need to incorporate autonomous capabilities and designate a Portfolio Acquisition Executive for autonomy.
Someone with an operational background should be in charge, Ferrari argued, though the PAEs were recently reorganized from a mix of officers and civilians to all civilians in charge, with uniformed deputies.
“If it's just led by an acquisition executive, then you're going to have the same problem that the Army always has, which is an acquisition executive's leading something, not a warfighter,” he said.
There are, though, some battlefield lessons the U.S. military can incorporate, Bondar said, to be able to work with the bureaucracy of a new command without making new technology acquisition so rigid.
“There's a lot of conversation about feedback loop, and it actually makes sense because…when every commander or every unit, whoever is buying drones, has the direct phone number of the manufacturer, they can immediately call and say what should be improved, what didn't work,” she said. “Because for them, giving this feedback, it's not some sort of obligation or part of procedure—they really feel this need because their lives depend on this, and the lives of their people.”

Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure final approval to launch in the country.
The remark came a day after Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. He then singled out Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network operator.
India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory.
Ambani and Reliance Group have not responded to Musk's remarks. The BBC has reached out to them for comment
The row comes as competition grows in India's satellite internet market, with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel also preparing to launch services.
The rivalry is complicated by the fact that Starlink has also partnered with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel.
In March 2025, both companies signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment and services in India, subject to government approval. The companies also said they could explore sharing network infrastructure. The BBC has also reached out to Bharti Airtel for comment.
Musk first made the allegations on Wednesday, accusing "certain oligarchs" of maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers.
"You can guess who they are," he wrote on X, external, adding that blocking Starlink was "a crime against the people of India".
On Thursday, India's Ministry of Communications responded, saying that three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services.
"The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said, without naming Musk directly.
Musk continued to question the delay, saying Starlink was already licensed in more than 165 countries.
"Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?" he wrote on X on Thursday.
Starlink, owned by Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install.
The company has been trying to enter India since 2021 and has secured key licences. But it still needs final security clearances and spectrum allocation before it can begin commercial services.
Wednesday's row unfolded as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in Delhi, where all three companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services.
Speaking at the event, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and Mukesh Ambani's son, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards regulatory approvals.
Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment and only said, "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Bharti Airtel chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said his company's satellite venture was also awaiting government approvals.
SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer, who oversees Starlink's business operations, said the company had spent years working with Indian regulators and had built security controls into its network to meet the country's requirements.
Security has been a key concern surrounding Starlink's entry into India. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had recovered Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the remote Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army operation in the northeastern state of Manipur.
Musk said at that time that Starlink's service had never been active in India, arguing that the equipment recovered by authorities could not have been using its satellite network.
Questions also remain over how affordable the service would be for Indian consumers, particularly those in rural areas.
India is one of the world's largest internet markets but access remains uneven, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to build.
Musk has argued that Starlink could help bridge this gap. "Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all!" he wrote on X on Wednesday.
The company has yet to announce prices for India, but some experts say its plans elsewhere suggest the service could be beyond the reach of many Indian households.
In the US, Starlink's residential plans start at $55 a month, although prices and equipment costs vary by plan and location.

722e78462e38.text:
Matthewâs view
Riyadh was once the Gulfâs escape route from the Iran war. No longer.
Several Western governments are advising against travel to Saudi Arabia. The US requires officials to obtain special approval to use the capitalâs airport. Iâm hearing of some executives leaving for Doha and the UAE.
Here in Riyadh, we now hear booms and see fires that have largely been absent since the conflict began on Feb. 28. This is a jarring reversal. Saudi Arabia has suffered fewer attacks than Gulf neighbours, its airspace has mostly stayed open, and the kingdom has projected a business-as-usual attitude.
That message is getting harder to sustain after Iran-backed Houthi fighters escalated attacks in response to the Saudi-led campaign against them in Yemen. One person was killed in a strike on Riyadh airport, a Saudia Airlines plane was reportedly in flames, and hundreds of flights have been canceled.
Some offices, schools, and the Expo 2030 construction site near the airport were evacuated on Thursday. Foreign governments suggested their citizens remain vigilant, but what can individuals do when threats come suddenly from the sky?
Over the next few weeks, Saudi Arabia is hosting the World Petroleum Congress and the Future Investment Initiative, drawing CEOs from the worldâs biggest energy and financial companies. While no postponements or cancellations have been announced, security teams are undoubtedly assessing what level of risk is tolerable for the titans of the global economy. Staying away could offend the kingdom, and firms that donât stand with Saudi Arabia now risk missing out when the economy bounces back.
Older residents here repeat a mantra that the country has been through worse, notably when Iraq launched Scud missiles in 1991 during the first Gulf War. But most of those strikes were on military structures.
Riyadh was different then, too. It had no ambitions to be a hub for finance, trade, and tourism. Today, it needs stability. Itâs harder to sell investors on its vision when the capital is under fire.

114ea300857a.text: Top executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies are privately gaming out scenarios for a public and political revolt after a catastrophic AI event . Why it matters : These officials anticipate a large-scale event, most likely a cyberattack, that shuts down access to financial services, internet connectivity, or even power and water. The first example of significant real-world harm caused by unsafe AI would turn an already wary public further against the technology and its leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, as well as President Trump for reluctance to regulate it. The risk : While scenario planning is common within many companies and national security settings — the Pentagon has been running war games for decades — the difference is that many top AI researchers and executives believe a major incident is inevitable . "OpenAI conducts preparedness exercises where teams discuss and work through a range of potential scenarios," a company spokesperson said. "These scenarios are not treated as inevitable, but are meant to help us prepare for a variety of circumstances." Anthropic declined to comment. Zoom in: The blame game will start whether a rogue-agent swarm breaks containment from an internal testing environment or a bad actor finds unexpected ways to use available models. A recent campaign targeting South Korean financial organizations — including reported breaches at two banks — shows the damage one person can do. A hacker from China allegedly used AI tools from China-developed models, including DeepSeek, to steal data from tens of thousands of bank customers. The attacker used Claude Code to ask for help finding places to sell the stolen data, according to cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike . Top AI planners assume Democrats , ascendant after the midterms, will move fast to shut down AI but will face significant challenges. An aging Congress, out of touch with the AI revolution, could find itself out of its depth. The global economy is now heavily intertwined with an AI infrastructure buildout. Slowing it down could hit an already fragile economy hard. Too many open-weight models exist that can already be freely downloaded and used to cause harm, a problem most cybersecurity pros see as solvable only by using AI to fight rogue AI . Between the lines : The planning involves red-teaming for worst-case scenarios. It focuses mainly on racing to educate members of Congress. Company executives know regulation has no chance of passing right now, but still want to shape the legislation and policies U.S. leaders will turn to after a first catastrophic event. What we're watching: Many AI industry insiders told Axios they believe a major event will occur in the next six to 12 months. Even with Democrats in control of the House and Senate, the companies see fractured politics as the norm, including within the Democratic Party. Some of the most heavy-handed Democratic proposals include banning superintelligence or pausing advanced AI development. Others have bipartisan support and even some industry buy-in, including a required kill switch on advanced AI. But experts have questioned the viability of trying to turn off all AI systems. The bottom line: In a real crisis, Washington can set partisan differences aside. One Democratic aide pointed to cooperation during COVID and the 2008 financial crisis.

A cadre of elite techies, financiers, and high-level Trump administration officials have spent a year quietly charting an extraordinary and rapid campaign to persuade Americans to use apps and other artificial intelligence-powered tools to manage their healthcare and medical records.
As that campaign has unfolded, administration officials have granted tech companies an unusual opportunity to nudge the nation’s health department toward a loosely regulated future for AI health apps in which the government reimburses them for services as it does medical professionals.
In February, federal health officials invited those businesses — including tech giants Microsoft, Anthropic, OpenAI, Apple, and Google — to a listening session on conversational AI products for patients, such as chatbots. Representatives from at least 35 industry organizations attended the meeting held by the Food and Drug Administration, which is responsible for regulating health apps as medical devices. Companies were prompted in advance to explain their AI products and how they access patients’ sensitive medical information.
But the meeting did not appear on the FDA’s public calendar or regulatory notices, nor was the public invited. Rather, the invitation for a select group to help shape federal policy governing AI in healthcare was extended in a chat room on the messaging service Slack.
“This is a great opportunity to support HHS’ goals and share your state-of-the-art understanding of safe Conversational AI development and monitoring to help FDA shape future guidance,” CMS senior policy adviser Morgan Taylor wrote in the Slack workspace.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has not formally announced the chat room through federal regulatory channels, though CMS officials have talked about it at industry conferences. Legal experts said the chat room resembles a federal advisory panel, which would be required to operate in public view.
KFF Health News reviewed thousands of Slack messages, meeting transcripts, and video recordings that reveal how the Trump administration has granted the industry a direct line to top government officials — including former head of the Department of Government Efficiency Amy Gleason.
The conversation took place behind the scenes as federal health officials publicly worked to integrate AI and other technology into nearly every aspect of healthcare, a plan they’ve branded the “Health Technology Ecosystem.”
“We wanted to give industry a chance to play in the sandbox of government-supported healthcare,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said in September at the public launch of an initiative that allows health apps to bill Medicare for AI services such as wearable device tracking. Last week, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. delivered an enthusiastic endorsement of AI in healthcare, claiming it is “much better informed than any doctor in the country.”
Meanwhile, HHS staff even promised that a recently launched Medicare App Library would serve as a lucrative pipeline for those businesses to get new users. The library’s webpage currently promotes only two dozen commercial apps to millions of American seniors and those with disabilities.
As Trump officials sell it, Americans will get easier access to their medical records so apps can swiftly provide health or wellness advice. In practice, however, so will the tech companies.
Doctors, meanwhile, are increasingly worried about how patients use and share their medical records with the nascent technology.
“Some of these tools just aren’t ready for primetime,” said John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association. “We don’t have enough data about them. We don’t understand how they work, how they’re using the information. There’s no liability if these tools get things wrong.”
CMS officials declined to answer several questions about the Slack workspace, including about its legality.
“CMS is focused on giving Medicare beneficiaries greater access to their health information and useful digital tools while promoting an open, interoperable healthcare system,” Gleason, now chief product officer for the newly created Office of Health Technology and Products at CMS, wrote in an emailed statement. “The Health Technology Ecosystem is an open, voluntary technical collaboration. CMS will continue working with patients, providers, payers, technology organizations, and other stakeholders to make health information more accessible and useful to the Americans it serves.”
The FDA did not respond to a request for comment.
The Conversation Begins
The behind-the-scenes effort to funnel more Americans to AI-powered health apps began in August 2025 in the Slack workspace.
“Welcome all!” Gleason wrote. “Please be sure to read the Code of Conduct and see the Channel list as well to help you find channels that are relevant to you.”
Gleason is best known for serving as the acting administrator of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, as it gained access to millions of Americans’ sensitive personal and financial data, including at the Social Security Administration.
As her work with DOGE wound down last year, Gleason welcomed a variety of tech leaders, investors, and entrepreneurs to the chat room.
The Slack workspace’s participants include representatives from major digital wellness companies like Oura Health, AI companies like Palantir, and investment outfits like 8VC, a venture capital firm associated with Kennedy’s son Finn. ‘We Are Seen as Disposable’: Rural Residents Fight a Proposed Gas Pipeline
CHATHAM COUNTY, N.C. — Despite being in one of the nation’s fastest-growing states, this rural county of roughly 85,000 people is still brimming with red foxes, coyotes, white-tailed deer, and wild turkeys.
But in recent months, Enbridge Gas North Carolina’s proposed plans for a natural gas pipeline have exposed how population growth, here and across the nation, is driving a divide between wealthy newcomers and longtime residents.
Chatham has grown into one of North Carolina’s most affluent counties, fueled by an influx of new residents in its northeastern corner. Yet the pipeline would run from Moncure to Siler City, two communities where the per capita income is roughly $25,000 a year, or about half the income typical for the region.
And it’s raising familiar concerns. A 2020 report from the Chatham County Public Health Department stated that “unjust, unfair, and uneven distribution of social and economic resources” in the county, including exposure to environmental hazards, limited people’s “ability to achieve optimal health.”
In September, the Chatham County Board of Commissioners unanimously voted to oppose the project, saying that “protecting public health, safety, environmental resources, and private property rights remains a priority.” The resolution states that the proposed pipeline could affect areas occupied by vulnerable, low-income residents. Under state law, Enbridge could still attempt to take land through eminent domain, and low-income communities affected would have fewer resources available to fight back.
The state Department of Environmental Quality typically would review applications for permits to build a natural gas pipeline. That department has not yet received a permit application for the pipeline, said Onotse Omoyeni, senior press secretary for the office of Gov. Josh Stein. The North Carolina Utilities Commission declined to comment.
Enbridge says the 12-inch-diameter pipeline is needed to meet growing energy demands in the area, including Chatham, where the population has soared 21% since 2016, as well as neighboring Lee County.
Yet the proposed pipeline has set off protests at public meetings and attracted hundreds of people to a Facebook group to express their opposition, many of them small farmers, retirees, or their relatives. They argue the pipeline would pose an environmental threat to wells used for drinking water and expose people in less affluent areas to toxic pollutants that could increase the risks of cancer, preterm births, and asthma — all for the benefit of people who live nowhere near the proposed route.
“Nobody wants to be next to a pipeline,” Dorasue Burns Christian, a retired dental hygienist, told KFF Health News. She said the proposed route cuts across the roughly 22-acre farm where she has lived for more than 50 years. “I’m stressed and I can’t sleep at night. I have been pushed as far as I can be pushed.”
Enbridge Gas North Carolina is a subsidiary of the Canadian energy company Enbridge. Residents point to other communities in which Enbridge has operated — such as Marshall, Michigan; Romeoville, Illinois; and Danville, Kentucky — where oil spills and a natural gas pipeline rupture led to evacuations, injuries, and at least one death.
Enbridge declined an interview request to answer questions about the location of the North Carolina pipeline and the company’s safety record. In a statement, spokesperson Persida Montanez said the pipeline is needed to accommodate population and business growth in Chatham and neighboring Lee County.
A company website says safety will be prioritized during construction and operation, including monitoring, maintenance, and compliance with regulatory rules.
Many residents believe the company is attempting to profit from a proposed data center, which many also oppose. The company website says that Enbridge does not intend to use the pipeline for that purpose and that serving a data center would require a pipeline at least twice the size of the one planned for Chatham.
The pipeline would connect to existing natural gas infrastructure in Siler City and near Moncure, the company said.
Still, pipeline opponents say they are fed up.
“They chose this route because they probably thought people would not fight back,” said Amanda Clark, a protest organizer who grew up in Chatham. Her family roots in the county date to the 1700s. “In rural communities, we are seen as disposable.”
‘Collateral Damage’
Chatham County’s fight comes amid a construction boom in the natural gas pipeline industry and the Trump administration’s promises of “American energy dominance.”
The U.S. produces more natural gas than any other country, about as much as China, Russia, and Iran combined.
Research shows natural gas pipeline leaks are concentrated in low-income and minority communities where people experience higher rates of poverty and physical disabilities and have fewer means to respond to crises.
Nationwide, there were nearly 2,600 pipeline incidents from 2010 to 2021 that were serious enough that they were required to be reported to the federal government, including fires and explosions that killed 122 people and injured more than 600.
In 2019, one person died and six were injured in Kentucky when an Enbridge natural gas pipeline ruptured, according to a federal government report.
Enbridge reached a $177 million settlement with the federal government after the 2010 oil spills in Michigan and Illinois. In the Michigan spill, a pipeline discharged 1 million gallons of oil into Talmadge Creek, in one of the largest inland oil spills in U.S. history.
“No Pipeline. No Compromise,” read the red T-shirts worn by some of the more than 300 people who attended a Chatham County Board of Commissioners meeting in Pittsboro, North Carolina, in early August. Outside the building, they displayed signs that said “People NOT Pipelines” and “Save Our Farms.”

Around 100 Baltimore residents packed a community hall in the Curtis Bay neighborhood on the evening of Oct. 1. One after another, they implored the Maryland Department of the Environment not to renew the air permit for the city’s largest trash incinerator.
The speakers—young residents and retirees, longtime neighbors, doctors, students and environmental advocates—described the daily ordeal of living with asthma and other respiratory illnesses amid the industrial pollution that surrounds Curtis Bay.
It was a day of conflicting emotions for residents.
Within just over a week, separate government regulators moved in sharply different directions over two high-volume incinerators operating in heavily industrialized portions of South Baltimore.
On Oct. 1, Maryland regulators announced that a medical-waste incinerator that has illegally spewed pollution would stop burning waste under a settlement with the state, while Baltimore County approved a contract that could provide a potentially decade-long lifeline to the WIN Waste trash incinerator, one of Baltimore’s largest sources of air pollution.
South Baltimore is a historically overburdened community surrounded by dozens of industrial facilities. Residents have long raised concerns about the cumulative impacts of environmental pollution on their health and daily lives.
Community groups such as the South Baltimore Community Land Trust partnered with environmental coalitions across Baltimore, as well as academics at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, to advocate for the closure of the medical-waste incinerator after repeated violations. In 2023, the facility was fined $1.75 million for repeat violations, “one of the largest penalties in an environmental criminal case,” according to the state attorney general’s office.
The WIN Waste facility is a well-known landmark to many passing through the city; its Baltimore-branded smokestack towers above Interstate 95. A recent study estimated that its emissions impose nearly $54 million a year in health damages, with much of the burden falling on surrounding communities.
“We are paying with our lungs. We are paying with our blood,” said Lindi Shepard, a former teacher and education researcher, who came to testify at the public meeting.
Abby Cook, a lifelong Baltimore resident who has worked as an environmental professional, told regulators she wants to have a child someday but fears raising one in the city.
“I’m afraid to raise a child in Baltimore City because it isn’t safe … not because of crime, but because of the air,” Cook said.
“We are paying with our lungs. We are paying with our blood.”
— Lindi Shepard, former teacher and education researcher
That same evening, as Baltimore residents were trying to convince state regulators how challenging it was to live with industrial pollution every day, some of the Maryland officials with power over the state’s environmental policies were somewhere else.
Roughly four miles away, senior officials from Maryland’s environmental agencies were gathered with political leaders and environmental groups at an event honoring environmental champions. Among them were MDE Secretary Serena McIlwain, Maryland Comptroller Brooke Lierman, Maryland Energy Administration Director Kelly Speakes-Backman and several lawmakers. Gov. Wes Moore was the chief guest at the event.
The juxtaposition came at a consequential moment, particularly for the Curtis Bay community, which has fought for years to convince policymakers to find ways to reduce waste incineration and saw some progress with the closure of the medical waste facility.
Just when MDE announced that the medical-waste incinerator would stop operating under a settlement with state regulators, Baltimore County approved a contract that could continue sending roughly 215,000 tons of garbage each year to WIN Waste, also called BRESCO, for as long as 10 more years.
Among the main concerns residents raised about the WIN Waste incinerator is the large volume of ash it generates, which is subsequently disposed of at the Quarantine Road Landfill in South Baltimore. Studies of municipal incinerator ash have identified contaminants including dioxins, lead and arsenic, but community researchers say they have been unable to independently test ash from WIN Waste to determine its composition and contaminant levels.
Now, MDE has to decide whether to renew the air permit that would allow the facility to continue operating. WIN Waste’s air pollution permit is due for renewal this year, but in a press release, SCBLT said MDE has already granted WIN Waste a tentative determination to renew.
For South Baltimore residents, it was a tough situation to reconcile. Inside the recreation center, the testimony grew increasingly confrontational.
Alex Smith, who said his workforce-development organization has received support from WIN Waste, urged residents to move in “a more positive direction.”
A Howard University researcher who said her lab had studied the community for four years responded. “People are tired of being resilient,” she said. “It’s not about being positive.”
Then came Nicole Fabricant, who said she has worked with young people in South Baltimore for more than 17 years. She dismissed industry-funded community projects cited by WIN Waste supporters as inadequate compensation for the pollution residents say they endure.
“These are the trinkets,” Fabricant said. “These are not jobs. This is not employment, and this is not a sustainable future for Baltimore.”

But as the Iran war squeezes Republicans ahead of the midterms, Democrats are aligning to call for the defense secretaryâs ouster or resignation.
With impeachment still a dirty word among many House Democrats, targeting Cabinet secretaries could be a pressure release valve for lawmakers itching for action against the Trump administration.
âI 100% believe Pete Hegseth needs to be impeached and removed from office, because not only is he the worst secretary of defense in American history, he is a dangerous war criminal,â said Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., who said it should be one of the caucusâ âtop three prioritiesâ next year.
Hegseth was reviled by the left even before the Iran war began, and since then heâs faced criticism from Republicans for his handling of the war. An impeachment vote could even be bipartisan: When the House returns after the midterms, itâll be forced to take up a Hegseth ouster resolution filed by iconoclastic Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.
Prioritizing Hegseth impeachment would solve a big problem for Democrats: If they win the House, their leaders will face intense pressure from the base to show a new level of fight against Trump. Yet theyâre leery of the internal divisions or appearance of overreach that a third Trump impeachment might create, and still smarting from his return to office after two impeachment votes.
In public, top Democrats are accordingly circumspect on targeting Hegseth. Jeffries says Hegseth should be fired and that Democrats âhavenât ruled anything outâ in their investigations. Democrats have filed impeachment articles against other Trump Cabinet officials, like Education Secretary Linda McMahon and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., has also filed impeachment articles against Hegseth.
Yet interviews with a half dozen Democrats pointed to Hegseth as the safest place to land. Itâs not just safe-seat Democrats willing to take the plunge: Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., who represents a Trump-won district, said she was open to the possibility.
âIf I were Pete Hegseth, Iâd be worried. Itâs certainly something that needs serious consideration, and I hear Democrats, yes, but I also hear some Republicans saying it as well. I think thereâs a lot he needs to answer for,â she said.
Of course, it may not be even up to Democratic leaders in the end. Impeachment politics next year could be driven by an incoming crop of progressive lawmakers who could form a sizable bloc in the caucus. Any member can force a vote on an impeachment resolution, which outgoing Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, repeatedly triggered during Trumpâs first term and his current one.

Massieâs Hegseth resolution, among other allegations, lays out charges of violating Congressâ war powers and carrying out extrajudicial killings.
âThey all should be impeached â President Trump and his cabinet thatâs enabled him to do everything that he has right now,â said Adam Hamawy, a fellow Justice Democrats-aligned progressive from New Jersey. âNow, whether weâre going to be able to do that is another thing, but itâs not something that, you know, we should just ignore because itâs not possible.â
The Pentagon defended Hegsethâs record in a statement.
âSecretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way,â said Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson, adding that the Pentagon âis better under President Trump and Secretary Hegsethâs leadership than before.â
Know More
Itâs unclear if Hegseth will leave the administration post-midterms. While Trump is known to be unpredictable, he likes Hegseth a lot, and those familiar with the situation are skeptical of any looming changes at the top of the department.
Still, other Democrats say they need to balance impeachment with acting on cost-of-living issues like healthcare that they believe will tip the midterms in their favor.
âThereâs going to have to be a balance of addressing needs and meeting our constituents where theyâre at, and also part of restoring the faith of the American people in our own government and restoring the integrity of our democratic institutions âÂ it requires holding bad actors to justice,â said Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J.
The Massie resolution will be a good test for Democratic support for going after Hegseth. Some Democrats are loath to support a measure drafted by a Republican and before any kind of investigative process has been completed.
But some leaders like Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the top Armed Services Committee Democrat, have signaled they could back the Massie measure.

The Signal Interview
âEverybody wrote this place off,â Shobi Khan says as he walks a visitor around Canary Wharf, the 130-acre estate he has overseen since 2019. After the UKâs banker-scaring vote to leave the European Union, and an office-emptying pandemic, the refrain he kept hearing was: âItâs over. Bad experiment. Why did we do that?â
Khan still remembers his fury when a rival London property developer wrote in 2024 that Canary Wharf needed âa drastic transformationâ to survive, but those doubts were widely shared at the time. Just when the east London business district might have been celebrating a post-COVID rebound, it lost a series of prominent tenants, including HSBC, Moodyâs, and Clifford Chance.
Fast forward to 2026, and Canary Wharf Group is reporting the highest rental rates in its history. Office occupancy now exceeds 92%, local retailersâ sales are 40% higher than they were in 2019, and visitor numbers, which fell from 54 million a year to just 20 million during the pandemic, are on track to exceed last yearâs record of 76 million.
Khan can also boast a string of new commitments from high-profile global tenants. Visa recently leased 300,000 square feet of office space, Barclays just bought its headquarters for Â£750 million, and Citi is investing more than $1 billion in its European HQ. Capping them all is JPMorganâs proposal to erect a Â£3 billion, 265-meter tower that will be Londonâs largest office building if its plans are approved. âWhat kind of vote of confidence is that?â Khan asks rhetorically.
What turned the tide, he says, was a multipart strategy to make Canary Wharf more competitive with the West End, the City of London, and Europeâs leading financial hubs. He now sees that approach as an intellectual property playbook that CWG could one day take to other markets.
âIâve got people from China, from the Middle East, Australia, all coming here for tours,â he says, âand we get offers.â
A âgreen and blueâ diversification
Canary Wharf was a product of Margaret Thatcherâs government, the centerpiece of an ambitious redevelopment of Londonâs crumbling docklands. But from the opening of its first towers in 1991, it suffered from a reputation as a sterile, remote outpost that appealed to few employers other than those in need of large trading floors that old buildings in the City of London could not provide.
Khan joined CWG as CEO in 2019, having been chief operating officer of the US real estate investment trust General Growth Properties. Even before he moved, he recalls: âIâd keep talking to London business leaders, and they were like, âOh, yeah, Canary, I remember it. So many bankers, nothing to do after five, and itâs really hard to get to.â That was the perception for 30 years.â
He has been much helped by the opening of the Elizabeth line in 2022, which he calls âa game-changerâ for improving access to the site. But Khan has also invested in bringing in a much broader array of companies and government agencies, so tenants from outside financial services now account for almost half of his office space.
He has simultaneously diversified a district that once had few apartments, shops, and dining options. About 3,500 residents now live in its apartment buildings â a figure he expects to double by next year. And Canary Wharf has more than doubled the number of retailers, restaurants, bars, and cafes since the pandemic. That has reduced the groupâs historic dependence on the office market.
Lately, Khan has focused on creating more âgreen and blueâ spaces like parks and riverside walkways, while âcuratingâ activities and amenities designed to make Canary Wharf feel more like a vibrant community than an office park.
As he walks around the property, he points out outdoor event spaces, a padel center where the booked-up courts cost Â£80 to Â£100 an hour, and an Olympic-sized open-water pool that attracted 30,000 swimmers in the month after it opened this summer.
Such attractions may sound like sideshows, but they help bring Khanâs strategy to life. It takes time to change perceptions, he notes, and he needs such tangible symbols to convince potential tenants that Canary Wharf has truly changed.
âItâs like a house renovation. Some people can visualize it, but some people need to see the renovation,â he says.
A playbook that could travel
CWG, owned by Brookfield and the Qatar Investment Authority, is not wholly confined to its 130 acres. The group has developed projects elsewhere in London, including 20 Fenchurch Street, the curving City skyscraper nicknamed âthe Walkie-Talkie.â
But Khan says CWG has developed âa lot of expertiseâ from honing its model, which it can deploy in other districts, cities, and countries.
It may do so over âthe medium term,â rather than sooner, he adds, because it still has land to build another 5-7 million square feet, equivalent to seven to 10 new buildings.
For now, âweâve got enough on our hands,â he says â even as he notes that Canary Wharf Group now prefers to be known by its initials, CWG, so that future partners wonât assume that its ambitions are limited to its current home.
Even as Khan worries about the impact of rising interest rates, he says the London market is âin an up cycle,â and predicts âgreat demand-supply fundamentalsâ for the coming years.
Appetite for top office space remains strong across the capital, while CWGâs latest earnings showed that availability in Central London fell 20% year on year as supply in Docklands stayed broadly steady. The shortage of supply elsewhere in London will get worse next year, Khan says, blaming it on UK regulations that have driven up construction costs, deterring new development.
A decade after the Brexit vote, âthereâs been minimal flightâ of bankers to European capitals, he notes. âBut growth is less because of that. 0887febd2b41.text: Democrats believe President Trump has committed impeachable offenses. But they're divided over whether they should try to impeach him if they win control of the House. Why it matters: If Democrats win the House, as expected, their 2027 decision on whether to try to impeach Trump could have major consequences for the 2028 presidential race. Zoom in: Theoretically, impeaching Trump would be easy for a unified, Democrat-controlled House. Many top Democrats note that Trump survived a record two impeachments in his first term — and that he'd be unlikely to be removed from office. That would require a two-thirds, bipartisan vote in a Senate that's likely to be closely divided. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said Trump has "already committed numerous impeachable offenses " in his second term, including usurping congressional authority. In 2021, Raskin led the second Trump impeachment, following the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Raskin said top Democrats are "very sober about what that two-thirds requirement means on the Senate side. If anything, Donald Trump has tightened his control over the Republican Party since the last round. He's gotten rid of the senators that he viewed as not sufficiently loyal and sycophantic." Zoom out: Other Democrats also are cautioning against an impeachment campaign if their party takes control of the House in January. Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a potential presidential candidate, told NBC's "Meet the Press" last Sunday that he supports investigations, not impeachment, "because it's not going anywhere and it's going to be a food fight." Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) said recently: "Don't be impeaching anybody ... Let's just get back to work." Friction point: Democrats' more progressive wing is already talking about an impeachment drive. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told The Floridian in March: "If you are asking me if I support impeachment, I do. I think that it's on very objective grounds of following the law or not." Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), a liberal who, like AOC, is weighing a White House run, also has argued for impeachment. " It's about setting a standard," he told NBC News , rejecting the notion that an impeachment would distract Democrats from pushing policy changes. "Democrats can impeach to uphold constitutional values, and at the same time have a first-hundred-day agenda that deals with the cost of living." What's next: Trump, who denies wrongdoing, is already preparing for his third impeachment. He told reporters Wednesday that he was "never even worried" about his first two impeachments. "I can do whatever I want, if I want," Trump said, calling the impeachments and subsequent criminal cases against him "very illegal things." "I view the presidency as a very sacred position," he said. "Very sacred position. Very important. Very sacred. A position where it has to be treated properly." Deep down , Trump might welcome an impeachment, one adviser said, "because he's in his element in chaos and when he's being persecuted." A longtime confidant said: "If Democrats win and start the investigations, he'll get more defiant ... Democrats won't be able to resist impeachment and he won't be able to resist daring them to do it. You think you control Donald Trump? Well, f*ck you. You don't." A senior administration official said the belief within the White House is that an impeachment would "just prove Democrats are all about getting Trump, and this stuff about affordability is just a hoax." Between the lines: Democrats know they face a conflict between holding Trump accountable and delivering on their campaign promises to restore Medicaid cuts and bolster the Affordable Care Act. Raskin said: "Does this make sense as a matter of law and politics and public policy to advance another impeachment? That's obviously a more complex question than whether or not he's violating the Constitution when he goes to war without congressional consent or he imposes tariffs outside of the law, or he engages in unprecedented scales of corruption in abusing his office." "So all this is to say, it is not a fetish with us," he added. "On the other hand, it's definitely not a taboo." Raskin, a law professor, is in line to lead the House Judiciary Committee, which would be involved in any impeachment. He emphasizes that "impeachment is by definition an intertwined question of both law and politics." In other words, it's not just a legal process. That's why the House impeaches and the president is then tried in the Senate, not the Supreme Court. The intrigue: Some Democrats have been at odds with themselves on impeachment. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), another potential 2028 candidate, said in April 2025 that he "strongly" supported impeaching Trump and that there's "no question" the president committed impeachable offenses. By this summer, however, Ossoff was no longer committed to it. Behind the scenes: Some Republicans have indicated that if they keep control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 election, they could bypass an impeachment trial by simply voting to dismiss the charges. Senate Democrats did that in 2024, after President Biden's homeland security secretary, Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by the House. Senate Republican leaders warned then that Democrats were setting a precedent they may not like when Republicans were in charge. Then there's Vice President Vance. He's likely to run for president over the next two years as Democrats debate impeachment. "JD relishes nothing more than defending the president," an administration official said. "More 'lawfare' against POTUS will unify Republicans even more." "If Democrats want JD to become president, please, impeach Trump."

But Neha's - who uses "they" and "them" as personal pronouns - visibility is no longer limited to campuses.
Viral videos over the past few days show them being dragged through the street by a group of female police officials, climbing on top of police barricades, raising their fist and shouting slogans, and being detained.
Photos of them smiling while being carried away by policewomen have also gone viral.
In a recent BBC Bangla interview, Neha played down the attention they've been receiving.
"I know it happened in front of the camera so it seems like it's something different," they said. "But I have seen all student activists with the Left doing the same things that I have been doing. It's just that there is a camera on me, so people think something different is happening."
The attention on Neha comes at a time when several high-profile protests are being held on India's streets in what is being seen as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power.
There's the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a Gen Z-led online satirical movement - that held weeks-long protests in Delhi in the summer over education reforms. It ended in July only after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.
Separately, some of India's opposition parties, especially the Congress, have also taken to the streets over electoral reforms. For the past few days, videos of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra being shoved and jostled and detained have gone viral and made headlines in India.
Saturday's protest in Delhi has been called by the CJP, which is seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating electoral rolls to favour Modi's BJP. Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the accusation.
Although not a member of the CJP, Neha has said their group would also participate.
Born in the northern state of Uttarakhand, Neha lived in different cities as a child as their army officer father moved for his postings.
After graduating from Delhi University, they did a master's degree from Ambedkar University in the capital and are now a PhD student at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU).
Neha first came into the spotlight in the summer during the CJP's protest over education reforms.
Neha and Aisa were at the protest from the start, but not many knew them at that point. That changed after 28 June, when educationist and scientist Sonam Wangchuk began a hunger strike in CJP's support and Neha and a few others from Aisa also joined him.
"It was an obvious choice for us. We've been protesting against paper leaks and education reforms for a long time," Neha later said in an interview.
While most of the attention was focused on Wangchuk, whose reputation and presence galvanised the movement, Neha's outspokenness and combative speeches began to get them noticed.
After Wangchuk and others were moved to hospital, Neha continued fasting despite having lost 8kg.
Even after being moved to hospital, they said in a video: "The fight continues. Once I've recovered, we'll meet you again on the streets to continue our fight for our right."
After the protests ended in July, Neha has established themselves as a Gen Z leader who's courted by the CJP and media, besides appearing alongside Rahul Gandhi at press conferences.
But Neha's involvement with Aisa and leftist politics and statements criticising PM Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and other BJP leaders have also led to "lots of disagreements with my family as my parents are staunch supporters of BJP".
And last month, at least three police complaints were lodged, external in Uttar Pradesh state by BJP against Neha for making "objectionable remarks" against the chief minister - they came two days after Aisa's police complaint that Neha had received death threats, external.
Neha, who has been travelling to many Indian cities to participate in protests in support of students, also made headlines when a man allegedly threw ink, external at them during a protest march in Jharkhand state. A photo Neha shared on Instagram showed their face streaked with ink stains. Police said they had detained the man.
The noisy protests and repeated detentions have earned Neha a reputation for being a street fighter.
"The streets have always dictated the course of politics in this country and they will continue to do so, more so in the coming few years," they told BBC Bangla.
"If we look at the social changes of the recent past, those social changes did not come from people sitting in parliament; they came from the streets," they said.
Now as the authorities gear up for 10 October's protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Kumar, Neha and Aisa have said they would be back in the streets with the CJP to "protect democracy".

ac899680f9bd.text: Navi Pillay, an outspoken supporter of international law who has served as a judge on multiple global courts and as the UN's top human rights official, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. Why it matters: President Trump once again did not win the prize he has openly coveted . Pillay, among other posts, previously served on the International Criminal Court — a body Trump sanctioned and last month called " rogue " and "evil." What they're saying: " The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order," the prize committee said in a social media post. "This year's laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted." Context: Besides the ICC and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, Pillay also served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Pillay , a native of South Africa in her mid-80s, was the first Black woman to serve on that country's highest court. The big picture: The Nobel Peace Prize is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about constantly and has frequently insisted he should have won. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, gave Trump her prize medal earlier this year — though the Norwegian Nobel Institute made clear the prize itself could not actually be transferred . This is breaking news.

ABB has in recent weeks rolled out a portfolio of products aimed at addressing the needs of AI data centers, while Schneider Electric acquired a US industrial software firm for $22.6 billion. Some of these solutions are not entirely new, but the energy demand surge from AI data centers, industrial electrification, and the need for more climate-resilient infrastructure is creating momentum to improve current systems.

Three Saudi nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country's civil aviation authority has said after Yemen's Houthis said they targeted the facility.
The attacks also resulted in "injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities", the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on X.
It said the first attack on Thursday targeted the airport while the second one struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia.
One of its pilots was among those killed, the airline said in a statement.
Air traffic had returned to normal, the civil aviation authority said.
Yemen's Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked the airport with two missiles, reports said.
The Iran-aligned group said it had also targeted an airport in Najran city near the Saudi border with Yemen, and Khamis Mushait air base further north. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed these attacks.
The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on October 6 and 7.
Two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, the civil aviation body said on Wednesday. Another person was killed at King Khalid airport.
The latest attacks come amid mark an escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.
The Houthi military spokesperson said the previous two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".
The group says it is targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.
The conflict has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.
That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.
But Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.
A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
But the informal ceasefire began to unravel in July.
The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating for what they say is a years-long Saudi blockade, and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

4c47e127ef02.text:
Charter rates for oil tankers hit a fresh record, driving a larger wedge between the nominal price of crude futures and what it costs to actually receive barrels. Crude oil exiting the Strait of Hormuz averaged about 10 million barrels per day over the past week, despite a rising number of attacks on tankers. But the time required for the largest tankers to rest outside the strait waiting for crude deliveries from smaller vessels has effectively created a tanker shortage. It now costs up to $77 million to hire a large tanker to move crude from the US to Asia, up from less than $10 million last year.
Crude futures, meanwhile, fluctuated based more on tradersâ perceptions of Trump administration statements than by the flow of physical barrels, which has made them âincreasingly unreliable as a proxy for genuine supply,â analyst Amrita Sen wrote in the Financial Times; the gap between the âdatedâ and futures prices for Brent is now the highest since the war started. And because emergency crude stocks have already been drained, if Gulf exports fall again, âyou do have that $200-a-barrel scenario,â the CEO of trading house Vitol warned.
Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency clarified that last weekâs G7 commitment to release diesel from strategic supplies will be drawn from the volume originally authorized in March, and not represent any new barrels; European diesel prices jumped 8% on the news.

Watch: Fleeing Kyiv for the countryside ahead of winter
Kyiv resident Olena Konoplia has decided to move to Ukraine's countryside, as Russian attacks on the city have intensified and the prospect of another cold winter looms.
Russia has been targeting Ukraine's power grid leaving locals without electricity and heating, and they will soon face prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures.
Olena told the BBC she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital.
"I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explained.

A former US Army sergeant who survived the mass shooting on Fort Hood has said that while he supports the execution of the gunman by firing squad, he is concerned about it being livestreamed.
Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times, told the BBC that the "method is befitting" for Nidal Hasan because other methods like lethal injection would be "doing him a favour".
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers in a medical building at Fort Hood, in Texas, in 2009.
But while Lunsford agreed with the method of execution, he said it was "not something you should view for entertainment purposes".
Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, he said: "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief."
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the public will be able to view a livestream of the execution, saying it is important for people to see the consequences of this kind of crime.
If it goes ahead, and legal experts told the BBC it might not ever happen, it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.
Lunsford explained that while he is concerned about the "effect" and "message" a livestream would send to younger people, when it comes to the survivors, their families and the families of the victims, they "should be able to look at it".
"I'm gonna be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude you failed, I'm still here,'" he said.
"I don't really have any sympathy for him as far as firing squad vs lethal injection, hanging or gas chamber, because he didn't have that same compassion when he did the deed on 5 November," the former sergeant explained.
"I think the method is befitting for him because the lethal injection - that's doing him a favour. Gas chamber? Is doing him a favour."
But Lunsford said that as a Christian, he has forgiven Hasan because "I cannot heal if I don't forgive him".
"We're taught that with your last breath you can ask for forgiveness and I think that's what he [Hasan] should do," he added.
Telling his account of what happened that day, he said Hasan got out of his chair and jumped onto a counter, before pulling out a weapon and discharging rounds.
Lunford said he was looking for an exit via the back door, which was "two or three strides" away from him when he was first shot above his left eye and then "hit two more times in my back" as he crawled behind a desk.
"At that point I played dead," he said. When Hasan moved on, he grabbed a nearby wounded soldier and went outside, where Lunsford said Hasan came up behind them and shot him again.
One memory he said that "bothers" him from the day was of a woman who told Hasan she was pregnant.
"We heard a gunshot and the last thing that girl was saying was: 'Oh my god, my baby, my baby.'"
Lunsford said personnel don't carry weapons in medical facilities, and that Hasan "took the coward's way out" to attack them there.
"And then for him to say he is fighting for his cause? I've read the Quran, and everything that he said he was doing that was in the Quran is not supported by the Quran," he explained.
Hasan's execution was announced by the Pentagon earlier this week, in what will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Legal experts have told the BBC there are a number of hurdles around the livestreaming of this which could mean it is successfully challenged in court.
Some politicians have been vocal in their opposition.
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN it was "disgusting" while Republican Senator Thom Tillis said public executions were what "oppressive dictators" did.
"It should not be happening in America," he added in a post on X., external

Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the tech firm.
"I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," Mikita Balesni posted on X, external alongside an open letter to the ChatGPT-maker, written with fellow ex-employees.
On 2 October, a spokesperson for the AI firm told the BBC its investigation "confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures".
OpenAI repeated these claims, external on Friday morning in a note from research leaders.
"We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," the note said.
"Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment."
The dismissals come amid a growing debate over AI safety and the potential risks advanced AI systems could pose to society.
The joint letter to OpenAI leadership was written by Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, who say they were all, until recently, safety or alignment employees at the company.
Alignment is the practice of building human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.
The former staff members raised concerns that their firings had made employees at the tech company "afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI".
Reposting the letter, Korbak wrote, external: "For months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave.
"I believe that was why I was fired."
OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and would announce details in the coming weeks.
"We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," Wang said in a post on X, external.
"Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of manoeuvre, I am concerned we will not be the last."

Thieves have stolen 30,000 bottles of wine collectively worth about â¬5m (Â£4.2m) from a prestigious Italian winery, Italian media reports.
Marchesi Antinori, one of Italy's biggest family-owned wineries, said the theft at its storage facility in Tuscany took place on Saturday as the company was preparing to ship a consignment to customers abroad.
At least seven masked men are believed to have deactivated the alarms, disabled the cameras and used company forklifts to load two large trucks of the company's prized Tignanello, Solaia and Guado al Tasso Tuscan reds.
Renzo Cotarella, the chief executive, told Corriere della Sera this was the largest theft of its kind in Italy.
"A theft of this scale and value has certainly never occurred in Italy," he said.
He added that he was hopeful the authorities would be able to trace the stolen wine.
"Two trucks full of merchandise can't just disappear into thin air. The Tuscan roads are full of cameras; perhaps with a bit of luck we'll be able to recover at least some of the bottles stolen from us."
He told the Financial Times: "These wines have a great value and I don't know how they can sell all this wine around the world without being seen."
The company believes the selection of bottles, which usually sell for between â¬150 and â¬500 each, suggests the thieves were wine connoisseurs and had inside knowledge.
The theft was only discovered on Monday morning as staff arrived on site. No arrests have been made.
Marchesi Antinori was founded in 1385 and exports to 170 countries. It had a revenue of â¬263m (Â£223m) last year.
There has been a spate of wine thefts in Italy this year, including two in the northern Piedmont region where hundreds of thousands of euros worth of bottles were reportedly taken.

21f063c90b6a.text:
Faisalâs view
Two statements by US Senator Chris Murphy and Secretary of State Marco Rubio signal that Washington takes Gulf security seriously. They have come at a critical juncture for Saudi Arabia and the region.
Senator Murphyâs comments carry weight because he has long criticized Saudi policy. Yet he traveled to Riyadh, spent two hours discussing his concerns with the kingdomâs leadership, and publicly stated that Washington canât achieve its goals alone. This has brought him closer to Riyadhâs view: If the US aims to enhance regional stability, contain Iranian influence, and advance a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, it must work with its regional partners.
Secretary Rubio â who is also the US national security advisor â affirmed Saudi Arabiaâs right to defend itself against Houthi aggression and Washingtonâs intention to honor its defense and security agreements with the kingdom.
Together, these statements matter at a time when some in Washington advocate a narrower role for the US. They show that American leaders recognize that threats against the Gulf have global consequences. While Saudi Arabia has considerable military capabilities, experience in Yemen, and powerful allies like Pakistan and TÃ¼rkiye, active US backing remains crucial, both strategically and politically.
I write this as a Saudi citizen whose country supports Yemenâs legitimate government. The military operation there aims to restore sovereignty and confront the Houthi militia thatâs attacking not just Saudi Arabia and Yemen, but the arteries of the global economy.
The Houthis are sometimes misrepresented as a Yemeni faction vying to share power with others in the state. But their slogan â âGod is the greatest, Death to America, Death to Israel, A Curse Upon the Jewsâ â is clear about their objectives and ideology.
Allowing them to consolidate control risks turning Yemen into a permanent breeding ground for international extremism and handing another Arab state to Tehran. We need only look at the painful legacy of Iraq to understand the disastrous consequences of allowing Iranian influence to swallow state institutions unchecked.
Beyond security, the economic risks are acute. An Iran-backed force dictating traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait threatens another chokepoint in the region, a scenario the global economy canât absorb as it deals with disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Keeping these waters open, which can only be achieved through Saudi-led deterrence, benefits the kingdom, but also serves US and global interests.
Some observers may question why Riyadh has turned up the heat now. The answer is simple: It was the Houthis who shattered years of goodwill and unilaterally escalated against the Yemeni government. Saudi Arabia was always clear that it wouldnât tolerate attacks in the Red Sea or inside its territory.
To truly understand Saudi foreign policy â which, at its core, balances diplomacy with resolve â I recently spoke to HRH Prince Turki Al-Faisal, the kingdomâs former intelligence chief, on the debut episode of the Arab Views podcast.
Prince Turki traced Saudi Arabiaâs engagement in Yemen through the eras of King Abdulaziz and his father, King Faisal, describing a policy shaped by strategic restraint within limits. With the kingdom now facing persistent provocations on multiple fronts from regional proxies, âthat restraint is no longer operable,â he said.
The Houthis appear to have mistaken Saudi restraint for an inability to act. With the militia stretched thin, Riyadh sees an opportunity to defeat it or force it back to negotiations. Washingtonâs support isnât a favor to the Gulf, but rather a clear-eyed assessment of its own strategic interests. By standing firmly with Saudi Arabia, the US is helping protect global trade, confront state-sponsored terror, and ensure that diplomacy in the Middle East is backed by unyielding strength.
There is a question of responsibility, too. Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries have suffered severe damage from the US and Israeli war against Iran. Yemen gives Washington a chance to show that they wonât be left to manage the regional consequences alone.
Faisal J. Abbas is an award-winning journalist and Editor-in-Chief of Arab News.

3928b9d92777.text:
The News
Zambia signed a $1.5 billion health financing agreement with the US after separating it from a critical minerals deal that is still being negotiated. The health pact had been jeopardized by privacy concerns over sharing citizensâ data.
Zambia is among several African countries that have signed bilateral health deals under the Trump administrationâs America First Global Health Strategy, but Africaâs second largest copper producer stands out for having publicly resisted key provisions and winning changes.
Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe said at the signing ceremony that the two memorandums of understanding âneeded to be decoupled and this has been done.â
Washington said the deal was worth $2.49 billion, with Zambia committing $975 million in ânew fundingâ and the US putting up $1.5 billion.
Global aid tumbled at its steepest rate on record last year as the US cut its budget by 57% when it dismantled the USAID model of unconditional funding, which researchers say has had an impact on health programs. A Lancet Global Health study published this week found that HIV testing dropped by more than 60% at four providers in Uganda and Zimbabwe, while treatment, which Washington had promised to protect, fell by about one third. âThe safety net that was supposed to preserve life-saving treatment did not hold,â lead author Henry Cust said.
Know More
President Hakainde Hichilema, who secured a second five-year term in August, held out for months against the US demands requiring it to hand over biological specimens and patient data in exchange for the funding.
The deal strips out the specimen clause and restricts data sharing to monitoring and evaluation of US-funded programmes. âThe government will not be sharing any specimens with the United States,â Health Minister Roma Chilengi said.
Zambia joins 35 countries, including several in Africa, which have signed the Trump administrationâs America First Global Health Strategy that replaces the old USAID and PEPFAR system. Kenya was among the first to agree, but its courts suspended the deal last December, first due to the data clauses and then because of privacy issues and a lack of parliamentary approval. Ghana and Namibia refused to sign up over concerns about data and specimens, while Zimbabwe lost all US health aid last month.
Notable
- Think Global Health, published by New York-based foreign policy think tank Council on Foreign Relations, found total health spending falls in most deals as the US steps back, by about 14% by 2030 in eight countries, including Mozambique, Lesotho, and Eswatini.

Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name.
The series will pick up events after the end of the hit film, with Constance Wu and Henry Golding playing their lead roles of Rachel and Nick, while Ronny Chieng is back as Eddie and Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh will have a recurring role as Nick's mother Eleanor.
"It's a 'Crazy Rich' family reunion!" said Adele Lim, who co-wrote the film, calling it the sequel we've been waiting for". It will "delve into the characters and worlds of Kevin Kwan's brilliant books" over eight episodes, she said.
The show will be made by HBO, and the news was announced days after HBO's parent company Warner Bros announced its Â£110bn (Â£82.8bn) merger with Paramount Skydance.
Adapted from Kwan's bestseller books, written between 2013 and 2017, the film topped the US box office and was nominated for two Golden Globes.
It featured an all-Asian cast and told the story of an Asian-American woman who gets a culture shock meeting her boyfriend's ultra-wealthy family in Singapore.
Lim is showrunner for the new TV series and will be one of the executive producers, as will the the film's director Jon M Chu.
He said the film had "changed his life", calling the cast and crew the "most creative and hilarious group of people I've ever known".
"Since then, this cast has become movie stars, superheroes, arena-filling performers and even an Oscar winner, so bringing everyone back together feels like coming home."
Lim added: "Our writers room is humming and we can't wait to share what we've come up with."
The series, co-produced by HBO and Warner Bros Television, will start production next year.
"Constance, Henry, Ronny, and Michelle are global superstars, and we know the passionate fans of the film and megahit novels can't wait to see more," said said Casey Bloys, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance Direct-To-Consumer.

Russia ramped up its military outlays, putting it on track to spend a record $200 billion on defense in 2026 with little sign of the Ukraine war coming to an end.
The huge increase â roughly 40% higher than its original plan for the year, with a similar amount expected in 2027 â comes with the countryâs budget and economy under growing pressure.
Russia can likely keep paying for the war by printing money, a leading analyst told Meduza, but ultimately, its people will pay the price: âThe Kremlin will have to determine who exactly needs to pay, how much they need to pay, and how publicly this process will unfold,â a Carnegie scholar wrote. âAll of this will have political consequences.â

Navi Pillay, a South African jurist who was the UNâs longest-serving human rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. Pillay was a pioneer long before taking on major international roles: She was the first non-white woman to serve as a judge in South Africaâs High Court. But it has been her time on the global stage â and her particular focus on genocide â that has won her most plaudits, beginning with the tribunal over ethnic cleansing in Rwanda.
The focus has made her a controversial figure, however, particularly in countries she argues have carried out genocide; she told The Guardian last year that she saw echoes of the Rwandan killings in Israelâs war in Gaza, which Israel angrily dismissed.
