Nigeria introduced a new discount on fuel, reigniting fierce debate over the wisdom of terminating a long-running subsidy program three years ago. The move comes ahead of Januaryâs presidential election, with high energy prices among the key campaign issues.
Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele announced a 30-day discount on petrol sold at government-owned pump stations, insisting that it was not a subsidy. But that framing, which was widely rejected by analysts, has opened a window of criticism for President Bola Tinubuâs top challengers.
Tinubu ended the subsidy following years of recommendations by the IMF and other economists that the program, whose $10 billion cost in 2022 exceeded the combined budgets for health and education, was wasteful and corrupt. But its removal raised fuel prices sharply, pressure that was exacerbated by the Iran war curtailing energy supplies.

Ariel Investmentâs John Rogers has been a longtime listener â he and the investment firmâs co-CEO Mellody Hobson have been consiglieri to everyone from Barack Obama to Howard Schultz. The company declined to comment on Authenticâs interest and said it would consider Arielâs views in the same way it considered the âviews of Mattelâs other shareholders.â (Ariel didnât respond to a request for comment.) But it may just be a matter of time before someone else â a real activist â decides to push on Mattelâs open door.

Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said.
The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years.
The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief.
Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement.
The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe.
The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).
The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled
"These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally.
Further details of their recovery were due to be revealed later on Friday.
The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.
Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.
Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul CÃ©zanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered in August.
France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris.
Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours.
They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with â¬88m (Â£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses.
The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security.

A doctor accused of a number of offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide is set to face trial in autumn next year.
Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group in Rwanda. He is the first person in the UK to have been charged over the genocide.
Brown, of Islington, north London, is charged with one count of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity.
A judge has now set his provisional trial date to begin in October 2027. He denies wrongdoing and has not yet entered a plea.
The defendant appeared via video link from Belmarsh prison on Friday for a pre-trial hearing at the Old Bailey during which Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb set a provisional eight to 12-week trial from October 4 2027.
A plea and case management hearing has also been set for 15 January.
He has indicated he will plead not guilty to the charges against him.
An estimated 800,000 Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus were killed during the 1994 Rwanda genocide which lasted for 100 days.
Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son.
Between April 6 and 13 1994, he was allegedly a party to six murders and was later charged following a seven-year British investigation into the killings.
The court heard on Friday that a Â£100,000 bail condition, imposed earlier in October, had not yet been met.
Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones KC told the court the events in 1994 were "the most devastating wave of mass killing in modern history".
Jones said: "One hundred thousand were murdered in Kigali especially in the first days and weeks of the genocide."

The French government has made its first sign of giving ground to teenage protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.
Education minister Edouard Geffray made the offer in a television interview on Thursday evening, at the end of another day of sometimes violent demonstrations by high-school students.
The government says 6,877 people have been arrested, 86% of whom are under the age of 18, since protests began centred around demands for more resources in secondary education.
In what unions have billed as Act Four of the three-week movement, some 71,000 people staged protests across the country on Thursday, with 24,000 gathering at the Bastille in Paris.
Police once again intervened with tear-gas to disperse groups who attacked them with paving stones and homemade fireworks.
In Bordeaux, a lycÃ©e, or high school, was ransacked by protesters, and in Marseille a deputy-head was beaten up.
On Friday, some 140 lycÃ©es - out of 3,500 - were totally or partially closed, a big drop on previous days. But another day of action has been called for next Tuesday.
Geffray's announcement was the first material concession to the protesters' complaints.
It has long been recognised by all concerned in French education that too many school hours are being lost because of absent teachers and their non-replacement by available supply staff.
The minister said that thanks to new software coming online at the ministry, it would be possible to direct 3,000 supply teachers to the 500 or so lycÃ©es identified as being in the greatest need.
Many of these schools are likely to be in high-immigration city suburbs, where the lack of teachers is most acute.
Geffray also said that more money would be made available under an already existing scheme for those teachers who want to work overtime hours in order to plug gaps.
And he promised that students' grievances would be taken into account in forthcoming discussions on the education section of the 2027 state budget.
But the offer contained no major promise of new investment on a scale likely to appease protesters.
The government is wary of appearing to buy social peace because it knows France's precarious debt situation is being followed closely by international money markets.
Reaction from student leaders has been guarded to say the least.
NathanaÃ«l Combary, who represents the most moderate of the three main lycÃ©e unions Renouveau LycÃ©en (LycÃ©e Renewal), said students were waiting to see how the promise was carried out in practice: "We've had some announcements which correspond to part of our demands. But obviously people want to see the money and more concrete results."
"As long as we do not have â¬10bn on the table, we will continue our action," said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Etudiante (Student Union), which is close to the radical-left France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party of presidential candidate Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon.
MÃ©lenchon praised Thursday's demonstrations, saying on X that the students had "retaken the Bastille".
But at the other end of the political spectrum, a spokesman for the hard-right National Rally (RN) condemned the government's concessions.
"The message is: if you break things, you get given stuff," said Laurent Jacobelli. "When you burn cars, attack police, you gain something in return. It's the legitimisation of violence."
The movement is the most serious student unrest in France in many years, and comes against a backdrop of rising tension in the country - with anger over rising fuel prices and distress in the farming sector also liable to trigger protests.
Next Saturday, 17 October, has been earmarked as a day of demonstrations by a revived "yellow vest" movement.
In addition, the approach of presidential elections in April and May - in which both hard right and hard left are expected to perform strongly - is exacerbating the mood of confrontation.
The government is hoping that the approach of half-term holidays at the end of next week - as well as the arrival of colder and wetter weather - will take some of the sting out of the protests.

63d6058846f0.text: The Trump administration said Thursday that it was suspending Microsoft from a key program used to sponsor employees for green cards. Later that day , the administration honored the tech giant's CEO with a medal for innovation. Why it matters: The split-screen day highlights the tension between the administration's championing of Big Tech and its immigration policies, which constrain an industry that has long relied on hiring foreign-born workers. Tech leaders have said that restrictions on hiring hamper the country's ability to compete — especially at a moment when the U.S. is in a race with China on AI. Driving the news: The administration's move Thursday also targeted Adobe and six IT services firms over the Permanent Employment Program, or Perm. It's typically the first major government approval step in employers sponsoring workers, often H-1B holders, for employment-based green cards . The administration accused these companies of hiring foreign workers and paying them less, at U.S. workers' expense. State of play: President Trump awarded Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House's New Golden Age Summit Thursday night. Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google co-founder Sergey Brin and CEO of AMD Lisa Su — like Nadella, all immigrants to the U.S. — were awarded the National Medal of Science. At the event, Trump called the honorees " national treasure s." What they're saying: Vice President Vance addressed the apparent contradiction at a press conference earlier Thursday, saying: "Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company; it's that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans." Microsoft "laid off 6,000 American workers while replacing them with 6,300 H-1Bs," he said. Vance didn't provide a timeline. "The suspension of Perm is going to last as long as it needs to," he said. "We have a number of tools to suspend it indefinitely." The other side: Microsoft said in a statement Thursday that 80% of the applications it submitted in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees — not to hire new people. "We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings." It didn't directly address the Perm program. Zoom in: The Department of Labor said it won't accept new Perm applications from the eight companies it named nor would it process those already in the pipeline. This is a process that can already take years for some workers — and many are long-time trusted employees inside those companies. By the numbers: In fiscal year 2025, the Labor Department certified nearly 140,000 of these Perm applications, and nearly 118,000 new ones were filed — down 22% from the previous year. Roughly 30% of certified applications were for software developers, computer systems analysts and data scientists. Microsoft's stock price fell about 1% after the news, but overall investors didn't seem flustered. Adobe shares rose nearly 4%. What to watch: Lawyers say the move could make companies more reluctant to sponsor workers for visas and permanent residency. And it could turn off talented foreign workers and students from coming to the U.S. The Perm program is "a fundamental way of getting a green card in the U.S. for workers," says Patricia Gannon, chair of the Immigration and Naturalization Group and the law firm Greenspoon Marder. "It's going to make foreign workers more hesitant to accept positions in the United States," says Hiba Anver, an attorney at Erickson Immigration Group. "I have concerns about a shrinking talent pool in the United States." Catch up quick: This isn't the administration's first effort on the H-1B labor force. In September 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced a $100,000 fee on H-1B visas. Roughly five months later, just 85 people had paid the fee, according to a court filing. Numerous federal judges have now struck down the fee. Brittany Gibson contributed reporting.

A man who lives in a log cabin and keeps wallabies, mongooses, porcupines, parrots and other rare birds has been told to move.
James Wale relocated to the rural Carmarthenshire site two years ago, having previously run a rare bird business in Pembrokeshire.
Neighbours said the site sounded like a "tropical jungle", especially at night.
Carmarthenshire Council issued Wale with an enforcement notice alleging he had broken planning rules, but he has been given more time to relocate the animals.
Planning agents representing the bird enthusiast said he wanted to create a "major tourism venture", and that his former business in the grounds of Picton Castle ended because the lease was not renewed.
Wale moved to the 17-acre woodland near Llannon and had hoped to set up an owl garden centre, but scaled back his plans to create a private bird welfare home along with some forestry and farming activities.
As well as the exotic animals, Wale also kept horses, goats, chickens and ducks, according to the enforcement appeal.
Documents said the abandoned venture planned to include "reptile, mongoose and several animal enclosures".
A planning application was then prepared for a smaller-scale venture including about 30 bird and animal enclosures, with Wale not intending to live onsite.
Two enforcement notices were issued by the council last year, one of which was withdrawn, and another sent this year which told him to stop living on the land, remove the cabin and stop keeping non-agricultural birds and animals.
During the subsequent appeal, seven objectors expressed concerns about the changes at the land linked to sanitation, stray animals and unusual noises.
One objector said the noises were "not those of native species".
Another claimed the noise "often sounds like a tropical jungle" which, along with the sound of generators and dog-barking, was "particularly troublesome late at night".
A further comment said the site had become waterlogged, turning a "once beautiful forest" into a "fly-tipping incident".
The person submitted a photo of goats and a Labrador to the council and said they had strayed onto their land.
Llannon councillor Llinos Mai Davies claimed the site adversely affected neighbouring properties and had a negative impact on the character of the area.
Photos of the land were submitted showing the boggy conditions and the woodland access track off the A476.
A planning inspector appointed by Welsh ministers has now dismissed the appeal after seeing the cabin during a visit to the land.
"The appellant keeps a few chickens, ducks and horses on site along with a variety of more unusual animals including eagles, falcons, parrots, hornbills, mongooses, skunks, porcupine and wallaby," they said.
The inspector said there was a minor element of forestry and agricultural activity taking place, but that the main operation was of a "fundamentally different character" and unauthorised.
Wale should be given 12 rather than six months to stop using the land to keep non-agricultural animals, remove the enclosures and restore the site to its original condition, the inspector concluded.
"Given the unusual type and mix of the animals, it may well take more time to find a suitable alternative location," they added.
Wale also has 12 months to stop living on the land, remove the cabin and its associated foul drainage.
His agents told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that a planning application would be drawn up in a bid to keep the birds on site.

It’s Nobels season — that time of the year when we find out which groundbreaking, paradigm-shifting, world-changing achievements beat out the rest to win what is arguably the most prestigious award on Earth.
From a light switch for the brain to the discovery of an ultra-elusive subatomic particle hailing from beyond our solar system to a solution to one of the most enduring puzzles in all of organic chemistry, the researchers behind this year’s scientific prizes each revolutionized the ways that scientists understand the world around them.
Take a look at the science behind each of this year’s awards.
Shining a light
A galaxy of nearly 90 billion neurons exists within a single human brain. But unlike stars in the void, neurons communicate with one another via some 100 trillion connections, allowing the human mind to learn, adapt and interact with its surroundings.
For scientists to understand how individual actions arise from such complexity, they needed a tool to directly link neural circuits to specific behaviors, said Abdel El Manira, a neuroscientist at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm. “Neuroscientists dreamed of a neuronal switch, a tool to turn specific neurons on or off with great precision,” El Manira said during the Oct. 5 announcement of this year’s prize in physiology or medicine by the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute.
Enter the bright idea that won. It’s a technology called optogenetics, which involves using light to precisely activate specific cells, like neurons, and watch how behavior changes. For their foundational contributions to optogenetics, biophysicists Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin and Georg Nagel, of the Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg in Germany, and neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University shared this year’s prize.
The prize winners’ story starts in an unlikely place: the eye spot of a single celled green alga called Chlamydomonas. In the early 2000s, Hegemann, then at the Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry in Martinsreid, Germany, and Nagel, at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt, discovered a unique protein in the alga’s eye spot. When illuminated, the protein generated an electrical impulse, enabling the organism to move. Further research revealed that when the protein, called channelrhodopsin, was exposed to light, it opened like a pore, allowing positively charged ions to flow into a cell, generating the electrical impulse. “They had just discovered the switch neuroscientists had long dreamed of,” El Manira said.
Building on the Hegemann and Nagel’s work, Deisseroth began testing whether channelrhodopsin could be used to activate brain cells. He and his colleagues first inserted the gene for channelrhodopsin into cultures of rat nerve cells and found that the cells reacted to light instantaneously. They then introduced the gene into nerve cells in the brains of living mice, along with optical fibers fed through the rodents’ skulls. By beaming blue light through the fibers, the researchers were able to control the movements of the rodents’ whiskers. This technology gave researchers the ability to test the links between certain brain circuits and behaviors.
“The technology, which soon became known as optogenetics, transformed neuroscience,” El Manira said. In addition to exposing the inner workings of healthy brains, he noted, “it has also helped reveal how brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression and dementia.”
For example, the technology has been used improve vision in some patients with retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that degrades light-sensing cells in the retina. It’s also helping researchers investigate the role that a person’s heart plays in how they experience and interact with their surroundings.
Capturing a ghost
At the South Pole, there exists a block of ice unlike any other on Earth. Buried deep beneath the surface of the Antarctic ice sheet, a cubic kilometer of ice is threaded with thousands of beadlike sensors. Known as the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, this immense instrument enables researchers to detect the most elusive particle in the universe — the neutrino.
Detecting neutrinos from beyond our solar system had been a goal of scientists for decades, as that could help understand where and how the universe accelerates particles to extraordinary energies.
The researcher who led the creation of the Antarctic observatory, physicist Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin–Madison, received this year’s Nobel Prize in physics. Halzen was awarded “for his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” Mark Pearce, a physicist and chair of the Nobel committee for physics, during the Oct. 6 announcement by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
Neutrinos are subatomic particles that are chargeless, incredibly small and so ethereal that they often pass through objects without interacting. In fact, billions of neutrinos pass through each of us every second, most of which are formed by nuclear fusion reactions in the sun. But some of these ghostly particles were thought to have originated much farther away, in high-energy particle collisions so distant as to lie beyond the limits of observations. Because neutrinos are not deflected by magnetic fields and rarely interact with matter, the detection of a high-energy neutrino’s trajectory could enable the identification of its distant source. An instrument capable of that task could therefore open a new window into the cosmos.
In the 1980s, Halzen realized that the South Pole was an ideal location for detecting the rare flashes of light that are generated when neutrinos collide with atomic nuclei. Ice deep inside the Antarctic ice sheet presented a large, transparent medium plunged in darkness, in a spot free from earthquakes and biological interference. It was the perfect stage for a neutrino lights

The 28-year-old man, whom city police identified as Oscar Belgal, survived and was treated at a hospital. DHS did not describe exactly what led to the shooting, saying only that "during the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon" and that the man was injured. But city Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Belgal was pulling into a parking space when a federal officer in plainclothes approached with gun drawn, followed by another federal officer who also wasn't in uniform. Belgal started to pull the car forward, and then at least one of the officers fired seven rounds, hitting the man below his left ear, Tisch said at a news conference near the shooting site late Thursday. Witnesses, he said, were screaming. Bystander videos and photos posted on social media showed a man sitting on the ground with his hands behind his back, in the immediate aftermath of the shooting. Another video shows New York City police officers picking up Belgal and carrying him into a police vehicle. Nearby, a damaged car sat blocking the roadway with small holes in two of its windows. Tisch said the shooting left the car with a bullet entry point on its front windshield and an exit point in one of its rear windows. The agency blamed "reckless sanctuary policies" in Democrat-led areas. d33471d6dda6.text: House races in Iowa , Pennsylvania, Washington , Michigan and more are shifting in Democrats' direction, according to a Friday update from the closely watched Cook Political Report. Why it matters: The GOP's midterm outlook was already bleak , anchored by an unpopular war and high fuel prices. But staving off a blue resurgence, despite heavy spending , is looking increasingly complicated as Election Day approaches. Driving the news: Cook's new moves put the likely midterm outcome at Democrats picking up nine to 19 seats, a range of 224 to 234. The shifts include: Five seats — in Iowa, Pennsylvania and Washington — moving from toss ups to leaning toward Democrats, including Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' (R-Iowa) tough rematch race against Democrat ⁠Christina Bohannan. Cook also nudged four races — in Iowa, Michigan, North Carolina and Virginia — from leaning toward Republicans to toss-ups. That's good news for Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.), whose district was warped by mid-decade redistricting. Republicans' hold on other races in Kentucky, Maine, Pennsylvania, Arkansas and Indiana slipped, shifting them to Lean R or Likely R. Meanwhile, Democrats' hold on Nevada, New York and Nebraska races tightened. Friction point: President Trump is crisscrossing the country to campaign for GOP candidates. But with the midterms serving as a referendum on his White House, his polling may well be a liability for Republicans in tight races. Republicans have quietly distanced themselves from the president — and it appears even some Trump voters get it: A Politico poll out Friday found that some one-in-four who voted for him in 2024 say the Republican candidate in their district would be better off breaking from Trump. Zoom in: Of the seats labeled "Toss Up" by Cook, six are held by Democrats, and 15 belong to Republicans. Per Cook, Democrats need to win 20% of the toss-up races to reach a majority, assuming the seats that favor them in the nonpartisan analysis go Democrats' way. The bottom line: The political environment keeps deteriorating for Republicans, even after the dust cleared from the redistricting battle and with their financial advantage . This month, Togo invited citizens to contribute texts, recordings, and translations to help AI models understand the West African countryâs 50 local languages.
The absence of African languages from large language models has become a major concern for the continentâs policymakers and tech leaders. But initiatives like Togoâs suggest the future of AI in Africa may hinge less on who builds the biggest model than on who makes the technology useful to the most people.
Global AI investment is expected to hit $2 trillion this year, according to research firm Gartner, as tech giants race to build computing power and infrastructure. But few African companies are capturing the cloud computing spending, and even then the numbers are tiny: Africa has 18% of the worldâs population, but only 0.6% of global data-center capacity, the World Bank says â and just 5% of that is equipped for advanced AI workloads.
For now, the continentâs main link to the boom is demand for minerals such as copper and cobalt. The bigger prize is productivity, from how farmers reach markets to how governments deliver services. The African Development Bank estimates inclusive AI adoption could add up to $1 trillion to Africaâs GDP by 2035. But without the infrastructure and energy to deploy it, AI is unlikely to add meaningfully to growth.
Thatâs why the World Bank argues in its biannual Economic Update, published this week, that most African economies should adopt and adapt AI rather than build frontier models from scratch â an expensive use of limited resources. Togo shows what adaptation looks like: A model that canât understand citizensâ languages is of little use in delivering government services.
African countries donât need to win the race to build the biggest model, but they do need to make AI productive across their economies. They also canât afford to merely be suppliers to the AI revolution or just consumers of finished AI products; they need to become places where that revolution delivers its biggest gains.
Notable
- The World Bank highlighted several low-cost but impactful uses of AI in Africa: Tools that âsupport student learning, help farmers detect and manage livestock diseases, and automate tasks such as accounting for small businesses.

a050e963d359.text: By — Adriana Morga, Associated Press Adriana Morga, Associated Press By — Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/your-child-may-be-automatically-enrolled-in-a-trump-account-heres-what-to-know Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Your child may be automatically enrolled in a Trump Account. Here's what to know Nation Oct 9, 2026 9:44 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Whether you realize it or not, your child may be enrolled in a "Trump Account." Rolled out earlier this year, the Trump Accounts program allows parents to claim special investment accounts for children who are 18 years old or younger. And some babies are eligible to receive a one-time $1,000 contribution from the government. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Now, because of automatic enrollment highlighted Wednesday by President Donald Trump, the Treasury Department says every eligible child with a valid Social Security number has a Trump Account. But parents and legal guardians would still need to formally activate the accounts if they haven't already. WATCH: Trump announces eligible U.S. children automatically enrolled in Trump accounts Here's what we know. How Trump Accounts work The accounts are a savings tool that invests money in the stock market on a child's behalf. The child can't access the money until they turn 18 and can use it only for specific purposes, such as paying tuition, starting a business or making a down payment on a home. Families can activate an account through the program's trumpaccounts.gov website or its mobile phone app. WATCH: How 'Trump accounts' for children work, and who will benefit most The government will make a $1,000 contribution for some babies after the account is claimed. To qualify for the $1,000 seed money, a baby must be a U.S. citizen, have a Social Security number and be born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028 — covering Trump's current term. Any parent — regardless of their immigration status — can open an account for a qualifying child. Parents of older children also are encouraged to open accounts. Even though they aren't eligible for the government's $1,000 contribution, some older children are eligible for seed money of $250 drawn from separate investments from wealthy donors. Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. Otherwise, family contributions will need to come out of pocket. Parents can contribute up to $2,500 annually in pretax income, much like retirement accounts. Employers, relatives, friends, local governments and philanthropic groups can also pitch in. Yearly contributions are capped at $5,000, although contributions from governments and charities don't count toward that total. Private banks and brokerages will manage the money. When the accounts were originally conceived, investments were restricted to broader index funds. But with updated rules from the Treasury Department late last month, eligible wealthy investors can now also donate stock from individual companies. Automatic enrollments — but not activation of accounts With automatic enrollment, Trump said 70 million children will now have the accounts, up from 8 million created since their launch in July. Researchers from the Brown School's Center for Social Development at Washington University in St. Louis advocated for the automatic enrollment. And Jin Huang, co-director of the center, called the administration's move "a big step." READ MORE: What experts want you to know about the Trump accounts and a new massive donation "Automatic enrollment is the most important policy design feature for early wealth building programs, in order to ensure full inclusion of all eligible children," said Huang, citing research from his team. Still, he says, more work needs to be done. Parents and legal guardians need to formally claim the accounts to activate them — as well as elect the $1,000 seed money if they're eligible — and Huang says "each of these steps will lower the participation," with particular barriers facing low-income families who may not already have access to similar investments. Wealthy investors can now donate individual stocks When Trump Accounts were first rolled out, investments were initially restricted to broad index funds — in theory to decrease risk while still yielding incremental growth. But among additional updates to the program, eligible wealthy investors can now also donate stock from individual companies. WATCH: Trump officially launches Trump Accounts for kids, ringing Wall Street opening bell "It's a way to encourage participation in the program," explained Nathan C. Goldman, a professor of accounting at North Carolina State University. He said many of the world's wealthiest people don't have "a whole lot of liquid cash sitting around" and might instead turn to shares. Still, he notes, individual stocks are more volatile than indexes. And families wouldn't get a say about which companies might donate to their children's portfolios. Once a child turns 18, they can access the money It's important to note that the child won't be able to access the money until they turn 18, except in rare circumstances. So the money can't help with immediate expenses. But once a beneficiary of a Trump Account turns 18, they can choose to use the money from it however they want. Trump account beneficiaries can also choose to roll the investment over to a Roth IRA account. "You're extending the life of this thing beyond the 18 years; you're going all the way out into the child's potential retirement," said Myranda Fabian, a certified financial planner with Plante Moran Financial Advisors. Moving the earnings from a Trump Account to a Roth IRA will be subject to taxation. Roth

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.
In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", following reported strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.
Fighting broke out between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), two weeks ago.
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended its civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea backs the TPLF, which it denies.
During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF.
But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.
Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.
Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.
US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.
One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.
Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.
Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."
But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.
On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".
In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.
This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.
Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.
Additional reporting by Kaleb Moges

d9bef991e55b.text: Congress has its best chance in years to pass sweeping permitting legislation, but a series of political and policy obstacles could derail the bipartisan Senate plan. Why it matters: Cutting hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors, and major business groups more broadly. Here are five risks to a lame-duck deal: 👱‍♂️ President Trump himself. The White House says it supports the bill, but Trump is mercurial, so nothing is final until it's final. His administration's willingness — or not — to loosen the screws on wind and solar projects it's restricting could also sway the lame-duck politics and complicate efforts to win Democratic support. Flashback: Co-author Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) last month cited "unresolved" questions about Trump officials returning to "regular order" for renewables, but credited their "very reasonable" proposal. 🗳️ A big blue wave. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), a senior House Democrat, has been arguing that Democrats will have more leverage next year. For now, there's little evidence that view is gaining traction among Democrats. The few definitive statements on the bill from lawmakers in both parties are supportive. But a strong Democratic showing in November could change that calculation. The big arguments against waiting: Dems won't have 60 votes even if they take the Senate, and Trump still needs to sign anything, limiting the prospects for a better deal next year. 🟩 Environmentalists. Groups with close ties to Dems — such as the Natural Resources Defense Council, League of Conservation Voters and Evergreen Action — are still weighing their positions on the bill. A coordinated push against it could make it harder for Democratic lawmakers to back the legislation. ⚡ Utilities. Regulated utilities would see new competition in transmission development and greater oversight of their planning and business. American Electric Power and Berkshire Hathaway Energy support the bill , but the sector's trade group — the Edison Electric Institute — has not taken a position. ⏰ The lame-duck squeeze. A busy legislative calendar, potential changes to the bill and uncertainty about lawmakers' appetite for legislating after the election could leave too little time to secure passage through both chambers. Already, House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) told Punchbowl News that he wants to modify the electricity provisions. If Republicans lose the House majority, their willingness to push a major bipartisan deal across the finish line could diminish. "It's hard to convince people to hang around and wait for something to happen when they're being constantly reminded that they lost," Jeff Navin , a former Democratic Hill staffer and co-founder of clean tech lobbying firm Boundary Stone Partners, said via email. The bottom line: This is a partial list! To riff on Mickey Rourke's advice to William Hurt in the great 1981 noir flick "Body Heat," there are 50 ways to mess up any bill, and if you can think of 25, you're a genius. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.
Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.
The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.
It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.
Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".
The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.
The BBC has approached him for comment.
A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.
Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.
University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".
"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.
Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".
"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

In the Grand Canyon, rock layers preserve a relatively continuous record of Earth’s geologic history going back about 2 billion years. But between 520 million and 1.8 billion years, the record is noticeably empty. It’s as if someone broke into a museum and made off with almost an entire wing’s worth of rocks, and sorting out “whodunnit” is one of the coldest cases in all geology.
Now, scientists studying the Grand Canyon’s rocks say that a gigantic Earth-spanning cliff —with a global glaciation as its accomplice — could be to blame for the heist.
The giant cliff started forming about 800 million years ago as an ancient supercontinent called Rodinia split apart, Thomas Gernon, an earth scientist at the University of Southampton in England, and colleagues report August 17 in Geology. Forces like rain and ice weathered and eroded the rock and, like waves at the beach steadily erasing one layer of sand after another, deleted a billion years of Earth’s history.
The group used computer models to simulate how ancient Earth evolved over hundreds of millions of years. They watched as the cliff — known as an escarpment — formed around the time in Earth’s history when rocks in the region vanished.
The escarpment most likely extended across much of a continent called Laurentia, the ancient precursor to North America. It stretched from what was to become Alaska all the way to Arizona and would have been about one to two kilometers high.
Spanning a continent
Some 65 million years ago, the Great Escarpment of Laurentia would have stretched across much of North America, including the spot that would one day become the Grand Canyon and the site of an enduring geologic mystery. The escarpment itself is thought to have formed around 800 million years ago.
“No study has previously suggested the existence of a continental-scale escarpment in the Grand Canyon region. Our study shows it’s a plausible, straightforward explanation for the immense erosion that took place in the Grand Canyon,” Gernon says. Such an immense cliff created steep slopes that were ideal places for the elements to loosen and make off with exposed rock.
And the escarpment had a lot of help when it came to its disappearing act: ice, lots and lots of ice. The theft of the rocks coincided with an extreme period of glaciation called Snowball Earth. Massive ice sheets formed and may have extended all the way from the poles to equatorial latitudes. As the ice expanded, it would have eroded great quantities of rock, helping create the gap in the record.
And the escarpment, due to its high elevation, would have created ideal conditions for Snowball Earth glaciers and ice sheets to form. In a separate study published in Science, Gernon and a team explained how an escarpment created by tectonic activity was responsible for the formation of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet starting some 34 million years ago. “The exposed rocky peaks of the escarpment would have acted as glacier factories,” Gernon says.
It remains unclear, however, whether the erosion that erased the rocks occurred before, during or after the Snowball Earth glaciations. “That’s the real hole that needs filling: pinning down the erosion history in space and time, continent by continent, precisely enough,” Gernon says.
Linking the disappearance of the rocks to verified events in Earth’s history such as the breakup of Rodinia bolsters the case, says Alan Collins, a geologist at Adelaide University in Australia who was not involved in the new study. Not only that, but Gernon’s team points to modern-day examples where similar erosive processes are at work, including a similar escarpment in Antarctica as well as one in South Africa.
Maybe not quite case closed yet, but “I find this very convincing,” Collins says.

aa94b213e25c.text: By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/in-combative-first-michigan-senate-debate-rogers-and-el-sayed-trade-attacks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter In combative first Michigan Senate debate, Rogers and El-Sayed trade attacks Politics Oct 9, 2026 10:59 AM EDT GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. (AP) — The first debate in Michigan's closely watched U.S. Senate race turned combative Thursday as Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed repeatedly traded personal attacks, talked over each other and even continued arguing during a commercial break. The contentious hourlong grudge match followed weeks of the two candidates sparring online and in advertisements that have flooded the state in the highly competitive campaign for an open Senate seat. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "I'd like to be a part of the debate, too," moderator Rick Albin said during the quarreling. "In 30 years of doing debates," he added later, "I've never seen it continue during the commercial. But it did." Rogers is a former congressman who ran unchallenged in the Aug. 4 Republican primary. He lost a previous Senate race to then-U.S. Rep. Elissa Slotkin by just under 20,000 votes two years ago. El-Sayed is a progressive and former public health official who defeated U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary this year by less than a percentage point. The seat is open because Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is retiring. Both parties see the race as pivotal to deciding which party wins control of the Senate in November. Rogers continues to distance himself from some of Trump's policies Rogers has broken with Trump on two major issues in recent weeks. In September, Rogers said the war with Iran needed to "end quickly." On Wednesday, he released an ad criticizing Trump's tariffs on Canada, saying, "we know that Canada is not our enemy" and "we need to end this tariff war now." Early in the debate, Rogers doubled down on both. Regarding the war, Rogers said: "I do believe it's going to come to an end. We need it to come to an end." READ MORE: Rogers and El-Sayed are set for their first debate in Michigan's Senate race after sparring online Later, Rogers said he had called the White House this week to push for a "deal" with Canada to end the trade dispute. "We were originally told that the Canadian tariff was going to be settled and settled quickly," Rogers told reporters after the debate. "It didn't happen. My argument is, and I made this to the administration, time to wrap it up." Rogers also criticized U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's actions earlier this year, saying the "efforts in Minnesota were probably not appropriate." "That to me was something that they could have done differently," Rogers said. Trump had surged immigration agents into the state, stirring outrage when two protesters were shot and killed. El-Sayed grilled on stance to not send funds to Israel El-Sayed worked during the debate to not only attack Rogers but also appeal to Democrats who may still contemplating their vote after a contentious primary divided the party's coalition. Some in the Jewish community have expressed concern about El-Sayed's past comments regarding Israel. El-Sayed was asked during the debate if he would support sending weapons to Israel if they were attacked by another country. He responded that he did not "want our tax dollars being used to subsidize war abroad." WATCH: Harris joins El-Sayed on campaign trail as Democrats focus on Michigan Senate race Asked later if Iran or Israel posed a more dangerous threat, he called it a "ridiculous question" and "both of them have proven dangerous in their own way." After the debate, El-Sayed was asked why he wanted Rogers to answer for his association with Trump while being dismissive of questions about his association with Hasan Piker, an online commentator with a history of controversial remarks. READ MORE: How Abdul El-Sayed rose from political oblivion to progressive breakthrough in Michigan "That's a serious question?" El-Sayed retorted. "To equate the most powerful person in the world with a streamer in California seems to me to just be — I'm not going to use the word — but silly." High-profile Democrats have tried to help El-Sayed bring together Democrats in recent weeks. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer appeared with him for the first time Thursday since she endorsed Stevens during the primary. Trump attacks El-Sayed on Truth Social the night before debate Trump assailed El-Sayed in a social media post late Wednesday, referring to him as "Mohammed" and saying he "goes back to the days of the Jihad." "He is a RADICAL Extremist, Terrorist Sympathizer," Trump wrote on Truth Social. El-Sayed, who was born in the U.S. to Egyptian immigrant parents, responded by pointing out that the president knows his name: "He says it every day." "He's not just attacking me. He's attacking all of us," El-Sayed wrote. "He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us." Former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.
The South African judge was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.
Pillay, 85, has taken part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations during a decades-long career, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.
Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
Pillay's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee JÃ¸rgen Watne Frydnes.
"Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," he said.
"At a time of existential challenges - including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time - international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity."
Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'".
Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader MarÃa Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom".
Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban.
She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court.
Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president.
From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law.
The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements.
The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies".
The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes.
Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice".
It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."
Frydnes said the Nobel organisation was not taking a position on whether the Israeli offensive in Gaza amounted to genocide.
Pillay is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused by The Gambia of genocide against the Rohingya people.
Myanmar has denied deliberately trying to destroy the minority Muslim population, with a government representative telling the court in January that the allegation was "unsubstantiated".
UN human rights chief Volker Turk said Pillay's recognition was "a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice, and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security, and prosperity".
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said she had been a "pioneering defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists" who had worked to "uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally".
Amnesty International Secretary-General AgnÃ¨s Callamard said she was with Pillay when she learned she had won - and called her an "inspired choice" for the award.
"At a time when both international law and justice are under attack, when too many states attempt to hollow them out, her Nobel Peace Prize could not come at a better time," she said.

0454eff904ce.text:
- Published
Convicted murderer Christa Pike is walking and talking in limited ways in her hospital room about a week after authorities in the US state of Tennessee botched her execution, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, was sent to hospital after surviving two attempts to execute her via lethal injection for the 1995 murder of a 19-year-old she met at a summer camp for troubled teens.
An independent review of what went wrong in the Nashville execution chamber on 30 September has been ordered by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee.
He has also halted executions in the state for the rest of the year.
Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing
How did Pike survive?
The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.
Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, says it was not the case that Pike had some "special immunity" but suggested it was simply that not enough of the drug pentobarbital reached her bloodstream to kill her.
Pike was injected with a second dose of the drug, according to the prison authorities' protocol, after the first did not kill her.
In interviews with the BBC, Zivot has suggested the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under Pike's skin than to have entered her bloodstream.
"Most of the pentobarbital, instead of circulating in her body, ended up in her arms, and that's how she lived," Zivot said.
Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition, was highlighted in advance by Pike's legal team as an additional issue that could scupper the process. Before the attempted execution, they had filed a legal case challenging the injection protocol.
If clots of blood formed at the injection site as a result of thrombocytosis, they would potentially have blocked the chemical from entering her veins, the lawyers warned.
As the attempted execution took place, prison officials used at least seven needles on Pike during their efforts to establish intravenous (IV) lines, Pike's lawyers said afterwards. The woman could simultaneously be heard "crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly".
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who was murdered by Pike and her then-boyfriend, told NBC the failed execution had been "a mess".
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
After it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the two doses, she was taken to hospital for life-saving treatment. States have a legal obligation not to deny medical treatment to prisoners.
What is pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded".
But the department said the lethal injection chemical had "consistently been effective".
What happens next?
The full picture of Pike's current physical condition is unknown.
Although she was said to be awake and speaking in hospital as of 6 October, and walking short distances around her room as of the next day, it remains unclear whether she has any long-term health defects.
At one stage she was reported by her lawyers to still be handcuffed to her bed.
There is then the question of what happens to Pike next.
Executions in the state have been paused for the rest of the year. During a court hearing on 7 October, a lawyer for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.
Meanwhile, an investigation is taking place into what happened. During the hearing, a judge ordered state authorities to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
The state's Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada is stepping down.
Pike's lawyers have made repeated calls for Lee to use his powers as state governor to commute her sentence to the lesser punishment of life in prison without parole.
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their plan to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier.
The Supreme Court has already been involved in Pike's case: it allowed the lethal injections to go ahead after a legal battle.
Has this happened before?

Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike is conscious and speaking.
There had been seven previous cases in which prisoners survived executions, but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.

1c025546f830.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/trumps-memorial-arch-faces-a-new-lawsuit-from-arlington-county-virginia Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's memorial arch faces a new lawsuit from Arlington County, Virginia Nation Oct 9, 2026 12:12 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Arlington County Board in Virginia filed a lawsuit Thursday opposing the construction of the Triumphal Arch, becoming the first governmental body to take legal action against President Donald Trump's planned monument. The lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, criticized the speed at which the project slated for Memorial Circle has moved without going through the full review process. WATCH: Retired general calls Trump's proposed arch near Arlington a 'sacrilege' "The National Park Service, the agency responsible for projects on national park land such as Memorial Circle, is proceeding full-speed toward ground-disturbing construction," the lawsuit said. "Although the agency has claimed that a final decision to construct the Arch has not yet been made and purports to be engaged in a routine decisional process, that rushed process appears to be a pretext designed to shore up justifications for building the Arch in accordance with the President's repeated marching orders." The lawsuit asks that "the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the arch" be halted to ensure that the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act be followed and proper analysis and testing be done."The Arlington County Board has filed this lawsuit because our community has the most to lose from this egregious and unlawful proposed project," Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said in a statement. He added that the county has acted in good faith in the review process, pointing out the "severe, unique, and wide-ranging negative impacts" the project will have on the county and its residents, only to see them ignored. READ MORE: Trump's arch could disrupt the significance of many of Washington's historical sites, National Park Service says Memorial Circle sits on federal parkland west of the Potomac River across the Memorial Bridge and immediately adjacent to Arlington County. The county is being represented in the lawsuit by legal advocacy group Democracy Forward. White House spokesman Davis Ingle said the Trump administration and White House have been "fastidiously compliant with all procedural and legal requirements and are certain this meritless and dilatory lawsuit will be dismissed." The arch will become one of the world's most iconic landmarks, he added. "It will enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike." The lawsuit came a day after the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA President Sara Nelson expressed concerns that the 250-foot (76-meter) arch compounds multiple safety issues that she said have gone unaddressed since a deadly January 2025, crash over the Potomac River that killed 67 people. Nelson also criticized Trump's plan to turn the arch into "a top grade military complex" able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition. READ MORE: Flight attendants' union raises safety concerns over Trump's Washington arch Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., saying the project needs to be approved by Congress. The judge in that lawsuit said the administration must give the court 48 hours before undertaking any activities related to or in preparation for construction of the arch. The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. The Trump administration has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), saying it wants to restrict the tribunal's resources and ability to operate.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
The announcement comes just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
US President Donald Trump has reacted sourly to the Norwegian prize's choice of winner this year and last, after having expressed a desire to receive it himself. He criticised Pillay for being part of a panel that accused Israel, as well as Hamas, of war crimes during the 7 October conflict.
The US says the ICC has no jurisdiction over it as it never ratified the statute founding it - but the international court has investigated US actions elsewhere.
Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."
The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.
Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.
He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories to "rein in" the institution.
The ICC responded by saying that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred".
The Trump administration has repeatedly criticised the court, including over its investigation into the actions of US forces in Afghanistan, a probe it has since deprioritised.
It has also been critical of the ICC issuing arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

fe5a664df615.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/the-plague-never-went-away-cases-are-reported-in-parts-of-africa-and-the-u-s-nearly-every-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The plague never went away. Cases are reported in parts of Africa and the U.S. nearly every year Health Oct 9, 2026 11:54 AM EDT The plague, the rare bacterial infection infamously known for killing tens of millions in 14th-century Europe, never went away. It is now easily treated with antibiotics. Since the 1990s, most human cases have been reported in Africa, especially Congo and Madagascar, according to the World Health Organization. READ MORE: What we know so far about a Russian lab worker's death and pneumonic plague There are an average of about seven human cases per year in the U.S., according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, mostly in rural areas of the American West. A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia recently died of pneumonia. The case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague. Russian authorities say testing showed no evidence of plague, but the research institute has been quarantined. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "People think the plague is gone, it was something that occurred 500 years ago. It's not. It's here amongst us," said Simon Clarke of the University of Reading in the U.K. "Unless you get rid of those wild animals, which of course is not possible, then you're not going to get rid of the bacteria." Surprised to hear the plague is still around? Here's what to know. Plague can attack lymph nodes, lungs and blood People in Siberia have been dying of plague for at least 5,500 years. The earliest evidence of a form of the disease was found in teeth from ancient hunter-gatherers north of the region's Lake Baikal. Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague — also called the Black Death — are caused by the same bacteria, called Yersinia pestis. The bacteria spread naturally among rodents like prairie dogs and rats. Fleas that jump from infected animals and bite people can spread the disease. WATCH: Understanding pneumonic plague after Russian lab worker's death The bubonic plague is the most common form of the infection. It causes painfully swollen lymph nodes that are most commonly found in the groin, armpit and neck, called buboes. Other symptoms include sudden high fever and chills, headaches, and pain in the abdomen, legs and arms, according to the Cleveland Clinic. There are two other forms of the plague: pneumonic plague, which can be caused by inhaling the bacteria, infects the lungs, while septicemic plague is an infection in the bloodstream. Both are fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization. Bubonic plague will often develop into the other two forms of plague if untreated. Plague can spread through fleas or bodily fluids Other than bites from infected fleas, people can also get plague by touching infected bodily fluids, so health experts recommend taking extra care when handling dead or sick animals. The plague can also spread through the respiratory droplets of someone who has pneumonic plague. READ MORE: The U.S. sees 7 plague cases a year. Here's why "If you cough, you can spread it to another person, but that doesn't travel very far," said Dr. Glenn Wortmann, MedStar Washington Hospital Center. "So you really need to be in face-to-face contact with that person to get pneumonic plague." That's why "the chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen," he said. Antibiotics can treat plague The plague was never eradicated, but we've gotten better at preventing its spread and treating it in humans. When treated early with antibiotics, the plague can be cured. The key is to get to a doctor fast — otherwise the plague can be deadly. There is a vaccine, but the WHO only recommends it for people who are at high risk of infection, like laboratory and healthcare workers. There isn't strong evidence that vaccines can work against the pneumonic form. There's no plague vaccine available in the U.S. AP video journalist Javier Arciga contributed to this story from San Diego. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. ae7ddd79e59d.text: By — Rebecca Santana, Associated Press Rebecca Santana, Associated Press By — Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ice-official-says-officers-shot-a-man-in-new-york-because-they-believed-they-were-in-danger Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter ICE official says officers shot a man in New York because they believed they were in danger Politics Oct 9, 2026 11:47 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal immigration officers opened fire on a Dominican man in New York because he drove his car into officers' vehicles and they believed their lives were in danger, a senior Immigration and Customs Enforcement official said Friday. The 28-year-old man, whom New York City police identified as Oscar Belgal, was shot "superficially" in the neck as ICE officers attempted to arrest him, Marcos Charles said. READ MORE: ICE officer shoots a man while making an arrest in New York, officials say Officers used their vehicles to block the man as he attempted to drive away, but he accelerated toward them, Charles said during a news conference with U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in Washington. The Department of Homeland Security said the news conference was about the "dangerous consequences of sanctuary city policies." Please check your inbox to confirm. "Our officers, using their training and believing that their life and the life of the partners and the general public were in danger, used their training and fired weapons," Charles said. Belgal had a 5-year-old boy in the car with him when the shooting happened, officials said. READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows Mullin said ICE agents didn't know the child was in the car, but that Belgal "was aware" and chose to knowingly put the boy at risk by trying to evade officers. ICE had issued a detainer on Belgal, who runs with a gang known for thefts using weapons and mopeds, Charles said. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, both Democrats, said late Thursday that they had pressed Mullin and Republican President Donald Trump to release Belgal, to no avail. They also urged the administration to immediately release body camera footage of the shooting and to halt immigration enforcement operations in the city. Mullin said Belgal is being held in a facility outside New York City but declined to provide the location. He confirmed ICE officers were wearing body cameras that were activated, but didn't say when any footage would be released. READ MORE: Shock gloves purchased by ICE cause pain, compliance and fear, Army study found Protesters and local officials had decried the shooting as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. "There is no justification for what we have seen today," Mamdani said late Thursday at the scene of the shooting. Federal officers who surrounded the vehicle wore construction vests and masks, making it difficult to identify them as immigration officers, he said. New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Belgal was pulling into a parking space when a federal officer in plainclothes approached with gun drawn, followed by another federal officer who also wasn't in uniform. Belgal started to pull the car forward, and at least one of the officers fired seven rounds, hitting the man below his left ear. Much of Mullin's remarks Friday were reserved for excoriating Mamdani and his immigration policy. "Sanctuary politicians, they create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for the American citizens to be safe," he said. Mullin said ICE has asked local officials in New York to hold onto more than 14,000 people for federal officers to collect and place in immigration detention. "Silence. Absolute silence is what we have gotten back," he said. "Why would they release these individuals back onto the streets?" "We're enforcing our nation's laws. We're not picking and choosing," Mullin continued. "Why is that controversial? We should all want law and order on our streets." Mullin also criticized the attention surrounding the case. "This was a thug. The absolute worst of the worst," he complained. "We're giving so much attention to this thug." Marcelo reported from New York. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
