0d64f2538f74.text: By — Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/el-ninos-storm-killer-winds-and-climates-warming-waters-in-fight-over-future-of-hurricane-isaias Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter El Niño's storm-killer winds and climate's warming waters in fight over future of Hurricane Isaias Nation Oct 9, 2026 11:35 AM EDT A supersized El Niño's decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico's toasty, storm-fueling waters are battling over the future strength of Hurricane Isaias. And the storm's tilt and eye show who's winning. For now, it's the waters charged by climate change. LIVE MAP: Track the path of Hurricane Isaias All Atlantic hurricane season there has been "this battle between shear and just the overall conducive conditions," said Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach. El Niño — the natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather worldwide — dominated. Its wind patterns smothered almost any wisp of a storm from strengthening in the Atlantic, while boosting what will soon be record high levels in the Pacific, Klotzbach said. Wind shear versus warm waters It's called wind shear and it pushes the tops and middle of storms around, making them lopsided and keeping them from making a complete circular eyewall, which is when storms can really power up, Klotzbach and University at Albany's Kristen Corbosiero said. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The other ingredients for a storm to turbocharge a storm are pushing back. There is plenty of fuel in warm water and moisture. The Gulf of Mexico is about 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5 degrees Celsius) warmer than normal. The 86 degree waters (30 degrees Celsius) are 100 to 500 times more likely to be that extra hot because of climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas, said climate scientist Kristina Dahl, vice president of the nonprofit Climate Central, which calculates the boost global warming causes to extreme weather. WATCH: Gulf Coast prepares for landfall as Hurricane Isaias gains power "But there's a certain point where it's like, I don't care how hot the waters are and how much moisture you have, if shear gets to a certain point, the shear is gonna win," Klotzbach said. The thunderstorm seeds of something bigger earlier in the week grew from circular winds over Central America but often were lopsided and couldn't quite form a crucial eyewall, all because of El Niño's high-level strong winds that pushed a would-be storm's top sideways, experts said. Then a window of moderation opened for just a couple of days, but it was enough, Corbosiero said. It makes sense it was in the Gulf of Mexico and in October, because El Niño has less of an effect in the Gulf than it does in the main Atlantic, she said. And storms often pop up in that region in October because of more northerly storm systems that help foster the right conditions. READ MORE: How El Niño is playing a role in Hurricane Isaias Wind shear wasn't exactly low, but it was a moderate level, when other factors like unusually warm waters and heavy moisture can kick in. Isaias rapidly intensified from 40 mph to 80 mph (64 kph to 129 kph) in a day and by late Wednesday, Isaias became the latest-in-the-season first Atlantic hurricane to form since 1914, Klotzbach said. "The warm waters and high moisture won," Klotzbach said. Isaias Friday was not tilting and had a strong eye, the hurricane center said. By Friday morning, Isaias blew past the threshold for becoming a major hurricane with winds of 111 mph (178 kph), strengthening to 120 mph winds (195 kph). The National Hurricane Center forecasts it to weaken to a strong Category 2 storm before landfall. What to expect before landfall Before Isaias comes ashore — forecast for probably somewhere from the Mississippi and Alabama coast to the Florida Panhandle late Friday night or early Saturday — the wind shear will strengthen from moderate levels of around 20 mph (32 kph) to 52 mph (84 kph) and then Isaias will start to struggle, which is good news for coastal residents, Klotzbach said. But as of Friday morning, hurricane center forecasters said the coast is in "a tenuous spot" because it would only take a six-hour delay in the onset of that more intense wind shear for Isaias to bring a stronger-than-expected landfall. Regardless of what will happen with wind shear, it will still be a dangerous hurricane when it hits land, forecasters said. WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns "Once it gets to the coast, we know that the storm surge is going to be deeper and farther reaching because of sea level rise caused by climate change," Dahl said. "So in this part of the world, there's been about six and a half inches of sea level rise over the past 100 years or so that's attributable directly to climate change." The National Hurricane Center is calling the surge "life-threatening." A warmer atmosphere means storms hold and then dump more rain, worsening flooding, Dahl said. The hurricane center is warning about urban, river and flash flooding in the Southeast this weekend. "There's a little bit of a battle here going on, but I think the really important thing to remember is that climate change is like this long-term big kahuna warming everywhere, and El Niño's like a little icing on the cake," Dahl said. Anthropic has raised eyebrows by announcing it will ban users from "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards its AI.
The Claude-maker said on Thursday it was updating its usage policy to let its tools end interactions where people are "cruel" - something it said it had done in "rare" cases prior.
It will now be included on a list of forbidden conduct which also contains bullying others, promoting self-harm and creating non-consensual intimate imagery.
While Anthropic said the policy would only apply in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse, it has reignited debate over how we should communicate with AI tools.
The company said it would not apply to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research" - suggesting it would only apply in clearly deliberate instances.
But what Anthropic would consider "abusive or cruel behaviour" towards its models remains unclear.
Screenshots of the new policy have been widely shared and commented on across social media - with some praising it as advancing good manners or "model welfare".
But others criticised the plan, with one person calling it "deeply wrong, external" and another suggesting it might undermine abuse directed at humans and animals.
"You can't be cruel to numbers and maths," wrote Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at Irish law firm William Fry, on LinkedIn, external.
"This level of anthropomorphisation of AI is harmful. It leads people to believe that it's something it's not."
Microsoft AI director Mustafa Suleyman, who in September criticised rival firm Anthropic for treating AI like it is human, reacted to Anthropic's update with a melting face emoji.
The changes, first reported by tech outlet The Verge, came following an annual review of the usage policy at the firm.
It was also updated to address new or emerging risks in other areas, including by forbidding use of Claude for "deceptive campaigns" or clarifying that, as US midterm elections loom, it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections".
Anthropic also said on Thursday its usage policy previously prevented its tools being used to develop weapons.
But none of the updates have attracted as much attention or scrutiny as its move to forbid users abusing its chatbots.
It has also tapped into the much-debated question of whether we should be curt or polite when using generative AI tools.
Some experts say writing or saying "please" or "thank you" to tools like ChatGPT is unnecessary and wastes tokens - used by the large language models powering generative AI tools to process and reply to you.
Others argue politeness can lead to higher quality answers or responses.
When a X user last year asked about electricity costs incurred by ChatGPT replying to users' "please" and "thank you" messages, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said it was, external "tens of millions of dollars well spent - you never know".
The Collins Dictionary meanwhile last November highlighted the re-emergence of the term "clanker" for disparagingly referring to AI tools.
Used to describe robots in Star Wars games and movies since the mid 2000s, the term made its shortlist of words reflecting the mood of 2025 after last July saw many take to TikTok to share their frustrations with AI-powered machines.
Some experts have also posited that being rude to AI chatbots could adversely impact human communication, by seeping into how we talk to and treat others.

Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.
Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.
Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.
Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".
Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".
Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".
The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.
The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.
Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.
Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.
Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".
Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".
Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.
Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.
Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.
But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

408f0293a797.text: The Department of Homeland Security is coming under fire for publicly attacking Democratic congressional candidate Janelle Stelson less than a month before the midterm election . Why it matters: The Stelson campaign is threatening a lawsuit over the allegations, while a watchdog group is seeking an investigation into whether an ICE official violated restrictions on partisan political activity by federal employees. "We are likely to take legal action to combat the blatant lies and coordinated misinformation campaign," Stelson campaign manager Alma Baker said in a statement to Axios. The campaign said Friday it has sent out cease and desist letters, viewed by Axios, to several news outlets that reported DHS's claims as fact. The race between Stelson and Republican Rep. Scott Perry in Pennsylvania's 10th district is one of the most competitive and expensive House elections in the country, attracting more than $26 million in spending, according to AdImpact. Driving the news: DHS published a press release on Wednesday announcing the arrest of what it said was an "illegal alien from Nigeria who exposed himself in public while working for congressional campaign in Pennsylvania." The migrant, Chimaobim Adedayo Igbojekwe, was arrested by ICE on Oct. 1 after pleading guilty to disorderly conduct last month, according to the press release. The release included a statement from ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall saying: "It's unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien to work on a Congressional campaign, let alone a pervert who exposed himself in public." Stelson herself quickly batted down the claim: "He's not an employee. He's not a volunteer," she said at an event on Wednesday. Nobody named Igbojekwe was paid by the Stelson campaign as of Sept. 30, according to disbursements tracked by the Federal Election Commission. The campaign also showed Axios a search of its volunteer database that turned up no results for the name. In its cease-and-desist letter, the campaign said Igbojekwe has also "never been employed by any vendors of the campaign." Asked Thursday for comment on this story, DHS sent Axios its initial press release. The agency did not respond to multiple follow-up emails requesting comment on the Stelson campaign's threat of legal action. Between the lines: DHS cited a New Jersey-based news outlet called "Shore News Network" as its source for the claim that Igbojekwe was a Stelson canvasser. That outlet cited a social media post from conservative activist Scott Presler. "A canvasser for democrat Janelle Stelson ... was reportedly charged for indecent exposure," Presler wrote in a post on X , which included a photo of a court document that did not make reference to the Stelson campaign. Presler did not respond to a request for comment from Axios. Axios obtained an affidavit in which Trevor Jeffers, the East Pennsboro, Pa., police officer who made the initial arrest, testified that Igbojekwe was sitting in a parked car in a residential neighborhood "wearing nothing but a shirt" with his "genitals ... exposed." "Igbojekwe advised that he was in the neighborhood for work and that he was waiting to hand out flyers for Janelle Stelson's political campaign," Jeffers said in the affidavit, adding that Igbojekwe "was able to provide a stack of flyers showing he was there for work." The East Pennsboro Police did not provide a comment and denied Axios' public records request for documents related to the case. Several news outlets that covered the initial arrest or the DHS press release have since deleted their stories and posts. None responded to Axios' requests for comment. The Stelson campaign, asked about the affidavit, referred Axios to Baker's statement on Wednesday saying Igbojekwe had "never been employed" by them and that they had "never heard of him prior to the news of his arrest." Zoom in: Igbojekwe was charged with indecent exposure and disorderly conduct, later pleading guilty to a single count of disorderly conduct, according to court records. The attorney listed as his representative in court documents, Cumberland County first assistant public defender Arla Waller, did not return multiple phone calls seeking comment. Igbojekwe did not respond to a request for comment sent to an email address listed under his name. The latest: The Office of Special Counsel "will open a file" in response to questions about whether Wall violated the Hatch Act, which prohibits mixing federal government work with political campaigning, according to emails shared with Axios. Donald Sherman, the executive director of ethics watchdog Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, wrote in an email to OSC that Wall's statement was "gratuitous partisanship that constitutes prohibited political activity." An OSC staffer replied to Sherman: "We received your complaint and will open a file to address this matter." An OSC spokesperson confirmed the authenticity of the emails but declined to comment further. Wall did not respond to a request for comment. What they're saying: Deborah Fleischaker, a former acting ICE chief of staff under the Biden administration, told Axios that legal counsel at the agency during her tenure "almost certainly would have recommended not to say something like" what Wall did in his statement. Directly referencing an election in an official statement "really is seen as a no no," she told Axios. Fleischaker acknowledged that federal ethics rules aren't the deterrent they used to be . The bottom line: Cook Political Report rates the race between Stelson and Perry for the Harrisburg-based House seat as a toss-up. The Freedom Caucus Fund, a hybrid PAC dedicated to electing and supporting House Freedom Caucus members, released a digital ad on Thursday calling Igbojekwe a "Nigerian illegal alien campaigning for Democrat Janelle Stelson."

619a6f6697eb.text: By — Steve Peoples, Associated Press Steve Peoples, Associated Press By — Jill Colvin, Associated Press Jill Colvin, Associated Press By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/the-midterms-stakes-are-high-for-these-2028-presidential-prospects Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The midterms stakes are high for these 2028 presidential prospects Politics Oct 9, 2026 1:04 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — As most of the political world focuses on next month's midterm elections, the shadow primary for the 2028 presidential contest is quietly playing out in public view. Democratic and Republican presidential prospects have been crisscrossing the country, raising money and tapping their political connections to help boost their parties' candidates — and their own White House ambitions. He's paid particular attention to the South, where he's campaigned with candidates up and down the ballot in states like Alabama, Mississippi, North Carolina and, not surprisingly, South Carolina, which hosts the party's first presidential primary contest in 2028. The Southern focus aligns with the mission of Newsom's Campaign for Democracy political action committee, which was established in 2023 to help his party compete in red states. But it could also help endear him to African American voters, who make up the heart of the Democratic base. Newsom's star power — and his extensive email list — has strengthened his relationships with key Democratic officials in states like Nevada and New Hampshire, where he's sent out fundraising emails that have generated a surge of donations in recent months. WATCH: Gavin Newsom on how to beat the GOP: 'Democrats need to grow a backbone' Perhaps Newsom's biggest midterm contribution was backing Proposition 50, California's response to the Texas Republican mid-decade gerrymander. The proposition, approved by California voters last year, created a new congressional map that may allow Democrats to pick up as many as five additional U.S. House seats in California this fall. As a presidential candidate, the California governor could argue that he was on the front lines of the redistricting battle. The 42-year-old has embarked on an aggressive midterm campaign schedule — from the Midwest, to the South, to Alaska — and focused on the administration's efforts to root out fraud. READ MORE: Erika Kirk backs JD Vance's potential 2028 presidential bid at Turning Point USA conference A key state will be Ohio, which Vance briefly represented in the Senate. Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vance's seat in 2025, is facing an aggressive challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. And in the governor's race, Democrat Amy Acton is in a close contest with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. The effectiveness of the conservative group Turning Point Action will also be scrutinized. Erika Kirk, the widow of Turning Point co-founder Charlie Kirk and the organization's new leader, has already endorsed Vance's potential presidential bid and leaders have said they intend to use the group to support his campaign. Vance has said he is not focused on running for president, but "trying to help elect Republicans." Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro speaks during an event to mark 100 days until the midterm elections with U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), and Congressional Candidate Bob Brooks (Pennsylvania's District 7) in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, July 26, 2026. He hasn't visited any early primary states or campaigned with any midterm candidates beyond his state. That's by design for a 53-year-old Democrat whose selling point as a presidential candidate might be his clout in Pennsylvania, which has emerged as perhaps the most important swing state in the nation. READ MORE: Pennsylvania's Democratic Gov. Shapiro wins his primary, as do his endorsed candidates Shapiro is expected to cruise to reelection over his Republican challenger, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, which has allowed him to spend his political capital elsewhere. Shapiro has gone all in to ensure Democrats win both chambers of the state legislature in November, and he's devoted significant time and resources to flipping four congressional seats. If Shapiro can demonstrate strength in swing counties like Beaver, Luzerne or Erie, it could help him make a credible claim to winning back some of the working-class voters that Democrats have lost in the Trump era. 5ff625cb38b6.text: By — Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-trump-rallies-with-new-yorks-gop-gubernatorial-candidate-bruce-blakeman Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Trump rallies with New York's GOP gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman Politics Oct 9, 2026 12:50 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — In his campaign to become the next governor of New York, Republican Bruce Blakeman has suggested Democrats might steal the election, played up fears about immigrant criminals and posted AI-generated videos depicting the state as dangerous and unaffordable. President Donald Trump is expected to speak at 7:30 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above And on Friday night, he'll rally with President Donald Trump in Syracuse. It is not exactly a message that seems geared toward winning over moderate voters. WATCH: Republican and Democratic strategists on closing messages and where they expect to win At a political moment where Republicans are hoping to capture centrists wary of an ascendent progressive left, Blakeman has instead embraced the president and his aggressive conservative tactics. The approach has puzzled some in a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans by more than 2-to-1. Please check your inbox to confirm. "If his advertising to get the job is to champion Trump, it's going to create a whole lot of problems," said former Gov. David Paterson, a Democrat. He said Blakeman's alliance with the president "could drive a lot of people who are in the middle over the edge." Blakeman, who serves as the Nassau County executive on Long Island, has framed himself as a bulwark against urban progressives, pushing policies related to transgender athletes and Trump's immigration crackdown. After the election of Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Blakeman pledged to erect a wall of surveillance gear to protect his suburban county. While visiting New York City last month, the president was chummy with Mamdani, one of the country's leading democratic socialists, and even expressed optimism about his work as mayor. "Hopefully you're going to be a great one," said Trump, who grew up in Queens, where Mamdani first entered politics. It's unclear what Trump will get out of his trip to Syracuse with the clock ticking toward midterm elections where his party's control of Congress is on the line. The most closely watched U.S. House race in the state is hours away, where Republican Rep. Mike Lawler is trying to fend off a challenge from Democratic candidate Cait Conley. However, Trump has steered clear of political battlegrounds in his travels so far, focusing on red states and friendly crowds at a moment when Republicans worry that his unpopularity could drag down the party. Blakeman says he doesn't always agree with Trump On the campaign trail, Blakeman argues he's winning over Democrats and independents, painting himself as the moderate candidate in his race against incumbent Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul. He dismisses the idea that his closeness with the president could hurt his chances in blue New York. "I don't think it has an effect," he said when asked about his relationship with Trump. "I've proved my independence over and over and over again. I make my own decisions. I call my own shots." Hochul has emphasized Blakeman's ties to Trump — mirroring much of the Democrats' national strategy for the midterm elections — hoping the president's dismal approval ratings help to sink her Republican foe at the ballot box. In an interview, Blakeman denied that he was aligned with the president on everything. "I am somebody who takes every issue and makes a decision based on good advice from smart people and common sense," he said. For example, Blakeman said of Trump, "he's pro-life. I'm pro-choice." He added: "I believe in a comprehensive guest worker immigration program. He hasn't embraced that yet." Despite a long history of Republican leadership, the party has not fared well in recent statewide elections. No Republican has taken up residence in the governor's mansion since former Gov. George Pataki lived there between 1995 and 2006. All levels of state government are firmly controlled by Democrats, and Democrats hold a wide majority of the state's House seats as well as both Senate seats. Blakeman emerged as the leading Republican candidate The Republican field for the governor's race this year was shaping up much differently before Trump waded in. U.S. Rep. Elise Stefanik, a Trump ally who represents a conservative district in northern New York, was expected to mount a strong candidacy but unexpectedly dropped out in December after Trump waffled on an endorsement. U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler, who represents a swing congressional seat in New York's Hudson Valley, had been teasing a statewide run but abandoned the plan not long after Trump endorsed him for reelection to the House, a move seen as a way to nudge Lawler back toward Congress. With Stefanik and Lawler out of the picture, Trump swiftly backed Blakeman. In the last governor's race, Lee Zeldin, a former Long Island congressman and current Trump administration Environmental Protection Agency head, was able to come within about 6 points of upsetting Hochul by focusing on concerns about crime. Blakeman is recreating elements of Zeldin's campaign on public safety even though crime rates have dropped significantly since then. US Vice President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter.
Talking with reporters, Vance expressed doubt that it would happen as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen".
He added, that "if it's through live stream, I'm not going to be watching it". Vance described the actions by former US Army major Nidal Hasan as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11".
Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.

Dems in majority could have familiar faces in key roles Politics Oct 9, 2026 2:05 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats hope to bring a new agenda to the House next year if they take the majority, but they will most likely do so with many of the same faces that have steered their party's legislative work for a decade or more. Potential committee chairs in the next Congress include Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, who has served as top Democrat on the House Homeland Security panel since 2005. Then, there's Adam Smith of Washington, who began serving as top Democrat on Armed Services in 2011, and Rep. Maxine Waters of California, who became the lead Democrat on Financial Services in 2013. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Other longtime committee leaders include Reps. Frank Pallone at Energy and Commerce and Bobby Scott at Education and Workforce, who assumed their leadership posts in 2015. Rep. Richie Neal became the top Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee in 2017. None would be able to continue in that position under the rules used by House Republicans, which generally limit lawmakers to three terms as chairman or ranking member. For Democrats, the question is whether to stick with their current system, which emphasizes seniority, or move closer to the one that Republicans have established. It's a discussion that some Democrats say they are having behind the scenes. WATCH: Republican and Democratic strategists on closing messages and where they expect to win "I think that the idea of term limits could be appealing to the American people, to the Democratic base. It sounds Democratic," said Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Va. "I'm open to the idea. I've spoken to a number of folks who are open to the idea." "I personally think it makes for a more vibrant Congress, but I know I'm in the minority in the minority," said Rep. Chrissy Houlahan, D-Pa. Party leaders are playing down the issue for now. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said seniority has always been a factor when it comes to committee leadership, but not the only one. "The caucus is going to work its will as we move forward," Jeffries told reporters. "At the end of the day, we can't put the cart before the horse. We've got to still go out and win this thing in November." Democrats have been here before Term limits are not a new discussion for Democrats. When they were weighing whether to return Nancy Pelosi as speaker in 2018, those opposing her bid wanted her to commit to limiting how long lawmakers could serve as House party leaders or committee chairs. She eventually agreed to serve in the post for no more than four more years. No such restrictions were added for committee chairs. In 2022, Democrats voted overwhelmingly against a six-year term limit for committee leaders. Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., who has served as top Democrat on the House Rules Committee since 2018, called term limits an "artificial, random mechanism that doesn't always serve the best interest of the institution." "I want people in chairs who are going to fight to get things over the finish line and make a real difference," McGovern said. "Some of those people may have been around for a long time and some of them may be relatively new." WATCH: Karl Rove and David Axelrod give their midterm predictions Pallone said he intends to be the next Energy and Commerce chairman or ranking member. He called term limits for chairs "very undemocratic." "If people want to vote for somebody they should be allowed to," Pallone said. He also said that term limits can lead to short-term thinking from chairs looking at their next opportunity in the private sector. "People serve for a couple years, then they go work for some lobbying firm," he said. "What they do when they're here is very much influenced by what lobbying firm they're going to work for." Thompson also said he would like to serve again as top Democrat on Homeland Security if he wins reelection. He dismissed the way Republicans limit committee leaders to three terms. "I don't want to be like Republicans. I'm a Democrat," Thompson said. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., says term limits have served Republicans well. "It's been really good to show younger members that you're always going to have a path to leadership if you keep working hard, if you do your job really well," Scalise said. "We definitely lose some good chairmen along the way, but we also get new leaders who otherwise would not have been able to rise up." Democrats have broken with seniority on occasion Democrats don't always stick with seniority. One recent exception is Rep. Jamie Raskin, the lead Democrat on the Judiciary Committee. He challenged Rep. Jerry Nadler for the job in late 2024, prompting Nadler, then 77, to step aside. Similarly, Democrats selected Rep. Angie Craig to become the top Democrat on the Agriculture Committee after she challenged the late Rep. David Scott for the post. Scott had been the panel's top Democrat for the previous two sessions, but was in poor health. Democrats also elected Rep. Robert Garcia last year to succeed Rep. Gerry Connolly on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. Connolly died after a battle with esophageal cancer. Garcia defeated veteran Rep. Stephen Lynch of Massachusetts for the job. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission issued an unusual warning this week to the country’s largest asset managers and a climate-focused investor group over their roles in a 2021 campaign that replaced board directors at ExxonMobil.
The commission published a letter saying it had concluded a probe into the entities, and while it found no evidence of violations, it expressed “serious concerns” about their actions.
Investor advocates and some former SEC staff say the letter clearly aims to suppress shareholder advocacy on climate change and pressure large asset managers like BlackRock, State Street and Vanguard, each of which were named in the letter, to steer clear of the topic entirely.
It is only the latest move by the SEC this year to limit investors’ ability to address climate risks and engage with corporate boards more broadly. The Trump administration and Republican officials across the country have spent years clamping down on efforts to press corporations for climate action.
In 2022, Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives opened an antitrust investigation into some of the same groups, accusing them of acting like a “cartel.” More than a dozen Republican state attorneys general also launched probes. Oil industry campaign contributions have gone overwhelmingly to Republican candidates.
Mika Morse, who was a policy counsel on climate risk to former SEC Chair Gary Gensler, said many investors and asset managers view climate change as a significant risk to their portfolios and feel a fiduciary duty to engage with companies on the topic, but may now hesitate to continue that work.
“Investors are feeling really inhibited because of this fear that they will become the target of investigations,” Morse said. “And this type of harassment is really effective, unfortunately.”
SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock, who began that position in May, was an attorney at Exxon during the investors’ campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. An SEC spokesperson said the investigation began last year and that Woodcock recused himself.
The investigation probed the communications of some of the country’s largest asset managers and pension funds—including BlackRock, State Street, Vanguard, the California Public Employees’ Retirement System and the New York State Common Retirement Fund—with a group called Climate Action 100+, an investor initiative that pushes for climate action by large corporate emitters.
“This type of harassment is really effective, unfortunately.”
— Mika Morse, former SEC policy counsel on climate risk
The report traced what it called a campaign by Climate Action 100+ beginning in 2019 to change Exxon’s board because of the company’s inaction on global warming. The California and New York pension funds were active in the climate group, and BlackRock and State Street joined the initiative in 2020.
By 2021, a small activist investor firm called Engine No. 1 had launched a campaign to replace some of Exxon’s directors. That campaign focused on what the firm said was the company’s poor financial performance—Exxon had been removed from the Dow Jones Industrial Average the previous year as its stock price lagged—rather than inaction on climate change. But the SEC letter said Engine No. 1 had communicated with some Climate Action 100+ members and with Ceres, a sustainable business advocacy group that helps coordinate the climate investor organization.
That year, the campaign succeeded in appointing three new members to Exxon’s board, in large part by convincing large asset managers like BlackRock to vote yes.
It was a huge blow to Exxon and came at a low point for the oil industry. Profits had plummeted during the COVID-19 pandemic. Some analysts were predicting peak oil consumption had passed. Major investors lined up behind the notion that climate risks were systemic, and President Joe Biden had won election the prior year after pledging to shift away from fossil fuels.
In the following years, the oil industry and its allies in public office and think tanks pushed back forcefully, filing lawsuits, investigations and legislation that targeted opponents in the financial sector, academia and elsewhere.
The Trump administration has incorporated this effort as public policy through the Department of Justice, SEC and other agencies, siding with the oil industry in numerous lawsuits, for example.
The SEC investigation examined whether the asset managers and other members of the climate organization coordinated their votes, which could have triggered onerous reporting requirements under SEC rules meant to give public insight into campaigns by activist investors to influence companies.
Firms like BlackRock are exempt from these reporting requirements even though they hold large stakes in many companies because they are considered passive investors. The SEC letter raised the question of whether the firms should have been required to report more extensively in the case of the Exxon campaign.
Experts in securities law say the difference is significant and that a finding of violation could have had serious implications. Ultimately, the commission did not find evidence to support any of these claims but still issued a public report.

Shareholder advocates have criticized the SEC report, arguing that it sought to intimidate investors.

- Published
US immigration officials have defended the actions of officers who shot and wounded a man in his car in New York on Thursday while his five-year-old son was in the back seat.
Markwayne Mullin, the head of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said officers fired their weapons while trying to arrest a man with a criminal history.
"We weren't aware the child was in the car," Mullin added at a news conference on Friday, arguing that it was the man, Oscar Belgal, who had put his child in danger. Belgal is now being held at a detention facility.
The legal organisation representing Belgal told the BBC that lawyers had not yet been able to speak to him.
The shooting happened in the residential neighbourhood of Marble Hill.
Marcos Charles, a top ICE official who was also at Friday's news conference, said agents used their vehicles to try and stop Belgal in his car but that he resisted orders to get out and instead accelerated, smashing into two ICE vehicles.
Charles said Belgal then "weaponised his vehicle and proceeded to accelerate going towards other officers", adding: "Our officers, using their training, and believing that their life and the life of their partners in the general public were in danger, used their training and fired weapons."
The number of officers who fired their weapons is being investigated.
Charles said Belgal "was struck by one of the bullets or fragments superficially in the neck".
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who called what happened "unconscionable and incredibly serious", said ICE agents surrounded Belgal's car before opening fire.
"They wore construction vests and masks that concealed their faces. There is no reasonable way to identify them as ICE agents," Mamdani said. He confirmed that the child was unharmed.
Mullin said the officers identified themselves and were wearing body-worn cameras that were turned on during the incident.
Video of the shooting, including body camera footage, has not been made public but unverified videos on social media appear to align with Mamdani's comments.
Body-worn camera footage released by the New York Police Department (NYPD) on Friday shows its officers arriving on scene and attempting to help Belgal after he has been shot. One ICE officer appears to be wearing a neon construction vest and carrying a large gun.
The NYPD officers then call for an ambulance and putting him in a police car to take him to hospital. They are later seen pulling Belgal from the vehicle and carrying him into the hospital.
Mamdani said on Thursday that he had spoken to US President Donald Trump and Mullin for two hours but failed to negotiate Belgal's release.
Mamdani said he would ask Trump, who has not yet commented publicly on the shooting, to end ICE enforcement actions in New York. Mullin has said he will not pause enforcement.
The DHS said Belgal, 28, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs and weapons possession".
Belgal was arrested by police officers in New York in December 2023 and released "a few days later", according to the DHS.
New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said there was also still a pending case against Belgal for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025.
DHS has also alleged Belgal was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group.
Mullin said the DHS believed Belgal "has either indirect or direct knowledge" of a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer shooting, "and that's why he became a target".
Mamdani is not the only New York official to have criticised the incident. Governor Kathy Hochul said federal officials needed to provide answers quickly about what happened.
"New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity," Hochul said, adding that she had spoken to Mullin and Trump as well.
There have been several high-profile shootings involving ICE officers this year, including one that caused the death of Renee Good in Minneapolis in January.

1b7f5cde801e.text: By — Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-wants-talarico-and-paxton-to-debate-talarico-couldnt-be-happier Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump wants Talarico and Paxton to debate. Talarico couldn't be happier Politics Oct 9, 2026 1:33 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — When Democratic nominee James Talarico stopped holding campaign events in the Texas Senate race, his Republican opponent Ken Paxton saw an opening to pounce. "Where is James Talarico?" he called out Wednesday during a rally with President Donald Trump in San Antonio. WATCH: Trump speaks at rally for Senate candidate Ken Paxton in San Antonio But that night, while flying back to Washington on Air Force One, Trump seemed to inadvertently throw Talarico a lifeline. The president said on social media that Talarico — who has the flu, according to his campaign — "should immediately report to a Debate Stage" to face off with Paxton. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. It was exactly what Talarico wanted to hear, since he had long been badgering Paxton for a debate. "President Trump just said Ken Paxton should debate. I agree," Talarico posted on Thursday morning. "Ball's in your court @KenPaxtonTX." No debate has been scheduled so far. Paxton has not publicly responded to Trump's debate demand. Some Republicans, worried Paxton may become the first Republican in nearly four decades to lose a Senate race in Texas, have also urged him to debate to help gain ground in an unusually competitive campaign in the Republican-leaning state. WATCH: What's making the Texas Senate race so competitive Talarico publicly challenged Paxton in July to three televised debates. Last month, he invited Paxton to debate him on Fox News, and he posted a video of himself calling Paxton with the invitation. "Hey Ken, it's James," Talarico said while leaving a voicemail. "Texans start voting in less than a month and they deserve to hear from both of us before they do." "So, if Fox News is where you'll be most comfortable, I'll be there," he added. So far, the campaign has played out almost entirely on the airwaves. The candidates' campaigns and more than a dozen outside groups have spent more than $247 million on advertising, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. The candidates have yet to appear jointly before voters. Later that month, it suggested an agreement with a news outlet was imminent, though none was announced. 28e9416835fb.text: Data: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios Middle- and lower-earners' inflation-adjusted incomes rose during the Biden years — but high earners saw their incomes fall. That's a surprising finding from one of the most thorough datasets on American household finances , released Friday morning by the Federal Reserve. Why it matters: The data sheds granular new information on a much-contested question: What happened to Americans' real incomes during the post-pandemic period? It featured an exceptionally tight job market and the highest inflation in decades, followed by aggressive Fed rate hikes. The median American family's income rose 7% in inflation-adjusted terms between 2021 and 2024. But that masked significant differences among income brackets. The average real income of families in the top 10% of earners fell 14%, to $652,000 from $757,000 (both figures are 2025 dollars). That implies, contrary to a common narrative about the K-shaped economy, that income inequality fell during the post-pandemic period. Yes, but: The story for wealth is very different. Families that were already wealthy — and tend to own stocks, houses and other assets — became much richer from 2022 to 2025. Among families in the top 10% of income, median net worth rose a whopping 31% from 2022 to 2025, compared with a 2% rise in net worth for the median family. Families in the bottom 40% of income actually saw their net worth decline slightly in that span. The intrigue: The data, from the Survey of Consumer Finances, is collected and released every three years. Friday morning's release is the 2025 survey — but questions about income cover the preceding calendar year. As such, the income numbers compare 2024 with 2021 — conveniently capturing the change from the early part of the Biden administration to near its end. Between the lines: While the compression in income inequality seen in this data may seem surprising, it aligns with other evidence that blue-collar workers saw bigger raises during the super-tight job market and inflationary episode of 2021 and 2022 than did higher-earning white-collar professionals. Moreover, in a footnote, the Fed researchers note that top earners tend to have income from volatile sources, mainly capital gains and business income. Big swings in those income sources among the highest earners can create outsized movement in the averages. Of note: The survey also sheds light on how the Fed's aggressive interest rate hikes in 2022 and 2023, meant to bring inflation under control, hammered borrowers. The median debt payment-to-income ratio rose 2 percentage points from 2022 to 2025, reaching 15.4%. The share of families with debt payment-to-income ratios above 40%, a threshold for high debt obligations, increased to 8.6% from 6.5%, reaching a level last seen in the 2013 survey. The bottom line: Low earners saw bigger percentage gains in their incomes' purchasing power amid the post-pandemic inflation than did high earners — but the rich got a lot richer at the same time.

Conservative commentator Katie Zacharia has been offered the job of White House press secretary, a White House official confirmed to the BBC.
Zacharia, who currently works as a communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group would become the president's sixth chief spokesperson across his two administrations. She previously had a brief stint as a spokesperson at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, who left the White House in August, has reportedly taken a job with Fox News.
The BBC has contacted Zacharia for comment.
The 42-year-old political strategist is a frequent fixture on conservative Newsmax and Fox News, and has been active in Republican politics for most of her adult life, having worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and for the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006.
Since June, she has been a senior communications adviser for Trump's media company and Truth Social platform, according to her LinkedIn profile. She worked in Homeland Security briefly from February to March this year.
While she was only briefly in government at DHS - which she later said she left because of the strain of travel between California and Washington on her family - she has long been a ferocious defender of President Trump and his administration's policies.
In a June interview with the BBC, for example, she dismissed criticism of Trump's controversial use of the White House to host a televised UFC fight, saying the principles of the UFC "are the kind of principles that founded our Constitutional Republic".
"It's about not giving up the fight until the bitter end," she said. "I think there's no better summation of the American ethos than a good UFC fight."
A lawyer educated at Pepperdine University in California, Zacharia also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally - and current Special Presidential Envoy for Special Missions - Ric Grenell.
In 2011, she spent nearly two years clerking at a law firm in Beijing, China.
The complex job of press secretary goes beyond the briefing room podium to include managing contentious relationships with the press, coordinating with other parts of the White House, and providing media advice to the president. The secretary also oversees an office that receives a significant amount of inquiries and requests on a daily basis.
Trump called Leavitt one of his "most trusted aides" when she left the role, saying she wanted to spend more time with her family, which set a high bar for her replacement.
A lawyer educated at Pepperdine University in California, Zacharia, 42, has four children. She has also worked as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative advocacy group headed by Trump ally Ric Grenell.

There was still "lots of room for improvement" when it comes to how much we recycle at work compared with our habits at home, according to an expert.
Figures suggest only 61% of people in Wales recycle often at their workplace, with one in five saying they do not recall seeing the appropriate facilities to do so.
Providing more bins or clearer labelling are some of the ways in which businesses could make a difference, said waste reduction charity Wrap.
But one business had already seen a "significant improvement" at their offices after removing staff's personal bins, a move that was initially met with resistance.
When recruitment firm Acorn by Synergie first moved into their offices on the outskirts of Newport in 2003, they were producing six large wheelie bins' worth of rubbish a week.
It now has just one weekly collection thanks to increased recycling, including food waste, which was their biggest adaptation, following the introduction of the Welsh government's Workplace Recycling Law in 2024.
"The main thing that we changed was removing desk bins and individual bins," said director Mark Rudge.
"We had quite a bit of resistance to that. Individuals liked having their own little waster station.
"But we put central recycling areas within each zone of the business, and eventually, people get the hang of that.
"A lot of home recycling is extremely similar, so people brought those good habits to the workplace."
Office worker Ann-Marie Derrick admitted fellow staff members had found it a pain to begin with, but it had now become "second nature".
"Anybody new coming to the office is just straight away onboard and I think we're probably quite proud as a team about how much recycling we do."
The company's environmental manager Anthony Lee said it had taken a few months for staff to fully mirror their home recycling habits at the workplace, and that there had been a "significant improvement in compliance".
Not all workers and business have adapted to the same degree.
WRAP's annual tracker survey indicated that although 94% of people in Wales say they recycle at home, only 61% do so "very often at work" with that figure dropping to below half for students at college or university.
Only 30% of respondents said they had seen lots of recycling facilities at their workplace, despite the new requirements, while 20% said they could not recall seeing any.
"It's still a relatively new thing to have recycling bins when we're away from home," said Angela Spiteri, senior marketing manager at WRAP.
"It's a very positive step in the right direction for Wales, but it's not perfect and there's a lot of things we can do to improve."
She said there was a responsibility on businesses to ensure that was possible, "providing the right bins and facilities for people to make that easier".
"I don't recycle as much when I am out and about, I just bin it," admits Gerwyn Pugh, 56, from Barry.
"It's routine [at home], but out and about every bin takes a bit more time to work out."
James Jenkins, 30, said he often took rubbish home with him given the limited options where he works.
"We only recycle cardboard because that's our only waste.
"The more industrialised businesses need to do more, because they'll have more of an impact than smaller businesses."
Natalie James, 47, said she recycled "probably about the same" at work and at home.
"Because I work at a hospital we've got the recycling categories everywhere, so we have to."
Although businesses in Wales are now required to sort their waste into six categories, collection arrangements can vary from area to area.
In the Vale of Glamorgan, businesses use a mix of council and private services, and the local authority said the change has resulted in a "higher quality of recycling".
Carys Stephens, the council's waste project officer, said there had been a "fantastic response from businesses."
"There's obviously going to be some that are critical of the idea, and they're worried about extra costs and effort that goes into segregated recycling.
"But we've been doing segregated recycling for a couple of years now, and most people just take it in their stride."
Although Wales' workplace recycling rates are "reasonably high", said consultant Rebecca Colley-Jones, "there's lots of room for improvement".
"It is a new system, so there's always a period of settling down."
She said that she was sure "we would see that 61% rise".
"Often they can be tourism or hospitality businesses, so they're having to educate their customers what to do."
Colley-Jones said individuals also needed to personally take more care.
"Our home is our castle, we're responsible for the waste and people are under a little bit of pressure, perhaps from their neighbours to look like they're recycling.
"Whereas you don't have that in the workplace.
"When people come to work, they come to work, they don't necessarily thing recycling is part of their job description.
She added: "It's trying to get people to understand that they also need to be buying into the culture of an organisation, and also the culture of Wales as a country. We are the second-best recycler in the world."
She added that the changes had inevitably led to some costs for businesses, and varying collection arrangements can sometimes be "confusing".
Natural Resources Wales, which monitors compliance on behalf of the Welsh government, said so far no workplace had been prosecuted for failing to follow the new regulations.
A spokesperson added that 56% of businesses were found to be compliant in the first two years of the new rules, but it had provided "advice and support" and the majority of non-compliant companies "had taken steps" to address their issues.

f898417baade.text: By — Ali Rogin Ali Rogin Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-relaxes-rules-around-political-events-for-blanche-other-senate-approved-appointees Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration relaxes rules around political events for Blanche, other Senate-approved DOJ appointees Politics Updated on Oct 9, 2026 2:59 PM EDT — Published on Oct 9, 2026 2:53 PM EDT The Department of Justice is making it easier for Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Senate-confirmed DOJ appointees to participate in political activities, according to a new internal memo obtained by PBS News. The memo, penned by the agency's top ethics official, includes new language noting that Senate-approved presidential appointees are exempt from strict restrictions that govern the political conduct of most senior officials. It specifically allows those employees, including the attorney general, to address political gatherings and endorse or oppose candidates – a swerve away from long-standing precedent within the DOJ that experts say may further erode trust in the U.S. justice system. WATCH: How Blanche is shattering DOJ's standard of political independence The document is the latest version of a memo the department's ethics office circulates from time to time, reminding employees of the restrictions on their political activities under a law known as the Hatch Act. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The existence of exceptions for presidential Senate-confirmed appointees themselves is not new, and is codified in the language of the Hatch Act, which governs the political activity of all federal employees. But presidential appointees at the Department of Justice have a history of holding themselves to a more restrictive code of conduct, noted Joseph Tirrell, who led the DOJ's Departmental Ethics Office before his dismissal last year. "This policy, and its recent update, have lowered the bar so that DOJ employees are now only held to the standard set by [the Hatch Act], as opposed to the higher and more restrictive standard set by attorneys general for the last 20-plus years that help ensure, to the greatest extent possible, that DOJ was above politicking," Tirrell wrote in an email to PBS News. "DOJ's lowering of its standards regarding political activism by senior officials means that Americans can no longer trust that Department decisions and actions are made fairly and without regard to political affiliation." The updated guidance comes as Blanche has made a number of appearances at political rallies and official events where political candidates spoke. Recent events have included an election rally for a Senate candidate in North Carolina, where Blanche introduced President Donald Trump, the Republican Party's midterm election convention, as well as a roundtable on violent crime in South Carolina, where Blanche sat next to Sen. Darline Graham, who is on the ballot in November. READ MORE: Attorney General Blanche blurs Justice Department boundaries by appearing at political events Tirrell said he believes these appearances still violate a separate Hatch Act prohibition on the use of official authority to influence the outcome of elections. Previous iterations of the same DOJ document said some individuals serving in "further restricted" positions, like those in the Senior Executive Service (SES), were barred from an even wider array of election activities – including addressing a political rally or endorsing a political candidate – than most other career executive branch employees. The latest revision lists most of the same "further restricted" roles, but adds a new line specifically exempting "employees appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate (PAS)." And in a section listing the prohibited activities for "further restricted employees," the memo explicitly states that it does not apply to "PAS." That acronym for presidential appointees is common in other contexts, but recent previous versions of the same DOJ ethics guidance make no such distinctions between those appointees and other "further restricted" employees. In a statement to PBS, a Department of Justice spokesperson said that the updated version of the memo clarifies, rather than changes, Hatch Act rules. "The updated guidance clarifies an existing exception under the Hatch Act for Presidentially-appointed, Senate-confirmed officials, and clarifies that appearances with partisan candidates should be reviewed by ethics officials to ensure proper designations," the spokesperson said. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche waves as he arrives on stage at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026. Photo by Brian Snyder/ Reuters The new language clarifying rules for employees' official appearances with partisan candidates no longer recommends employees avoid appearing alongside political candidates at official events taking place shortly before a political election. The previous guidance, released when Blanche's predecessor Pam Bondi was serving in the top role, said: "Previous Attorneys General have made an effort, and also encouraged Presidentially appointed officials, or those acting in such positions, to avoid making public appearances in any state shortly before a primary or general election in that state, to the greatest extent practicable. The Attorney General has determined that this precedent should be followed." The new October memo says such appearances "warrant heightened scrutiny — especially when close to an election" and that the Office of Special Counsel has identified several factors to consider when determining whether an event is "official vs. political for purposes of the Hatch Act." A no-holds-barred televised debate between Michigan Senate rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers has highlighted how ugly personal attacks are ramping up in the US midterms elections race.
In Thursday evening's duel, Rogers questioned whether someone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist". El-Sayed, a Democrat, called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration".
Moderator Rick Albin said the barbs continued off camera, spilling into the commercial break - something Albin said he has never seen in 30 years of doing debates.
On the morning after the debate, US President Donald Trump posted on social media attacking the Democrat and bringing up his Muslim identity.
The Michigan race could affect which party controls the Senate after November's midterm elections as Democrats campaign to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from the Republicans.
Little was considered off limits in the verbal jousting between Rogers and El-Sayed, which saw the Republican repeatedly suggest the Democrat and his family had ties to terrorist organisations.
El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, denied this.
A fact-check from a state news outlet, Bridge Michigan, has said there is no evidence, external that El-Sayed is personally connected to the Muslim Brotherhood, branches of which have been designated as terrorist organisations by the US.
The Democrat questioned whether Rogers was even from Michigan and labelled his opponent a "Florida man", with yachts and a mansion in the Sunshine State. Rogers denied the Florida ties and boat ownership.
"Weak, cowardly, won't stand up until his poll numbers drop," El-Sayed said during one heated exchange.
The economy, immigration and support for Israel were topics that came up as expected during the debate.
But tensions flared as Rogers appeared to attack El-Sayed's family.
The rivals were discussing Flock cameras, the controversial AI-powered surveillance system, which El-Sayed said should be federally regulated.
"And why would that bother you?" Rogers shot back. "Well, if you have someone in your family that might be on the watchlist."
El-Sayed challenged Rogers to "go ahead and say it", adding: "Are you going after my mom?"
The Democrat's mother, Fatten Elkomy, previously worked as a nurse practitioner for the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA), according to the Midwesterner, external, a conservative regional news outlet.
The US treasury department designated IARA, external in 2004 for supporting terrorism.
The US justice department charged figures within IARA, external in 2007 with illegal wire transfers to Iraq, but El-Sayed's mother was not among those indicted and she left the agency in 2004.
The BBC has contacted El-Sayed's campaign and Elkomy for comment.
One academic told the BBC that Thursday's debate underscores how anti-Muslim sentiment is becoming increasingly normalised at the highest level of US politics.
Quardricos Driskell, a George Washington University political science professor, pointed to the period after the 9/11 attacks as a time when there was similar rhetoric, but he noted the distinction in presidential leadership.
In the wake of the attacks, then-President George W Bush stood in front of a mosque and defended the Muslim faith, saying: "Islam is peace."
Driskell said: "Islamophobia has long existed, I think across American political society from both parties.
"What distinguishes the current moment is that the explicit use of Muslim identity as a political attack is by prominent Republican leaders."
On Friday morning, President Trump issued the latest in a series of attacks on the Democrat.
"Mohammad is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country," Trump wrote on social media.
Some questioned why Trump chose to refer to El-Sayed as Mohammad - his full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed ElâSayed, but he has been known as Abdul since kindergarten, according to the Detroit News, external.
Trump's comment follows several other similar anti-Muslim remarks from elected officials, including Tennessee Republican congressman Andy Ogles posting on X earlier this year: "Muslim's don't belong in American society."
After Zohran Mamdani was elected as the first ever Muslim mayor of New York City, he faced similar attacks.
"After 9/11 we said 'Never Forget.' I think we sadly have forgotten," Republican congresswoman Nancy Mace wrote on X, after Mamdani's election.
Gregg Nunziata, a Republican policy adviser, told the BBC these types of comments were "extremely destructive and deeply alarming".
He also noted the absence of condemnation for these remarks, saying it's "the responsibility of leaders to tamp down that type of rhetoric and police their own side and that's not happening today".
There has been a rise in anti-Muslim sentiment across the US, according to the Pew Research Center.
In 2002, 25% of adults said Islam "is more likely" to encourage violence than other religions. That number jumped to 51% in 2026.
It comes amid a rise in hatred more broadly in the US, including antisemitism.
Haris Tarin, vice-president of the Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC), said Trump's comments like his social media post on Friday morning make him feel "sick".
He said his organisation had tracked an eight-fold increase in anti-Muslim speech over the last year.
"This rise has coincided with elections, and it has allowed for candidates who oppose American Muslims licence to openly attack their faith," Tarin said.
Driskell said such attacks often exploit voters' fears.
"We have to keep in mind the motivating factor often in politics, and particularly during campaigning, which is fear," he said.
"That's what ultimately Islamophobia is - the fear," he continued, "instilling fear that people get out and vote".

A massive magnitude 7.7 earthquake has hit Panama, damaging buildings and prompting a wide-ranging tsunami warning for neighbouring countries.
About 4.6 million people felt moderate to severe shaking as a result of the quake, according to the US Geological Survey, which has said that the effects of the disaster were "likely to be widespread".
The quake, which hit just before 15:00 local time (18:00 GMT), could trigger tsunamis in Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile and Mexico, according to the US Tsunami Warning System.
The epicentre of the earthquake was about 6.2 miles (10km) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in south-central Panama, with a series of shallow aftershocks following it.
Footage shared online, which has not been verified by the BBC, appears to show collapsed buildings in the towns of PenonomÃ© and SonÃ¡.
The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface.
However, the full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, nor whether there have been any casualties as a result.
Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km (124 miles) away, according to new agency AFP.
The earthquake comes just three days before Panama was scheduled to hold a national evacuation drill for dealing with a major earthquake.
It also follows devastating earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela earlier this year.

Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers, Jake and Callum Robinson, and their American friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.
During the trial, the court heard the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area. Their bodies were later found with gunshot wounds to their heads, dumped down a well.
The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence in other parts of Mexico.
The verdict was handed down on Friday in the Mexican state of Baja California.
The parents of the two Australian brothers, Martin and Debra Robinson, have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial and they delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments heard earlier on Thursday.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," said their father, Martin.
Family members of Rhoad joined the trial by video link.
Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".
During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.
In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, JesÃºs "El Kekas" Gerardo, was sentenced in a separate trial to twenty years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.
At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.
The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers and the chilling murders revealed much about how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.
The only explanation the authorities appeared able to give was that the surfers â all in their early thirties â had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Their killings took place barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them.
At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to commemorate the men by paddling out at one of the area's best known surfing spots and throwing flowers into the sea.
Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.
Amid the demands for action, the governor of Baja California, Marina del Pilar Ãvila, tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence in her state.
"Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said.
"I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

(AP) — Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, "I'm not going to be watching it." Watch the clip in the video player above. The Republican vice president said, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the shocking plans for a public execution and said Hasan's crimes should not be forgotten. READ MORE: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at the military base in 2009. "So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it," he added. Vance is a convert to the Catholic Church, which has long opposed capital punishment. Watch Vance's full remarks in the video below. Earlier Friday morning, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the U.S. government's decision to livestream Hasan's execution. "It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War's decision to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hassan. Our God is the God of life. In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," said Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the Conference, in a statement. Earlier, President Donald Trump told a White House event that Hasan will be getting "the death penalty through firing squad. And he deserves it." Trump, who approved Hasan's execution, called him "a maniac." The president approved the method of execution by firing squad days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection late last month pushed Tennessee's governor to halt further executions in that state this year. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military hasn't executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging. Trump, who has long been a vocal supporter of capital punishment, didn't mention the plans that the Pentagon has announced to livestream the execution so that the broader public can see it. Associated Press writers Will Weissert in Washington and Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
