b1c4f142c2db.text: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is going to have his hands full next Congress, even without a threat to his leadership or a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Why it matters: Schumer (D-N.Y.) will have to grapple with the presidential ambitions of up to eight of his senators who may care more about winning the White House than following their leader. Roughly one in six Democratic senators eyeing the campaign trail would add a degree of difficulty to a job that rarely lacks challenges, as former President Obama acknowledged this week. "Being the head of the Democratic Party is a pain in the butt, because you've got people from every walk of life," Obama said of Schumer at a fundraiser Wednesday. Flashback: This year's ICE funding fights gave Schumer a taste of how presidential ambitions can complicate governing. Potential 2028 contenders competed to take the toughest stance against ICE funding, even at the risk of a government shutdown. Zoom in: The tension between individual ambition and party unity could surface early in Schumer's tenure if he becomes majority leader. Democrats are promising to lower costs and govern responsibly, while insisting they'll challenge and investigate the Trump administration at every turn. Schumer and President Trump have a long, complicated relationship — and each other's cell numbers. Between the lines: Democrats could control majorities in both chambers, giving them immense power against Trump. But majority power is dependent on members being present and unified. Presidential contenders have incentives to spend time outside Washington and show how they differ from their fellow 2028 hopefuls in the Senate. They also may want to pick high-profile fights with the party establishment to prove their progressive bona fides. But Schumer faced a similar challenge during the 2020 presidential cycle, when he was minority leader and seven sitting senators sought the Democratic nomination. Attendance was the biggest headache as candidates crisscrossed the country, complicating Senate scheduling. But Democrats didn't lose any major votes despite their presidential hopefuls being on the campaign trail. Who we're watching: Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) has visited South Carolina, New Hampshire and Nevada (twice). Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.): South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Iowa. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.): South Carolina (twice), Nevada and Michigan. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.): South Carolina. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.): Iowa and Nevada. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.): Iowa and New Hampshire (twice). Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.): Nevada (twice) and New Hampshire. Honorable mention: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is focused on winning reelection, so he has no documented early-primary-state visits yet. That hasn't stopped presidential rumors from swirling. Zoom out: First, Schumer needs to get to at least 51 seats in November, navigate a high-stakes lame-duck session, and then win a secret-ballot election to reclaim his title as majority leader. Some of his potential new members — especially if Democrats have a good night on Nov. 3 — aren't overly enthusiastic about supporting him. Candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas have not committed to voting for him. The bottom line: Presidential candidates want to stand out. Senate majority leaders need their members to blend in — and fall in line.

fce783ce77c1.text: By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-establishes-committee-to-investigate-federal-reserves-lisa-cook-in-latest-effort-to-fire-her Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her Politics Oct 9, 2026 4:33 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a "committee of inquiry" to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications. The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook "shall" attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn't be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said. READ MORE: Trump administration proceeds with efforts to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook Trump's extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve's independence. The president has repeatedly called for the central bank to cut its key interest rate, but just last month, the Fed raised it instead, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump's attempts to fire Cook from the Fed's seven-member board of governors represent the first time in the central bank's 113-year history that a president has sought to remove a Fed governor. Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden and is the first Black woman on the Fed's board. Trump's attacks on her followed other efforts to oust or indict Black officials, such as New York Attorney General Letitia James and Gen. Charles Q. Brown, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. "As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law," Trump wrote in the memorandum. Cook's attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norman Eisen, said they were considering having Cook appear at the Nov. 5 hearing and respond to the charges. READ MORE: No criminal wrongdoing in Federal Reserve building renovation, watchdog says, but it was mismanaged "We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise," Lowell and Eisen said in a statement. "Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her." The "committee of inquiry" will be composed of Kevin Hassett, the president's top economic adviser, who has frequently echoed Trump's criticisms of the Fed; Keith Sonderling, the acting director of the Office of Government Ethics, whom the president has also appointed to lead the Labor Department, and Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, whom Trump appointed in November 2025. Trump initially tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after alleging she had committed mortgage fraud by declaring two different properties to be her "primary" residence in mortgage applications in 2021. Mortgages on primary homes can often receive a lower interest rate or other beneficial terms. Cook has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime. Lowell and Eisen have previously said Cook committed an "inadvertent error" and did refer to one of the properties as a vacation home in other documents. "An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing," Lowell and Eisen said in August. The Federal Reserve declined to comment on Trump's announcement. Trump and some of his economic advisers have blamed the Fed's broader rate-setting committee, which includes 12 voting members and 19 officials in total, for forcing last month's rate hike, even though it followed comments by Warsh in August that signaled higher rates were likely. As a member of the board of governors, Cook is also one of the 12 voting members of the committee. The vote to lift rates Sept. 16 was unanimous. The move also follows a Supreme Court ruling in June that Cook could keep her job after Trump sought to fire her last year. That ruling included a footnote that said nothing prevented Trump from "trying again" as long as she was given proper notice and an opportunity to respond to the charges. Trump said the committee of inquiry will seek to establish whether there is "cause" to fire Cook, as required under the law governing the Fed. The Supreme Court said in June that a for-cause firing required an alleged offense that was serious and related to an official's job. Scott Alvarez, formerly the chief counsel for the Fed, said that President William Howard Taft set up a similar commission in 1912 to remove two officials from an independent agency. The commission created by Trump goes beyond the type of process the Supreme Court said was needed to fire Cook. "It's an attempt to show that he's really giving Cook as much process as possible," Alvarez said. Still, the allegations against Cook don't appear to meet the "for cause" standard set out by the Supreme Court, Alvarez said. Other analysts said that Trump will likely use the process to ultimately fire Cook. "We do not see why the White House would start this process if it were not trying to create a way to justify removing Cook from her job," Jaret Seiberg, managing director of TD Cowen's Washington Research Group, said in a note to clients. Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.
The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.
As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public â stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation â has soured.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
It is these states â places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio â that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.
For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.
He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms â an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.
His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return â besides much-needed hard currency â is unclear.
It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.
It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.
The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.
Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes â attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.
With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.
But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.
Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

Oil companies will no longer be required to conduct environmental reviews before exploring for fossil fuel reservoirs in the Western Arctic, the largest tract of federally managed public land in the United States.
The Bureau of Land Management announced a categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act for winter oil and gas exploration in the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska, also known as the Western Arctic. Published Friday in the Federal Register, the exemption comes as the Trump administration moves to accelerate oil and gas drilling in Alaska.
The categorical exclusion will allow developers to “more nimbly locate energy resources in the Petroleum Reserve,” increasing domestic energy supply and lowering costs for the public, said Kevin Pendergast, Alaska State Director for the Bureau of Land Management. The agency said its decision reflects a “long history” of exploration in the region without “significant or lasting environmental impact.”
During Arctic exploration, oil and gas firms construct temporary roads, drill test wells and conduct seismic surveys, in which “thumper trucks” weighing up to 45 tons send shock waves through the ground to detect oil deposits. The activities are mostly limited to winter, when heavy machinery can travel over frozen ground without sinking into the delicate tundra and permafrost below.
Even then, exploration activities pose a significant risk to residents and an already threatened ecosystem.
The Western Arctic is the traditional land of the Iñupiat people and serves as a critical wildlife habitat for hundreds of thousands of caribou across three major herds. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s 2024 Arctic Report Card, caribou populations in the region have fallen by more than half since their historic highs in the 1990s.
Industrial development in the Arctic directly interferes with seasonal migration routes and the areas where herds return year after year to calve. United States Geological Survey research has documented changes in Arctic caribou behavior even at low vehicle traffic volumes.
The petroleum reserve is also home to millions of migratory birds, as well as polar bears and seals threatened by habitat loss due to rapidly melting sea ice.
The Arctic is warming at two to four times the global average rate. As snow and ice melt in the polar region, they expose a darker surface that absorbs more sunlight and drives further warming in a feedback loop scientists have dubbed “ice-albedo” feedback. Critics of the exemption say that signing off on oil exploration without any environmental review process further harms a fragile ecosystem.
“It is no secret that the Trump administration will ignore impacts to public lands and our nation’s laws if it benefits resource extraction corporations, but recent efforts to remove any and all public review of Arctic oil extraction are particularly egregious,” said Andy Moderow, senior director of policy for the Alaska Wilderness League in a statement by the organization. “This drill first and discover the impacts later approach puts Arctic lands, waters, and wildlife at risk.”
Opponents also question the legality of the categorical exclusion.
“The administration finalized this new approach with zero public input,” said Janet Bering, an Alaska-based attorney with the environmental law organization Earthjustice. “Combined with a similar proposal that rubber stamps new oil production, this is a one-two punch. It’s bad policy, and it is unlawful.”
Last month, the Bureau of Land Management proposed a rule to expedite all oil and gas drilling across the Western Arctic by cutting environmental review and public input for projects beyond the exploration phase.
The rule stemmed from a petition by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing oil and gas firms exploring and producing offshore and in Alaska’s northernmost reaches, including the National Petroleum Reserve. The association did not respond immediately to requests for comment on Friday’s decision.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
The Trump administration’s push to accelerate oil extraction in the Arctic has drawn mixed responses from Alaska Natives. Some Iñupiat communities in the region say they stand to benefit economically from drilling and corporate investments. Others see the development as a blow to already imperiled lands critical for subsistence hunting and, with it, their traditions and culture.
Rosemary Ahtuangaruak, a former mayor of the majority-Iñupiat community of Nuiqsut and founder of the organization Grandmothers Growing Goodness, said caribou have been pushed farther away from Nuiqsut as ConocoPhillips expands drilling operations in the area.
The community is located just four miles outside the petroleum reserve. For years, Nuiqsut residents have fought for stronger environmental mitigation measures in pending drilling permits. Ahtuangaruak has advocated for practices that would reduce air pollution from gas flares and protect caribou migration to their seasonal calving grounds.
By eliminating the environmental review process, Nuiqsut residents will have even fewer opportunities to weigh in through public comment, she said.
“We should not let the greed of profiteering lead our tables of decision-making over the cost of people and the life, health and safety of the generations to come,” Ahtuangaruak said.
First designated as a petroleum reserve for the U.S. Navy in 1923, the Department of the Interior assumed authority for oil and gas leasing in the region in 1976. Yet the 36,000-square-mile tract of wild Arctic tundra, wetlands and coastline was largely preserved as wilderness until the turn of the 21st century.

A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations." Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy." The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement. Trump and Putin's deal draws immediate backlash Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels." The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt. It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. A crude oil pipeline spill last month in the Detroit suburbs has prompted federal authorities to open an investigation into the safety of all 20,000 miles of hazardous liquids pipelines operated by Energy Transfer.
The 600-gallon spill at a commercial intersection in Sterling Heights, Michigan, has received little media coverage. Local news reports at the time, based on a statement from the city, described a much smaller spill and stressed that no residents or homes were in danger. Neither the city nor news reports mentioned the name of the Dallas-based pipeline operator, one of the nation’s largest and most politically connected oil and gas companies.
But in a corrective-action order issued Sept. 21 without a press release, the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration revealed the failure on Energy Transfer’s 59-year-old, 130-mile crude oil pipeline between Marysville, Michigan, and Toledo, Ohio. The federal agency, part of the U.S. Department of Transportation, initially directed the company to shut down a 16-mile segment at the site of the spill. An agency spokesperson said the pipeline was restarted the following day at reduced pressure, slowing the flow of oil.
In an extraordinary move, due to “a system-wide risk of additional similar failures,” PHMSA gave Energy Transfer 90 days to submit a detailed inventory of past repairs made throughout its hazardous liquid pipeline network nationwide, as well as a plan to remediate vulnerabilities.
It was the only one of 23 corrective-action orders PHMSA has issued this year that seek to address safety issues on a company’s entire pipeline network. According to Energy Transfer’s website, that network includes about 20,000 miles of crude oil, refined product and natural gas liquids pipelines.
PHMSA said Energy Transfer’s initial investigation confirmed the spill occurred at the site of a past repair—a steel encasement sleeve that had been welded onto the Michigan pipeline in 2010 to fix a defect. The same kind of encasement sleeve failure caused a jet fuel leak discovered last year on another Energy Transfer pipeline that contaminated the drinking water source of a residential neighborhood north of Philadelphia, the PHMSA order said.
“Considering the characteristics of Energy Transfer’s larger pipeline network, the failures underneath at least two repair sleeves, each with indications of improper installation, point to a likelihood of future failures,” said the order, signed by the agency’s top official, Administrator Paul Roberti.
Last year, after Energy Transfer made a large political donation to a PAC supporting President Donald Trump, PHMSA backed off a proposal that would have forced the company to scrutinize all past repairs on its Twin Oaks pipeline in Pennsylvania and remediate any vulnerabilities. Now, the agency essentially is ordering Energy Transfer to develop such a remedial action plan for all of its hazardous liquids pipelines, including both the Twin Oaks and the Marysville-to-Toledo lines.
The agency issued the order three days after the Michigan spill was discovered, saying it was acting without giving Energy Transfer notice or an opportunity for a prior hearing because of the risk of “serious harm.” The company has since requested a hearing, which has not been scheduled yet, according to a PHMSA spokesperson.
Energy Transfer in an email declined to answer questions about the incident. “Please refer to PHMSA documents, which have all the available information,” said an unsigned email from the company’s media relations team.
A factor that figured into PHMSA’s decision on the nationwide order: Energy Transfer could not locate the original records for the steel repair sleeve at Sterling Heights, nor could it find records that would enable the agency to verify the integrity of 11 other such sleeves along the length of the Marysville-to-Toledo pipeline, the agency said.
In the Michigan order, PHMSA revealed for the first time that Energy Transfer also was not able to find records for four of the 45 repair sleeves along the length of its Twin Oaks pipeline that failed last year in Pennsylvania.
PHMSA had ordered Energy Transfer to submit records on the Twin Oaks repair sleeves to the agency last year, but the submission was not made public despite at least 11 Freedom of Information Act requests, including from Inside Climate News. PHMSA said it could not make the Twin Oaks documents public due to an ongoing enforcement investigation.
An agency spokesperson declined to answer further questions on the Michigan incident, saying by email that the investigation remains ongoing.
Energy Transfer inherited both the Michigan and Pennsylvania pipelines in 2012 when the company purchased Philadelphia-based Sunoco for $5.3 billion. The acquisition transformed Energy Transfer from mainly a natural gas pipeline firm into a diversified giant with crude oil and refined product pipelines in 10 states. Both spill sites, like much of the Sunoco network, are located in PHMSA-designated “high consequence areas,” locations where a pipeline rupture could have significant adverse impact on human health, safety, property or the environment.
Pipeline Politics
Energy Transfer has become a major player on the political scene, due largely to its founder and executive chairman Kelcy Warren’s support for President Donald Trump.
Last year, one week after PHMSA sent the company notice of a proposed safety order over the Pennsylvania spill, Warren and Energy Transfer donated a total $25 million to MAGA Inc., the political action committee established after Trump’s election. The president directly controls its $400 million war chest. It was the largest political donation Warren had ever given, and it made Energy Transfer the biggest oil and gas industry donor so far in the 2026 election cycle, according to data compiled by the nonprofit OpenSecrets for Inside Climate News. 5bb985bbde8e.text: By — Ed White, Associated Press Ed White, Associated Press By — Claudia Lauer, Associated Press Claudia Lauer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/legal-path-seems-narrow-to-challenge-livestream-of-fort-hood-shooters-execution-experts-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Legal path seems narrow to challenge livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution, experts say World Oct 9, 2026 5:55 PM EDT Any effort to challenge the Trump administration's plan to livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan might rest solely with the man sentenced to death for killing 13 people at the Texas military base in 2009, experts say. Broadcasting the event worldwide isn't mentioned in the Army rules governing how rare military executions are carried out. But that doesn't mean there is a viable legal path to oppose it by anyone besides Hasan. And he hasn't signaled whether he will even try to stop anything related to his Dec. 3 death sentence. WATCH: Vance says he's 'not going to be watching' livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution Officials at the Pentagon said Thursday that Hasan's execution by a firing squad would be livestreamed and that more details would follow. A day earlier, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said, "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public." "Other than Hasan, I'm not sure anyone could" have legal standing to stop a livestream, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova University's law school and an expert in military justice. Could U.S. parents try to halt livestream? Fissell, however, tossed up a novel possibility: parents who don't want their children to see a person blasted with bullets on the internet, either in real time or viewed later. Army regulations say, "No person under the age of 18 shall witness" a military execution. "That's explicit," Fissell said. "It's a question of whether a livestream counts as a presence. ... I think it violates the spirit of the regulation." READ MORE: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed The regulations, he added, weren't written to contemplate witnesses outside the actual site of an execution — and certainly not a livestream. "This actually has not been explored enough," Fissell said. Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law, said he doesn't see a lot of legal options to challenge most of the unfolding details of Hasan's execution, though he agrees that Hasan would have standing to object with a petition, known as habeas corpus, in U.S. District Court. "Arguing the Army can't livestream it because some parent wouldn't be able to stop their kid from watching it on the computer strikes me as a very unlikely piece of litigation," Fidell said. "Better legal minds than me maybe can come up with a way to make that argument, but I don't see it." Last firing squad was in WWII Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers at Fort Hood were waiting to receive medical clearance for deployment. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire and also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot. Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He is paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair. Clergy, including U.S. Catholic bishops, and some officials criticized the livestreaming announcement. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, told reporters that he wouldn't watch it and expressed some doubt whether a livestream would happen. President Donald Trump signed off on Hasan's execution, which would be the first by a firing squad since World War II. The last military execution happened on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was killed by hanging. A 2023 update to the Army regulation on executions gave the Secretary of the Army discretion on choosing a method, in part to ease hurdles to conducting executions at Guantanamo Bay, Fidell said. A firing squad is "clearly a legal method of execution in the military," Fissell said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. MARTINEZ, Calif.—Scores of people tired of living near accident-prone refineries packed an elementary school auditorium to hear what their government officials were doing to protect them.
Two local refineries, Marathon Martinez Renewables and Martinez Refining Co., have racked up hundreds of air quality violations over the past five years. MRC agreed in February to pay $10 million in fines for 163 violations that included an accident that blanketed residents’ homes with 24 tons of metal-laden dust four years ago on Thanksgiving Day.
The settlement did not cover a similar episode in 2025, when a fireball sent thick clouds of smoke across town, leaving residents wondering, again, if it was safe to go outside or eat from their gardens.
Marathon’s Martinez Renewables, which recently locked out more than 100 workers in a labor dispute, has received more than 100 violations from the air district for flaring and other infractions since 2021.
Such incidents inspired U.S. Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, a Democrat, to meet with his constituents in this small city an hour northeast of San Francisco on Thursday night. DeSaulnier, a former air regulator whose district includes four refineries, stressed the need to balance the economic benefits refineries bring to the region with the risks they pose to workers and communities.
Refineries are among the county’s top property-tax contributors and provide thousands of good-paying jobs, DeSaulnier said. The region needs these refineries as it transitions toward renewable energy, but they need to be safe, he said. “It’s a constant battle.”
Flaring incidents have increased in recent years, spiking to nearly 70 in 2023. Flaring involves the controlled burning of flammable gases to manage a buildup of pressure in equipment and reduce the risk of explosions. It also releases a mixture of toxic chemicals, fine particles and climate pollutants.
Recognizing residents’ concerns about ongoing flaring, county officials at the meeting announced the release of a new public dashboard that allows people to track incidents, something residents like Heidi Taylor have been asking for.
Taylor, who co-founded Healthy Martinez after MRC showered her home with heavy metals, wants the refinery to undergo a new health risk assessment, which hasn’t been done in 36 years, she said.
“We need to know what health risks Martinez residents are facing, when that information will be made public and how quickly any unacceptable risks will be addressed,” Taylor said.
MRC did not respond to a request for comment from Inside Climate News.
These incidents require greater enforcement but the Trump administration is working to undermine federal oversight of refineries, DeSaulnier said.
The administration has repeatedly tried to eliminate the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, an independent federal agency that investigates the root causes of industrial chemical accidents. So far, Congress has continued to fund the agency.
Keeping refinery workers and surrounding communities safe requires real-time accountability measures that trigger automatic investigations or corrective actions after incidents, DeSaulnier argued in a recent op-ed. He suggested following Chemical Safety Board recommendations such as tracking equipment failures, overdue inspections, leaks and failed safety systems.
DeSaulnier has a long history of trying to improve refinery safety, dating back to his days as a Contra Costa County supervisor. The congressman was briefly overcome with emotion during Thursday’s hearing as he recounted the deaths of five men at the Tosco Avon Refinery in the 1990s, when he said the county averaged one refinery-related death or serious injury every year.
“I went to a couple of funerals,” he said, regaining his composure, “and I will never forget hearing about the lives of five individuals who, in my opinion, never should have died.”
The Avon refinery is now operated by Marathon Petroleum as Martinez Renewables, where an explosion in 2023 left Jerome Serrano, an operator with four children, fighting for his life for months. Workers with the United Steelworkers Local 5 blamed understaffing and unsustainable overtime shifts for the accident.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
More than 100 employees went on strike for safer conditions after Marathon refused to give them the same contract it had negotiated with the USW for more than 200 other bargaining units across the petroleum and renewables industry.
The strike turned into a lockout when the company rejected union members’ unconditional return to work offer. Workers have now been out of the plant for 165 days.
Nick Plurkowski, USW Local 5 president, was glad to see so many people show up to learn about refinery safety. The meeting covered current regulations and other important topics in a way “only the congressman can do,” Plurkowski said, referring to his personal connection to the workers who died. “He understands that the worst possible outcome isn’t the refineries paying fines, it’s when someone we know gets hurt or killed.”
“The amount of flaring is concerning to say the least,” said Plurkowski. He filed a complaint with state occupational health and safety regulators, alleging that the workers who replaced the USW Local 5 workers, who he said were illegally locked out, aren’t qualified to operate the plant safely. As a result, he said, the state is investigating Marathon’s training of the workers currently running the plant.
Marathon spokesperson Jamal Kheiry said the company continues to staff the Martinez Renewables facility with highly qualified personnel, including supervisors, engineers and technical experts with extensive experience and training in safe, reliable plant operations.

e97c16fe6261.text: President Trump decided to make a diesel fuel deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored half a dozen U.S. requests to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, a U.S. official with direct knowledge told Axios. Why it matters: Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin sparked a new crisis with Ukraine and threatens to derail a new push by the Trump administration for a deal to end the war. "Zelensky is misreading the room. By continuing to hit refineries, he is eroding the good will that he has built with Trump over the last six months," the U.S. official said. Zelensky, in an interview with Axios after the announcement, said he was blindsided by the deal, which he called "not fair and not honest" and an unwarranted gift to Putin. Driving the news: Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries in recent months were highly effective and caused an energy crisis in Russia. Russia imposed a ban on diesel exports in response, which added more pressure to global diesel markets under strain from the war in Iran. Zelensky told Trump and his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that he was prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if the Russians halted attacks on Ukrainian power plants. The U.S. official said Trump wanted Ukraine to unilaterally stop attacking Russian refineries because the strikes were contributing to high gas prices in America. Trump didn't see the attacks on refineries as equivalent to Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid, the U.S. official said. Inside the room: During eight hours of talks in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner told a Ukrainian negotiating team that the president was expected to speak to Putin and lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports. They were told that Trump decided to move forward after Ukraine ignored multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, which were directly affecting U.S. consumers. A Ukrainian official claimed that during the talks, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could cut off Ukraine from U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. The U.S. official denied such a threat was made and said Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, Witkoff and Kushner said. "The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the U.S., too," the U.S. official said. Zoom in: The official said the new crisis over the diesel deal erupted after the U.S. mediators had constructive talks with Ukrainian and European diplomats in Miami on Friday. The main focus was on finalizing security guarantees that the U.S., Europe and NATO would provide to Ukraine as part of a deal to end the war. New proposals for territorial solutions were also raised. Witkoff and Kushner presented a postwar package for Ukraine that included ways to fund reconstruction and rebuild the Ukrainian military, as well as ideas on how to deal with budget deficits stemming from the war. The participants also discussed a roadmap for Ukraine's accession to the EU and the relationship Ukraine would have with NATO after the war ends. In addition, Witkoff and Kushner raised the possibility of a Europe-Russia postwar security framework that could appeal to both sides. What to watch: Witkoff and Kushner briefed the Ukrainians and Europeans on potential energy deals with Russia that the U.S. hopes would bring down energy prices and induce Russia to make concessions in peace talks, the U.S. official said. What's next: The U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner are considering visiting Moscow and Kyiv next week to discuss peace proposals, but it's unclear how Friday's blowup will affect their plans. "Putin is hitting [Ukraine] hard but we think he is open to a discussion on ending the war. We want to work on a new proposal that will be good enough for him in order to get him to stop," the U.S. official said. Yes, but: During his 90-minute phone call with Trump, Putin declined to commit to resuming peace talks with Ukraine, his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters. He said that Ukrainian strikes on Moscow and other cities during the Russian parliamentary elections "thwarted the possibility of an immediate resumption of the negotiation process." "The president said, we will think about when these negotiations can be resumed," Ushakov added.

A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-UÃ©lÃ©, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.

As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.
"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.
"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."
He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycÃ©es, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.
"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."
The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.
The protests - ignited at the LycÃ©e Antoine-de-Saint-ExupÃ©ry in the deprived Paris suburb of CrÃ©teil - have struck a chord across the country.
Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycÃ©es soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.
The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.
The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.
On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.
But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.
Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.
It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.
When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).
"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.
On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.
Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.
But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.
"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycÃ©e student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la RÃ©publique, a place synonymous with protest.
"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."
The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.
So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.
More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.
But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.
Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.
A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.
"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."
Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.
But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.
"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."
Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.
Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.

Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday.
The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists.
The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on the resignation demand.
Police say they have denied permission for the gathering and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed with huge metal barricades.
Several trains to Delhi have been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering.
But Abhijeet Dipke, founder â of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may".
"If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing âPrime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X.
The CJP's weeks-long protest in the summer seeking education reforms was its first major challenge to Modi's government. The CJP scored a major victory when it forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July.
The CJP protesters returned to streets last week with a rally in Mumbai city to press for CEC Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held a huge rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore).
Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days.
Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups.
CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi.
In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests.
Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference, external that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP.
"Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said.
Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them.
"In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied."
The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather.
At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.
The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission.
For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue.
Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media.

4196f8786645.text: Hurricane Isaias has strengthened into a Category 3 hurricane as it heads toward the Gulf Coast. Residents are rushing to prepare for the storm, which is packing winds up to 120 mph and is expected to make landfall Friday night. Amna Nawaz speaks with Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, for more. Amna Nawaz: Hurricane Isaias has now strengthened into a Category 3 major hurricane as it heads towards the Gulf Coast. The storm is packing winds up to 120 miles an hour and is expected to make landfall later tonight. States of emergency have been declared in parts of Alabama, Florida, and Georgia, warning of storm surge up to nine feet and as many as 15 inches of rain in some coastal areas. All along the coast, residents are rushing to prepare, lining up for gas and boarding up their homes ahead of the storm. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis today urged people to get ready. Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL): You will face very hazardous conditions prior to the storm making landfall. So you really need to finish your preparations now. You have to execute your plans now. There's going to be a point in the not-too-distant future where it's not going to be safe to go outside, even though the storm may still be a distance away from reaching the shore. Do it now. Amna Nawaz: Joining us now is Michael Brennan. He's director of the National Hurricane Center. Michael, welcome back. So, give us the latest that we know about Hurricane Isaias' path. where and when is it expected to make landfall? Michael Brennan, Director, National Hurricane Center: Well, I can just tell you, Isaias is still a Category 3 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale, with maximum sustained winds of 115 miles per hour, down just a little bit from earlier in the day, but that's just a really minuscule change. You can see the center of circulation just offshore of the Florida Panhandle here, probably going to move inland on the coast and make landfall in the next couple of hours. And that's when the worst of the conditions will begin to materialize. But as you can see here behind me, all of this weather is pushing onshore now. So conditions are going downhill really, really rapidly. Amna Nawaz: Yesterday, you mentioned to us that it could weaken further as it approaches landfall. Is that still true? Michael Brennan: Yes, so it's experiencing what we call vertical shear, which hurricanes don't -- they don't strengthen usually in those types of environments. The storm so far has been able to cling to Category 3 status. A little bit more weakening is possible right before it makes landfall. But, for all practical purposes, it really won't matter because the hazards are already baked and set in place. Even if the storm comes down a little bit from a wind speed perspective, the rain and the storm surge and the wind impacts really won't change much. Amna Nawaz: And are your concerns still largely the same based on what's happened since the last day we spoke, flooding and storm surge mainly for coastal areas, or should folks inland be concerned as well? Michael Brennan: So we're a bit more concerned about inland impacts. The forward speed has increased today. It's now moving really, really rapidly at 17 miles per hour. And what that means is, it can carry the momentum a little bit farther inland. So I think what we're going to see is the winds and potential power loss extending deep into Alabama portions of Georgia and even Eastern portions of Mississippi, so absolutely not a coastal phenomenon. These winds are going to spread deep inland. Amna Nawaz: And at this point, would you say it is too late for people to try to evacuate? If they're not able to, what should they do to prepare? Michael Brennan: At this point, it is much too late to be moving around. Sun will be going down soon. Conditions are deteriorating rapidly. We're already seeing tornadoes form in some of these outer bands. You just need to be where you're going to be, hunker down, ride out the storm. Don't be out venturing around looking at it. Amna Nawaz: We're thinking about everybody in the storm's path and wishing them well. That is Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, joining us tonight once again. Thank you. Michael Brennan: Thank you.

a00c8973c245.text: An investigation is underway after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shot a man in New York City Thursday. William Brangham reports. Amna Nawaz: An investigation is under way after ICE agents shot a man in New York City yesterday. Federal authorities say 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, who is illegally in the U.S., attempted to ram officers with a vehicle when they tried to detain him. ICE agents then fired at his car where a young child was in the back seat. William Brangham has this report. William Brangham: Bodycam footage released today shows New York City police arriving at the scene of the ICE shooting finding plainclothes ICE officers, one seemingly dressed as a construction worker, carrying a long gun, another tending to Oscar Belgal, the man they'd shot in the neck minutes before, in the background, the car Belgal was driving with his 5-year-old son. The boy was unharmed and is now with family members. Man: It was really quick. It was boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Zohran Mamdani (D), Mayor of New York City: Let me say this plainly. Tonight, millions of our neighbors are wondering whether they will be safe on our streets, in our schools, at their worksites. William Brangham: That night, protesters gathered at the site. Protester: Whose streets? Protesters: Our streets! Protester: Whose streets? Protesters: Our streets! William Brangham: The growing crowd clashed with police. Federal authorities say ICE agents were attempting to arrest Belgal when he tried to flee, and agents shot at least seven rounds at his car believing their lives were in danger. Marcos Charles, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement: Mr. Belgal was struck by one of the bullets or fragments superficially in the neck. He stopped his vehicle. We arrested him, rendered first aid information and then took him to the hospital. William Brangham: DHS said the 28-year-old suspect has now been transferred to an undisclosed detention facility outside New York. Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary: It is shameful that we're giving this particular case so much attention when this was a thug. William Brangham: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Belgal had a criminal history and blamed this escalation on the actions of New York officials. Sen. Markwayne Mullin: Sanctuary politicians, they create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for the American citizens to be safe. Underneath President Trump, he made it very clear he was going to restore law and order in our cities and our towns and our states, despite what happens with career politicians that put criminals in front of law-abiding citizens. William Brangham: Mayor Mamdani and New York Governor Kathy Hochul both talked with President Trump trying to negotiate Mr. Belgal's release and pressed him to stop immigration enforcement operations in New York. In a statement posted to social media, Governor Hochul wrote -- quote -- "New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity." Federal immigration agents have now reportedly shot at least two dozen people since the start of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in January 2025. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham.

c9b1934a01d2.text: Candidates for U.S. Senate in three battleground states faced off in fiery debates Thursday night that frequently veered into personal attacks. David Brooks of The Atlantic and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW join Amna Nawaz to discuss the week in politics, including the battle for control of Congress. Amna Nawaz: Candidates for U.S. Senate in three battleground states faced off in fiery debates last night that frequently veered into personal attacks. In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers tried to tie Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's family to terrorism, despite there being no evidence. Abdul El-Sayed (D), Michigan Senatorial Candidate: You go after my mom? Mike Rogers (R), Michigan Senatorial Candidate: I'm not going after your mom. Abdul El-Sayed: That's exactly what you're doing. Mike Rogers: What your mom was working at, I was going after that organization that was indicted for funneling money to al-Qaida. Amna Nawaz: In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff accused Republican Congressman Mike Collins of bigotry and racism. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA): It's not just that you have hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office and you have promoted neo-Nazi content online. It's that you're robbing your constituents to subsidize your donors. If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA), Senatorial Candidate: I have condemned racism, antisemitism, hate. I don't care where the source is. And I tell him that too. It's wrong. We have no place in this world for that. Amna Nawaz: And, in Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins demanded that Democrat Troy Jackson apologize after he accused her of corruption. Troy Jackson (D), Maine Senatorial Candidate: She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they're making money. I mean, Senator Collins and her husband are making money more off of this war, and so is a whole bunch of other people, and that's why this doesn't stop. Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME): That is absolutely outrageous, and you owe me an apology. Troy Jackson: No, you owe me an apology. Amna Nawaz: For more on the battle for control of Congress, we turn now to the analysis of Brooks and Capehart. That is "The Atlantic"'s David Brooks and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW. Good to see you both. Jonathan Capehart: Hey, Amna. Amna Nawaz: Speaking with those debates last night, some policy discussions, but very heavy on the personal attacks. And in the context of this, we should say The Cook Political Report just this week shifted eight house races and three Senate races in Kansas, North Carolina, and New Hampshire toward Democrats. Jonathan, Senate control is on the line here. Is that why these are getting so heated? Jonathan Capehart: Yes. I mean, I have said many times -- excuse me -- I have said many times here that this election cycle, midterm election cycle, reminds me of 2006, exactly 20 years ago. These same conversations were happening, particularly with the Senate. The Senate map then and now was supposed to be extremely difficult, if not impossible for Democrats to retake the majority. And here we are in just Georgia, Michigan, Maine. I mean, Maine would be the only pickup of the three. But the fact that these debates are so nasty and personal shows that Democrats feel they are within striking distance. Republicans feel perhaps that they are on their on their back foot -- on their back feet. And, I mean, given who the president is, same -- president of their party, they should feel that they're on their back feet. Amna Nawaz: David, you agree? David Brooks: Some -- I agree with Jonathan, but I think something has changed since 2006, which is we have had 10 years of political, moral decay, and sound a lot -- the candidates used to be inhibited a bit by the sense that, if I lie, if I'm a total sleazebag, it might hurt me. And now they realize it won't hurt me at all. And, in fact, my partisans may actually like it. And so you had -- I think, in those three cases, all three of those things were sleazy behavior, Troy Jackson. Susan Collins has some Boeing stock in her portfolio. And he calls her a war profiteer because of that? That's ridiculous. The insinuations that El-Sayed is involved in terrorism because he's Muslim, ridiculous. Jon Ossoff, my advice to him is, if you start calling your political opponents Nazis, maybe it's time to shut up. That's just not what we do here in this country. And the Bull Connor stuff -- and a lot of these candidates have real weaknesses. Like, Mike Collins, who's the Georgia Republican, I think what's accurate to say about him is, he has a disturbing number of young men on his -- around him who have ties to the alt-right and some of the vile antisemitic stuff online. El-Sayed can... Amna Nawaz: Who have shared, we should say, white nationalist content online, right. David Brooks: Right. Amna Nawaz: That's the accusation. David Brooks: El-Sayed, he can't tell the difference between Iran and Israel. When asked whether -- which was a greater threat, he couldn't tell the difference. Iran has killed thousands of Americans. Iran is the leading cause of -- or leading sponsor of terrorism around the world. If you can't tell the difference, then something's wrong here. And so they could have gone after legitimate weaknesses. But in each case, they took it to 11 and it was dishonest. Amna Nawaz: Meanwhile, we know the cost of living, price of gas, these are the things at the top of all voters' minds. And I want to ask you about what we heard from the president himself late today, which was a deal with Vladimir Putin to get diesel from Russia. That reverses years of pressure on Moscow for their war in Ukraine. It also flies in the face of new legislation that Congress just passed that would allow the president broad powers to punish countries that buy Russian oil. It also follows Trump pledging that there would be no more strikes on Iran, David, until after the midterm e

bbeaae5bcbb3.text: Actor Ke Huy Quan went from arriving in America as a refugee to starring in Indiana Jones and The Goonies. Decades later, he made an Oscar-winning comeback. In the latest episode of our PBS News podcast “Settle In,” Amna Nawaz spoke with him about his debut memoir “Never Say Die,” which starts with his family’s harrowing attempts to escape post-war Vietnam. Amna Nawaz: Actor Ke Huy Quan went from arriving in America as a refugee to starring in "Indiana Jones" and "The Goonies." Decades later, he made an Oscar-winning comeback. In the latest episode of our PBS News podcast "Settle In," I spoke with him about his debut memoir, "Never Say Die," which starts with his family's harrowing attempts to escape postwar Vietnam. Ke Huy Quan, Author, "Never Say Die": My parents have nine kids, so there's 11 of us. So their whole idea was that if we were to all escape at the same time, the chance of us making out, it's unlikely. So, very early on, they decided we're going to separate. So my mom took three of my siblings, including my best friend, David. They got on a boat and went to Malaysia. And they made it on the first attempt. And so my mom and three of my siblings were separated for more than a year-and-a-half. Amna Nawaz: I mean, for a parent to have to make that kind of decision, I can't even imagine. Have you talked to your parents about that, about that moment and having to make those kinds of decisions for your family? Ke Huy Quan: Interestingly, no. We never spoke about it. I think that's why I love that quote that I put in the very beginning of the boat. "No one ever puts their kids on a boat unless the unless the water is safer than land," from Warsan Shire. Amna Nawaz: Yes, the poet, yes. Ke Huy Quan: And that really speaks volumes to what my parents were going through, the incredibly difficult decision that they had to make. Amna Nawaz: I love you quoted Warsan Shire as well that line from the poem about no one leaves home unless home is the mouth of a shark. Is that what it felt like? Ke Huy Quan: Yes. It was really incredible, and I didn't really know -- it was -- believe it or not, it's been almost 50 years. None of our family members ever talked about it, and because... Amna Nawaz: Never? Ke Huy Quan: Never. And because they were so -- such distant memories, I wanted to make sure that what I remembered is accurate. Amna Nawaz: Yes. Ke Huy Quan: So, right before I sat down to write this book, I actually called some of my older siblings, which I know because of they were -- they were at a -- at that age where they remember much more than I did. Amna Nawaz: And did they? Ke Huy Quan: They were older. And they did. So, having that conversation with them was unbelievable. And it was just as traumatic for them, but I -- each of us dealt with that trauma in our own separate and individual ways. And what they told me was exactly how I remembered it. But they had it even more tough because they were older. I was 7. I was well protected, even though, being in that circumstances, they did everything they can to shield me from, honestly everything, that was going on. I just -- I didn't know much of it. So, having that conversation with them was really unbelievable, and I'm glad I did. Now I get to understand a little bit of what they went through. And, interestingly enough, they have -- they have to read the book to fully understand what I went through, because we never shared. Amna Nawaz: And you can watch that full conversation and more episodes of "Settle In" on our YouTube page or wherever you get your podcasts.
